NCRS Summary Sheets — PCM1 Fall 2026

Every bottom line, exam lock, trap and pattern table in the module

This companion holds every Bottom Line, Exam Lock, Trap and pattern table from the master deck, lecture by lecture, with the practice questions collapsed to stem-and-answer. It is built to be read last — the night before, and the morning of.

How it is organised

  • One sheet per lecture, in module order, with the lecture's own summary sheet reproduced in full.
  • Each system closes with a consolidated sheet: every lock in that system on one page.
  • The filter box (or /) narrows to any term across the whole document.
  • Print / Save as PDF produces the Letter-portrait version, one lecture per page break.

L01 · Arteriosclerosis

PATH · Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology · source pp. 1–37

Bottom line

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Arteriosclerosis is a family of four wall-thickening processes; only atherosclerosis builds an intimal atheroma, and the atheroma's danger is decided not by its size but by cap thickness, core size and inflammation.

Exam Locks

Exam Lock
The five that get asked
  • Atherosclerosis is asymptomatic until occlusion is > 70% — that number is the boundary between silent disease and angina.
  • Mönckeberg does not narrow the lumen and is not clinically significant.
  • Fatty streaks are not raised, cause no obstruction, and are present in almost everyone's aorta.
  • Vessel order: lower abdominal aorta and iliacs → coronaries → popliteal → internal carotid → circle of Willis.
  • BP = CO × PR, and hypertension is 95% primary / 5% secondary.

Traps

Trap
Three ways this lecture is made to look harder than it is
  • Confusing hyaline (protein, benign HTN + diabetes) with hyperplastic (SMC onion-skin, malignant HTN) arteriolosclerosis.
  • Assuming the tightest stenosis causes the infarct — the vulnerable plaque usually is not the tightest one.
  • Reading blue toes as large-vessel occlusion when the stem hands you intact pulses.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Carry this forward
  • When you reach Diuretics, Antihypertensives I and II, hold each drug against this equation: diuretics and aldosterone antagonists cut volume → CO; β-blockers cut HR → CO; ACE-I/ARB, CCBs, α-blockers and direct vasodilators cut PR.
Exam Lock
Why this revision slide is not optional
  • Every entity in this lecture is defined by which layer it damages: atheroma = intima; Mönckeberg = media; fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia = intima; hyaline and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis = small vessel wall.
  • Robbins Basic Pathology, 11th Ed. Chapter 8, p.275 — regional specialisations of the vasculature.
Exam Lock
Memory line for the order
  • A-C-P-I-C — the vessels get smaller and more proximal-to-distal as you go down the list; the abdominal aorta below the renals is the single most involved segment, which is why AAA is infrarenal.
Trap
The trap in this set
  • Mönckeberg is the one that is radiologically dramatic and clinically silent. A stem that describes impressive calcification but normal pulses and no ischaemia is steering you away from atherosclerosis, not toward it.
Trap
Why “intact pulses” is the whole question
  • Blue toe syndrome looks like acute limb ischaemia but the pulses are normal — the emboli are microscopic. A stem with painful blue toes and absent pulses is large-vessel occlusion, not atheroembolism.
  • The other giveaway is timing: days after a catheterisation, often with a rising creatinine and eosinophilia.

Pattern tables

Pattern lock — telling the four apart in one question stem

If the stem says…It is…Because
“calcification of the media of the radial artery, incidental finding on X-ray, patient 78, pulses normal”Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosisMedia, does not narrow the lumen, no ischaemia
“onion-skin concentric thickening, BP 220/130, fibrinoid necrosis”Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosisMalignant hypertension, SMC proliferation
“homogeneous pink hyaline thickening of arterioles in a long-standing diabetic”Hyaline arteriolosclerosisProtein deposition, benign HTN and diabetes
“restenosis 6 months after balloon angioplasty”Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasiaHealing response to mechanical injury
“yellow raised intimal lesion in the abdominal aorta with a lipid core”AtherosclerosisIntimal atheroma in a large elastic artery

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 62-year-old man has a coronary angiogram after two episodes of chest pain at rest. A 40% eccentric lesion in the LAD is described as having a thin fibrous cap, a large lipid core and dense macrophage infiltration at the lesion shoulders. Which feature best predicts his risk of acute myocardial infarction?

B. The thin fibrous cap with a large lipid core — Vulnerable plaques have thin fibrous caps, large lipid cores, and increased inflammation with fragile neovascularisation; shoulder areas are more susceptible. Degree of stenosis predicts angina (symptoms begin above ~70% occlusion) but not rupture — most infarcts arise from non-critical lesions.

Three days after cardiac catheterisation a 70-year-old develops painful, purple discolouration of several toes. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable and symmetric. Creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL. What is the pathological hallmark of the responsible lesion?

B. Cholesterol clefts within the embolus — Blue toe syndrome with intact pulses, days after an arterial procedure, with acute kidney injury = cholesterol emboli syndrome. The pathological hallmark is the presence of a cholesterol cleft in the embolus.

A radial artery from a 79-year-old shows heavy calcification of the media centred on the internal elastic lamina. The lumen is patent and the patient has no ischaemic symptoms. Which process is this?

C. Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis — Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis: calcific deposits in the media of medium-sized arteries, usually centred on the internal elastic lamina, in patients older than 50. The lesions do not encroach on the vessel lumen and are not clinically significant.

Which cell is directly responsible for converting a fatty streak into a mature fibrofatty atheroma?

D. The smooth muscle cell, by proliferating and depositing ECM — Intimal SMC proliferation and ECM deposition lead to the conversion of the earliest lesion, a fatty streak, into a mature fibrofatty atheroma. The other four cells all contribute signals (PDGF, IL-1, IFN-γ) — but the structural conversion is the smooth muscle cell's work.

A 44-year-old woman has a blood pressure of 168/104 mm Hg on three occasions, an unexplained hypokalaemia and an abdominal bruit. Under the lecture's classification, which category and cause does this pattern point to?

B. Secondary hypertension — renal (renal artery stenosis) — 95% of hypertension is primary, but the stem gives a renovascular signature: young-ish patient, abdominal bruit, hypokalaemia from secondary hyperaldosteronism. Renal causes — glomerulonephritis and renal artery stenosis — head the secondary list.

Under the ACC/AHA table used in this lecture, a reading of 136/78 mm Hg is classified as:

C. Stage I hypertension — Stage I hypertension is 130–139 systolic or 80–89 diastolic. Because the categories are joined by *or* above the high-normal band, the systolic value alone (136) fixes the stage.

CLSK · Peripheral Vascular System

CLSK · Dr. Onika Miguel · Department of Clinical Skills · source pp. 38–91

Bottom line

Bottom Line
Two words decide it
  • Pulses and ulcer site. Pulseless + toe/pressure-point ulcer = arterial. Pulses present + medial malleolus + brown pigmentation = venous.

Exam locks

Exam Lock
The mnemonic the slide ends on
  • Pulseless · Pallor · Paresthesia · Pain · Paralysis — the arterial-occlusion Ps. Add Poikilothermia (cold) and you have the classic six.
Exam Lock
Arterial vs neurogenic claudication
  • Arterial claudication is reproducible at a fixed walking distance, relieved by standing still, with absent pulses. Neurogenic (spinal stenosis) claudication is relieved by flexion — leaning on a shopping trolley, cycling — and the pulses are normal.

Traps

Trap
Why a high ABPI is bad news, not good news
  • An ABPI above 1.2 does not mean excellent perfusion — it means the vessels are too calcified to compress (classically diabetes, chronic kidney disease). That is why the action is to measure the toe pressure instead.
Trap
Do not treat Homan's sign as a rule-out
  • The lecture prints its own numbers to make the point: a sensitivity as low as 10% means a negative Homan's sign tells you almost nothing. The Wells score plus D-dimer is what excludes DVT in a low-risk outpatient.

DLA · Clinical approach to leg swelling

DLA · Department of Clinical Skills · source pp. 94–112

Exam locks

Exam Lock
Map every differential back to one of the five
  • CHF → hydrostatic · nephrotic and cirrhosis → oncotic · cellulitis → permeability · filariasis and post-radiotherapy → lymphatic obstruction · NSAIDs and CCBs → Na⁺ and water retention.

Traps

Trap
The single most testable line on this slide
  • Diuretics do not treat lymphedema. The fluid is not there because of a hydrostatic/oncotic imbalance — the drainage route is blocked. A stem offering furosemide for a woody, non-pitting, post-mastectomy arm is the distractor.

Pattern tables

Edema vs lymphedema — the discriminating table

FeatureEdemaLymphedema
CauseFluid accumulation due to venous or systemic conditionsLymphatic dysfunction or obstruction
PittingUsually pitting (except in late stages)Non-pitting
SymmetryOften bilateralCan be unilateral or bilateral but asymmetric
Skin changesMinimal unless chronicThickened, fibrotic skin (woody texture)
Response to elevationImproves with limb elevationDoes not improve significantly
Associated symptomsMay have pain, redness, or warmth (if inflammatory)Heaviness, tightness, and reduced range of motion

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 58-year-old man had a myocardial infarction 1 year ago, which was the first major illness in his life. He now wants to prevent another acute coronary event and is advised to begin a program of exercise and to change his diet. After one year, a reduction in the level of which of the following analytes in the serum would be the best indicator of the success of his diet and exercise regimen?

B. LDL cholesterol — Faculty answer key: B. LDL is the causal lipoprotein in atherogenesis — lowering LDL (not raising it) is the endpoint. A *reduction* in HDL would be harmful, which is why option A is a trap.

A 50-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of exercise-induced angina pectoris. BP 145/85, HR 79 and slightly irregular. Coronary angiography shows a fixed 75% narrowing of the anterior descending branch of the left coronary artery. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes for 20 years and his serum cholesterol is typically over 230 mg/dL. Which of the following is the earliest event that gives rise to narrowing of the artery?

C. Endothelial dysfunction — Faculty answer key: C. The response-to-injury hypothesis begins with endothelial injury and dysfunction. Note the distractor in B — foam cells derive from macrophages, not smooth muscle cells, and they are not the earliest event.

A 42-year-old man dies after a motor vehicle accident. At autopsy the aorta shows multiple flat, yellow lesions that do not significantly narrow the vascular lumen; microscopy shows numerous lipid-filled macrophages within the intima. Which of the following best describes the vascular lesion?

A. Fatty streak — Faculty answer key: A. Flat (not raised) + no luminal narrowing + lipid-filled macrophages in the intima = fatty streak. The word that eliminates B and D is “do not significantly narrow”.

DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations

DLA · Dr Michon Sukhoo-Pertab · Department of Clinical Skills · source pp. 113–150

Exam locks

Exam Lock
The one-line rule the session is built to teach
  • Syncope in association with palpitations should prompt a work-up for serious arrhythmia — and the diagnosis of an anxiety disorder does not preclude the diagnosis of an arrhythmia.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 25-year-old man with well-controlled panic disorder reports 6 months of rapid, regular palpitations occurring only during his morning jog. Three days ago he developed tunnel vision at the end of a run and lost consciousness. His aunt died suddenly while swimming 5 years ago. Examination and resting ECG are normal. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

C. Exercise (treadmill) ECG test — The palpitations are reproducibly exertional and accompanied by syncope with a family history of sudden death — a catecholamine-driven ventricular arrhythmia. Holter monitoring was unrevealing in the case; the treadmill test reproduced VT with syncope. Panic disorder can cause palpitations but would not cause syncope.

An 80-year-old woman describes a rapid, irregular heartbeat with no clear start or stop. Her pulse is irregularly irregular. Her ECG shows absent P waves replaced by fine fibrillatory waves and a narrow QRS at 130/min. Which single ECG feature most reliably separates this from multifocal atrial tachycardia?

C. The complete absence of discrete P waves — MAT also has an irregular rhythm and a narrow QRS, but it has discrete P waves of ≥ 3 different morphologies. Atrial fibrillation has no discrete P waves at all — they are replaced by fibrillatory waves. The lecture itself notes that AF, flutter and MAT can be difficult to separate.

Which physical finding on this session's table would most specifically raise the possibility of an atrial myxoma as the cause of palpitations?

C. Crescendo mid-diastolic murmur — The session's table pairs the crescendo mid-diastolic murmur with atrial myxoma. The mid-systolic click is mitral valve prolapse (SVT); the Valsalva-augmented holosystolic murmur is HCM.

L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection

PATH · Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology · source pp. 151–190

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Hypertension damages vessels two ways — slowly (hyaline → benign nephrosclerosis) or suddenly (hyperplastic + fibrinoid necrosis → malignant nephrosclerosis) — and a weakened media then fails either by ballooning outward (aneurysm) or splitting along its length (dissection).
Exam Lock
The eight that get asked
  • Malignant HTN = > 200/120 with end-organ damage; urgency vs emergency is decided by end-organ damage, not by the number.
  • Hyaline = chronic/benign + diabetes. Hyperplastic = malignant, onion-skin, PAS+, fibrinoid necrosis.
  • Cor pulmonale: acute dilates (PE), chronic hypertrophies (COPD).
  • AAA is infrarenal, atherosclerotic, male, > 50, smoker — and rupture risk tracks size.
  • Syphilis → ascending thoracic aorta, tree bark, cor bovinum.
  • Berry → circle of Willis, ACA branches, ADPKD, SAH on straining.
  • Mycotic is not a true aneurysm — septic embolus, usually from infective endocarditis.
  • Type A > Type B in frequency; Type A needs surgery; dissection plane = middle/outer third of media.
Trap
Three traps
  • Calling a pulsating haematoma a true aneurysm — it is a false aneurysm; the wall is adherent tissue, not vessel.
  • Attributing an ascending aneurysm to atherosclerosis — atherosclerosis starves the inner media and gives you the abdominal aneurysm; hypertension narrows the vasa vasorum and gives you the ascending one.
  • Reading dissection pain as MI. Both are severe anterior chest pain — the discriminators are radiation between the scapulae, absent or unequal pulses, and a normal-to-high blood pressure.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
The single sentence that separates the two
  • In malignant hypertension, the vascular damage is acute. In benign hypertension, vascular damage is chronic. Everything else — the morphology, the organ damage, the urgency of treatment — follows from that one word.
Exam Lock
The morphology term to attach
  • Cystic medial degeneration — marked elastin fragmentation with areas devoid of elastin that resemble cystic spaces, against the regular layered pattern of elastic tissue in normal media.
Trap
The distinction the objective is actually testing
  • Acute cor pulmonale dilates; chronic cor pulmonale hypertrophies. A saddle embolus gives you a thin, ballooned RV at autopsy — not a thick one. There has been no time to hypertrophy.
Trap
Why plaque protects here but causes AAA elsewhere
  • Atherosclerosis causes abdominal aneurysm by starving the inner media — but a dense plaque is also a mechanical barrier that arrests a propagating dissection. That is why the tear itself occurs in relatively plaque-free aorta.

Pattern tables

Hyaline vs hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis — the pair that gets asked

Hyaline arteriolosclerosisHyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
SettingChronic (“benign”) hypertension — and diabetesSudden and severe elevation in blood pressure (malignant hypertension)
MechanismHemodynamic stress → plasma protein leakage and smooth muscle cell matrix productionThickened reduplicated basement membrane (PAS positive) and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia
MorphologyDeposition of homogenous pink material (hyaline) in the vessel wall causing wall thickening and luminal narrowingConcentric laminated “onion skin” thickening with luminal narrowing
Accompanied by—Fibrinoid necrosis (necrotising arteriolitis)
End resultImpairment of blood supply to the tissue and ischemic changesAcute ischemic injury

Hyaline vs hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis — the pair that gets asked

OrganLesion
KidneyHyaline arteriolosclerosis → benign nephrosclerosis · Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis → malignant nephrosclerosis
BrainBoth hyaline and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis seen → can cause hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhages
RetinaHyperplastic arteriolosclerosis → cotton wool spots

The five named aneurysms — location, cause, complication

AneurysmLocationPathogenesisSignature complication / clue
Abdominal aortic aneurysmAbdominal aorta and common iliac arteries; most distal to the renal arteries and proximal to the bifurcationAtherosclerosis. Males >>> females; older, rarely below age 50; smokersRisk of rupture is directly related to the size of the aneurysm. Usually fusiform, may be saccular; lined by raised, ulcerated and calcified (complicated) plaque and thrombi
Syphilitic aneurysmAscending thoracic aortaTertiary syphilis → inflammatory response to the spirochete → obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum → ischemic injury of the elastic tunica media → medial destruction, chronic inflammation and scarring“Tree bark” appearance of the intima; may narrow or occlude coronary ostia; aortic valve ring dilation → valvular insufficiency → massive LV hypertrophy = cor bovinum (cow's heart)
Marfan's syndromeAscending aorta and arch of aortaAutosomal dominant; mutation in the gene for fibrillin-1, required for normal elastic tissue development → elastic fibers become incompetent to resist normal stressCystic medial degeneration → aneurysms, aortic dissection, valve lesions. Elongated axial bones, tall slender body, lower body > upper body length, long thin extremities and fingers; subluxation of the lens (ciliary body is rich in fibrillin)
Berry aneurysmCircle of Willis — most common site: anterior cerebral artery branches; small and saccularNot present at birth but develop over time because the arterial media is congenitally attenuatedClinically silent until they rupture — often during increased intracranial pressure (straining at stool or sexual orgasm) → subarachnoid hemorrhage → severe headache, coma. Association: autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)
Mycotic aneurysmAnywhere — usually smallNot a true aneurysm. Weakening and rupture of the vessel wall by a microbial infection. Called mycotic (a misnomer) because initially people thought it was caused by fungal infectionA dislodged septic embolus, usually as a complication of infective endocarditis, damages the wall → hemorrhage and abscess at the site of rupture. Usually clinically silent

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 38-year-old man presents with BP 226/128 mm Hg, headache and blurred vision. Fundoscopy shows flame-shaped haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and papilloedema. Creatinine is 3.4 mg/dL. A renal biopsy is most likely to show which arteriolar change?

B. Concentric laminated onion-skin thickening with fibrinoid necrosis — Malignant hypertension (> 200/120 with retinopathy and end-organ damage) produces hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis — onion-skin concentric thickening, PAS-positive reduplicated basement membrane, smooth muscle hyperplasia, accompanied by fibrinoid necrosis (necrotising arteriolitis) — i.e. malignant nephrosclerosis. Hyaline change belongs to chronic benign hypertension and diabetes.

A 66-year-old man with severe COPD has a raised JVP, hepatomegaly and pedal edema. At autopsy the right ventricular free wall is 8 mm thick and the right atrium is enlarged; the left ventricle is normal. What is the diagnosis, and what distinguishes it from the acute form?

B. Chronic cor pulmonale; the acute form shows RV dilation without hypertrophy — Chronic cor pulmonale: RV (± RA) hypertrophy, COPD is the most common cause. Acute cor pulmonale follows massive pulmonary emboli and shows a dilated RV with no hypertrophy — there has been no time to remodel.

A 24-year-old man, 196 cm tall with arachnodactyly and upward lens subluxation, dies suddenly. The ascending aorta is dilated and shows elastin fragmentation with cystic spaces devoid of elastin. Which protein is defective?

B. Fibrillin-1 — Marfan syndrome — autosomal dominant mutation in the gene for fibrillin-1, required for normal elastic tissue development. The aneurysm sits at the ascending aorta and arch; the histology is cystic medial degeneration; the ocular sign is lens subluxation because the ciliary body is rich in fibrillin.

A 52-year-old man with a two-week history of fever and a new murmur develops sudden severe abdominal pain. Imaging shows a small saccular dilation of the superior mesenteric artery. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which aneurysm type is this, and by what mechanism?

C. Mycotic aneurysm from a dislodged septic embolus damaging the wall — Fever + new murmur + S. aureus bacteraemia = infective endocarditis; a dislodged septic embolus weakens the arterial wall — a mycotic aneurysm, which the lecture is explicit is not a true aneurysm and is a misnomer (not fungal).

A 58-year-old hypertensive man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the interscapular region and a 24 mm Hg difference in systolic pressure between arms. CT shows a dissection flap beginning 2 cm above the aortic valve. Which statement is correct?

B. This is a proximal (Type A) lesion, is more common, carries high mortality and needs rapid medical and surgical treatment — Ascending involvement = proximal / Type A: more common, high mortality, requires rapid medical and surgical treatment. The plane is between the middle and outer third of the media; the most common cause of death is rupture into the pericardial, pleural or peritoneal cavities; and the tear typically occurs in aorta largely free of plaque.

L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular System

CLSK · Dr. Michon Sukhoo-Pertab (MBBS, PGCME) · Department of Clinical Skills · source pp. 191–254

Bottom line

Bottom Line
Use this as your template
  • Note the order: JVP → hepatojugular reflux → carotids (auscultate, then palpate) → inspection → palpation (heaves, thrills, PMI) → auscultation (S1, S2, extra sounds, murmurs) — exactly the sequence of the examination itself. Write in that order and you cannot forget a component.

Exam locks

Exam Lock
3 / 2 / ≤1
  • The count is the whole classification: 3 features = typical, 2 = atypical, 1 or 0 = non-cardiac. Learn the three features as a set — quality, provocation, relief.
Exam Lock
Never forget the four “killer” causes of chest pain
  • Myocardial infarction or ischemia · Pulmonary embolism · Aortic dissection · Pneumothorax. Alongside them, always ask: is the patient stable or unstable, what are the characteristics of the pain, and what are the risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease?
Exam Lock
Platypnea is the one people miss
  • Orthopnea and PND both point at heart failure. Platypnea is the reverse — worse sitting up, better lying down — and it points at an atrial myxoma or hepatopulmonary syndrome.
Exam Lock
Timing S1 at the bedside
  • Palpate the carotid artery while auscultating. S1 occurs with the pulse; S2 does not.
Exam Lock
The two that move the other way
  • HCM and MVP are the exceptions: less filling makes them louder, more filling makes them softer. Everything else follows preload.

Traps

Trap
Nitroglycerin response is not a diagnostic test
  • The slide says so explicitly. Oesophageal spasm relaxes to nitrates too — “it got better with GTN” does not confirm ischaemia, and “it did not” does not exclude it.

Pattern tables

Types of chest pain — the definitions to reproduce

TypeDefinition (verbatim)
Angina pectorisDiscomfort in the chest and/or adjacent areas (jaw, shoulder, back, arm), usually, but not always, due to myocardial ischemia.
— Typical anginaSubsternal chest discomfort with all three: characteristic oppressive quality (described as “pressure”, “squeezing”, or “heaviness”, but almost never sharp or stabbing) and duration (typically minutes) · provoked by exertion or emotional stress · relieved by rest or nitroglycerin (within several minutes).
— Atypical chest painChest discomfort that meets 2 of the typical angina characteristics.
— Non-cardiac painChest pain that meets 1 or none of the typical angina characteristics.
PleuriticSudden and intense sharp, stabbing, or burning pain in the chest when inhaling and exhaling. Exacerbated by deep breathing, coughing, sneezing, or laughing. Pleuritic inflammation near the diaphragm — pain can be referred to the neck or shoulder. It is inflammation of the parietal pleura.

The positional dyspnoeas — four words, four diseases

TriggerNameAssociated with
SOB with physical activity, improves with restExertional dyspneaMany causes. Respiratory → COPD · Cardiac → CHF · Hematologic → anemia. May not indicate disease at all — just tolerance for that level of activity.
SOB when lying flat, relieved by sitting or standingOrthopneaClosely associated with CHF
SOB in the upright position with relief in the supine positionPlatypneaLeft atrial myxoma or hepatopulmonary syndrome
SOB that awakens the patient, often after 1 or 2 hours of sleep, usually relieved in the upright positionParoxysmal nocturnal dyspneaClosely associated with CHF
SOB in one lateral decubitus position as opposed to the otherTrepopneaUnilateral pleural effusion / unilateral lung disease

Murmur maneuvers — the supplemental table that shows up in comprehensives

ManeuverEffect on cardiac parametersEffect on murmurs
Inspiration↑ RV preload · ↓ LV preload · no effect on LV afterload↑ intensity of murmurs arising from the right side of the heart; ↓ intensity of murmurs arising from the left side
Valsalva maneuver / standing↓ RV preload · ↓ LV preload · ↓ LV afterload↑ intensity of MVP (with early mid-systolic click) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmurs; ↓ intensity of murmurs arising from the left side
Squatting / lying down quickly / raising the leg↑ RV preload · ↑ LV preload · no effect on LV afterload (afterload may increase with squatting)↑ intensity of all murmurs; ↓ intensity of MVP (with late mid-systolic click) and HCM murmurs. Tetralogy of Fallot: severity of tet spells and associated murmurs decrease with squatting. MVP: click occurs later in systole

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 58-year-old woman describes 4 months of substernal heaviness that comes on climbing two flights of stairs, lasts about 5 minutes, and goes away when she stops. Under the classification used in this lecture, how is this chest pain classified?

C. Typical angina — All three features are present: characteristic oppressive quality lasting minutes, provoked by exertion, and relieved by rest. Three of three = typical angina. Two of three = atypical; one or none = non-cardiac.

A 63-year-old man is short of breath when he sits up and feels better lying flat. Which of the following should be at the top of the differential?

C. Left atrial myxoma — SOB in the upright position relieved by lying supine is platypnea, associated with left atrial myxoma or hepatopulmonary syndrome. Orthopnea and PND (the reverse pattern) are the ones associated with CHF; trepopnea is the lateral-decubitus one associated with unilateral pleural effusion.

You auscultate a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border. It becomes louder when the patient performs a Valsalva maneuver and softer when he squats. Which lesion behaves this way?

D. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — Valsalva and standing decrease preload; almost every murmur gets softer — except HCM and mitral valve prolapse, which get louder. Squatting increases preload and does the reverse. AS, MR, VSD and TR all follow the normal preload rule.

A 71-year-old with long-standing uncontrolled hypertension has a fourth heart sound at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position. What does this sound indicate?

B. Atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant left ventricle — S4 is the atrial kick in late diastole — blood entering a stiffened (non-compliant) LV against high atrial pressure. It is the sound of severe LVH from uncontrolled hypertension or severe aortic stenosis, and is usually a sign of diastolic heart failure. Option A describes S3.

L05 · Vasculitides

PATH · Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology · source pp. 255–303

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Sort by vessel size, confirm with age, and prove it with serology and the presence or absence of granulomas and eosinophils.
Exam Lock
The seven locks
  • GCA > 50, Takayasu < 50 — the histology will not separate them for you.
  • PAN spares the lungs and is HBV-associated in ⅓ of cases; lesions are of different ages.
  • MPA lesions are all the same age and there are no granulomas.
  • Kawasaki = fever ≥ 5 days + 4 of 5 criteria; coronary aneurysms in 20% if untreated; IVIG + aspirin.
  • Buerger = male smoker < 40, tibial/radial, corkscrew collaterals, autoamputation.
  • c-ANCA/PR3 = Wegener's. p-ANCA/MPO = Churg-Strauss and MPA.
  • All three small-vessel vasculitides are pauci-immune — ANCA-positive but no immune-complex deposition.
Trap
Two traps
  • Treating a negative temporal artery biopsy as excluding giant cell arteritis — involvement is segmental.
  • Reaching for immunosuppression before excluding infectious vasculitis — the lecture calls this out explicitly as counterproductive.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
The clinical decision this lecture is really about
  • Pathogenesis is either immune-mediated or direct infection, and it is very important to differentiate between them: immunosuppressives are used for immune-mediated conditions and will be counterproductive in an infectious pathology.
Exam Lock
Giant cell vs Takayasu — the only reliable separator
  • The histology is essentially the same. Age is the discriminator: > 50 = giant cell; < 50 = Takayasu. Territory helps — temporal/ophthalmic vs aortic arch and great vessels.
Exam Lock
Three questions separate all three
  • Upper airway involved? → Wegener's. Asthma and eosinophilia? → Churg-Strauss. Neither, plus no granuloma, all lesions the same age? → microscopic polyangiitis.
Exam Lock
“All lesions the same age” is the MPA lock
  • PAN shows different stages of activity at the same time; MPA shows lesions all of the same age. That single phrase is how a histology stem separates them.
Trap
Why “segmental” matters clinically
  • Because involvement is segmental, a temporal artery biopsy can miss the lesion — a negative biopsy does not exclude the diagnosis, and treatment is not delayed for it when vision is at risk.
Trap
The exception written into the criteria
  • Children who fall short of the full criteria but have cardiac abnormalities on echocardiogram meet the diagnosis of Kawasaki disease. If untreated, 20% develop cardiovascular sequelae — coronary arteritis, aneurysm rupture and hemorrhage, myocardial infarction.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 60-year-old woman has a 1-month history of headache, jaw claudication, pain over the shoulder and lower back pain. Physical examination shows rope-like thickening of the temporal artery. Labs show anemia and elevated ESR. Which histopathological finding is seen in her temporal artery?

B. Granulomatous inflammation of intima and inner media with multinucleated giant cells and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina — Case 1 — giant cell arteritis. Age > 50, female, rope-like temporal artery, jaw claudication, polymyalgia rheumatica (shoulder and lower back pain), anemia and high ESR. Morphology: segmental, intimal hyperplasia, granulomatous inflammation with giant cells, fragmented internal elastic lamina.

A 25-year-old woman has a 1-month history of flu-like symptoms and difficulty with vision. Examination shows weak pulses in her upper extremities; an aortic arch angiogram shows narrowing of the carotid and subclavian arteries. What will the carotid artery show?

A. Destruction and collagenous fibrosis of the media with mononuclear infiltrates and inflammatory giant cells — Case 2 — Takayasu arteritis. Age < 50, young woman, pulseless disease with aortic-arch branch narrowing. Histology is very similar to giant cell arteritis: media destruction and collagenous fibrosis, mononuclear infiltrate, inflammatory giant cells. Age and territory are the separators.

A 30-year-old man has 1 month of recurrent abdominal pain, worse after meals, and rashes over the forearm. He had Hepatitis B infection 2 months ago. What will the mesenteric artery show?

B. Transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis at branching points, patchy, with different stages of activity present at the same time — Case 3 — polyarteritis nodosa. Young adult, ⅓ of cases follow Hepatitis B, mesenteric ischaemia (post-prandial abdominal pain) and rash. Morphology: transmural inflammation, fibrinoid necrosis, predilection for branching points, patchy, lesions of different ages, superimposed microaneurysms.

A 3-year-old boy has 3 weeks of chest pain, rashes, and edema of the hands and feet. Examination shows painful cervical lymphadenopathy, a sore and swollen tongue and multiple oral ulcers. What is seen in the coronary artery, and what is the treatment?

B. Transmural necrotising inflammation with more acute inflammatory cells and less fibrinoid necrosis; IVIG and aspirin — Case 4 — Kawasaki disease. Under 4, fever with conjunctivitis, mucositis / strawberry tongue, cervical node > 1.5 cm, erythema and oedema of the extremities. Histopathology is very similar to PAN but with more acute inflammatory cells and less fibrinoid necrosis. Management is IVIG + aspirin — one of the few paediatric indications for aspirin.

A 35-year-old man who smokes 2 packs daily for 15 years has 1 month of severe lower-extremity pain, cold sensitivity in his hands, rest pain, and gangrene of the great toe. What will the tibial artery show?

B. Segmental inflammation with luminal thrombosis containing neutrophil microabscesses surrounded by granulomatous inflammation, extending to contiguous nerves and veins — Case 5 — Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans). Male smoker under 40, Raynaud + instep claudication + rest pain + digital gangrene. The three parts of the name are the three findings: thrombus with microabscesses, segmental angiitis, obliteration of the lumen — with nerves and veins encased in the same fibrous tissue.

A 30-year-old man has 2 months of flu-like symptoms, haematuria and weight loss. He has a nasal ulcer, and chest X-ray shows a cavitary lesion in the left lung. Which serology and lung-biopsy finding fit?

B. c-ANCA/PR3; necrotising granulomas with geographic necrosis and accompanying vasculitis — Case 6 — granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's). The triad: upper-airway necrotising granulomas (nasal ulcer), lower-airway granulomatous vasculitis (cavitating nodule), and focal necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis (haematuria). Serology is c-ANCA / PR3-ANCA. Untreated, 80% mortality within 1 year.

A 30-year-old woman with asthma since age 10 has 2 weeks of flu-like symptoms and cannot extend her left wrist and some fingers (wrist drop). She has palpable purpura on both hands and eosinophilia. Which diagnosis, and what additional serology supports it?

C. Churg-Strauss syndrome (EGPA); p-ANCA/MPO with raised IgE — Case 7 — Churg-Strauss. Asthma + eosinophilia + mononeuritis multiplex (wrist drop) + palpable purpura. Serology: p-ANCA / MPO-ANCA, plus raised IgE and tissue as well as peripheral blood eosinophilia. Asthma is the feature that is present in Churg-Strauss and absent in both Wegener's and MPA.

A 20-year-old man has 2 days of muscle pain and a raised, non-blanchable rash over both lower limbs. A week earlier he had a sore throat treated with oral penicillin. What does the skin biopsy show?

B. Fibrinoid necrosis with all lesions of the same age and no granulomas — Case 8 — microscopic polyangiitis. Antibody responses to antigens such as drugs (penicillin) or microorganisms (streptococci). Pathology: fibrinoid necrosis, all lesions the same age, no granulomas — that combination separates MPA from both PAN (different ages) and Churg-Strauss (granulomas + eosinophils).

PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)

PHAR · Lucy Clunes PhD · source pp. 304–368

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Each class is defined by one transporter at one segment: CA-inhibitor/PCT, NKCC2/thick ascending limb, NCCT/DCT, aldosterone-receptor or ENaC/collecting duct — and the electrolyte disturbance is simply what that segment normally handles.
Exam Lock
The six locks
  • Loops lose calcium (→ hypercalcaemia treatment); thiazides keep it (→ stone prevention).
  • Both loops and thiazides cause hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis by increasing distal Na⁺ delivery.
  • Spironolactone = antiandrogen effects; eplerenone does not.
  • Acetazolamide = metabolic acidosis + alkaline urine; used for glaucoma, epilepsy, mountain sickness.
  • Mannitol is contraindicated in CHF and pulmonary oedema — it expands the extracellular volume first.
  • Conivaptan is IV-only, a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor, contraindicated in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia.
Trap
Three traps
  • Giving a thiazide when GFR < 30 — it will not work; use a loop (or metolazone).
  • Combining an ACE inhibitor or ARB with spironolactone/amiloride and not checking potassium — hyperkalaemia.
  • Forgetting that NSAIDs blunt loop diuretics by blocking the COX-2/prostaglandin arm of their action.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
Calcium is the whole loop-vs-thiazide question
  • Loops lose calcium (they abolish the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ reabsorption) → used in hypercalcemia. Thiazides keep calcium → used in hypercalciuria / recurrent stones. Loops Lose calcium; Thiazides Take it back.
Exam Lock
Loop-specific extras the reading adds
  • Loops abolish the lumen-positive potential from K⁺ recycling → ↑ Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ excretion; loop diuretics should be avoided in postmenopausal osteopenic women because increased Ca²⁺ excretion may have deleterious effects on bone metabolism. Loops also induce COX-2 expression — the prostaglandins mediate part of the diuretic/natriuretic action, which is why NSAIDs blunt them.
Trap
Why the biggest reabsorber is not the strongest diuretic
  • The proximal tubule reclaims 65% of filtered sodium, so acetazolamide ought to be the most powerful diuretic. It is not — most of the excess fluid delivered out of the proximal tubule can be reabsorbed more distally, particularly in the loop of Henle. The loop is the high-ceiling site because nothing downstream can compensate for it.

Pattern tables

Where the thiazide adverse effects come from — the mechanisms named in the reading

Adverse effectMechanism (verbatim from the reading)
HypokalemiaIncreased delivery of Na⁺ to the distal tubule → enhanced exchange of Na⁺ for K⁺ → greater excretion of K⁺
HyponatremiaReports of fatal or near-fatal hyponatremia, attributed to inappropriate secretion of ADH. Plasma electrolytes should be monitored.
HyperuricemiaCompetition for the organic secretory pathway in the proximal tubule by thiazides and uric acid. Can precipitate gout in some patients.
HypercalcemiaThiazides inhibit sodium reabsorption but at the same time increase the reabsorption of calcium
HyperglycemiaThiazides decrease glucose tolerance and latent diabetes mellitus may be unmasked. Appears to involve reduced insulin secretion (due to depletion of K⁺) and alterations in glucose metabolism.
HyperlipidemiaMay increase plasma LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol and total triglycerides (~5–15% increase); may return toward baseline after prolonged therapy
Metabolic alkalosis (objective PHAR.0226)Increased urinary excretion of K⁺ and titratable acid, from increased distal Na⁺ delivery — the same mechanism as loop diuretics

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 68-year-old woman with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones and hypertension needs a single agent that helps both problems. Which diuretic, and by what mechanism?

B. Hydrochlorothiazide — blocks NCCT and increases calcium reabsorption — Thiazides inhibit sodium reabsorption in the DCT but increase the reabsorption of calcium — this fall in calcium excretion is useful in recurrent kidney stones due to hypercalciuria, and they are first-line for hypertension. Furosemide does the opposite and would make her stones worse.

A patient on high-dose intravenous furosemide for decompensated heart failure develops sudden bilateral hearing loss and tinnitus. Which adverse effect is this, and which other diuretic class shares the sulfonamide hypersensitivity risk?

B. Ototoxicity; thiazides — Ototoxicity is the signature loop-diuretic adverse effect (worse with rapid IV infusion and with aminoglycosides). Both loops and thiazides are sulfonamide-based and carry hypersensitivity risk — the reading lists hypersensitivity for both.

A man with cirrhosis and ascites is started on spironolactone and develops tender gynaecomastia. What is the mechanism, and which agent avoids it?

B. Antagonism at progesterone and androgen receptors; switch to eplerenone — Spironolactone has affinity for progesterone and androgen receptors, where it acts as an antagonist — gynecomastia, impotence, menstrual irregularities. Eplerenone has low affinity for these receptors and is less likely to produce these effects.

Why is acetazolamide a weak diuretic despite acting where 65% of filtered sodium is reabsorbed?

B. Fluid escaping the proximal tubule is reabsorbed more distally, particularly in the loop of Henle — The reading states it directly: a proximally acting diuretic might be expected to induce large losses, but most of the excess fluid delivered out of the proximal tubule can be reabsorbed more distally, particularly in the loop of Henle. Downstream compensation is what caps its ceiling.

A 74-year-old with GFR 22 mL/min and volume overload is prescribed hydrochlorothiazide with little effect. What is the correct change, and why?

B. Switch to a loop diuretic; thiazides should be replaced by loops in moderate-to-severe CKD — Objective PHAR.0230: in moderate-to-severe CKD (e.g. GFR < 30 mL/min) thiazides should be replaced by loop diuretics. The one thiazide-like exception the lecture names is metolazone, the most potent, which causes Na⁺ excretion in advanced kidney failure.

L07 · Heart Failure

PATH · Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology · source pp. 369–411

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Compensation (neurohormonal → Frank-Starling → hypertrophy) buys time at the cost of an under-vascularised, stiff myocardium; when it runs out, the heart fails forward into the organs it should perfuse and backward into the veins that drain into it.
Exam Lock
The seven locks
  • Concentric = pressure = sarcomeres in parallel. Eccentric = volume = sarcomeres in series.
  • HFrEF = systolic; HFpEF = diastolic, EF ≥ 50%.
  • The commonest cause of right-sided failure is left-sided failure; isolated right failure from lung disease is cor pulmonale.
  • Heart failure cells (lung, hemosiderin) = left. Nutmeg liver = right.
  • High-output failure: anemia, hyperthyroidism, thiamine deficiency, pregnancy.
  • Stable angina ≈ > 70% fixed stenosis; unstable ≈ 90% or plaque rupture.
  • Acute coronary syndrome = unstable angina + MI + sudden cardiac death.
Trap
Two traps
  • Assuming hypertrophy means a thicker wall — in eccentric hypertrophy the wall thickness can be normal.
  • Assuming the heart is failing because it is weak — in high-output failure the pump is fine and the demand is the problem.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Why five axes and not one taxonomy
  • These are not competing classifications — they are five independent questions about the same patient. A single case is, for example, systolic, low-output, left-sided, backward, decompensated. Answer all five and you have described the failure completely.
Exam Lock
Two numbers that decide autopsy questions
  • A left ventricle over 1.5 cm is hypertrophied. A heart over ~360 g (male) is enlarged. And because valves are avascular and nourished by diffusion, they heal by scarring, not regeneration — which is why rheumatic valve disease is progressive.
Exam Lock
Two named appearances
  • Heart failure cells = hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the lung, from left failure. Nutmeg liver = chronic passive congestion with hemorrhagic centrilobular necrosis, from right failure. If a stem gives you one, it is telling you which side failed.
Exam Lock
The definition of acute coronary syndrome used in this module
  • The term acute coronary syndrome is applied to any of the three catastrophic manifestations of IHD: unstable angina, MI, and sudden cardiac death.
Trap
The line students miss
  • There can be significant hypertrophy without any increase in thickness of the walls. In eccentric hypertrophy the mass rises in proportion to the dilatation, so wall thickness can measure normal while the heart weighs 600 g.

Pattern tables

Systolic vs diastolic dysfunction

Systolic dysfunctionDiastolic dysfunction
DefectInability to contract properlyInability of the heart to relax and fill properly

Also calledHeart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) — left ventricular ejection fraction ≥ 50%

Both can coexist.

Pathogenesis — the two percentages that separate stable from unstable

Stable plaque / stable anginaUnstable plaque / unstable anginaMyocardial infarction
LesionFixed (stable) lesion obstructing > 70% of vascular cross-sectional area — CRITICAL STENOSISObstruction of 90% of cross-sectional areaUnpredictable and sudden conversion of a stable plaque into an unstable plaque
ConsequenceThreshold for symptomatic ischemia precipitated by exercise — EXERTIONAL ANGINA. Compensatory vasodilation is no longer sufficient to meet myocardial demandInadequate flow even at rest. Collateral circulation will mitigate stenosis; neovascularization indicates increased inflammationRupture, superficial erosion, ulceration, fissuring, deep hemorrhage → unstable angina, myocardial infarction and sudden death

> 90% of patients with IHD have atherosclerotic lesions that cause stable fixed narrowing of one or more coronary arteries.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 60-year-old man has 10 minutes of severe diffuse chest pain radiating to the left shoulder. He has had the same pain repeatedly when walking uphill or climbing stairs; it is relieved by rest or by vasodilators. ECG shows no ST elevation; troponin and CK-MB are normal. Angiography shows a fixed lesion obstructing > 70% of the vascular cross-sectional area. What is the diagnosis?

B. Stable angina from a fixed critical stenosis — Case 2 — stable angina. The lecture's own numbers: a fixed lesion obstructing > 70% is critical stenosis and is the threshold for exertional angina; enzymes and ST segments are normal because there is no infarction.

The same 60-year-old returns with 20 minutes of worsening chest pain that began at rest while watching TV, only slightly relieved by vasodilators. ECG shows no ST elevation; troponin and CK-MB are normal. Angiography shows a ruptured plaque with thrombus formation. What is the diagnosis?

B. Unstable angina — Case 3 — unstable angina: pain at rest, incomplete relief, ruptured plaque with thrombus, but normal troponin and no ST elevation, so no infarction has occurred yet. Unstable angina is one of the three manifestations grouped as acute coronary syndrome.

A third presentation: 30 minutes of sharp chest pain radiating to the left shoulder that began suddenly at rest with no relief from vasodilators. ECG shows ST-segment elevation and troponin is elevated. Angiography shows a ruptured plaque with superimposed thrombus completely occluding the left coronary artery. What changed?

B. A stable plaque converted suddenly and unpredictably into an unstable plaque, with thrombotic occlusion — Case 4 — myocardial infarction. The lecture's phrase is exact: “unpredictable and sudden conversion of a stable plaque into an unstable plaque” by rupture, superficial erosion, ulceration, fissuring or deep hemorrhage. Elevated troponin is what separates this from Case 3.

A 55-year-old woman with severe iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 5.8 g/dL) develops dyspnoea, oedema and a hyperdynamic circulation. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart with an ejection fraction of 62% and a high cardiac output. Which classification applies?

B. High-output failure — High-output failure occurs due to increased demands — anemia, hyperthyroidism, thiamine deficiency, pregnancy — and the defining feature is that symptoms of heart failure occur in spite of a well-functioning heart with a high cardiac output.

PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)

PHAR · Lucy Clunes PhD · source pp. 412–486

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Four first-line classes — ACEI, ARB, CCB, thiazide — chosen by the compelling indication in front of you: kidney or diabetes → RAAS blockade; black or elderly → CCB or thiazide; post-MI or heart failure → β-blocker plus RAAS blockade.
Exam Lock
The eight locks
  • ACEI = cough + angioedema + hyperkalaemia; ARB = the same minus the cough.
  • Both are contraindicated in pregnancy and bilateral renal artery stenosis — and both are first-line for unilateral renal artery stenosis.
  • Never combine ACEI + ARB; never add aliskiren to either in diabetes.
  • Verapamil → constipation and the greatest cardiac depression; dihydropyridines → ankle oedema and reflex tachycardia.
  • Do not combine verapamil or diltiazem with a β-blocker (AV block, negative inotropy).
  • Nitroglycerin for emergencies with cardiac ischaemia; esmolol for aortic dissection; fenoldopam for renal failure; phentolamine for catecholamine excess.
  • Nitroprusside → cyanide toxicity → sodium thiosulfate.
  • Clonidine must never be stopped abruptly — rebound hypertension.
Trap
Three traps
  • Reading a creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor as a reason to abandon RAAS blockade — a modest rise is the mechanism working; a large one means stenosis.
  • Treating dihydropyridine ankle oedema with a diuretic.
  • Giving a short-acting dihydropyridine at high dose — the notes say it can increase the risk of MI.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
Special considerations with black patients (current guidelines, verbatim)
  • Hypertension occurs at a younger age and is often more severe; black patients are particularly vulnerable to strokes and hypertensive kidney disease — 3–5 times as likely to have renal complications and end-stage kidney disease. They usually respond well to calcium channel blockers and diuretics but have smaller blood pressure reductions with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and β-blockers. Appropriate combination therapies provide powerful responses that are similar in black or white patients.
Exam Lock
Two safety lines
  • High doses of short-acting dihydropyridines can increase the risk of MI (excessive vasodilation and reflex cardiac stimulation) — sustained-release preparations are preferred.
  • Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil & diltiazem) are relatively contraindicated in patients taking β-blockers, or with 2nd or 3rd degree AV block, or severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Patients with bradycardia, conduction defects or heart failure should not be given CCBs, especially verapamil and diltiazem.
Trap
The paradox to hold in one sentence
  • The short-term creatinine rise on starting an ACE inhibitor and the long-term renal protection have the same cause — efferent dilation. A modest early rise is expected; a large one means you have unmasked stenosis.
Trap
Two combinations the notes tell you not to make
  • A combination of an ACEI and an ARB is not recommended — each is beneficial in kidney disease, but together they increase harm.
  • Adding aliskiren to an ACEI or ARB might increase cardiovascular and renal events in patients with diabetes and should be avoided.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria is started on lisinopril. Two weeks later his creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.9 mg/dL and he is oliguric. Which underlying lesion does this suggest, and why?

B. Bilateral renal artery stenosis; GFR depended on angiotensin II–mediated efferent constriction — In bilateral renal artery stenosis, perfusion pressure is low and filtration is maintained by angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. An ACE inhibitor removes that constriction → acute renal failure. Bilateral stenosis is a listed contraindication; unilateral stenosis, by contrast, is a first-line indication.

A patient on enalapril develops a persistent dry hacking cough. What is the mechanism, and what is the appropriate substitution?

B. Accumulation of bradykinin; switch to an ARB such as losartan — ACE also degrades bradykinin; inhibiting it raises bradykinin (and prostaglandin E₂ / prostacyclin), producing the cough and contributing to angioedema. ARBs block the AT1 receptor downstream and do not affect bradykinin, so they do not cause the cough and carry a much lower angioedema risk.

A 66-year-old man with hypertension and gout needs a single antihypertensive. Which agent has the additional benefit of lowering plasma uric acid, and by what mechanism?

B. Losartan — inhibits the URAT1 transporter — Losartan reduces plasma uric acid levels by inhibiting the URAT1 transporter — can be useful in patients with gout. Thiazides do the opposite: they cause hyperuricemia by competing for the proximal organic secretory pathway and can precipitate gout.

A 72-year-old woman with hypertension develops bilateral ankle swelling on amlodipine. Her JVP is normal, there are no crackles, and BNP is normal. What is the mechanism and best next step?

B. Precapillary arteriolar dilation without venular dilation causing a local pressure gradient; consider reducing the dose or switching class — a diuretic will not fix it — Dihydropyridine peripheral edema, especially feet and ankles, is a listed adverse effect and is not volume overload — it is a local Starling-forces problem from selective arteriolar dilation, which is why it responds poorly to diuretics. A normal JVP, clear chest and normal BNP exclude heart failure.

A 44-year-old man presents with BP 240/140, headache, papilloedema and a creatinine of 2.8. He is admitted to the ICU. What is the correct blood pressure target in the first hour?

B. Reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25%, aiming for a diastolic of about 100–110 mm Hg — Hypertensive emergency (severe hypertension with target-organ damage): lower BP by no more than 25% within minutes to 1 hour (goal DBP 100–110), then toward 160/100 within 2–6 h, then gradually to normal over 8–24 h. Abrupt decreases must be avoided — they cause watershed hypoperfusion.

L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease

PATH · Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology · source pp. 487–532

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Angina is ischaemia without necrosis; infarction is ischaemia past 20–40 minutes; and after that a single clock — neutrophils days 1–3, macrophages and softening days 3–7, scar at 2 months — predicts every complication.
Exam Lock
The nine locks
  • Prinzmetal: ST elevation, normal troponin, normal arteries.
  • ⅔ of infarcts arise from plaques with < 50% stenosis.
  • Contractility stops < 2 min; irreversible injury 20–40 min.
  • Transmural = STEMI = one artery; subendocardial = NSTEMI = inner ⅓, often global hypoperfusion.
  • Troponin: rises 2–4 h, peaks 48 h, persists 7–10 d. CK-MB clears by 72 h → detects reinfarction.
  • Rupture day 3–7 (free wall → tamponade; septum → VSD; papillary muscle → MR).
  • Aneurysm is late and rarely ruptures — the fibrotic wall is tough.
  • Arrhythmia is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death post-MI.
  • Dressler = weeks later, autoimmune.
Trap
Three traps
  • Calling ST elevation with a normal troponin an infarct — check whether it is vasospasm.
  • Attributing a circumferential subendocardial infarct to a single vessel.
  • Expecting the largest plaque to be the culprit lesion.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Why the subendocardium goes first
  • It is the last territory perfused — the coronaries run epicardium → endocardium and most flow occurs in diastole. Any global insult (shock, prolonged hypotension, severe anaemia) starves that layer first, which is why a circumferential subendocardial infarct means hypoperfusion, not a single blocked artery.
Exam Lock
The one that breaks the pattern
  • Prinzmetal angina gives ST elevation with normal troponin and normal arteries. Every other combination of those three findings points somewhere else — ST elevation *with* raised troponin is an infarct; no ST elevation with raised troponin is NSTEMI.
Exam Lock
The two-minute / twenty-minute rule
  • Contractility stops at < 2 minutes — that is why a wall-motion abnormality appears on echocardiography long before any necrosis. Irreversible injury begins at 20–40 minutes — that is the window reperfusion is racing.
Exam Lock
Contraction band necrosis has three homes
  • Reperfused infarct · catecholamine excess (cocaine, pheochromocytoma) · around the edge of any infarct. All three are the same mechanism — calcium flooding a myocyte with no ATP.
Exam Lock
Why CK-MB still matters
  • Troponin stays up for 7–10 days, so it cannot tell you whether a patient who reinfarcts on day 4 has a *new* event. CK-MB clears by 72 hours, so a second rise is a second infarct.
Exam Lock
The single most examinable relationship in this lecture
  • Peak macrophage activity (days 3–7) = maximum softening = maximum rupture risk. The heart is weakest exactly when the patient feels best, which is why day-4 sudden deterioration after an uncomplicated MI is rupture until proven otherwise.
Trap
The most counter-intuitive number in the lecture
  • Two-thirds of infarcts arise from plaques causing less than 50% stenosis. The plaque that kills you is usually not the one that was causing your angina. That is why plaque stability, not plaque size, is the object of the previous lecture.

Pattern tables

Transmural infarctionSubendocardial infarction
ExtentInvolve the full thickness of the ventricular wall in the distribution of a single coronary artery (regional) — also called STEMILimited to the inner one third, or at most one half, of the ventricular wall — also called NSTEMI

Microscopic infarctions are also seen.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 45-year-old man is woken at 3 a.m. by severe chest pain that does not resolve with rest but goes away with sublingual nitrate. ECG during the episode shows ST-segment elevation; troponin and CK-MB are normal. Angiography the next day shows no significant narrowing. What is the diagnosis?

D. Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina — Case 3 in the lecture — Prinzmetal angina. Occurs at rest and wakes the patient, ST-segment elevation during episodes (transmural ischaemia), normal enzymes, and no significant narrowing on angiography because the mechanism is coronary artery spasm. It responds to vasodilators and can occur in atherosclerotic or normal coronaries.

A patient with an acute MI dies on day 4. At autopsy the infarct centre is soft and yellow-tan with a hyperaemic border, and there is 400 mL of blood in the pericardial sac. Which histological finding explains the rupture?

B. Peak macrophage activity with breakdown of myofibers and no collagen yet laid down — Days 3–7: macrophages appear and break down myofibers, but collagen has not yet been laid down — maximum softening, maximum rupture risk. Free-wall rupture → haemopericardium and cardiac tamponade. Neutrophils dominate days 1–3; dense scar takes > 2 months.

Four days after an inferior STEMI a patient develops a new loud holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, with flash pulmonary oedema. Which vessel was occluded and what has ruptured?

B. RCA/PDA; posteromedial papillary muscle — The lecture pairs inferior wall MI (PDA) with mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture. The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply from the PDA, so it is the vulnerable one. A septal rupture (LAD) gives a harsh murmur at the left sternal border with a step-up in oxygen saturation.

A 78-year-old diabetic woman is found to have Q waves in II, III and aVF on a routine ECG. She reports no chest pain, ever. What phenomenon is this and how common is it?

B. Silent MI; as many as 25% of cases — Silent MI occurs in as many as 25% of cases — asymptomatic infarction discovered only by ECG changes and laboratory tests, common in the elderly and in patients with diabetes mellitus or hypertension (autonomic neuropathy blunting afferent pain signalling).

After successful primary PCI a patient's infarct is grossly haemorrhagic, and microscopy shows prominent hyper-eosinophilic cross-striations spanning myofibers. What are these bands and why do they form?

B. Contraction band necrosis; calcium influx driving actin-myosin interaction with no ATP to permit relaxation — Contraction band necrosis is the microscopic signature of reperfusion injury: an influx of calcium heightens actin-myosin interactions and, in the absence of ATP, the sarcomeres cannot relax and get stuck in an agonal tetanic state. Up to 50% or more of final infarct size may be attributable to reperfusion injury.

A hypotensive patient in septic shock survives, but troponin is elevated and the ECG shows T-wave depression without ST elevation. Autopsy of a similar case shows necrosis confined to the inner third of the ventricular wall, circumferentially. What is the mechanism?

B. Global hypoperfusion of the last-perfused layer, on a background of diffuse stenosing atherosclerosis — A circumferential subendocardial infarct is not the territory of one artery — the lecture attributes it to diffuse stenosing coronary atherosclerosis or prolonged hypotension. The subendocardium is the last region perfused, so it dies first in any global insult. ECG shows no ST elevation, maybe T-wave depression (NSTEMI).

Six weeks after a large anterior MI a patient develops fever, pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial friction rub, with a raised ESR. What is this, and how does it differ from the pericarditis of day 2–3?

B. Dressler syndrome; it is autoimmune, from autoantibodies targeting damaged pericardial antigens, whereas the early form is direct irritation in transmural infarcts — Two pericarditides follow MI. The early one (day 2–3) is acute fibrinous/fibrinohaemorrhagic, from direct irritation of the pericardium in transmural infarcts. Dressler syndrome occurs several weeks post-MI and is autoimmune — autoantibodies targeting damaged pericardial antigens.

PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)

PHAR · Lucy Clunes PhD · source pp. 533–579

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • In a crisis the drug is chosen by the organ that is failing — ischaemia → nitroglycerin, dissection → esmolol, kidneys → fenoldopam, catecholamines → phentolamine, pregnancy → hydralazine or labetalol.
Exam Lock
The seven locks
  • Emergency = target-organ damage → IV, ICU, ≤ 25% drop in the first hour.
  • Urgency = no organ damage → two oral drugs, outpatient follow-up.
  • Pregnancy: methyldopa (chronic), hydralazine (eclamptic crisis), labetalol (β-blocker of choice). No ACEI/ARB/aliskiren/bosentan.
  • Nitroprusside → cyanide → sodium thiosulfate; t½ 1–2 min, IV only.
  • Fenoldopam preserves renal perfusion; contraindicated in glaucoma.
  • Labetalol does not cause reflex tachycardia; nicardipine and diazoxide do.
  • Sildenafil + nitrate = contraindicated (cGMP accumulation).
Trap
Three traps
  • Stopping clonidine abruptly, or pairing it with a β-blocker — rebound hypertension.
  • Using doxazosin as monotherapy for hypertension — it increases the rate of congestive heart failure.
  • Correcting a hypertensive emergency too fast — the complication is MI, stroke or visual loss.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Objectives PHAR.0240 and PHAR.0241 in one line
  • ACE inhibitors and ARBs are used in diabetic nephropathy because they dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria — and this benefit is great enough that they are used in normotensive diabetics with albuminuria, where the indication is renal protection rather than blood pressure.
Exam Lock
Why both preserve renal blood flow
  • Central sympatholysis lowers pressure without constricting the renal vasculature. That is why these two survive in patients where renal perfusion matters — and why methyldopa remains the classic choice in pregnancy, where uteroplacental flow must be preserved.
Exam Lock
Objective PHAR.0245 — why nitrate + sildenafil is dangerous
  • Both act on the same pathway: nitrates donate NO which raises cGMP, and sildenafil blocks the PDE5 that degrades cGMP. Together they cause runaway cGMP accumulation → profound, refractory hypotension — potentially fatal. This same pairing reappears in the Antianginal Drugs lecture.
Trap
Two drugs, one lupus-like syndrome
  • Hydralazine and methyldopa both produce a reversible lupus-like syndrome. Methyldopa additionally produces a Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia — the two are frequently offered as distractors for each other.

Pattern tables

Central α₂ agonists — clonidine vs methyldopa

ClonidineMethyldopa

Renal effectDOES NOT reduce renal blood flow or GFRDOES NOT reduce renal blood flow or GFR
UseHypertension management including hypertensive crises (other drugs with fewer side effects are now generally preferred)Usually treatment of choice for pregnancy-induced hypertension (other drugs with fewer side effects are now generally preferred for other patients)

Rebound hypertension following abrupt withdrawal — avoid concomitant use with β-blockers.Sedation, drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, headache, weakness, fatigue, sexual dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia · nightmares, mental depression, vertigo (infrequent) · reversible lupus-like syndrome · positive Coombs test in 10–20% on long-term treatment (> 1 year), which can result in hemolytic anemia, hepatitis & drug fever

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation has BP 176/118, headache and proteinuria. Which two agents are named in this lecture as the pregnancy choices for acute lowering and for chronic control?

B. Hydralazine acutely; methyldopa chronically — Hydralazine is the drug of choice for hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy related to eclampsia, and methyldopa is usually the treatment of choice for pregnancy-induced hypertension. Labetalol is the commonly used β-blocker in pregnancy. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aliskiren and bosentan are all contraindicated in pregnancy.

A patient with a phaeochromocytoma has a hypertensive crisis. Which agent is the drug of choice, and why is starting with a β-blocker alone dangerous?

B. Phentolamine; unopposed α-stimulation after β-blockade worsens vasoconstriction — Phentolamine — a non-selective α blocker — is named as the drug of choice for catecholamine-related emergencies: pheochromocytoma, cocaine and amphetamine toxicity, clonidine withdrawal and MAOI interactions. β-blockade first leaves α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed.

A 61-year-old man with hypertensive emergency has a creatinine of 4.2 mg/dL. Which IV agent both lowers blood pressure and maintains or increases renal perfusion?

B. Fenoldopam — Fenoldopam is a peripheral dopamine-1 receptor agonist: it evokes arteriolar dilation while maintaining or increasing renal perfusion and promoting natriuresis, which is why the lecture calls it particularly beneficial in renal insufficiency. Its one contraindication is glaucoma.

A man taking sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension is given sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain and becomes profoundly hypotensive. What is the mechanism?

B. Nitrates raise cGMP and sildenafil blocks the PDE5 that degrades it, so cGMP accumulates unopposed — Objective PHAR.0245. Nitrates donate NO → guanylyl cyclase → ↑ cGMP; sildenafil inhibits PDE5, the enzyme that breaks cGMP down. Given together, cGMP accumulates without limit → profound, refractory vasodilation and hypotension. Nitrates are an absolute contraindication with PDE5 inhibitors.

A patient on long-term methyldopa develops fatigue and jaundice; haemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL with a raised reticulocyte count. Which test is most likely to be positive, and in what proportion of long-term users does it occur?

B. Direct Coombs test; 10–20% of patients treated for over a year — Methyldopa causes development of a positive Coombs test in 10–20% of patients on long-term treatment (> 1 year), which can result in haemolytic anaemia, hepatitis and drug fever. It also causes a reversible lupus-like syndrome — as does hydralazine.

L11 · Valvular Heart Disease

PATH · Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology · source pp. 580–623

Bottom line

Bottom Line
Two mnemonics that carry the table
  • Aortic stenosis = Angina, Syncope, CHF — “ASC” in the order severity is reached. Mitral stenosis pushes pressure backwards into the lungs — so haemoptysis and orthopnoea, with a left atrium that enlarges and fibrillates.
Bottom Line
How the choice is actually made
  • Mechanical = durability bought with anticoagulation. Bioprosthetic = freedom from warfarin bought with a second operation. That trade-off is why mechanical valves go to younger patients and bioprostheses to older ones or to those who cannot be anticoagulated.

Exam locks

Exam Lock
The asymmetry to remember
  • Stenosis is always the leaflet, and always chronic. Regurgitation can be leaflet or apparatus, and can be acute — which is why a ruptured chord or papillary muscle presents as sudden flash pulmonary oedema, while stenosis never does.
Exam Lock
Three sterile-vegetation tells
  • Cancer + bland thrombus + no inflammation = NBTE. SLE + vegetations on *both* surfaces = Libman-Sacks. Previous rheumatic fever + tiny warty nodules on the line of closure = RHD.

Traps

Trap
Why the free edges matter
  • In calcific aortic stenosis the calcium sits on the outflow surface and the free edges are spared; in rheumatic aortic disease the commissures fuse and the free edges are thickened. That single feature separates senile from rheumatic aortic stenosis on a gross photograph.

Pattern tables

The four common valvular lesions — causes, symptoms, signs

LesionCommon causesSymptomsSigns
Mitral stenosisPost-inflammatory scarring (rheumatic heart disease)Dyspnea (pulmonary edema), orthopnea and hemoptysisLate low-pitched diastolic murmur and crepitations in lung
Mitral regurgitation1. Post-inflammatory scarring (rheumatic) · 2. Infective endocarditis · 3. Mitral valve prolapseDyspnea (pulmonary edema), palpitations and fatiguePansystolic murmur radiating to axilla

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 10-year-old boy has one week of fever, chest pain and joint pain; his parents report a throat infection 3 weeks earlier. He has a subcutaneous nodule on the extensor surface of his right forearm and a raised ESR. What histological lesion is pathognomonic in his heart?

B. Aschoff bodies containing Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells — Case 1 — acute rheumatic fever. The Aschoff body is the pathognomonic feature: T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and plump activated macrophages (Anitschkow cells) whose chromatin condenses into a slender wavy ribbon — “caterpillar cells”. Verrucae are present but not pathognomonic.

A 70-year-old man has syncope and exertional chest pain. Echocardiography shows a thickened, calcified aortic valve with left ventricular hypertrophy. Where will the calcium be found, and what is spared?

B. Mounded on the outflow surfaces of the cusps, with the free edges usually not involved — Case 3 — calcific aortic stenosis: mounded calcified masses on the outflow surfaces of the cusps, heaped within the sinuses of Valsalva, with the free edges usually not involved. Commissural fusion with thickened free edges would indicate a rheumatic aetiology.

A tall, thin 35-year-old woman with scoliosis and a high arched palate has palpitations; echocardiography shows mitral cusps protruding into the left atrium during systole. Which layer of the valve is abnormal?

B. The fibrosa is thinned and the spongiosa expanded with myxoid ground substance — Case 4 — myxomatous mitral valve / mitral valve prolapse, here with a Marfan-like connective tissue phenotype. Microscopy: thinning of the fibrosa layer, expansion of the spongiosa layer with loose, oedematous, faintly basophilic ground substance.

A 30-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever, chest pain, palpitations and low urine output. He had a tooth extracted a month ago. Echocardiography shows nodules at the line of closure with destruction of the mitral valve. Which organism is most likely, and why is the urine output low?

B. Viridans streptococci; immune-complex glomerulonephritis — Case 5 — subacute infective endocarditis after a dental procedure: Viridans streptococci on a valve that becomes deformed, insidious course over weeks. The renal impairment is one of the immune-complex phenomena listed alongside Osler nodes and Roth spots — glomerulonephritis.

A 75-year-old man with colon carcinoma has small nodules at the line of closure of the mitral valve on routine echocardiography, with no valve destruction. What is the diagnosis and the histology?

B. Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis; bland thrombus with virtually no inflammation, loosely attached to the cusp — Case 6 — NBTE (marantic endocarditis): small thrombotic vegetations on previously normal valves in a debilitated patient with an adenocarcinoma / hypercoagulable state. The nodules are fibrin and platelets, not invasive, with no destruction of the valve and no inflammation.

L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1

MICR · A. Malur PhD · Department of Microbiology, Immunology, and Pharmacology · source pp. 624–655

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Four vegetations, told apart by size, site, destructiveness; and one organism rule — virulent organism on a normal valve = acute; low-virulence organism on a deformed valve = subacute.
Exam Lock
The ten locks
  • AS = angina, syncope, CHF; ejection systolic to the carotids. MR = pansystolic to the axilla. MS = late diastolic. AR = early diastolic + bounding pulses.
  • Aschoff body with Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells is pathognomonic for rheumatic carditis.
  • Rheumatic MS: commissural fusion + short chordae → fish-mouth orifice.
  • Calcific AS: calcium on the outflow surface; free edges spared.
  • MVP: thin fibrosa, expanded spongiosa; women 7:1; mid-systolic click.
  • IE hallmark = vegetation that destroys the valve; ring abscess; IVDU → tricuspid.
  • Osler = painful (immune); Janeway = painless (embolic).
  • NBTE = cancer/hypercoagulable, bland, non-destructive. Libman-Sacks = SLE, both surfaces.
  • 3 sets of blood cultures detect 96–98%; 10% are culture-negative.
  • Early PVE < 1 y = CoNS/S. aureus; late PVE > 1 y = native-valve organisms.
Trap
Three traps
  • Assuming a negative pharyngeal culture excludes rheumatic fever — cultures are negative by the time the illness begins; you need anti-streptolysin O or anti-DNase B.
  • Calling every mitral vegetation infective — check whether the valve is destroyed.
  • Forgetting mitral valve prolapse as a predisposing lesion for infective endocarditis.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
Why NBTE is step 2 of infective endocarditis
  • The sterile platelet–fibrin thrombus of NBTE is the scaffold that circulating bacteria adhere to. That is why the pathology and microbiology lectures describe the same lesion from two directions, and why any condition producing endothelial injury is a risk factor.
Exam Lock
The time-based rule for prosthetic valves
  • Early PVE (< 1 year, usually < 2 months) = skin flora introduced at surgery → coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus. Late PVE (> 1 year) behaves like native-valve disease — the organism comes from the community, not the theatre.
