Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 58-year-old man with no history of heart disease has 4 days of high fever and chills, worsening confusion, and sudden left-sided hemiparesis. He had a recent deep skin infection. He has a grade III murmur and bibasal crepitations. Which organism, and which form of endocarditis?

B. Staphylococcus aureus; acute IE on a previously normal valve — Case 1 — a previously normal valve, a highly virulent organism seeded from a deep skin infection, rapid destruction and an embolic stroke within days = acute IE due to S. aureus. S. aureus carries an increased risk of embolism, stroke, persistent bacteraemia and death.

A 75-year-old man has 14 days of low-grade fever, fatigue and painful bumps on his hands and feet. He had a mitral valve replacement 4 years ago and a recent colonoscopy. He has Osler nodes, splinter haemorrhages and petechiae. What category of endocarditis is this?

B. Late prosthetic valve endocarditis — organisms as for native valve disease — Case 2 — the valve was replaced 4 years ago, so this is late PVE (> 1 year), whose organisms are the same as native valve endocarditis (viridans streptococci, S. aureus, enterococci, HACEK) rather than the perioperative skin flora that cause early PVE. Osler nodes are painful; Janeway lesions are painless.

Two sets of blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The isolate is catalase-positive, coagulase-negative, mannitol-negative and novobiocin-sensitive. Which organism and which clinical context?

B. S. epidermidis; device-related or early prosthetic valve IE — Catalase + (staphylococcus), coagulase − (not S. aureus), mannitol − and novobiocin sensitive = S. epidermidis — the most frequently isolated species from human skin, a major cause of early PVE and of infections associated with inserted devices, via fibrinogen-binding adhesins and biofilm. Novobiocin resistance would indicate S. saprophyticus.

Under the Modified Duke criteria as taught in this lecture, a patient with one positive echocardiogram showing an intracardiac mass, a temperature of 38.4 °C, IV drug use and a Janeway lesion has how many major and minor criteria, and what is the diagnostic category?

B. 1 major, 3 minor — definite IE — Major: the positive echocardiogram (1). Minor: temperature > 38 °C, predisposing risk factor (IV drug use), vascular phenomenon (Janeway lesion) = 3. 1 major + 3 minor = definite IE.

L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease

PATH · Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology · source pp. 839–877

Exam locks

Exam Lock
The four infiltrates
  • Lymphocytes → viral. Neutrophils + lymphocytes + plasma cells → fungal. Eosinophils → hypersensitivity (methyldopa, sulfonamides). Giant cells → giant cell myocarditis. The cell in the infiltrate *is* the answer.
Exam Lock
Beck's triad is in the slide, unnamed
  • Faint distant heart sounds + distended neck veins + declining cardiac output (hypotension) is Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade. The lecture lists all three and adds shock as the endpoint.

Pattern tables

Dilated vs hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)
DefinitionProgressive cardiac dilatation leading to progressive heart failure (ejection fraction < 25%). Most common form of cardiomyopathy — 90% of cases.Primary myocardial hypertrophy of the left ventricle with marked reduction in diastolic filling, and in one-third of cases with left ventricular outflow obstruction
PhysiologySystolic dysfunction — flabby, hypocontractingPrimarily diastolic dysfunction — thick-walled, overweight and hypercontracting, in striking contrast to DCM
Genetics / etiologyIdiopathic (small number) · genetic: autosomal dominant mutation affecting cytoskeletal protein (most common titin) and X-linked mutation in the dystrophin gene · chemotherapy: doxorubicin · alcohol · end result of viral myocarditis, thiamine deficiency and postpartumAutosomal dominant with variable expression. Missense point mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins → gain of function: β-myosin heavy chain (most common), myosin-binding protein C, cardiac troponin T
Who / clinicalMost commonly affects individuals 20–50 years. Progressive CHF refractory to therapy, usually end stage by the time of diagnosis. Secondary mitral regurgitation and abnormal rhythms are common; embolism from mural thrombi. Treatment: cardiac transplantMassively hypertrophied LV with reduced stroke volume → CHF · increased O₂ demand → angina · decreased cardiac output → exertional dyspnea · harsh ejection systolic murmur · sudden death due to arrhythmias — one of the most common causes of sudden, otherwise unexplained death in young athletes
GrossDilation and hypertrophy of all chambers · flabby and heavy (2–3× normal weight) · mural thrombosis → embolizationMassive myocardial hypertrophy without dilation · asymmetric septal hypertrophy, most prominent in the subaortic region · on longitudinal section a banana-like configuration of the ventricular cavity · endocardial plaque/sclerosis in the left outflow tract
MicroscopyInterstitial and endocardial fibrosis · small subendocardial scars replacing individual cells or groups of cells · combination of hypertrophied and atrophied myocardial cellsMarked myocyte hypertrophy with myofiber disarray — haphazard arrangement of hypertrophied, abnormally branching myocytes · interstitial fibrosis

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 25-year-old woman has 2 days of fever and severe chest pain radiating to her left shoulder, not related to exercise. She recovered from “flu” two weeks earlier and has felt weak since. Angiography shows no coronary blockage. Which infiltrate would a biopsy show, and what is the main complication?

B. Lymphocytes with focal myocyte necrosis; may end up as dilated cardiomyopathy — Case 1 — viral myocarditis (Coxsackie A & B6, enteroviruses): interstitial inflammation of mainly lymphocytes with focal necrosis of myocytes adjacent to the inflammatory cells; gross shows a dilated flabby heart. It may mimic acute MI and may end up as dilated cardiomyopathy.

A 20-year-old footballer dies suddenly. His uncle died suddenly at 25. Autopsy shows a thick myocardial wall without dilation, asymmetric septal hypertrophy and myocardial disarray. Which protein is most commonly mutated?

C. β-myosin heavy chain — Case 3 — hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: autosomal dominant, missense gain-of-function mutations in sarcomeric proteins, of which β-myosin heavy chain is the most common (then myosin-binding protein C and cardiac troponin T). Titin and dystrophin belong to DCM; plakoglobin and desmin to ARVC.

A 65-year-old woman with 25 years of rheumatoid arthritis has exertional dyspnoea, syncope and fatigue; echocardiography shows impaired ventricular diastolic filling, and post-mortem shows amyloid in the myocardium. What will the chamber sizes look like?

B. Both atria dilated with ventricles of approximately normal size and undilated cavities — Case 4 — restrictive cardiomyopathy secondary to amyloidosis: both atria dilated from impaired ventricular filling and pressure overload, with the ventricles approximately normal size and the cavities not dilated. Option E describes constrictive pericarditis, which produces very similar physiology — that is the classic distractor.

A 50-year-old man has a month of dyspnoea, chest pain and palpitations with a raised JVP, tender hepatomegaly and pedal oedema. He dies suddenly; post-mortem shows a dilated right ventricle with focal replacement of myocardium by adipose tissue and fibrosis. Which syndrome should be considered, and which skin finding would support it?

A. Naxos syndrome; hyperkeratosis of plantar and palmar surfaces — Case 5 — arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, from mutations in desmosomal proteins (plakoglobin) or desmin, so that desmosomes detach after strenuous exercise. Naxos syndrome = ARVC + hyperkeratosis of plantar and palmar skin surfaces, associated with plakoglobin mutations.

A patient with end-stage renal failure has pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward and a high-pitched friction rub. What type of exudate is expected, and what is the underlying category?

B. Fibrinous (“bread and butter”); secondary pericarditis due to uraemia — Uraemia is the most common systemic disorder associated with pericarditis — a secondary pericarditis with a fibrinous “bread and butter” exudate, the same exudate seen in rheumatic heart disease and post-MI. Haemorrhagic points to malignancy, caseous to TB, fibrinopurulent to bacteria.

L14 · Cardiovascular Infections 2

MICR · A. Malur PhD · Department of Microbiology, Immunology, and Pharmacology · source pp. 878–902

Bottom line

Bottom Line
Why this closes the loop
  • Rheumatic damage deforms the valve, and a deformed valve is the substrate for subacute endocarditis by low-virulence organisms such as viridans streptococci. The same organism genus causes both, by two entirely different mechanisms — immune mimicry, then direct colonisation.

Exam locks

Exam Lock
Two tests separate all four
  • Catalase splits staph from strep/enterococcus. Then coagulase splits S. aureus from S. epidermidis, and MSA/haemolysis splits S. sanguinis (alpha, no growth on MSA) from E. faecalis (gamma, yellow on MSA).

Traps

Trap
Why this objective exists (MICR.78)
  • A negative culture is not a negative diagnosis. If you stop at “no growth”, you miss Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) and Bartonella — organisms with specific serological tests and specific therapy. The most common reason for no growth is simply that antibiotics were given first.

Pattern tables

The biochemistry table for the Gram-positive cocci that cause IE

OrganismCoagulase testCatalase testMSAMost common haemolysis on blood agar
Staphylococcus aureus++YellowBeta-haemolytic
Staphylococcus epidermidis−+RedNon / gamma haemolytic
Streptococcus sanguinis−−No growthAlpha-haemolytic
Enterococcus faecalis−−YellowNon / gamma haemolytic

MSA = mannitol salt agar. Note the trap: E. faecalis ferments mannitol like S. aureus — but it is catalase negative.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 5-year-old boy has 2 days of chest pain and decreased energy, with tachypnoea and intercostal retractions, resting tachycardia, an irregular rhythm and weak peripheral pulses. He had a recent gastrointestinal illness and has no cardiac history. Which organism and receptor are involved?

B. Coxsackievirus B; the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR) — Case 1 — viral myocarditis in a child after a gastrointestinal (enteroviral) prodrome. Coxsackievirus B, especially B3, enters myocytes via the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR); injury comes from direct viral assault and the host immune response.

A 32-year-old man has sudden sharp anterior chest pain, worse on deep inspiration and when lying down, relieved by sitting forward. He is diaphoretic and tachycardic with a pericardial friction rub and recent cold symptoms. Which is the most likely category of cause?

B. Viral — Case 2 — acute viral pericarditis. The lecture lists a long viral differential (Coxsackievirus A and B, CMV, EBV, hepatitis, measles, mumps, HHV-6, parvovirus B19, HIV, VZV); bacteria are uncommon, TB is rare, and fungi occur in the immunocompromised. The positional chest pain and friction rub are the signature.

Blood cultures from a patient with a new murmur remain sterile after 5 days. He keeps goats and has had intermittent fevers for months. What is the diagnostic strategy?

B. Serology and PCR for fastidious organisms such as Coxiella and Bartonella — Culture-negative IE (~5% of cases) is caused by prior antibiotics or by fastidious / non-bacterial pathogens — Bartonella, Coxiella (Q fever, classically animal exposure), Aspergillus. The stated solution is further microbiological testing: serology and molecular testing (PCR). Modern instruments already detect HACEK within 5 days, so slow growth no longer explains it.

A blood isolate is a Gram-positive coccus in short chains: catalase negative, coagulase negative, gamma-haemolytic, and it turns mannitol salt agar yellow. The patient had a recent urological procedure. Which organism?

C. Enterococcus faecalis — Enterococcus faecalis: catalase −, coagulase −, gamma haemolysis, and ferments mannitol like S. aureus (yellow MSA) — the deliberate trap in the lecture's table. Enterococci are enteric flora and the named risk factors are genitourinary and gastrointestinal procedures.

L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac Neoplasms

PATH · Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology · source pp. 903–939

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • The direction of the shunt sets the colour, the volume load sets the long-term damage, and every unrepaired left-to-right shunt is on a path to Eisenmenger.
Exam Lock
The eight locks
  • ASD = most common CHD diagnosed in adults; secundum is 90%.
  • VSD = most common CHD overall; 90% membranous; most close spontaneously.
  • PDA = machinery murmur; PGE keeps it open, indomethacin closes it; reversal gives differential cyanosis.
  • Eisenmenger = the shunt reverses when pulmonary resistance ≥ systemic; the defect is then irreparable.
  • Tetralogy = most common cyanotic CHD; the degree of subpulmonic stenosis sets the severity; squatting helps.
  • Transposition = parallel circulations; survival depends on a shunt; maternal diabetes.
  • Truncus = DiGeorge / 22q11, one great artery over a VSD.
  • Coarctation = Turner, bicuspid aortic valve, rib notching (postductal), lower-limb cyanosis (preductal).
Trap
Three traps
  • Calling a left-to-right shunt “cyanotic” — it is acyanotic until it reverses.
  • Forgetting that trisomy 21 is the most common genetic cause of CHD, with a defect in 40%.
  • Missing cardiac myxoma as a cause of positional syncope and embolic stroke in a middle-aged woman.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
Why prostaglandins are the whole story
  • Made in the placenta, destroyed in the lungs. Cut the placenta and inflate the lungs and PG levels collapse — the duct closes. That is why PGE₁ keeps a duct open (transposition, preductal coarctation) and indomethacin closes it (isolated PDA).
Exam Lock
Two counting mnemonics from the lecture
  • Acyanotic = the three D's (ASD, VSD, PDA). Cyanotic = the T's — and the number of letters counts the anatomy: 1 vessel (truncus), 2 switched (transposition), 3 (tricuspid atresia), 4 (tetralogy), 5 (total anomalous pulmonary venous connection).
Exam Lock
Position-dependent syncope is the myxoma question
  • A left atrial mass that obstructs the mitral orifice only in certain positions produces syncope on standing or bending, a crescendo mid-diastolic murmur (from the palpitations DLA), and constitutional symptoms from IL-6. It is the one cardiac tumour with a classic bedside story.
Trap
Two lower-limb cyanoses that are not the same
  • Preductal coarctation gives lower-limb cyanosis because deoxygenated blood reaches the descending aorta through the PDA. Differential cyanosis in a reversed PDA gives the same picture for the same reason — but with a normal aortic arch. The clue is the blood pressure difference between arms and legs, which belongs to coarctation.

Pattern tables

The three left-to-right shunts

Atrial septal defect (ASD)Ventricular septal defect (VSD)Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
DefinitionAbnormal and fixed opening between the left and right atrial septumIncomplete closure of the ventricular septum allowing free communication between the left and right ventriclesDuring intrauterine life the ductus permits flow from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the unoxygenated lungs. In healthy term infants it constricts and is functionally closed within 1 to 2 days of birth
EpidemiologyUsually asymptomatic until adulthood — the most common congenital cardiac malformation diagnosed in adults. Incidence: 10% of all congenital heart diseasesMost common form of congenital heart disease. Associated with trisomy 21, 13, 18 and fetal alcohol syndromeFemales >> males. Higher incidence with maternal rubella infection. Accounts for about 7% of CHD; 90% of these are isolated defects
Types / anatomySecundum ASD (90%) — deficient septum secundum formation near the centre of the atrial septum · Primum (5%) — adjacent to the AV valves, often with AV valve abnormalities and/or a VSD · Sinus venosus (5%) — near the entrance of the superior vena cavaMost commonly (90%) membranous. Most VSDs close spontaneously in childhood.—
MurmurOften present as a result of excessive flow through the pulmonary valve and/or through the ASDPansystolic murmurCharacteristic continuous, harsh, “machinery-like” murmur
Complications / managementEisenmenger physiology if untreatedPulmonary hypertension; CHF. Large unclosed VSDs almost universally lead to irreversible pulmonary vascular disease, ultimately resulting in shunt reversal and cyanosis — Eisenmenger complex.Because the shunt is initially left-to-right, there is no cyanosis. The shunt may reverse, leading to lower-extremity cyanosis — differential cyanosis: blue toes, normal fingers. May need to be kept open with prostaglandin E if associated with other malformations (coarctation, TGA). Closes with indomethacin.

The right-to-left shunts

Tetralogy of FallotTransposition of great arteriesTruncus arteriosus
AnatomyFour cardinal features: 1. ventricular septal defect · 2. obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonic stenosis) · 3. an aorta that overrides the VSD · 4. right ventricular hypertrophyAorta arises from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle — ventriculoarterial discordance → parallel circulationsFailure of partitioning of the embryologic truncus into aorta and pulmonary artery, due to failure of neural crest cells to drive formation of the aorticopulmonary septum. A single great artery receives blood from both ventricles
Embryology / associationResults embryologically from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum; RVH is a secondary consequence of pressure overload. Associated with Down syndrome and DiGeorge syndromeAssociated with maternal diabetes. Incompatible with postnatal life unless a shunt (VSD or PDA) is present — the more common presentation. In utero the foramen ovale and ductus ensure mixing; after birth they close → no mixing → severe refractory progressive cyanosisAssociated with DiGeorge syndrome (microdeletion chromosome 22, 22q11). There is an underlying VSD which turns the right and left ventricles into a single chamber → mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
ClinicalMost common cyanotic congenital heart disease, usually present by 6 months. More outflow obstruction → more right-to-left shunting → more cyanosis → more severe ToF; the more severe the subpulmonic stenosis, the more hypoplastic the pulmonary arteries. Cyanotic disease with reduced pulmonary blood flow. “TET SPELLS” with vigorous crying, feeding or agitation · dyspnoea on exertion, syncope · polycythaemia → cerebral thrombosis · right-to-left shunt increases risk of infective endocarditis and systemic embolizationOutcome depends on the degree of blood mixing, tissue hypoxia, and the ability of the RV to maintain the systemic circulation. VSD present in about ⅓ of casesToo much blood may flow to the lungs — flooding makes it difficult to breathe; may lead to pulmonary hypertension
The manoeuvreSquatting, or knees to chest, as a compensatory mechanism — increases peripheral vascular resistance and thus decreases the magnitude of the right-to-left shunt across the VSD——

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 32-year-old woman is found to have a fixed, widely split S2 and a systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. Echocardiography shows a defect near the centre of the atrial septum. Which type is this, and what proportion of ASDs does it represent?

B. Secundum ASD; 90% — Secundum ASD — resulting from deficient septum secundum formation near the centre of the atrial septum — accounts for 90% of all ASDs. Primum defects (5%) sit adjacent to the AV valves; sinus venosus defects (5%) sit near the SVC entrance. ASD is the most common congenital cardiac malformation diagnosed in adults.

A neonate has cyanosis of the toes but pink fingers, with a continuous machinery murmur. What is the mechanism?

B. Reversal of flow through a patent ductus arteriosus, delivering deoxygenated blood distal to the left subclavian artery — Differential cyanosis — blue toes, normal fingers — is the PDA slide's own phrase. The duct joins the aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, so when the shunt reverses, only the lower body receives deoxygenated blood. Head and right arm stay pink.

A 4-month-old becomes deeply cyanosed while crying and improves when the mother holds his knees to his chest. Why does that manoeuvre work?

B. It increases peripheral vascular resistance and so decreases the right-to-left shunt across the VSD — Tetralogy of Fallot: squatting or knees to chest increases peripheral vascular resistance and thus decreases the magnitude of the right-to-left shunt across the ventricular septal defect, sending more blood through the obstructed outflow to the lungs. The severity of a tet spell tracks the degree of subpulmonic stenosis.

A newborn of a diabetic mother has severe refractory cyanosis from day 2. Echocardiography shows the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left. What is the immediate pharmacological priority?

B. Prostaglandin E to keep the ductus arteriosus open and preserve mixing — Transposition of the great arteries creates parallel circulations and is incompatible with postnatal life unless a shunt (VSD or PDA) is present. In utero the foramen ovale and duct provide mixing; once they close there is none. PGE keeps the duct open — indomethacin would be lethal here.

A 16-year-old girl of short stature with a webbed neck has upper-limb hypertension, weak femoral pulses and rib notching on chest X-ray. Which lesion, which syndrome, and which associated valve abnormality should be sought?

B. Postductal coarctation; Turner syndrome; bicuspid aortic valve — Postductal coarctation: upper-limb hypertension, weak low-pressure lower limbs, rib notching from collaterals, intermittent claudication. Associated with Turner's syndrome, and in the non-isolated half of cases with a bicuspid aortic valve. Preductal coarctation presents in infancy with CHF and lower-limb cyanosis through a PDA.

PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)

PHAR · Lucy Clunes PhD · source pp. 940–1015

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Four drugs change the trajectory — ARNI, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor — and everything else in the lecture makes the patient feel better without making them live longer.
Exam Lock
The eight locks
  • Sacubitril must always be paired with an ARB — neprilysin inhibition also raises angiotensin II.
  • No ACEI within 36 hours of an ARNI (angioedema).
  • Monitor NT-proBNP, not BNP, on an ARNI.
  • β-blockers: start low, go slow; contraindicated in cardiogenic shock.
  • MRAs stop at eGFR ≤ 30 or K⁺ ≥ 5.0.
  • SGLT2i help regardless of diabetes; contraindicated in T1DM and eGFR < 25.
  • Ivabradine needs sinus rhythm; digoxin needs a symptom or AF, and never claims survival.
  • Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate: intolerant of RAAS blockade, CKD, or African American patients with advanced HF.
Trap
Three traps
  • Treating HFpEF as if it were HFrEF — the four pillars were trialled in reduced ejection fraction.
  • Giving a calcium channel blocker or NSAID in HFrEF — both are on the avoid list.
  • Reading a rising BNP on an ARNI as decompensation.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
Why the mortality drugs are all anti-compensatory
  • Chronic activation of the SNS and RAAS is associated with cardiac tissue remodeling, which prompts additional neurohumoral activation — a vicious cycle. Every drug that prolongs survival (ARNI/ACEI/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) blocks a compensation. Every drug that only relieves symptoms (diuretics, digoxin) treats the consequence.
Exam Lock
Objective PHAR.0253 in one line
  • Chronic HF = block the compensations (ARNI, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) and relieve congestion (loop diuretic). Acute decompensated HF = relieve congestion first (IV loop diuretic), then support the pump short-term (milrinone, dobutamine) — never long-term, because PDE inhibitors increase mortality.
Trap
The interaction that kills
  • Every drug that causes hypokalaemia — loop diuretics, thiazides — makes digoxin more toxic at the same serum level. A patient stabilised on digoxin who is started on furosemide can become toxic without a dose change. Check the potassium, not just the digoxin level.

Pattern tables

The four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT)

PillarDrugsWhy it worksKey adverse effects / cautions
1 · ARNI (or ACEI/ARB)Sacubitril / valsartanIn HF the natriuretic peptide system is activated alongside RAAS and works antagonistically to it — vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, lower BP and sympathetic tone, reduced aldosterone. Natriuretic peptides are broken down by neprilysin. Sacubitril blocks neprilysin, prolonging their favourable effects. Because neprilysin also breaks down angiotensin II, sacubitril can never be used alone — it must always be combined with an ARB. Preferred over ACEI in new guidelines; absolute 4.7% reduction in CV death or HF hospitalisation vs ACEI.Hypotension · hyperkalemia · angioedema · teratogenic (valsartan component) · worsening renal function with NSAIDs · cough (very small %). Contraindicated: history of angioedema with ACEI/ARB; recent ACEI use (< 36 hours); severe hepatic impairment; pregnancy; diabetics on aliskiren
2 · β-blockersBisoprolol · carvedilol · metoprololReverse cardiac remodeling; 30–40% reduction in mortality and hospitalisation in NYHA II–IV. Main benefit in HFrEF is inhibition of renin release, plus preventing the deleterious effects of norepinephrine on cardiac muscle fibres (remodeling, hypertrophy). Recommended for all stable patients with reduced LVEF, and for asymptomatic Stage B.Can get initial exacerbation of symptoms — start at low dose and increase gradually over several weeks. Bradycardia, reduced exercise capacity, hypotension, AV block. Use cautiously in decompensated HF; contraindicated in cardiogenic shock. Considerable care with verapamil (additive negative inotropy)
3 · MRASpironolactone · eplerenonePatients with advanced heart disease have elevated aldosterone from angiotensin stimulation and reduced hepatic clearance. Aldosterone antagonism prevents Na⁺ retention, myocardial hypertrophy and hypokalemia. Benefits are thought to be relatively independent of the diuretic effect and due to a beneficial influence on cardiovascular remodeling. Decrease morbidity and mortality in severe HF.Hyperkalemia — especially with ACEI/ARB/ARNI, K⁺ supplements or renal failure · GI disturbances (gastritis, peptic ulcer) · CNS effects (lethargy, confusion) · endocrine abnormalities (gynecomastia, decreased libido, menstrual irregularities — less with eplerenone). Contraindicated at eGFR ≤ 30 or serum K⁺ ≥ 5.0 mEq/L
4 · SGLT2 inhibitorsDapagliflozin · empagliflozinRecommended in symptomatic chronic HFrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and CV mortality irrespective of the presence of diabetes. Mechanism remains unclear: osmotic diuresis and natriuresis, decreases in arterial pressure and stiffness, reduction of preload/afterload → blunting of cardiac stress → less hypertrophy and fibrosis, and a shift to ketone-based myocardial metabolism.Increased incidence of genital and urinary tract infections (glycosuria) · osmotic diuresis → volume depletion, increased serum creatinine. Contraindicated: type 1 diabetes (↑ risk of ketoacidosis), eGFR < 25, hypersensitivity

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 64-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 28%) on lisinopril, carvedilol and furosemide is to be switched to sacubitril/valsartan. What must happen first, and why?

B. Wait at least 36 hours after the last ACE inhibitor dose, because of the increased risk of angioedema — Neprilysin also breaks down bradykinin; inhibiting it with sacubitril causes bradykinin to accumulate. Adding it to an ACE inhibitor (which already blocks bradykinin degradation) markedly raises angioedema risk, so sacubitril cannot be used with an ACEI, or dosed within less than 36 hours of one.

Six months after starting sacubitril/valsartan, a patient's BNP has risen although he is clinically improved. What explains this, and which test should be used instead?

B. Neprilysin inhibition prevents BNP degradation, falsely elevating it; use NT-proBNP — BNP is degraded by neprilysin, so ARNIs can cause misleading elevations. NT-proBNP is not degraded by neprilysin, so it is the more clinically useful marker for monitoring HF during ARNI therapy.

A patient with HFrEF in sinus rhythm has a resting heart rate of 82 bpm on the maximum tolerated dose of bisoprolol. Which agent should be added, and what must be true for it to work?

B. Ivabradine; the patient must be in sinus rhythm — Ivabradine inhibits the I_f current in the sinoatrial node, so it only works in sinus rhythm — being out of sinus rhythm is a listed contraindication. It is an adjunct after the β-blocker dose has been optimised, and is contraindicated alongside verapamil or diltiazem (CYP3A4).

A 78-year-old on digoxin and furosemide develops nausea, confusion and describes yellow-tinged vision with halos around lights. Her ECG shows atrial tachycardia with AV block. Which single laboratory value most likely precipitated this?

B. Serum potassium (low) — Hypokalaemia — caused here by the loop diuretic — increases digoxin binding to the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase because potassium decreases the enzyme's affinity for digoxin, enhancing both therapeutic and toxic effects. Treatment: withdraw/reduce, correct K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, lidocaine and/or Mg²⁺ for ventricular tachyarrhythmias, and digoxin immune Fab if severe.

Which statement about drugs used in HFrEF is correct?

B. Digoxin reduces symptoms and hospitalisation but does not increase survival — Digoxin decreases symptoms, increases exercise tolerance and decreases hospitalisation — but does not increase survival. Diuretics have no mortality benefit except MRAs; long-term PDE III inhibition increases mortality; SGLT2 inhibitors benefit HFrEF irrespective of diabetes; and β-blockers must be started low and titrated over weeks.

PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs I

PHAR · Dr. Lucy Clunes · source pp. 1044–1155

Exam locks

Exam Lock
Use / state-dependence — one idea that explains the whole class
  • Drugs bind more rapidly to open or inactivated Na⁺ channels, so they have a greater effect in tissues that are more frequently depolarizing. Cells discharging at abnormally high frequency are preferentially blocked — which is why an antiarrhythmic can suppress a tachycardia while barely touching normal myocardium, and why toxicity appears in hypoxia and acidosis, when normal cells behave abnormally.

Traps

Trap
The three drugs that raise digoxin levels
  • Quinidine, verapamil and amiodarone. All three are themselves antiarrhythmics, so the combination that seems most rational — adding a rhythm drug to a rate drug — is exactly the one that pushes digoxin into its toxic range.

Pattern tables

Mechanisms of arrhythmia — and how each is treated

MechanismWhat happensHow antiarrhythmics treat it
Abnormal automaticityThe SA node sets the pace, but if other cardiac sites show enhanced automaticity they generate competing stimuliMost antiarrhythmics suppress automaticity by blocking Na⁺ or Ca²⁺ channels to reduce the ratio of these to K⁺ → decrease the slope of phase 4 depolarization and/or raise the threshold of discharge to a less negative voltage → ↓ frequency of discharge
Re-entrant circuitsNormal impulses are conducted down bifurcated pathways to activate the entire ventricular surface. Re-entry occurs if a unidirectional block creates an abnormal conduction pathway, with abnormally slow retrograde conduction around a non-excitable area. Re-entry is the most common cause of arrhythmias.Slow conduction and/or increase the refractory period — i.e. convert the unidirectional block into a bidirectional block
Early afterdepolarizations (EADs)Occur during the inciting action potential (phase 2 or 3); triggered by conditions that prolong the action potential (e.g. drugs that prolong the QT interval). Phase 2 EADs are carried by inward Ca²⁺; phase 3 EADs by partially recovered Na⁺ channels. If sustained, they lead to torsades de pointes.Slow conduction and/or increase the refractory period — make cells less excitable
Delayed afterdepolarizations (DADs)Occur shortly after repolarization is complete (interrupting phase 4). Mechanism not well understood; classically calcium overload, as in digoxin toxicityAs above
Accessory tract pathwaysAn extra conduction route bypassing the AV nodeSlow conduction and/or increase the refractory period — goal: enhance conduction through ‘normal’ pathways

PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II

PHAR · Dr. Lucy Clunes · source pp. 1193–1258

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Match the class to the phase — I blocks phase 0 Na⁺, II slows phase 4, III blocks phase 3 K⁺, IV blocks phase 0 Ca²⁺ in the nodes — and then match the tissue: nodes for II and IV, ventricle for IB, atrium and accessory pathways for IA, IC and III.
Exam Lock
The ten locks
  • IA ↑ QRS, ↑ QT, ↑ ERP. IB small ↑ QRS, insignificant ↓ QT. IC significant ↑ QRS.
  • Binding speed: IB fastest, IA intermediate, IC slowest.
  • Lidocaine works on ischaemic (depolarised) tissue and has no negative inotropy.
  • Flecainide/propafenone are lethal in structural heart disease.
  • Quinidine → cinchonism + raises digoxin. Procainamide → lupus-like. Disopyramide → antimuscarinic + negative inotropy.
  • Amiodarone: t½ 25–60 days, loading dose, > 50% long-term adverse effects, check TSH first.
  • Dronedarone has no iodine — fewer effects, less efficacy — contraindicated in decompensated HFrEF and permanent AF.
  • Sotalol = β-blocker + K⁺ blocker; lowest adverse-effect rate but torsades.
  • Adenosine is first line for PSVT; CCBs are second line.
  • Magnesium is the treatment for torsades.
Trap
Three traps
  • Giving a β-blocker or verapamil for acute rate control in decompensated heart failure.
  • Forgetting that quinidine, verapamil and amiodarone all raise digoxin.
  • DC cardioversion in digoxin toxicity — it can provoke ventricular fibrillation.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
Why lidocaine works only where the tissue is sick
  • Class IB drugs are less prominent blockers of Na⁺ channels at rest but effectively block channels in depolarized tissue. In ischaemic tissue, cells are partly depolarized because they lack sufficient ATP to run the sodium pump, so their Na⁺ channels spend more time inactivated — and IB drugs have the greatest affinity for the inactivated state. That is the whole reason lidocaine is a post-MI drug.

Pattern tables

Class I — the three subclasses on one page

Class IAClass IBClass IC
DrugsQuinidine · procainamide · disopyramideLidocaine · mexiletineFlecainide · propafenone
Action potentialSlow the rate of change of phase 0; slow conduction, prolong the action potential and increase the ventricular effective refractory period; prolong phase 3 by inhibiting K⁺ channelsSlow phase 0 and decrease the slope of phase 4; shorten phase 3 repolarization; little effect on depolarization in normal cellsMarkedly depress phase 0 → marked slowing of conduction, but little effect on duration or the ventricular effective refractory period; prominent effects even at normal heart rates
ECG↑ QRS, ↑ QT, ↑ ERP (moderate Na⁺ block + prolonged repolarization)Small ↑ QRS; clinically insignificant ↓ QT (mild Na⁺ block, shortened repolarization)Significant ↑ QRS, no change in repolarization
Clinical useAtrial fibrillation; supraventricular and ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Largely replaced by safer antiarrhythmics because of proarrhythmic risk. Procainamide still maintains a niche as the drug of choice for stable pre-excited atrial fibrillation.Lidocaine: acute ventricular arrhythmias from MI or cardiac manipulation; digitalis-induced arrhythmias. Its use for VT has declined because IV amiodarone is superior. Little effect on atrial or AV junctional arrhythmias. Mexiletine: oral derivative for severe ventricular arrhythmiasSevere symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias resistant to other therapy; severe symptomatic supraventricular arrhythmias and prevention of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Propafenone also maintains sinus rhythm in symptomatic AF
Signature toxicityAnticholinergic effects — tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision, constipation; diarrhoea, nausea, headache, dizzinessLidocaine: wide toxic-therapeutic ratio; CNS effects (drowsiness, slurred speech, agitation); no negative inotropic effect; toxic doses → convulsions, coma. Mexiletine: mainly CNS & GINegative inotropy (aggravates CHF); CNS and GI effects. Flecainide and propafenone are associated with the potential for fatal ventricular arrhythmias in persons with structural heart disease.

Class III — the K⁺ channel blockers

AmiodaroneDronedaroneSotalolDofetilide
MechanismStructurally related to thyroxine (contains iodine). Complex: class I, II and III (and some IV) effects, with K⁺ channel blockade dominant. Decreases AV conduction and sinus node function; blocks mostly inactivated Na⁺ channels; weak Ca²⁺ blocker; inhibits adrenergic stimulation (α and β blocking). Antianginal as well as antiarrhythmicRelated to amiodarone but with NO iodine content → decreased adverse effects but decreased efficacy. K⁺ blockade dominant, with Na⁺, Ca²⁺ and β-blocking effectsPotent non-selective β-blocker that also inhibits the rapid outward K⁺ current → prolongs repolarization and action potential duration, lengthens the refractory periodPotent and pure K⁺ channel blocker
Clinical applicationsOne of the most commonly employed antiarrhythmics despite its side-effect profile. Ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias. Drug of choice for acute VT refractory to cardioversion shock. Low doses maintain sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillationAtrial fibrillation / flutterLife-threatening ventricular arrhythmias; maintenance of sinus rhythm in patients with AF/flutter who are currently in sinus rhythm. Because of pro-arrhythmic effects, do not use for asymptomatic arrhythmias.Conversion of atrial fibrillation/flutter to sinus rhythm, and maintenance of sinus rhythm in chronic AF/flutter of longer than one week's duration after conversion
PharmacokineticsOral (very well absorbed) and IV. t½ several weeks (25–60 days) — extensively distributed in adipose tissue, loading dose required; full clinical and adverse effects may take 6 weeks—Use with caution in renal impairmentExcreted in urine (~80% unchanged)

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 68-year-old man on long-term amiodarone develops a dry cough and progressive exertional dyspnoea; chest imaging shows reticular changes. Which two baseline tests should have been performed before starting the drug, and which organs does it classically affect?

B. Thyroid function and pulmonary/liver assessment; thyroid, lung, liver, cornea and skin — Amiodarone contains iodine and is structurally related to thyroxine — serum TSH should be tested before initiation. Classic long-term toxicities: interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, hyper-/hypothyroidism, liver toxicity, photosensitivity, corneal deposits and blue-grey skin discoloration, plus neurological effects. More than 50% of long-term users stop it.

A patient with a narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 180 bpm is given a rapid IV bolus of a drug with a 15-second half-life and converts to sinus rhythm after a brief flush and chest discomfort. Which drug, and which structure does it act on most?

B. Adenosine; the AV node — Adenosine — a P1 purinergic agonist that opens a G-protein-coupled K⁺ channel and inhibits cAMP-mediated Ca²⁺ influx, causing hyperpolarization. The AV node is more sensitive than the SA node, which is why it terminates AV-nodal re-entrant PSVT. Flushing, burning, chest pain and bronchoconstriction in asthmatics are the expected effects.

A patient with a previous anterior myocardial infarction and an ejection fraction of 32% is started on flecainide for symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. What is the concern?

B. Class IC drugs carry the potential for fatal ventricular arrhythmias in persons with structural heart disease, and are negatively inotropic — Flecainide and propafenone are associated with the potential for fatal ventricular arrhythmias in persons with structural heart disease, and flecainide's negative inotropy aggravates CHF. Class IC markedly depresses phase 0 with slow dissociation, so the QRS widens significantly even at normal rates. Lupus-like syndrome is procainamide; cinchonism is quinidine.

Which class IA drug is described as the drug of choice for stable pre-excited atrial fibrillation, and which chronic adverse effect occurs in 25–30% of long-term users?

B. Procainamide; reversible lupus-like syndrome — Procainamide — the lecture states it “still maintains a specific niche as the drug of choice for the management of stable pre-excited atrial fibrillation”. Its chronic toxicity is a reversible lupus-like syndrome in 25–30%; it is metabolised in part to NAPA, which adds a class III effect.

Which single feature separates class IB from class IA on the ECG, and why?

B. IB produces only a small QRS increase and a clinically insignificant QT decrease, because it dissociates rapidly and shortens phase 3 — IA blocks Na⁺ and K⁺ → ↑ QRS, ↑ QT, ↑ ERP. IB has the most rapid binding and dissociation, shortens phase 3 repolarization, and so gives only a small QRS increase with a clinically insignificant QT decrease. IC dissociates most slowly → significant QRS increase with no change in repolarization.

PHAR · Antianginal Drugs

PHAR · Dr. Lucy Clunes · source pp. 1296–1351

Exam locks

Exam Lock
Objectives PHAR.0275, 0278 and 0279 on one slide
  • Why nitrate + β-blocker (or CCB) is better than either alone: nitrates ↓ preload but cause reflex tachycardia and increased contractility; β-blockers and rate-limiting CCBs ↓ heart rate and contractility but increase end-diastolic volume. Together, each cancels the other's compensatory penalty.
  • Why nitrate + sildenafil is dangerous: sildenafil inhibits PDE5, the enzyme that breaks down cGMP; nitrates raise cGMP. Combined, cGMP accumulates unopposed → profound hypotension.

Traps

Trap
Two β-blocker traps in angina
  • β-blockers are contraindicated in variant angina — non-selective agents such as propranolol can exacerbate vasospasm by blocking β2-mediated vasodilation. Treat vasospasm with CCBs or nitrates.
  • NEVER discontinue a β-blocker abruptly — it causes rebound hypertension or angina.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 62-year-old man with stable angina on a nitroglycerin patch worn continuously reports the patch no longer helps. What has happened and what is the fix?

B. Nitrate tolerance; institute a daily nitrate-free interval of 10–12 hours — Nitrate tolerance develops rapidly as vessels desensitize to vasodilation, and is overcome by a daily nitrate-free interval of 10–12 hours — patches on for 12 h, off for 12 h. Increasing the dose without a nitrate-free window makes tolerance worse.

A 54-year-old man has chest pain at rest, at night, with transient ST elevation and normal coronary arteries on angiography. Which drug should be avoided, and why?

B. Propranolol; non-selective β-blockade removes β2-mediated vasodilation and can exacerbate vasospasm — This is variant (Prinzmetal's) angina — coronary spasm without overt plaque. The reading is explicit: non-selective β-blockers such as propranolol can exacerbate variant angina by blocking β2-mediated vasodilation. Treat with nitroglycerin and calcium channel blockers, which are all equally effective here.

Why does adding a β-blocker to a nitrate produce better angina control than either drug alone?

B. The β-blocker abolishes the nitrate's reflex tachycardia and increased contractility, while the nitrate offsets the β-blocker's increase in end-diastolic volume — Objective PHAR.0275. The lecture's own table: nitrates alone → reflex increase in HR and contractility and ↓ EDV; β-blockers/CCBs alone → ↓ HR and contractility but ↑ EDV. Combined → HR down, contractility unchanged, EDV none-or-decreased — each drug cancels the other's penalty.

DLA · Cardiac Arrhythmias 1 & 2

DLA · Theofanis Kollias, MD · Department of Pharmacology · source pp. 1352–1385

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Angina is one equation with four levers; arrhythmia is one strip read in a fixed order — rate, rhythm, P wave, PR, QRS, ST, QT — and each abnormal answer names a mechanism.
Exam Lock
The eight locks
  • Nitrates dilate veins > arteries → ↓ preload; the reflex tachycardia is why you pair them with a β-blocker.
  • Nitrate-free interval of 10–12 h prevents tolerance.
  • Nitrate + sildenafil = contraindicated.
  • β-blockers are contraindicated in variant angina and must never be stopped abruptly.
  • Ranolazine is last-line and prolongs the QT.
  • Mobitz I: PR lengthens then drops, above the His. Mobitz II: drops without warning, below the His.
  • WPW = short PR + delta wave + wide QRS (bundle of Kent).
  • PIRATES for AF; ABCDE drugs + low K/Mg/Ca for torsades.
Trap
Two traps
  • Giving a short-acting dihydropyridine alone — increased mortality unless combined with a β-blocker.
  • Cardioverting a stable patient in AF without 3–4 weeks of anticoagulation first.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
Above vs below the bundle of His
  • Mobitz I is above the His bundle — the node is fatiguing, so the PR stretches before it fails, and the block is usually benign and vagally responsive. Mobitz II is below it — an all-or-nothing infranodal failure that progresses to complete block, which is why it needs a pacemaker.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 58-year-old woman with coronary artery disease presents with 18 hours of palpitations, BP 100/70, pulse 150. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Flecainide is given, which works by prolonging the QRS duration. Which ECG intervals does this drug affect?

D. The QRS complex, and therefore the QT interval which contains it — The DLA's own question. Flecainide is class IC — it markedly blocks Na⁺ channels and produces a significant increase in QRS with no change in repolarization. Because the QT interval contains the QRS, widening the QRS necessarily lengthens the measured QT even though phase 3 is untouched.

A 39-year-old man has 12 hours of palpitations after several days of binge drinking. He is dehydrated, BP 125/75, pulse 110. The ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves and a narrow QRS. Which cause from the mnemonic fits, and what is the rhythm?

C. Atrial fibrillation; ethanol (the 'E' of PIRATES) — Irregularly irregular + absent P waves + narrow QRS = atrial fibrillation. The binge drinking is the classic “holiday heart” presentation — E for ethanol in PIRATES: Pulmonary disease, Ischemia, Rheumatic heart disease, Age/Anemia/Atrial myxoma, Thyrotoxicosis, Ethanol, Sepsis.

A rhythm strip shows progressive lengthening of the PR interval until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle repeats. Where is the block, and what are the classic causes?

B. Above the bundle of His; excess vagal tone, myocardial infarction, digoxin toxicity — Mobitz type I (Wenckebach): gradual increase in refractoriness at the AV node, so the PR progressively prolongs until a beat is dropped. The block is above the bundle of His. Causes: excess vagal tone, myocardial infarction, digoxin toxicity. Mobitz II drops beats without PR prolongation and sits below the His bundle.

A patient on a macrolide antibiotic and a tricyclic antidepressant develops a polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia whose QRS amplitude twists around the baseline. What is the rhythm, what predisposes to it, and what is the treatment?

B. Torsades de pointes; QT prolongation from the 'ABCDE' drug classes and hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia; magnesium — Torsades de pointes — polymorphic VT on a background of a prolonged QT. Causes: congenital; hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia; and drugs — AntiArrhythmics (IA/IC/III), AntiBiotics (macrolides), AntipsyChotics, AntiDepressants (TCAs), AntiEmetics. Magnesium is the treatment (from the antiarrhythmics lecture).

Bottom line

Bottom Line
Where the marks actually are
  • The rubric scores asking permission, hand hygiene, draping and comfort before it scores any clinical finding — and it scores verbalising as heavily as doing. Rehearse the opening 30 seconds and the closing 30 seconds; the middle you already know.

Exam locks

Exam Lock
Deep inspiration is the fastest discriminator at the bedside
  • Pain that worsens on deep inspiration is pleuritic — PE, pneumothorax, pericarditis, pleuritis, musculoskeletal. Pain unaffected by breathing or position but reproduced by exertion is ischaemic. Pain relieved by sitting forward is pericarditis.

Source notes

Source note
Also in this workbook
  • Appendix B images: Baker's cyst · dry calluses · the characteristic toe in Buerger's disease · skin changes in PAD. Appendix D: AAA screening — abdominal ultrasound is noninvasive, inexpensive and highly accurate (94–100% sensitivity, 98–100% specificity); physical examination by palpation is not reliable; screening can reduce AAA-related deaths by about 50%. USPSTF Grade B: one-time ultrasound for men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked (> 100 cigarettes lifetime); Grade C: selective screening for men 65–75 who never smoked; insufficient evidence for women.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 34-year-old woman has 2 days of unilateral right calf pain and swelling after a long flight. The calf is 4 cm larger than the left, warm and tender, with no fever or sharply demarcated erythema. Which diagnosis heads the SG03 list, and which physical measurement supports it?

B. Deep vein thrombosis; calf circumference difference greater than 3 cm measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity — Acute (< 72 h), unilateral, no infective features, with a recognised risk factor. The measurement the checklist requires: palpate the tibial tuberosity, measure 10 cm below, and compare — a difference of more than 3 cm is a positive result. Erythema nodosum is bilateral and on the anterior shins; erysipelas is sharply demarcated.

A 68-year-old man with breathlessness has bilateral pitting oedema, orthopnoea and PND. Which additional history question best separates the cardiac from the hepatic and renal causes on the SG04 list?

B. Ask about frothy urine and facial swelling, and about alcohol use and liver disease — Bilateral oedema opens the systemic differential. The workbook's own cues: kidney → swelling of the face, haematuria, frothy urine, oliguria; liver → history of liver disease or alcohol use; cardiac → SOB, PND, orthopnoea, past ischaemic heart or chronic lung disease; and hypothyroidism → cold intolerance, weight gain, mood changes.

A 46-year-old man has sharp anterior chest pain, worse on deep inspiration and lying flat, better sitting forward, with a rub. Which of the SG06 differentials fits, and which one would be excluded by the positional relief?

B. Pericarditis; excluded: myocardial infarction, whose pain is usually unaffected by position — Pericarditis: pleuritic, positional, relieved by sitting forward, with a friction rub. The CLSK lecture states it directly — the pain of myocardial infarction is usually unaffected by changes in position, though not always. Aortic dissection radiates between the scapulae with unequal pulses.

Bottom Line
If you have five minutes before the exam
  • Read the drug table on the previous slide top-to-bottom once, then answer this question out loud for each row: *what is its antidote, and what does it get monitored with?* Almost every coagulation question is one of those two axes.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
How the exam uses this
  • The stem tells you the vascular bed. Coronary/cerebral artery → the answer is almost always an antiplatelet (or, in the acute window, a fibrin-specific thrombolytic). Deep vein or pulmonary artery → the answer is an anticoagulant. Getting the compartment right eliminates three of five options before you read them.
Bottom Line
Two axes, four drugs
  • Prodrug vs drug on one axis; reversible vs irreversible on the other. Clopidogrel and prasugrel are the prodrugs and the irreversible pair; ticagrelor and cangrelor are the active drugs and the reversible pair. Cangrelor is the only IV agent — which is why it is the one used when you need P2Y12 blockade *now* in the cath lab.
Bottom Line
Why fondaparinux is the cleanest illustration of the mechanism
  • It is *only* the ATIII-binding pentasaccharide — no chain at all. So by the ternary-complex rule it must be a pure anti-Xa agent with no effect on thrombin. UFH → both; LMWH → mostly Xa; fondaparinux → Xa only. The gradient follows chain length exactly.
Bottom Line
Why the delay, in one sentence
  • Warfarin stops new factor synthesis; it does nothing to factors already circulating. The onset is therefore governed by the half-life of the longest-lived factor (up to 60 h) — which is exactly why a fast parenteral agent must cover the first days.
Bottom Line
A memory hook that survives the exam
  • Inducers: B-C-P-R — Barbiturates, Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Rifampin. Three are antiepileptics/sedatives and one is an antimycobacterial; all four are the classic P450 inducers you will meet again in the antiepileptics lecture. Everything else on the list inhibits — and inhibition means INR up, bleeding.
Exam Lock
Vitamin K sits on both sides of the balance
  • Vitamin K is required for factors II, VII, IX and X *and* for the anticoagulant proteins C and S (PHAR.0281). A drug that blocks vitamin K therefore lowers procoagulants and anticoagulants — and the anticoagulants fall first.
Exam Lock
The anuclear-platelet argument is the whole answer
  • Any question asking *why aspirin's antiplatelet effect outlasts its plasma half-life*, or *why 5–7 days must elapse before surgery*, is answered by the same sentence: irreversible COX acetylation in a cell that cannot make new protein, so the effect lasts the platelet's 10-day lifetime and recovers only as new platelets are produced.
Exam Lock
15% and "no effect"
  • Two numbers carry this objective: only 15% of absorbed clopidogrel is activated, and polymorphisms have no effect on prasugrel. If a stem gives you a poor metabolizer on a PPI with recurrent stent thrombosis, the answer is to switch agent — prasugrel or ticagrelor — not to raise the clopidogrel dose.
Exam Lock
The two-line version
  • aPTT → intrinsic + common → UFH and parenteral DTIs. PT/INR → extrinsic + common → warfarin. Everything modern (LMWH, fondaparinux, DOACs) is predictable and unmonitored; that predictability *is* the selling point.
Exam Lock
Management of HIT (PHAR.0290) — verbatim
  • Patients are treated by discontinuance of heparin and administration of a direct thrombin or factor X inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin, dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban) or fondaparinux.
Exam Lock
The bridging rule, verbatim
  • For treatment of acute venous thromboembolism, heparin, LMWH, or fondaparinux is usually continued for at least 5 days after warfarin therapy is begun, and until the INR is in the therapeutic range on 2 consecutive days. This overlap allows for adequate depletion of the vitamin-K-dependent coagulation factors.
Exam Lock
Skin necrosis is a protein C/S problem, not a bleeding problem
  • The paradox resolves once you remember PHAR.0281: proteins C and S are vitamin-K-dependent anticoagulants with short half-lives, so warfarin creates a transient hypercoagulable window before the procoagulant factors fall. That is why the treatment includes heparin, not more warfarin.
Exam Lock
The four antidotes, in one block
  • Protamine sulfate → heparin (partial for LMWH, inactive against fondaparinux). Vitamin K → warfarin (fresh frozen plasma if immediate). Idarucizumab → dabigatran (antibody Fab fragment). Andexanet alfa → apixaban / rivaroxaban (decoy modified factor Xa).
Exam Lock
3 – 4.5 hours
  • This is the single most examinable number in the lecture. Alteplase is the only agent listed for acute ischemic stroke, and the window is 3–4.5 hours from onset with a measurable neurologic deficit. Reteplase and tenecteplase are STEMI only.
Exam Lock
Long term vs short term is the whole point
  • DAPT after a noncardioembolic stroke/TIA is a short-term strategy only; extending it long term trades ischemic benefit for hemorrhage. Note also the word noncardioembolic — a cardioembolic stroke (e.g. AF) is an anticoagulation problem, not an antiplatelet one.
Trap
Aspirin is not the same as the other NSAIDs here
  • In the MI appendix the lecture states that nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (except aspirin) should be discontinued — reversible COX inhibitors compete for the same site and can blunt aspirin's irreversible effect, and they carry their own cardiovascular risk.
Trap
Cilostazol vs dipyridamole is a classic one-word swap
  • Both are PDE inhibitors; the indications are not interchangeable. Cilostazol → claudication (legs). Dipyridamole → stroke prevention (brain). Mnemonic: Cilostazol = Calves.
Trap
Pregnancy is the cleanest discriminator in this lecture
  • Heparin = drug of choice in pregnancy. Warfarin = never in pregnancy — category X, crosses the placenta, causes fetal hemorrhage and serious birth defects. A pregnant patient with a DVT is a one-step question.
Trap
Stopping heparin alone is the wrong answer
  • HIT type II is a prothrombotic state — the antibodies activate platelets. Removing the trigger does not remove the circulating immune complexes or the activated platelets, so an alternative anticoagulant must be started. Note also that warfarin alone is not on the list.
Trap
Protamine does not fully rescue these
  • Protamine sulfate partially reverses LMWH and is inactive against fondaparinux.
Trap
Dabigatran is not a monotherapy option
  • It is easy to lump the three DOACs together. The lecture separates them explicitly: dabigatran needs a parenteral lead-in; only rivaroxaban and apixaban are approved as monotherapy. It adds: LMWH or UFH should be administered if there is a delay in obtaining these anticoagulants.
Trap
"MONA" is not a priority order
  • The lecture lists aspirin, oxygen, nitroglycerin and morphine — but explicitly de-emphasises morphine (avoid IV morphine if possible) and removes non-aspirin NSAIDs. Reflex mnemonics are exactly where these two modifiers get lost.
Trap
Protamine has its own toxicity — and can itself cause bleeding
  • Given in the absence of heparin, protamine can interfere with coagulation, since the basic protein interacts with platelets and fibrinogen. Adverse effects: hypersensitivity, dyspnea, flushing, bradycardia and hypotension.

Venous vs arterial thrombosis — the pattern that decides which drug you reach for

Arterial thrombosisVenous thrombosis
Dominant componentPlatelet-rich ("white clot") on a ruptured plaqueFibrin- and red-cell-rich ("red clot") in stasis
Typical eventsMI, ischemic stroke, TIA, peripheral arterial occlusionDVT, pulmonary embolism
Drug class that fitsAntiplatelets — aspirin, P2Y12 blockers, GP IIb/IIIa blockersAnticoagulants — heparins, fondaparinux, warfarin, DOACs
Established clotThrombolytics — STEMI, acute ischemic strokeThrombolytics — acute *massive* pulmonary embolism

Clopidogrel pharmacogenetics — the CYP2C19 story, in the three forms it is examined

Question the exam asksThe lecture's answer
Why is clopidogrel's effect variable between patients?Clopidogrel is a prodrug converted to an active metabolite mainly by CYP2C19. Patients who are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers have lower plasma levels of the active metabolite — alternative treatments should be considered for them.
Which common drug must not be co-prescribed, and why?Omeprazole, a CYP2C19 inhibitor, reduces plasma levels of the active metabolite of clopidogrel. Concurrent use of clopidogrel and omeprazole should be avoided. More generally: concomitant use of clopidogrel and CYP2C19 inhibitors should be avoided.
Why does prasugrel not have this problem?Prasugrel is also a prodrug and requires hepatic activation by several P450 enzymes, but polymorphisms have no effect on prasugrel activation. Its activation is more efficient: most of the absorbed prasugrel undergoes activation, versus only 15% of absorbed clopidogrel

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A drug raises intracellular cAMP inside the platelet. What is the predicted effect on platelet function, and which endogenous mediator works the same way?

B. Inhibition; prostacyclin (PGI₂) — Elevation of intracellular cAMP results in the inhibition of platelet function — adhesion, aggregation and secretion. PGI₂, secreted by healthy endothelium, is the endogenous mediator that raises platelet cAMP (and also vasodilates by raising cAMP in smooth muscle). ADP and TXA₂ do the opposite: they decrease cAMP or increase Ca²⁺.

Which receptor pair does the platelet use to adhere to exposed subendothelium, and which receptor is the final common pathway for aggregation?

B. GPVI for collagen and GPIb for vWF; final pathway GP IIb/IIIa — The reading is explicit: platelets have collagen receptors (GPVI) and vWF receptors (GPIb), and activation of GP IIb/IIIa — the fibrinogen receptor — is the final common pathway for platelet aggregation. That is why GP IIb/IIIa blockers are the most complete antiplatelets.

A 66-year-old is admitted with an occlusive thrombus in the left anterior descending artery. Which compositional feature best explains why an antiplatelet, not warfarin, is the chronic secondary prevention?

B. Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich, forming on a ruptured plaque under high shear — Arterial ("white") thrombi are platelet-rich and form on ruptured plaque; venous ("red") thrombi are fibrin-rich and form in stasis. The composition dictates the class. Note option 5's trap: antiplatelets and anticoagulants prevent thrombus formation but are ineffective against pre-existing clots — only thrombolytics lyse them.

A 61-year-old with a drug-eluting stent is on clopidogrel and develops reflux. Which acid-suppressing strategy is contraindicated by this lecture, and what is the mechanism?

B. Omeprazole, because it inhibits CYP2C19 and lowers the active metabolite of clopidogrel — Concurrent use of clopidogrel and omeprazole should be avoided — omeprazole is a CYP2C19 inhibitor, and CYP2C19 is the enzyme that converts the clopidogrel prodrug to its active metabolite. Less active metabolite, less P2Y12 blockade, more stent thrombosis.

Which single agent blocks the final common pathway of platelet aggregation, and what is its molecular nature?

C. Abciximab — a chimeric mouse–human monoclonal antibody against GP IIb/IIIa — GP IIb/IIIa is the fibrinogen receptor and its activation is the final common pathway for aggregation. Abciximab is the chimeric mouse–human monoclonal antibody against it; eptifibatide and tirofiban are the other two blockers. All three are adjuncts to PCI.

A patient with peripheral arterial disease has reproducible calf pain at 100 m. Which antiplatelet does this lecture pair with that complaint?

B. Cilostazol — Cilostazol — a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that promotes vasodilation and inhibits aggregation — is the agent listed for intermittent claudication. Aspirin + extended-release dipyridamole is the combination for secondary prophylaxis of cerebrovascular disease.

Why does LMWH inhibit factor Xa efficiently but have little effect on thrombin?

B. The short chain cannot bridge ATIII and thrombin into a ternary complex, which Xa inactivation does not require — Both bind ATIII through the same pentasaccharide. The difference is purely geometric: inactivation of IIa requires a ternary complex in which the heparin chain binds ATIII and thrombin simultaneously — LMWH is too short. The ternary complex is not necessary to accelerate inactivation of Xa by ATIII. Note ATIII does inhibit thrombin, IXa and Xa — just very slowly without heparin.

Day 7 of UFH for a DVT: platelets have fallen from 240 to 62 ×10⁹/L and the patient has a new right-leg arterial occlusion. What is the correct management?

C. Stop heparin and start argatroban — This is HIT type II — immune-mediated, and characteristically thrombocytopenia *with* thrombosis. The lecture's management is discontinue heparin and give a direct thrombin or factor X inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin, dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban) or fondaparinux. Observation alone leaves a prothrombotic state untreated. Contrast HIT type I: common, mild, nonimmunologic, within the first 5 days.

A pregnant woman at 26 weeks is diagnosed with a proximal DVT. Which agent does this lecture identify, and what disqualifies the main alternative?

B. Heparin; warfarin crosses the placenta and is pregnancy category X — Heparin is listed as the drug of choice during pregnancy. Warfarin crosses the placenta and can cause a hemorrhagic disorder in the fetus and serious birth defects; it should never be administered during pregnancy — category X. Option 4's trap: thrombolysis is reserved for acute massive PE, not routine DVT.

On day 3 of warfarin (started without a parenteral agent) a woman develops painful purpuric skin lesions over the breast and thigh that progress to necrosis. What is the underlying mechanism and the correct treatment?

B. Protein C or S deficiency — these fall before factors II and X, causing thrombosis; stop warfarin, give vitamin K if needed, and give UFH or LMWH — Warfarin-induced skin necrosis occurs in patients with deficiencies of protein C or S; warfarin lowers proteins C or S before it lowers factor X and factor II — the result is thrombosis. Treatment is discontinuation of warfarin and reversal with vitamin K if needed; UFH or LMWH should be given to patients with thrombosis. It is a clotting problem being treated with an anticoagulant — that is the counter-intuitive step.

A patient on warfarin for AF is started on a new drug and the INR climbs from 2.4 to 6.1. Which of these could be responsible?

D. Metronidazole — Metronidazole is on the lecture's list of drugs that inhibit warfarin metabolism, thereby potentiating anticoagulation — INR rises, bleeding risk rises. The other four (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates) are the four inducers that reduce anticoagulation. Full inhibitor list: cimetidine, chloramphenicol, disulfiram, fluconazole, metronidazole, TMP-SMX.

A 58-year-old with an unprovoked proximal DVT wants to avoid injections entirely. Which regimen is supported, and which DOAC would NOT satisfy the request?

B. Rivaroxaban or apixaban monotherapy; dabigatran would require a parenteral lead-in — Rivaroxaban and apixaban are the only direct oral anticoagulants that have been studied and approved as monotherapy (no pre-treatment with heparin) for the treatment of VTE. Dabigatran requires parenteral anticoagulants transitioning to dabigatran, and warfarin requires a ≥ 5-day bridge.

A 72-year-old presents 2 hours after sudden right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia. CT shows no hemorrhage. Which drug is indicated, and what property makes it preferable to streptokinase?

B. Alteplase; it is fibrin-specific, with low affinity for free plasma plasminogen, so it acts on the thrombus without evoking systemic fibrinolysis — Alteplase is the only agent this lecture lists for acute ischemic stroke, started within 3–4.5 hours of onset in a patient with a measurable neurologic deficit. It is fibrin-specific: low affinity for free plasminogen, preferential activation of fibrin-bound plasminogen, accumulation onto the thrombus, degradation of fibrin without evoking systemic fibrinolysis. Reteplase and tenecteplase are listed for acute STEMI only.

Which statement about antithrombin III is correct as this lecture presents it?

B. ATIII inhibits thrombin, IXa and Xa very slowly in the absence of heparin; heparin acts as a cofactor that accelerates the reaction — Antithrombin III inhibits clotting factor proteases — thrombin, IXa and Xa. In the absence of heparin, antithrombin III inhibits them very slowly. Binding of heparin to antithrombin III accelerates the inhibition; heparin functions as a cofactor for the antithrombin–protease reaction. ATIII is an endothelial anticoagulant factor (with PGI₂, proteins C and S, TFPI and t-PA); the vitamin-K-dependent proteins are II, VII, IX, X, C and S.

A man on long-term warfarin for AF requires urgent surgery for a bleeding duodenal ulcer; INR is 6.8. What achieves the fastest correction?

C. Fresh-frozen plasma — Vitamin K works by allowing new γ-carboxylated factors to be synthesised, so reversal following administration of vitamin K takes approximately 24 h. For rapid reversal — immediate hemostasis — fresh/frozen plasma is infused, because it supplies the factors directly. Protamine antagonises heparin, not warfarin; idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.

Which pairing of anticoagulant and its reversal agent is INCORRECT?

D. Fondaparinux — protamine sulfate — Protamine can partially reverse the anticoagulant effects of LMWHs but is inactive against fondaparinux. The other four pairings are exactly as the lecture gives them. Remember protamine works electrostatically — a cationic, arginine-rich protein complexing anionic heparin — and fondaparinux is too small a pentasaccharide for that interaction to neutralise.

Which of these is a property of LMWH relative to UFH, per the lecture's comparison?

B. Higher bioavailability, longer half-life, less frequent dosing, equal efficacy — LMWH have equal efficacy to UFH, higher bioavailability, longer half-life, and less frequent dosing requirements, and are replacing UFH in many clinical settings. Their MW is 1,000–5,000 (UFH is 5,000–30,000), they efficiently inhibit Xa but have less effect on thrombin, and monitoring is not usually necessary (anti-Xa assay if needed).

A patient undergoing PCI for NSTEMI is high-risk. According to Appendix 1, which combination of adjunctive antithrombotic therapy is described?

B. Aspirin + an ADP receptor blocker + a GP IIb/IIIa antagonist, with UFH or bivalirudin — For PCI the lecture gives Antiplatelet therapy: aspirin + ADP receptor blocker; additionally a GP IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist in high-risk patients. Anticoagulant therapy: UFH or bivalirudin. Note also that fibrinolytic therapy is only for STEMI, which rules out option 3 for an NSTEMI.

A haemophilia A patient has persistent oral bleeding after a dental extraction despite factor replacement. Which adjunct does this lecture name, and what is its mechanism?

B. Tranexamic acid; inhibits plasminogen activation — Aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid inhibit plasminogen activation and are used as adjunctive therapy in hemophilia, and therapy for bleeding from fibrinolytic therapy. They are the exact mirror of the thrombolytics on the plasmin axis. Note the lecture's own line on plasma fractions: factor VIII deficiency and factor IX deficiency account for most of the heritable coagulation defects.

Which statement about the timing of warfarin therapy is correct?

B. The anticoagulant effect is apparent within 24 h, peaks at 72–96 h, and a single dose lasts 2–5 days — The coagulation factors involved have half-lives of 6–60 hours; the anticoagulant effect is apparent within 24 h; peak effect may take 72–96 h; a single dose lasts 2–5 days. Warfarin does not touch circulating factors — it blocks synthesis of functional new ones, which is why the overlap rule exists: heparin/LMWH/fondaparinux for at least 5 days after warfarin is begun and until the INR is therapeutic on 2 consecutive days.

Which pairing of monitoring test and pathway is correct?

B. aPTT — intrinsic and common; PT/INR — extrinsic and common — The aPTT is a test of the integrity of the intrinsic and common pathways (used for UFH and parenteral DTIs); the PT — expressed as the INR — is a test of the extrinsic and common pathways (used for warfarin, every 2–4 weeks). DOACs do not require monitoring; LMWH potency can be assessed with an anti-factor Xa assay but this is not routine.

Which drug is a synthetic pentasaccharide with negligible antithrombin activity, approved for prevention and treatment of DVT and usable in HIT?

B. Fondaparinux — Fondaparinux — a synthetic pentasaccharide, the sequence of five carbohydrates that bind to antithrombin III, a specific inhibitor of Xa with negligible antithrombin activity, approved for prevention and treatment of DVT. The lecture's summary table lists its uses as VTE and HIT. Enoxaparin is a LMWH (a chain, not a bare pentasaccharide); bivalirudin and dabigatran are direct thrombin inhibitors.

L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology

PATH · Dr. Mathew Oyelami · Department of Pathology · source pp. 1016–1043

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Ask three questions in order: which compartment (glomerulus, tubule/interstitium, vessel), acute or chronic (tempo, kidney size, GFR for 3 months), and nephrotic or nephritic (bland urine and > 3.5 g vs RBC casts and hypertension).
Exam Lock
The seven locks
  • Pre-renal BUN:Cr > 20:1; intrinsic 10–15:1; post-renal 10–20:1.
  • CKD = GFR < 60 for ≥ 3 months with albuminuria; ESRD = GFR < 5% of normal.
  • Creatinine slightly OVERestimates GFR because it is moderately secreted.
  • Azotemia = raised BUN and creatinine. Uremia = azotemia + symptoms.
  • Deposits: subepithelial humps = post-strep; regular subepithelial = membranous; subendothelial = lupus/MPGN; mesangial = IgA.
  • Nephrotic loses antithrombin III → hypercoagulable.
  • RBC casts are nephritic and nothing else.
Trap
Two traps
  • Reading a normal creatinine as a normal GFR in a frail, low-muscle-mass patient.
  • Biopsying a child with nephrotic syndrome, or a pair of small shrunken kidneys.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Why pre-renal raises the ratio
  • Urea is reabsorbed with sodium and water; creatinine is not. When perfusion falls, avid proximal reabsorption drags urea back with it, so BUN rises out of proportion to creatinine — hence a ratio above 20:1. Once the tubule itself is injured, that reabsorption fails and the ratio falls back toward 10–15:1.
Exam Lock
The compartment triad is the diagnostic algorithm
  • Glomerulus → immune. Tubule/interstitium → toxic, ischaemic, infectious. Vessels → local or systemic vascular disease. Every lecture that follows sits in exactly one of these three rows, and the urinalysis tells you which.
Exam Lock
Deposit location is the single most efficient fact in the renal block
  • Subepithelial humps → post-strep. Regular subepithelial → membranous. Subendothelial → lupus and MPGN. Mesangial → IgA. Learn these four before any of the individual diseases and half of the nephritic lecture becomes recall.
Trap
Why the child with nephrotic syndrome is not biopsied
  • In a young child, nephrotic syndrome is minimal change disease until proven otherwise — it responds to steroids, and light microscopy would be normal anyway. Biopsy is reserved for failure to respond.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 72-year-old man with severe gastroenteritis has a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL and a BUN of 62 mg/dL. Urinalysis is bland. Which category of acute kidney injury does the BUN:creatinine ratio point to, and why?

B. Pre-renal; the ratio is above 20:1 because avid tubular reabsorption returns urea with sodium and water — BUN:Cr ≈ 26:1. The lecture's own thresholds: pre-renal is more than 20:1 (think inadequate blood flow — volume depletion here), intrinsic renal 10–15:1, post-renal 10–20:1. A bland urinalysis supports pre-renal rather than tubular injury.

A renal biopsy shows immune complexes as regularly spaced deposits on the subepithelial side of the glomerular basement membrane. Which disease does this pattern indicate?

B. Membranous nephropathy — Regularly spaced subepithelial deposits = membranous nephropathy. Post-streptococcal GN gives isolated subepithelial humps; lupus nephritis and MPGN give subendothelial deposits; IgA nephropathy gives mesangial deposits.

A patient's urine is tea-coloured with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; proteinuria is 1.8 g/day and blood pressure is 168/98. Which syndrome, and what is the underlying mechanism?

B. Nephritic syndrome; glomerular injury due to acute inflammation — RBC casts + dysmorphic RBCs + hypertension + sub-nephrotic proteinuria = nephritic syndrome, whose mechanism is acute inflammation (“itis” → “itic”). Nephrotic syndrome would give bland urine, > 3.5 g/day proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia and hypercoagulability.

Which of these is a listed contraindication to renal biopsy in this lecture?

B. A 4-year-old with nephrotic syndrome — The lecture lists four situations where biopsy should not be performed: advanced disease with small shrunken kidneys, a young child with nephrotic syndrome, a clinical picture that is already specific (diabetes, post-streptococcal), and normal creatinine, complement and BP with proteinuria < 1 g/day.
