Bottom Line
Read the type from the particle
  • Chylomicrons → I (the LPL/apoC-II machine is broken). LDL alone → IIA (the receptor is broken). LDL + VLDL → IIB. IDL → III (apoE is the remnant ligand). VLDL → IV. VLDL + chylomicrons → V. The particle names the defect.
Bottom Line
Why this diagram is worth memorising instead of five mechanisms
  • Four of the six classes lower LDL by the same final step — depleting hepatocyte cholesterol so that LDL receptors are upregulated and plasma LDL is cleared. They differ only in *how* they deplete it. PCSK9 inhibitors are the exception and act on receptor degradation, which is exactly why the lecture calls them complementary to statins.
Bottom Line
Bempedoic acid is a statin one step earlier in the pathway
  • ACL sits upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, and bempedoic acid is a prodrug activated by an enzyme not present in skeletal muscle — which is the clinical reason it appears in statin-intolerant patients. Note it still elevates uric acid, like niacin.
Exam Lock
The one number from this section
  • The relationship between LDL and CHD risk is log-linear: for every 30 mg/dL reduction in LDL, the relative risk for CHD is reduced by about 30%. This is the quantitative justification for treating to a target rather than to a threshold.
Exam Lock
The two statin sentences most likely to be tested
  • High-dose statin immediately after ACS regardless of lipid levels — the benefit is not a lipid-number benefit. And homozygous FH benefits much less — no functional LDL receptor means the drug's final common pathway is missing, which is precisely why PCSK9 inhibitors appear in the FH row of the treatment table.
Exam Lock
Niacin's profile in one line
  • Flush (aspirin-preventable, prostaglandin-mediated) · hyperglycemia · hyperuricemia/gout · hepatotoxicity. A diabetic with gout is the patient in whom niacin is hardest to justify — especially since adding niacin to a statin has not been shown to reduce ASCVD risk.
Exam Lock
If a question pairs a fibrate with a statin, the answer hinges on which fibrate
  • Both drugs independently cause myositis; the danger is pharmacokinetic and belongs to gemfibrozil alone — two mechanisms (blocked hepatic uptake and competition for glucuronosyl transferases), both raising statin levels. Fenofibrate does not do this. Add renal insufficiency to the stem and the risk rises further.
Exam Lock
Why PCSK9 inhibitors and statins add up
  • Statins upregulate LDL receptors, and PCSK9 inhibitors increase LDL receptors on the membrane of the hepatocyte — PCSK9 inhibitors are complementary to statins. Two different points in the receptor's life cycle: synthesis versus recycling.
Exam Lock
Three superlatives run this table
  • Biggest LDL drop → PCSK9 monoclonals (60–70%). Biggest HDL rise → niacin (20–35%). Biggest TG drop → fibrates (30–60%). And two classes move something the wrong way: fibrates can raise LDL, resins raise TG.
Exam Lock
The pregnancy answer is a resin
  • Statins are category X. The only category B drug in the lecture is colesevelam, and the resins are separately named drugs of choice for pregnant women and for children. That is two independent statements pointing at the same answer.
Trap
Bile acid sequestrants appear on the TG list
  • A lipid-lowering drug that raises a lipid: resins may increase TG and are contraindicated in hypertriglyceridemia. Thiazides and atypical antipsychotics are the two agents that appear on both lists — expect them in a stem about a patient whose lipids worsened after starting a drug for something else.
Trap
Fibrates may RAISE LDL
  • Fibrates may increase LDL, particularly if the TG level is greater than 400 mg/dL. In the lecture's summary table the LDL column for fibrates is written as ↑ or ↓ — the only class with an ambiguous entry.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 52-year-old starts rosuvastatin. Which sequence correctly describes how plasma LDL falls?

B. Statin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase → intracellular cholesterol is depleted → HMG-CoA reductase and LDL receptors are upregulated → LDL clearance from blood increases — Statins are competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, the first committed step of cholesterol biosynthesis. Depletion of intracellular cholesterol leads to upregulation of HMG-CoA reductase, and upregulation of the LDL receptor; upregulation of LDL receptors results in increased clearance of LDL from the blood. Option 4 is the PCSK9 mechanism; option 5 is ezetimibe.

Which patient benefits LEAST from statin monotherapy, and why?

B. A homozygote for familial hypercholesterolemia — no functional LDL receptors, so the final common pathway of statin action is absent — Homozygotes for familial hypercholesterolemia lack functional LDL receptors and thus benefit much less from statin therapy. Note the distractors' errors: statins stabilize plaque (pleiotropic effect), their TG-lowering efficacy is similar to their LDL-lowering efficacy, and the HDL rise is described as small (5–15%).

Which monitoring plan matches this lecture's recommendation for a patient starting atorvastatin?

B. Aminotransferases at baseline, 1–2 months, then every 6–12 months; CK at baseline and immediately if muscle pain or weakness appears — Aminotransferase activity should be measured at baseline, at 1–2 months, and then every 6–12 months. CK should be measured at baseline. If muscle pain or weakness appears, CK should be measured immediately and the drug discontinued if activity is significantly elevated. Rhabdomyolysis is rare but can cause myoglobinuria → renal injury.

A 58-year-old on simvastatin is started on a fibrate for TG of 780 mg/dL and develops severe muscle pain with CK 12,000 U/L. Which fibrate was most likely used, and what are the two mechanisms?

B. Gemfibrozil; it inhibits hepatic uptake of statins and competes for the glucuronosyl transferases that metabolize most statins — Gemfibrozil inhibits hepatic uptake of statins, thus increasing plasma concentration of statins, and competes for the glucuronosyl transferases that metabolize most statins. As a consequence, levels of both drugs may be increased when they are co-administered — this increases the risk of rhabdomyolysis. Fenofibrate does not inhibit statin metabolism and is much less likely to increase risk of rhabdomyolysis. Fibrates act on PPAR-α, not γ.

A patient starting niacin reports intense facial flushing after each dose. What is the mediator, and what prevents it?

B. Prostaglandins; give aspirin before the niacin dose — Administration of aspirin prior to niacin decreases the flush, which is prostaglandin-mediated. The flush is intense, cutaneous, after each dose, and occurs when the drug is started or the dose increased. Niacin's more serious effects are hepatotoxicity and hyperglycemia (via insulin resistance), plus ↑ uric acid → gout.

A woman planning pregnancy has LDL 205 mg/dL. Which agent is supported by this lecture?

B. Colesevelam — Statins are absolutely contraindicated — category X. Resins are the drugs of choice for pregnant women and for children, and among them colesevelam is category B ("appears to be safe in animal reproductive studies"). Fibrates, niacin, ezetimibe and cholestyramine/colestipol are all category C; PCSK9 inhibitors have not been tested and are not approved in pregnancy.

Which lipid abnormality would make bile acid-binding resins a poor choice?

B. Elevated LDL with triglycerides of 620 mg/dL — Resins may increase TG — they are contraindicated in hypertriglyceridemia, and in patients with hypertriglyceridemia as well as elevated LDL, VLDL levels may increase. They are useful only in hyperlipidemias involving isolated increases in LDL, and are the drugs of choice for pregnant women and children — which is why the other options are appropriate uses.

Which mechanism correctly describes inclisiran?

B. A small interfering RNA that binds PCSK9 mRNA and prevents translation of PCSK9 — Inclisiran is a small interfering RNA (siRNA) directed to PCSK9 mRNA; it binds to PCSK9 mRNA and prevents protein translation of PCSK9, resulting in decreased PCSK9 and LDL. It is given SC at month 0, month 3, and then every 6 months, by a healthcare provider, and added to maximally tolerated statin therapy it reduces LDL by about 50%. The antibodies are alirocumab and evolocumab; ACL is bempedoic acid; NPC1L1 is ezetimibe.

A 63-year-old with clinical ASCVD is on maximally tolerated rosuvastatin with LDL still 118 mg/dL. Which is the first non-statin agent this lecture says should be considered?

B. Ezetimibe — Ezetimibe is the first non-statin drug that should be considered as an adjunct to a statin, with maximal LDL-lowering of about 20%. Note the lecture's separate warning that addition of niacin to statin therapy has not been shown to reduce ASCVD risk, and that PCSK9 inhibitors sit further down the ladder — reserved in the treatment table for familial hypercholesterolemia not responsive to oral therapy and for high-risk ASCVD.

Which Fredrickson type is caused by an abnormal apoE, and which lipoprotein accumulates?

C. Type III; IDL — Type III — familial dysbetalipoproteinemia — ↑ IDL, caused by abnormal apoE. ApoE is the ligand for remnant clearance, so remnants (IDL) accumulate. For contrast: type I = ↑ chylomicrons from deficiency in LPL or apoC-II; IIA = ↑ LDL from decreased or no functional LDL receptor; IIB = ↑ LDL and VLDL from hepatic VLDL overproduction; IV = ↑ VLDL; V = ↑ VLDL and chylomicrons.

Which statement about ezetimibe is correct?

B. It inhibits NPC1L1, reduces cholesterol absorption by 54%, and remains effective without dietary cholesterol because it also blocks reabsorption of biliary cholesterol — Ezetimibe inhibits the intestinal transport protein NPC1L1; cholesterol absorption is reduced by 54%; it is also effective in the absence of dietary cholesterol because it inhibits reabsorption of cholesterol excreted in the bile. Maximal LDL lowering is about 20%, and bile-acid sequestrants inhibit absorption of ezetimibe — the two should not be administered together.

Which combination of "best-in-class" claims matches the lecture's percentage table?

B. PCSK9 monoclonals best for LDL; niacin best for HDL; fibrates best for TG — From the table: evolocumab/alirocumab ↓ LDL 60–70% (largest); niacin ↑ HDL 20–35% — and the lecture states outright that niacin is the most effective drug for raising HDL; fibrates ↓ TG 30–60%, and as monotherapy fibrates offer the highest TG reduction, followed by niacin, ω-3 fatty acids, statins, and ezetimibe.

Which is a pleiotropic effect of statins as listed in this lecture?

B. Stabilization of atherosclerotic plaque — The four pleiotropic effects given are: improve endothelial function, decrease platelet aggregation, stabilize atherosclerotic plaque, and reduce inflammation. ↑ LPL belongs to niacin and fibrates; ↓ adenylyl cyclase in adipocytes is niacin; PPAR-α is fibrates; NPC1L1 is ezetimibe.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Immunofluorescence is the discriminating test
  • This table *is* the immunofluorescence result. Granular IgG + C3 along the GBM → membranous. No pattern → the podocyte diseases (MCD, FSGS). The lecture's own summary table repeats this exactly, so learning the classification and learning the IF column are the same task.
Exam Lock
Two barriers, two failures
  • The filtration barrier is both a size barrier (slit diaphragm) and a charge barrier (anionic GBM). Albumin is anionic, so charge loss alone lets albumin through — which is why minimal change disease produces massive selective proteinuria with a normal light microscope. Structural collapse (FSGS, membranous) adds size failure, and the proteinuria becomes non-selective.
Exam Lock
PATH.6007 in one sentence
  • The thrombotic risk in nephrotic syndrome is two-hit: antithrombotic factors are lost in the urine through the damaged glomerulus, and the liver's compensatory protein synthesis increases pro-thrombotic factors. Renal vein thrombosis is the named complication — and it is listed again under membranous nephropathy.
Exam Lock
PLA2R + membrane attack complex
  • Membranous is an in situ immune-complex disease: the antibody meets its antigen (PLA2R) *on the podocyte itself*, which is why the deposits are subepithelial. The injury is done by C5–C9, not by neutrophils — which is why the light microscope shows thickening without hypercellularity and the urine is nephrotic rather than nephritic.
Exam Lock
The three negatives are the diagnosis
  • No LM finding · no IF pattern · no deposits on EM. All that is left is foot-process effacement. Add no hypertension, preserved renal function, selective proteinuria and >90% steroid response and MCD becomes the most "negative" disease in the lecture — which is exactly how it is recognised.
Exam Lock
Three columns, four diseases, one exam question
  • The stem gives you one of the three columns and asks for the disease, or gives the disease and asks for a column. Spike and dome + granular IgG/C3 + subepithelial deposits → membranous. Nothing + nothing + effacement → minimal change. Segmental sclerosis + (IgM/C3 sometimes) + diffuse effacement → FSGS. Nodules + no pattern + earliest GBM thickening → diabetic.
Trap
A child with nephrotic syndrome who does not respond to steroids
  • This is the single most common way the pair is tested. MCD: >90% of children respond to a short course of corticosteroids. FSGS: poor response to corticosteroid therapy. Add hematuria, hypertension or a reduced GFR to the stem and the answer moves from MCD to FSGS even before the biopsy is described.

FSGS vs minimal change disease — the six differences, verbatim

#Clinical features of FSGS differ from MCD in the following ways
1Acute or sub-acute onset of nephrotic syndrome
2Higher incidence of microscopic hematuria, reduced GFR (renal insufficiency), and hypertension

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 4-year-old develops periorbital swelling and anasarca two weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. Urine protein is 5 g/24 hr and is almost entirely albumin. BP is normal and creatinine is normal. What will the renal biopsy show?

B. Normal light microscopy, no immunofluorescence pattern, and effacement of foot processes on EM — Minimal change disease — the most frequent cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, most common between ages 1 and 7, often follows a respiratory infection or prophylactic immunization, with selective proteinuria (chiefly albumin), no hypertension, and preserved renal function. The biopsy is a triple negative: no LM finding, no IF pattern, and effacement or fusion of foot processes with absence of deposits on EM.

The same child is given a short course of corticosteroids and does not respond; repeat urinalysis now shows microscopic hematuria, and BP is 128/86. Which diagnosis becomes most likely, and which feature of the proteinuria supports it?

B. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; proteinuria is more often non-selective — The lecture lists the six ways FSGS differs from MCD: acute or sub-acute onset · higher incidence of microscopic hematuria, reduced GFR and hypertension · proteinuria more often non-selective · poor response to corticosteroid therapy · degree of proteinuria is an important prognostic indicator · most common glomerular disorder that progresses to chronic kidney disease. Steroid failure plus hematuria plus hypertension is three of the six.

A 54-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome has a biopsy showing diffusely thickened capillary walls; silver stain shows spikes projecting between deposits, and immunofluorescence is granular for IgG and C3 along the GBM. Which antigen underlies the primary form, and what does the injury?

B. Phospholipase A2 receptor on podocytes; the membrane attack complex C5–C9 — Membranous nephropathy. Primary disease is caused by antibodies against antigens (Phospholipase A2 Receptor, PLA2R) on podocytes, which leads to complement activation on the surface of podocytes and generates the membrane attack complex (C5–C9) → damages podocytes. 75% of cases are primary and 25% secondary. Because the injury is complement-mediated rather than neutrophil-mediated, the LM shows thickening without hypercellularity.

Which secondary cause of membranous nephropathy is an EXOGENOUS antigen in this lecture's scheme?

D. Penicillamine — The lecture splits secondary causes into endogenous antigens — SLE, malignancies (lung, colon, melanoma), other autoimmune conditions like autoimmune thyroiditis — and exogenous antigens — drugs like gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs, captopril, and infections like hepatitis B, malaria, syphilis, schistosomiasis**==.

A nephrotic patient develops flank pain and a CT shows thrombus in the right renal vein. Which two mechanisms does this lecture give for the hypercoagulability?

B. Loss of anti-thrombotic factors in the urine, plus increased hepatic synthesis of pro-thrombotic factors — There is loss of anti-thrombotic factors in the urine due to glomerular damage, and the liver's compensatory increase in protein synthesis produces an increase in pro-thrombotic factors — giving an increased risk of thrombosis, illustrated in the lecture with a CT showing right renal vein thrombosis. Renal vein thrombosis is also listed as a complication of membranous nephropathy.

Which urinary finding in nephrotic syndrome is produced by the liver's compensatory response, and how is it identified?

B. Oval fat bodies and fatty casts, showing a Maltese cross under polarized light — Hypoalbuminemia → compensation by the liver → increased protein synthesis → hyperlipidemia → lipiduria. Urinalysis shows oval fat bodies, fatty casts and lipid droplets, seen with Sudan III stain, with the classic Maltese cross under polarized light. Red cell casts belong to the nephritic syndromes of the next lecture.

A 63-year-old with 18 years of type 2 diabetes has 4 g/24 hr proteinuria. Which is the EARLIEST structural change, and by which modality is it identified?

B. GBM thickening, identified on electron microscopy first — The lecture lists the earliest features in order: 1. GBM thickening (identified on EM first), 2. mesangial widening, 3. tubular BM thickening. Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules — ball-like deposits of a laminated matrix in the periphery of the glomerulus containing trapped mesangial cells — and hyaline arteriolosclerosis are later, and grossly the kidneys become granular and contracted.

Which statement about the timeline of diabetic nephropathy matches the lecture?

B. Microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/24 hr) appears after 7–13 years; macroalbuminuria (>300 mg/24 hr) after 10–20 years — Initially, hyperglycemia leads to hyperfiltration (increased GFR) and increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure → polyuria and nocturia. After 7–13 years of disease: microalbuminuria 30–300 mg/24 hr appears in incipient nephropathy. After 10–20 years: macroalbuminuria >300 mg/24 hr, overt nephropathy. Note that GFR rises first — option 3 inverts the sequence. Urine protein is the important screening tool for tracking progression.

A patient on haemodialysis for nine years develops nephrotic-range proteinuria. Biopsy shows material in the mesangium that obliterates the glomerular tuft. Which protein is implicated, and what is the prognosis?

B. β2-microglobulin; very poor prognosis, with many dying of end-organ failure — Renal amyloidosis is most commonly seen in patients undergoing prolonged dialysis (β2-microglobulin). The kidney is the most commonly involved organ of systemic amyloidosis, renal insufficiency is present in 50% at the time of diagnosis, diagnosis is by biopsy of the organ involved, and the prognosis is very poor — many die of end-organ failure from amyloid deposition.

Which grouping correctly separates the nephrotic entities by immune complex deposits?

B. (+) membranous, amyloidosis, diabetic; (−) MCD, FSGS — The lecture's classification is: (+) immune complex deposits — membranous nephropathy, amyloidosis, diabetic nephropathy; (−) immune complex deposits — minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. This is also the immunofluorescence result: granular IgG and C3 along the GBM in membranous, no pattern in the podocyte diseases (FSGS sometimes granular for IgM and C3), no specific pattern in diabetic nephropathy.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
The clearance rule explains PSGN's natural history
  • Subendothelial deposits are rapidly cleared, accounting for the resolution of hematuria and renal failure. Later in the disease — by the time of biopsy — there are subepithelial deposits, which are cleared slowly because they are separated from circulating cells and factors. That is why the biopsy shows humps in a child who is already recovering.
Bottom Line
Lupus can imitate every disease in both glomerular lectures
  • Class 5 is membranous nephropathy. Class 4 is a proliferative nephritic picture. Class 3/4 can present as RPGN (it is listed under immune-complex-mediated RPGN, type 2). The one finding that stays lupus-specific is the "full house" immunofluorescence — IgG, IgM, C3, C1q, C4 all positive.
Exam Lock
Normal complement with mesangial IgA is the giveaway
  • The lecture states plainly that IgA nephropathy's pathogenesis involves activation of the alternative complement pathway, yet C3/C4 are normal — production is keeping up with consumption. If a stem gives you gross hematuria after a sore throat with normal complement, the answer is IgA nephropathy; low complement moves it to PSGN.
Exam Lock
Three eponymous appearances, one disease
  • Lumpy-bumpy and starry sky are the immunofluorescence; humps are the electron microscopy. All three belong to post-streptococcal GN. Compare with membranous nephropathy, whose subepithelial deposits give spike and dome on silver stain light microscopy — the same anatomical compartment, different stain, different disease.
Exam Lock
C3NeF is the mechanism you must be able to state
  • An autoantibody that stabilises an enzyme rather than blocking it: it protects the alternative-pathway C3 convertase from inactivation, so C3 is consumed continuously. Serum C3 falls with normal C1 and C4 — the signature of pure alternative-pathway consumption — and Factor B and properdin fall with it. Recurrence after transplant in 90% follows from the fact that the antibody, not the kidney, is the disease.
Exam Lock
Linear · granular · nothing
  • Three immunofluorescence patterns map one-to-one onto the three mechanisms. Linear = an antibody bound continuously along the GBM (anti-GBM). Granular = discrete immune complexes. Pauci-immune = no antibody in the tissue at all, because the antibody (ANCA) is acting on neutrophils, not on the GBM. Any RPGN question resolves to this row.
Trap
Nephritic vs nephrotic is a proteinuria threshold *and* a mechanism
  • Nephrotic = podocyte injury, > 3.5 g/24 hr, bland urine. Nephritic = inflammation, sub-nephrotic proteinuria, and red cell casts and dysmorphic RBCs. The two overlap in real patients — MPGN and lupus can present either way — which is exactly why the lecture keeps returning to the biopsy.
Trap
Synpharyngitic vs post-streptococcal — the timing is the discriminator
  • IgA nephropathy gives gross hematuria at the same time as, or within days of, the infection; PSGN manifests 1 to 4 weeks after the child recovers. Add normal complement (IgA) vs low complement (PSGN) and the pair separates cleanly.
Trap
Haemoptysis plus haematuria is not automatically Goodpasture
  • Anti-GBM disease cross-reacts with alveolar basement membrane, so the lungs are affected — but the ANCA vasculitides (Wegener's granulomatosis, microscopic polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss) also produce a pulmonary-renal syndrome. The immunofluorescence pattern is what separates them: linear vs pauci-immune.

2MesangioproliferativeMesangial hypercellularity with expansion of mesangial matrixElevated creatinineNephritic
3Focal nephritisFocal endocapillary ± extracapillary proliferation with focal subendothelial depositsElevated creatinineNephrotic

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 19-year-old develops visible haematuria on the second day of a sore throat. He has had similar episodes before, with microscopic haematuria in between. Protein is 1.1 g/24 hr; C3 and C4 are normal. What will immunofluorescence show?

B. Granular IgA with C3, principally in the mesangium — IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) — the most common type of glomerulonephritis worldwide, with episodes of gross hematuria associated with respiratory, GI or urinary tract viral infections and persistent microscopic hematuria between these episodes, non-nephrotic proteinuria (< 3.5 g/day) and normal C3/C4. IF shows characteristic deposition of IgA (with C3), principally in mesangial regions — granular and patchy, with early complement components usually absent. Note the timing: same-day hematuria, not 1–4 weeks later.

A 7-year-old has cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema and BP 132/88, three weeks after impetigo. C3 is low and anti-DNase B is elevated. What does electron microscopy show, and why is the child already improving?

B. Subepithelial "humps"; the earlier subendothelial deposits are rapidly cleared, which accounts for resolution of hematuria and renal failure — Post-streptococcal GN. Initially: subendothelial immune complex deposits → pathogenesis of nephritic syndrome. Later: subepithelial deposits form → at the time of biopsy. And: subendothelial deposits are rapidly cleared, accounting for the resolution of hematuria and renal failure; the subepithelial deposits are cleared slowly because they are separated from circulating factors. Diagnosis rests on elevated ASO or anti-DNase B with low serum complement.

Which pair of eponymous descriptions both belong to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

B. Lumpy-bumpy; starry sky — PSGN's immunofluorescence shows granular deposits of IgG and C3 in the mesangium and along capillary walls, described as "lumpy-bumpy" and "starry sky". Spike and dome is membranous nephropathy (silver stain, previous lecture); tram track is MPGN; crescents are RPGN; Maltese cross and oval fat bodies are the lipiduria of nephrotic syndrome.

A 21-year-old has nephritic syndrome; biopsy shows a tram-track GBM on silver stain, and immunofluorescence is positive for C3 but negative for IgG, C1q and C4. Serum C3 is low with normal C1 and C4. What antibody explains the findings, and what is the transplant outcome?

B. C3 nephritic factor, which binds and protects the alternative-pathway C3 convertase; recurrence in 90% after transplantation — MPGN type II — dense deposit disease. Circulating autoantibody termed C3 nephritic factor (C3NeF) binds the alternative pathway C3 convertase and protects it from inactivation → persistent C3 activation; C3 synthesis is also decreased by the liver, resulting in hypocomplementemia. The lecture gives decreased serum C3 and normal C1 & C4; decreased Factor B and Properdin, poor prognosis, and high incidence of recurrence following renal transplantation (90% of cases).

Which statement correctly matches an RPGN type to its immunofluorescence?

D. Anti-GBM disease — linear immunofluorescence; ANCA-associated disease — pauci-immune — The lecture's table: Type I (35%) anti-GBM antibody mediated → linear immunofluorescence; Type 2 (40%) immune-complex mediated → granular immunofluorescence; Type 3 (40%) ANCA mediated → no immunofluorescence (pauci-immune). Type I cross-reacts with alveolar basement membrane, therefore the lungs are affected (Goodpasture syndrome); type 3 associations are Wegener's granulomatosis, microscopic polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss syndrome.

Which of these is listed as an association of immune-complex-mediated (type 2) RPGN?

C. Henoch-Schönlein purpura — Type 2 (immune-complex-mediated) RPGN associations are idiopathic, post-infectious glomerulonephritis, IgA glomerulonephritis, Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), and lupus nephritis. Wegener's, microscopic polyangiitis and Churg-Strauss are type 3 (ANCA); Goodpasture is type I (anti-GBM).

What is the composition of the crescent in RPGN?

A. Fibrin and plasma proteins with glomerular parietal cells, monocytes, and macrophages — Crescents contain fibrin and plasma proteins with glomerular parietal cells, monocytes, and macrophages. They arise from proliferation of glomerular epithelial cells, migration of macrophages into the urinary space, and fibrin deposition due to escape of procoagulant factors, and are initially more cellular, later more fibrotic. Option 5 describes the tram track of MPGN.

A woman with SLE has a renal biopsy showing diffuse endocapillary proliferation with diffuse subendothelial and mesangial deposits, and creatinine of 1.9 mg/dL. Which class is this, and what immunofluorescence pattern is expected?

B. Class 4 (the most common); a full house pattern of IgG, IgM, C3, C1q and C4 — Class 4 — diffuse nephritis (most common): diffuse endocapillary ± extracapillary proliferation with diffuse subendothelial and mesangial deposits, elevated creatinine. Immunofluorescence in lupus nephritis is positive for IgG, IgM, C3, C1q, C4 and more → "full house" pattern (everything is positive!). Class 5 is membranous nephritis — thickened GBM with diffuse subepithelial deposits; class 6 is global sclerosis → ESRD.

Which statement about serum complement in glomerular disease is correct as this lecture states it?

B. Normal levels indicate that production of complement components is keeping up with consumption, and do not exclude complement involvement — Serum complement levels can help to distinguish glomerular diseases. Normal levels indicate that production of complement components are keeping up with the consumption of complement factors. Normal levels do not exclude complement involvement in the inflammatory process of glomerular injury. In dense deposit disease it is C3 that falls with normal C1 and C4 — pure alternative pathway; IgA nephropathy has normal C3/C4 despite alternative pathway activation.

Which feature is shared by MPGN type I and type II?

B. Tram-track (double contour) appearance of the capillary wall on silver or PAS stain — In both cases, the basement membrane will appear to be split in light micrographs — "tram track" appearance, and these findings are seen in type 1 and type 2 disease. The splitting is due to extension of processes of mesangial and inflammatory cells into the peripheral capillary loops. IgG subendothelial deposits and classical pathway activation belong to type I; C3NeF to type II.

L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases

PATH · Dr. Ravi Singh · Department of Pathology · source pp. 1482–1520

DiseaseCauseClinical pictureUrine / lab signatureMorphology
Acute tubular injuryIschemic (shock, burns, pancreatitis, GI/septic haemorrhage, vasculitis) or nephrotoxic (myoglobin, haemoglobin, light chains, bile; drugs, contrast, heavy metals, solvents)Most common cause of acute renal failure. Three stages: initiation (~36 h) → maintenance (40–400 mL/day, hyperkalemia) → recovery (up to 3 L/day, hypokalemia, infection risk)Muddy brown granular casts, epithelial cell casts, free epithelial cells; ↑ creatinine and BUN; metabolic acidosisDetachment of tubular cells from basement membrane; casts in DCT and collecting ducts; peritubular capillary congestion
Drug-induced interstitial nephritisHaptens → modified self-antigens → IgE or cell-mediated injury. Sulfonamides (first described), methicillin/ampicillin, rifampin, thiazides, NSAIDs2–40 days after exposure (average 15); fever, eosinophilia, rash; hematuria, mild proteinuria; 50% with rising creatinine/oliguriaEosinophils, sterile pyuria, WBC casts; ↑ eosinophil count; high K⁺, low HCO₃⁻Chronic interstitial infiltrate with prominent eosinophils; biopsy confirms; stop the drug, steroids help
Acute pyelonephritisE. coli > Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter; ascending (most common) or haematogenous; polyomavirus/CMV/adenovirus if immunocompromisedSudden costovertebral angle pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, malaise; dysuria, frequency, urgencyPyuria, bacteriuria; leukocyte (pus) casts — indicate renal involvement; quantitative urine culture establishes the diagnosisGrey-white cortical inflammation and abscesses; neutrophilic exudate in tubules and interstitium. Complications: papillary necrosis, pyonephrosis, perinephric abscess
Chronic pyelonephritisReflux nephropathy (UTI on congenital vesicoureteral/intrarenal reflux) or chronic obstructive pyelonephritis (posterior urethral valves, stones)Polyuria and nocturia, hypertension, mild proteinuria; usually found as gradual renal insufficiency; may develop FSGS → nephrotic syndrome↑ creatinine, urine albuminAsymmetrically contracted, coarsely scarred kidney; polar scarring with calyceal dilatation in reflux, diffuse calyceal dilatation in obstruction; "thyroidization" of tubules
Obstructive uropathy / hydronephrosisIntrinsic or extrinsic lesions at any level, urethra to renal pelvisSudden complete → renal colic. Bilateral partial → inability to concentrate urine, polyuria, nocturia. NephrolithiasisCalcium 70% · struvite 15% · uric acid 5–10% · cystine 1–2%Silent in the pelvis; renal colic — flank pain radiating to groin, haematuria; UTI; hydronephrosisHaematuria (urothelial ulceration)Prevention: 2 L/day fluid, low sodium diet, urinary alkalinisation for uric acid

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Endogenous toxins are the ones examinations hide inside a story
  • Myoglobin — crush injury, rhabdomyolysis, a statin-fibrate interaction from the antihyperlipidemics lecture. Hemoglobin — a transfusion reaction or intravascular haemolysis. Monoclonal light chains — myeloma. Bile/bilirubin — obstructive jaundice. Each is a different chapter's disease that ends in the same tubule.
Bottom Line
Prevention answers follow directly from the stone's chemistry
  • Uric acid stones precipitate at low pH → alkalinise the urine. Calcium stones follow urinary calcium → a low-sodium diet lowers calcium excretion. Struvite stones follow urea-splitting organisms → the infection is the target. Every preventive measure is the mechanism run backwards.
Exam Lock
What makes this lecture different from the last two
  • Glomerular disease announces itself in the glomerular urine — protein and red cell casts. Tubulointerstitial disease announces itself as failure of tubular jobs: concentrating urine (polyuria, nocturia), reabsorbing salt (salt wasting), and excreting acid (metabolic acidosis). Learn the three failures and most of the clinical pictures follow.
Exam Lock
The potassium flips
  • Maintenance → HYPERkalemia (you cannot excrete it). Recovery → HYPOkalemia (you are losing it in a 3 L/day diuresis through tubules that still cannot reabsorb). Same patient, opposite emergency, a week apart — and this is exactly how it is asked.
Exam Lock
Fever + rash + eosinophilia + sterile pyuria ≈ 15 days after a new drug
  • That tetrad is the entire diagnosis, and sterile pyuria is the finding that separates it from pyelonephritis — white cells in the urine with no growth on culture. Treatment is withdrawal of the drug; steroids help recovery.
Exam Lock
Papillary necrosis — the four-cause mnemonic the lecture hands you
  • Diabetes · Sickle cell disease · Chronic obstruction · Analgesic excess. The presentation is fever plus renal colic, because the sloughed papilla behaves like a stone.
Trap
The FSGS link is the crossover question
  • A patient with old renal scarring who later develops nephrotic-range proteinuria has developed FSGS — the hyperfiltration injury mechanism from the nephrotic lecture (reduction in renal mass → compensatory hypertrophy and hyperfiltration → intraglomerular hypertension → segmental sclerosis). Two lectures, one patient.

Pattern tables

ATI — the three clinical stages, and what kills in each

StageTiming / definitionWhat to watch for
InitiationAround 36 hours; dominated by the inciting medical, surgical or obstetric eventSlight decrease in urine output with a rise in BUN and creatinine — due to a transient decrease in blood flow and declining GFR
MaintenanceAcute kidney injury (acute renal failure) — sustained decrease in urine output between 40–400 mL/dayRising serum creatinine and BUN. Watch for electrolyte abnormalities (like hyperkalemia), acidosis, and the signs and symptoms of uremia and fluid overload.
RecoveryWith supportive care, patients usually survive and have a good chance of recovering renal function. Early recovery: steady increase in urine volume up to 3 L/day → diuresis and polyuriaTubules are still damaged, so sodium, potassium and water are lost. Watch for life-threatening HYPOkalemia and a peculiar vulnerability to infections.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 68-year-old is admitted after a ruptured AAA repair complicated by hypotension. On day 2 urine output is 180 mL, creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 3.4 mg/dL, and K⁺ is 6.1 mmol/L. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts. Which stage is this, and what is the immediate danger?

B. Maintenance; hyperkalemia, acidosis, uremia and fluid overload — This is the maintenance stage of acute tubular injury — sustained decrease in urine output between 40–400 mL/day with rising serum creatinine and BUN; watch out for electrolyte abnormalities (like hyperkalemia), acidosis and the signs and symptoms of uremia and fluid overload. Initiation is around 36 hours with only a slight fall in output; recovery brings diuresis up to 3 L/day and the opposite danger, life-threatening hypokalemia. Muddy brown granular casts and epithelial cell casts confirm ATI.

Ten days after starting ampicillin for pneumonia, a 44-year-old has fever, a maculopapular rash, creatinine 2.6 mg/dL and eosinophilia. Urine shows white cells and eosinophils but no growth. Which mechanism underlies this?

B. The drug acts as a hapten, covalently binding a tubular cell component; the modified self-antigen provokes IgE or cell-mediated injury — Drug-induced interstitial nephritis. Drugs function as haptens and covalently bind to some plasma membrane or extracellular component of tubular cells; these modified self-antigens then become immunogenic; the resultant injury is due to IgE or cell-mediated immune reactions directed against the tubular cells or their basement membranes. Onset is 2 to 40 days after drug exposure (average: 15 days) with fever, eosinophilia and rash, and the urine shows eosinophils and sterile pyuria.

Which drug class named in this lecture was the FIRST in which drug-induced interstitial nephritis was identified?

B. Sulfonamides — First identified in patients taking sulfonamides. The lecture's full list is sulfonamides · synthetic penicillins like methicillin and ampicillin · rifampin · diuretics like thiazides · NSAIDs.

A 26-year-old woman has fever 39 °C, right costovertebral angle tenderness, dysuria and frequency. Urine shows pyuria, bacteriuria and casts packed with neutrophils. Which finding proves the kidney — not just the bladder — is involved, and why?

B. Leukocyte (pus) casts, because casts are formed only in tubules — Leukocyte casts — typically rich in neutrophils (pus casts) — indicate renal involvement, because casts are formed only in tubules. Pyuria and bacteriuria occur in lower tract infection too. The diagnosis of infection is established by quantitative urine culture, and E. coli is the commonest organism, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella and Enterobacter.

A diabetic with recurrent pyelonephritis develops fever with renal colic; imaging shows a filling defect and CT shows fragmented necrotic tissue in the papillae. Which four settings does this lecture list for this complication?

B. Diabetes, sickle cell disease, chronic urinary tract obstruction, excessive analgesic intake — Papillary necrosis is seen mainly in diabetics, sickle cell disease, chronic urinary tract obstruction and excessive analgesic intake. It is an ischemic, suppurative necrosis that leads to sloughing of the papillae, which can obstruct the lower urinary tract → presenting acutely with fever and renal colic. The other complications listed are pyonephrosis and perinephric abscess.

Which histological feature is characteristic of chronic pyelonephritis?

C. Dilated tubules containing pink-to-blue glassy casts resembling thyroid follicles — Many of the dilated tubules may contain pink to blue, glassy-appearing casts — it looks like thyroid, hence this change is called "thyroidization". The other microscopic findings are foci of chronic inflammation, tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis, and grossly an asymmetrically contracted kidney with irregular, coarse scars — polar scarring with calyceal dilatation in reflux nephropathy versus diffuse calyceal dilatation in chronic obstruction.

A man with prostatic hyperplasia has bilateral partial obstruction. What is the EARLIEST manifestation, and how long can obstruction persist before damage becomes irreversible?

B. Inability to concentrate urine causing polyuria and nocturia; 2–3 weeks — Bilateral partial obstruction — the earliest manifestation is inability to concentrate urine → polyuria and nocturia. Sudden complete obstruction gives renal colic, and unilateral hydronephrosis may remain silent for long periods because the unaffected kidney can maintain adequate renal function. Renal function is fully recovered if relieved fast; irreversible damage and renal failure occur if obstruction is not relieved by 2–3 weeks.

Urine culture in a patient with recurrent stones grows Proteus. Which stone type is expected, and what is its composition?

B. Struvite (triple) stone; magnesium ammonium phosphate — Triple / struvite stones (15%) — magnesium ammonium phosphate — are formed by urea-splitting bacteria like Proteus. Urease raises urinary pH and supplies ammonium. For comparison: calcium stones (70%) — calcium oxalate and phosphate, with hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria; uric acid stones (5–10%) — with or without hyperuricemia, tendency to excrete urine at low pH; cystine stones (1–2%) — genetic defects in renal reabsorption of amino acids including cystine.

Which preventive measure does this lecture pair with uric acid stones specifically, and why?

B. Alkalinisation of urine, to increase the solubility of uric acid — The lecture's prevention list is increased fluid intake (2 L/day) · low sodium diet → decrease urinary calcium excretion · alkalinisation of urine to increase solubility of uric acid. Uric acid stones form because of a tendency to excrete urine at low pH, so raising the pH dissolves them — the mechanism run backwards.

Which of the following is a NEPHROTOXIC (rather than ischemic) cause of acute tubular injury in this lecture's classification?

D. Myoglobin released after crush injury — Nephrotoxic causes = direct toxic damage to tubular cells. Endogenous toxins like myoglobin, hemoglobin, monoclonal light chains, bile/bilirubin; exogenous toxins like drugs, radiocontrast dyes, heavy metals and organic solvents. The other four options are all ischemic — diffuse involvement of intra-renal vessels (microscopic polyangiitis, microangiopathies) and decreased effective circulating volume (burns, acute pancreatitis, hemorrhagic shock, septic shock).

L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders

Extrarenal: hepatic cysts (most common), berry aneurysms, colonic diverticulae, mitral valve prolapse

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Malignant hypertension is a thrombotic microangiopathy
  • The lecture lists malignant hypertension among the secondary causes of thrombotic microangiopathy two slides later — and the pathogenesis says why: endothelial injury → platelet activation → intravascular thrombosis. So a patient with BP 220/130, schistocytes and a falling platelet count is not two diseases; it is one.
Bottom Line
Two "split basement membrane" appearances, two very different diseases
  • MPGN gives a "tram track" — the GBM is duplicated by interposed mesangial cell processes and the disease is inflammatory. Alport gives a "basket weave" — the lamina densa itself splits and laminates because the type IV collagen network is defective, and the disease is inherited. Deafness and lens problems settle it clinically.
Exam Lock
Hyaline vs hyperplastic — the one-word answer
  • Benign → hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Malignant → hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ("onion-skin") plus fibrinoid necrosis of the afferent arteriole. The mechanistic reason is in the diagrams: benign disease reduces pressure transmission downstream, while malignant hypertension causes breakthrough transmission of high pressure that injures the endothelium directly.
Exam Lock
The two kidneys look different — and that is the diagnosis
  • The stenotic kidney is protected from the systemic pressure and becomes atrophic and ischemic; the contralateral kidney takes the full pressure and develops hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Asymmetric kidneys in a hypertensive patient with a bruit is the classic picture.
Trap
"Bland sediment" is the discriminator, not the creatinine
  • Almost every renal disease raises creatinine. What makes benign nephrosclerosis recognisable is what is absent: no cells, no casts, no crystals, and no microscopic hematuria, with proteinuria under 1 g/day. Compare the cast gallery from the tubular lecture — this is the one entity whose urine is empty.
Trap
Do not let the shared triad hide the discriminator
  • Both produce MAHA + thrombocytopenia + renal impairment + neurological signs + fever. What separates them is the weighting (kidney-dominant = HUS, brain-dominant = TTP) and the mechanism (Shiga toxin after bloody diarrhoea vs ADAMTS13 deficiency).

Pattern tables

HUS vs TTP — the pair that is always tested together

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
Classic settingClassically seen in children one week after an episode of bloody diarrhea caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7).Due to deficiency of ADAMTS13 enzyme.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 62-year-old with 20 years of hypertension has creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, urine protein 0.6 g/day, no haematuria, and a completely bland sediment. Which vascular lesion is expected on biopsy?

B. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis with medial and intimal thickening — Benign nephrosclerosis: patients are asymptomatic with slowly progressive elevation in serum creatinine, mild proteinuria (< 1 g/day), no microscopic hematuria, and a bland urine sediment — no cells, casts or crystals. The vascular lesion is hyaline arteriolosclerosis with medial and intimal thickening, and grossly the cortex has a fine, even granularity resembling grain leather. Options 1 and 3 belong to malignant nephrosclerosis.

A 41-year-old presents with BP 226/134, headache, retinal haemorrhages and papilloedema, and creatinine 3.8 mg/dL. Which mechanism explains the renal lesion?

B. Breakthrough transmission of high pressure injures arteriolar and capillary endothelium, allowing fibrinogen and plasma protein leakage with platelet activation — Malignant nephrosclerosis — ~5% of hypertensives develop rapidly rising blood pressure (200/120 mm Hg and more) with evidence of end-organ damage — renal failure, retinal hemorrhages and exudates, with or without papilledema. The pathogenesis: medial and intimal thickening plus duplication of the basement membrane → luminal narrowing, then severe hypertension results in breakthrough transmission of high pressure → endothelial cell injury → fibrinogen, platelet activation and plasma protein leakage → fibrinoid necrosis and intravascular thrombosis. Option 1 is the benign pathway.

A 34-year-old woman develops severe hypertension over three months with an abdominal bruit. Angiography shows a beaded mid-renal artery. What is the mechanism of her hypertension, and what will the contralateral kidney show?

B. Increased renin production from the ischemic kidney; contralateral hyaline arteriolosclerosis — Renal artery stenosis from fibromuscular dysplasia — > 10% of cases, more common in women, third and fourth decades (atherosclerosis accounts for > 70%). Hypertension secondary to renal artery stenosis is caused by increased production of renin from the ischemic kidney, and hypertension due to renal artery stenosis leads to hyaline arteriolosclerosis in the contralateral kidney. Investigations: elevated plasma or renal vein renin, response to an ACE inhibitor, with arteriography required to localise the lesion.

A 5-year-old is admitted with anuria, platelets 42 ×10⁹/L and schistocytes on the smear, one week after bloody diarrhoea. Which diagnosis and which organ emphasis?

B. HUS; more severe renal failure, less pronounced CNS involvement — Hemolytic uremic syndrome — classically seen in children one week after an episode of bloody diarrhea caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7), with more severe renal failure and less pronounced CNS involvement. TTP is the mirror image: due to deficiency of ADAMTS13, with CNS involvement more pronounced and renal failure less severe, often associated with SLE, HIV and haematological malignancy.

Which of these is listed as a SECONDARY thrombotic microangiopathy?

D. Malignant hypertension — The lecture splits TMA into primary — those with a known etiology: Shiga-toxin-mediated HUS and atypical HUS (complement-mediated TMA), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and secondary — develop in the background of other diseases or conditions without well-defined etiologies, like malignant hypertension and scleroderma-associated TMA. The triad in all of them is microvascular thrombosis, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.

A 38-year-old with bilateral flank masses, hypertension and haematuria has a family history of renal failure in her father and grandmother. Which extrarenal complication most threatens her life, and which gene is most commonly responsible?

B. Berry aneurysm rupture causing stroke; PKD1 — ADPKD. PKD1 on chromosome 16p13 → polycystin 1 (most common); PKD2 (4q21, polycystin 2) gives a milder phenotype with later onset. Extrarenal manifestations: hepatic cysts (most common), cysts in pancreas, spleen and lungs, colonic diverticulae, berry (intracranial) aneurysms — which can rupture and cause stroke — and mitral valve prolapse. Note the inheritance signature in the stem: no skipped generations, equally transmitted by men and women, 50% per child. PKHD1/congenital hepatic fibrosis belongs to ARPKD.

Which cystic disease shows dilated elongated channels arranged at right angles to the cortical surface, completely replacing medulla and cortex?

B. ARPKD — Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease — the kidney is enlarged with a smooth external surface; dilated elongated channels are present at right angles to the cortical surface, completely replacing the medulla and cortex. It is caused by mutation in the PKHD1 gene on chromosome 6p21 coding for fibrocystin protein, manifests in neonates, infants and children, and its common extrarenal manifestation is congenital hepatic fibrosis. Medullary sponge kidney is multiple cystic dilations of the collecting ducts in the medulla, in adults, with normal renal function.

A 14-year-old boy has persistent microscopic haematuria with red cell casts, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and anterior lenticonus. What will electron microscopy show?

C. Splitting and lamination of the lamina densa in a basket-weave pattern — Alport syndrome — an inherited disease of basement membrane collagen type IV, which is crucial for normal function of the lens, cochlea, and glomerulus, caused by mutations in COL4A4 and COL4A5 and most commonly X-linked (males > females). Electron microscopy shows pronounced splitting and lamination of the lamina densa, often producing a distinctive "basket weave" appearance, and immunohistochemistry with antibodies against alpha chains is negative in basement membranes. The other features are nerve deafness, lens dislocation, posterior cataracts and corneal dystrophy.

Which renal manifestation of ADPKD is explained by cysts compressing the renal vasculature?

C. Hypertension — The lecture maps each manifestation to a mechanical consequence: cysts compress renal vasculature → release of renin and aldosterone system → hypertension; rupture into the collecting duct → haematuria; stretch the renal capsule → flank/back pain; distal tubule secretion and absorption defects → nephrolithiasis (uric acid and calcium oxalate stones). Infections are common as infected cysts and acute pyelonephritis caused by gram-negative bacteria.

Which statement about nephrosclerosis pathogenesis is correct as this lecture states it?

B. Hyalinization is caused by extravasation of plasma proteins through injured endothelium and by increased deposition of basement membrane matrix — Hyalinization of arteriolar walls, caused by extravasation of plasma proteins through injured endothelium and by increased deposition of basement membrane matrix. The sequence continues: thickened walls → affected vessels have narrowed lumens → focal parenchymal ischemia → glomerulosclerosis and chronic tubulointerstitial injury, and nephrosclerosis is strongly associated with hypertension.

L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis

MICR · A. Malur PhD · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology · source pp. 1785–1817

AxisWhat to know
DefinitionsAsymptomatic bacteriuria = bacteriuria without symptoms. Lower UTI = bladder/urethra; upper UTI = kidney/ureter. Uncomplicated = healthy, pre-menopausal, non-pregnant woman, no risk factors, no treatment failure; everything else is complicated. Ascending is the most common route.
EpidemiologyMost common bacterial infection in US outpatients; more frequent in women; rises with age; paediatric peak 1–2 years, associated with vesicoureteral reflux; UPEC dominates both uncomplicated and complicated UTI.
DefencesUnidirectional flow · urine pH 4.6–8.0 · immunoglobulin · lactoferrin · Tamm-Horsfall protein (most abundant urinary protein; inhibits calcium crystallization; blocks type 1 fimbriae) · vaginal lactobacilli
PresentationLower: frequency, urgency, dysuria, suprapubic tenderness. Upper: the above + fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting. Children: incontinence, malodorous urine, irritability, poor feeding. Elderly: acute confusion/delirium, urosepsis. Pregnancy: increased risk of pyelonephritis.
DiagnosisDipstick: leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pH, blood. Microscopy: pyuria ≥ 5 WBC/HPF (8–10/mm³), haematuria, leukocyte casts. Culture is the gold standard (95% sens / 85% spec) — not routine in uncomplicated lower UTI; indicated in pregnancy, complicated/healthcare-associated UTI, pyelonephritis/urosepsis, recurrence, resistance concern, age > 65.
ComplicationsGeneral: pyelonephritis, perinephric abscess, urosepsis, emphysematous pyelonephritis. Men: prostatitis, epididymitis, orchitis, urethral stricture. Pregnancy: preterm labour and birth, chorioamnionitis.
PathogensE. coli (#1, lactose fermenter, nitrite +, urease −) · S. saprophyticus (2nd in young women, novobiocin resistant, nitrite −, urease +) · K. pneumoniae (3rd, nosocomial, capsule, mucoid, urease +) · P. mirabilis (CAUTI, swarming, H₂S +, urease +, non-lactose fermenter) · Enterococci · Pseudomonas. Viruses: adenovirus, CMV, BK virus.
VirulenceUPEC: type 1 fimbriae, P fimbriae (pyelonephritis-associated pili), LPS (O antigen, lipid A), K and H antigens, α-hemolysin, siderophore. Klebsiella: capsule (K antigen), LPS, fimbriae type 1 (host cells) and type 3 (medical devices), siderophore, biofilm. Proteus: fimbriae, proteases, hemolysins, LPS, and urease → alkaline urine → struvite and apatite stones → obstruction and crystalline biofilm.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Two defences, two drugs' worth of consequences
  • Tamm-Horsfall protein does two jobs the exam likes: it inhibits calcium crystallization (link to the stone lecture) and it blocks type 1 fimbriae from binding urothelium (link to UPEC virulence). Lactobacilli keep vaginal pH low; menopause and antibiotics remove them, which is one mechanism behind the hormonal risk factor.
Bottom Line
One enzyme ties three lectures together
  • Urease raises urinary pH and supplies ammonium → struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones from the tubular/interstitial lecture → stones cause obstruction and stasis → obstruction and stasis predispose to pyelonephritis from the same lecture. A single Proteus stem can be asked from any of the three angles.
Exam Lock
"Uncomplicated" is a definition, not an impression
  • It means a healthy, pre-menopausal, non-pregnant woman with no risk factors and no treatment failure. Everything else — men, pregnancy, catheters, stones, diabetes, structural abnormality, recurrence — is complicated, and that word changes the diagnostic pathway (urine culture required) and the complication list.
Exam Lock
Why a negative nitrite does not exclude a UTI
  • The nitrite test detects the conversion of nitrates to nitrites by bacterial nitrate reductase — an enzyme E. coli, Klebsiella and Proteus have but S. saprophyticus does not (nitrite test negative). A young sexually active woman with dysuria and a negative nitrite is the classic S. saprophyticus stem.
Exam Lock
P fimbriae are named after the disease they cause
  • Type 1 fimbriae bind the bladder urothelium — and are the target of Tamm-Horsfall protein. P fimbriae — pyelonephritis-associated pili (PAP) are what let UPEC ascend and colonise the kidney. Same organism, different adhesin, different level of the tract.
Trap
The classic symptoms are the ones most likely to be missing
  • In the very young and the very old, UTI does not present with dysuria and frequency. Irritability and poor feeding in an infant, and acute confusion or delirium in an elderly patient, are the presentations this lecture asks you to recognise (MICR.84).

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 22-year-old woman has three days of dysuria, frequency and suprapubic tenderness after becoming sexually active. Dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase but NEGATIVE for nitrites. Which organism is most likely, and which two laboratory features confirm it?

B. Staphylococcus saprophyticus; novobiocin resistant and urease positive — S. saprophyticus is the 2nd leading cause of UTI in young, sexually active women — "honeymoon cystitis", and is a member of the natural flora of the female genital tract and perineum. Its features: Gram-positive cocci, non-motile, facultative anaerobe, catalase positive, coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant, nitrite test negative, urease positive. The negative nitrite in the stem is the discriminator — the nitrite test depends on bacterial nitrate reductase, which E. coli, Klebsiella and Proteus have.

Which urinary protein both inhibits calcium crystallization and prevents type 1 fimbriated E. coli from binding urothelial receptors?

C. Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin) — Tamm-Horsfall protein (THP or uromodulin): the most abundant protein excreted in urine; a constitutive inhibitor of calcium crystallization; and the key urinary anti-adherence factor, serving to prevent type 1 fimbriated E. coli from binding to the urothelial receptors. The other listed defences are unidirectional flow of urine, urine pH 4.6–8.0, immunoglobulin, lactoferrin, and the normal vaginal microbiome (lactobacilli).

A 79-year-old nursing home resident is brought in with acute confusion, tachypnea and hypotension. Which UTI presentation does this represent, and what does this lecture say about the diagnostic approach?

B. Complicated UTI with urosepsis in the elderly; clinical history, urinalysis and urine culture — culture is also indicated over age 65 — Elderly population: acute confusion / delirium; tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension (urosepsis). This is a complicated UTI, for which the approach is clinical history, urinalysis and urine culture. The lecture also lists over 65 years among the specific indications for culture, alongside pregnancy, complicated or healthcare-associated UTI, pyelonephritis or urosepsis, recurrent UTIs, and concern for multi-resistant pathogens.

A man with a chronic indwelling catheter develops recurrent obstruction; urine pH is 8.4 and culture grows a swarming, H₂S-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod. Which enzyme explains the stones, and what is their composition?

B. Urease; magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and calcium phosphate (apatite) — Proteus mirabilis, one of the leading causes of CAUTI. Urease: urine urea → ammonia (rapid hydrolysis) → urine pH ↑ → precipitation of magnesium and calcium ions → magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and calcium phosphate (apatite) calculi / stone formation. And: urinary stones can obstruct urinary flow and cause tissue damage; precipitated minerals can form crystalline biofilms, also blocking urine flow.

Which virulence factor allows uropathogenic E. coli to ascend and colonise the kidney specifically?

B. P fimbriae (pyelonephritis-associated pili) — The lecture names them explicitly: P fimbriae: pyelonephritis-associated pili (PAP). The other UPEC surface factors are type 1 fimbriae (bladder adherence — the target of Tamm-Horsfall protein), LPS (O antigen and lipid A), K antigen and H antigen; the secreted factors are α-hemolysin and siderophore.

A 5-year-old boy after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation develops sudden gross haematuria with irritative voiding symptoms. Which organism does this lecture link to this picture?

C. BK virus — Acute hemorrhagic cystitis presents with lower UTI symptoms with sudden onset of gross hematuria and irritative voiding symptoms, and the lecture's causes are E. coli, adenovirus 11 and 21 (pediatric population), BK virus (hematopoietic stem cell transplant patients), and influenza A virus. The transplant context in the stem points to BK virus; adenovirus 11/21 is the paediatric association without transplantation.

Which biological feature correctly distinguishes Klebsiella pneumoniae from E. coli in this lecture's tables?

B. Klebsiella is non-motile with a large mucoid capsule and is urease positive, whereas E. coli is motile and urease negative — Both are Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, nitrite-positive, H₂S-negative Enterobacteriaceae. The differences the lecture gives are that Klebsiella is non-motile, has a large mucoid capsule forming pink mucoviscous colonies on MacConkey, is urease positive (delayed on urea agar) and is multidrug resistant, while E. coli is motile, urease negative==, and gives a green metallic sheen on EMB agar.

Which statement about urine culture in this lecture is correct?

B. It is the gold standard, with 95% sensitivity and 85% specificity, and is NOT routinely ordered in uncomplicated lower UTIs — Urine culture (gold standard) has 95% sensitivity and 85% specificity. Not routinely ordered in uncomplicated lower UTIs. Its indications are pregnant women, suspicion for complicated or healthcare-associated UTI, pyelonephritis or urosepsis, history of recurrent UTIs, concern for multi-resistant pathogens, or over 65 years. The clinical approach is uncomplicated → history and urinalysis; complicated → history, urinalysis and culture.

Which of the following is a Klebsiella virulence factor whose stated function is attachment to MEDICAL DEVICES rather than host cells?

C. Type 3 fimbriae — The lecture separates them: fimbriae type 1 and type 3 — attachment to host cells; type 1 → host cell, type 3 → medical devices. The capsule (K antigen) is anti-phagocytic, LPS is endotoxin, the siderophore increases iron binding capacity, and biofilm formation gives resistance to host cell and antibiotic killing — the reason Klebsiella is prominent in nosocomial UTI.

Which organism is NOT on the lecture's "PUNCH KiSS" list of urease-positive organisms?

C. Escherichia coli — "PUNCH KiSS": Proteus · Ureaplasma · Nocardia · Cryptococcus · Helicobacter · Klebsiella · S. Saprophyticus · S. Epidermidis. The urea agar results the lecture illustrates make it explicit: Proteus mirabilis is rapidly urease positive, Klebsiella pneumoniae is delayed urease positive, and Escherichia coli is urease negative.

Bottom line

Bottom Line
How to prepare, using the objectives as the checklist
  • The five objectives are themselves a complete study frame. For renal tumors, build one row per tumour with the seven columns the objective names: age · etiology · risk factors · pathogenesis · clinical features · complications (paraneoplastic and metastatic) · genetic basis. For bladder, the objectives ask for exactly three things: the two congenital anomalies (urachus, diverticulum); the two cystitis types (infectious vs interstitial) compared on etiology, pathogenesis, clinical course and morphology; and bladder cancer's risk factors, clinical features, classification, microscopic staging, and the morphological difference between papillary and flat lesions.

CLSK · Nervous System I — History and Cranial Nerves

CLSK · Dr Frik J Kotze · Department of Clinical Skills · source pp. 1818–1861

Bottom line

Bottom Line
"Lick your wounds" is worth the ten seconds
  • LMN → tongue points at the lesion (the weak side cannot push, so the healthy genioglossus wins). UMN → tongue points away. The same logic explains the pronator drift on the next lecture's motor exam: the weak side loses to gravity.

Exam locks

Exam Lock
Localise before you name
  • The lecture's own four-step map puts "where" between the findings and the diagnosis. In neurology the level of the lesion — cortex, brainstem, cord, root, nerve, junction, muscle — is usually a stronger discriminator than the symptom itself, which is why the examination is organised by system rather than by complaint.
Exam Lock
One pupil beats four in an emergency
  • Bilateral pinpoint → opioids or pons. Bilateral dilated + fixed → post-arrest or anticholinergic. Bilateral dilated + reactive → sympathomimetic. Unilateral dilated and fixed → temporal lobe (uncal) herniation — the only one in the table that is a surgical emergency of mass effect, and it links straight to the herniation figure in the pathology lectures.

Source note

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Romberg is a proprioception test, not a cerebellar test
  • The rule of 2 out of 3 explains it: with the eyes closed you remove vision, so a patient who still has proprioception and cerebellar/vestibular function stays upright. A patient who is unsteady only after closing the eyes has lost proprioception — sensory ataxia. A cerebellar patient is unsteady with the eyes open.
Exam Lock
The Babinski sign, and when it is normal
  • Present in babies up to 2 years of age — normal. After that it is a sign of a UMN lesion (corticospinal tract): the lecture lists amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig disease), brain tumor or injury, meningitis, multiple sclerosis, spinal injury / defect / tumor, and stroke.
Exam Lock
Why the numbers matter clinically
  • Brudzinski's and Kernig's signs add no diagnostic value to the diagnosis of meningitis if negative — at 5% sensitivity they miss 19 of 20 cases. They are 100% specific, so a *positive* sign is close to diagnostic. This is the cleanest example in the module of the rule that a specific test rules in (SpPin) and a sensitive test rules out (SnNout).
Trap
Spasticity and rigidity are not synonyms
  • Spasticity is velocity-dependent and belongs to the corticospinal (UMN) lesion; rigidity is "lead-pipe", constant through the range, and belongs to Parkinson's disease. Hypotonia points to the cerebellum. Three tones, three localisations.

Pattern tables

Special test — meningeal signs, with the actual test characteristics

SignTechniqueSensitivitySpecificity
Nuchal rigidityEnsure there is no cervical vertebral injury · flex the head forward until the chin touches the chest. Normal: supple (no resistance). Abnormal: resistance to flexion. Frequently absent in a child under 2 years.30%77%
Brudzinski's signPatient supine, in extension. The examiner gently grasps the patient's head in the occipital region and attempts flexion of the neck. Flexion of the neck causes involuntary flexion of the knee and hip.5%100%
Kernig's signPatient supine. Hip and knee are flexed by the examiner up to 90°. The examiner attempts to passively straighten the leg at the knee. The patient experiences pain along the spinal cord and the pain limits passive extension of the knee.5%100%

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 68-year-old has a left hemispheric stroke. On examination the tongue deviates to the right when protruded, with no wasting or fasciculations. Which lesion is this, and why does the tongue deviate that way?

B. UMN lesion affecting the left hemisphere; the tongue deviates away from the lesion and the affected side is stiff without wasting or fasciculations — UMN lesion — the tongue deviates AWAY from the lesion; the affected side will be stiff with no muscle wasting or fasciculations. In an LMN lesion the tongue deviates TOWARDS the lesion side and that side is wasted with fasciculations — the lecture's mnemonic is "lick your wounds". Absence of wasting and fasciculations is what makes this UMN.

A comatose patient has one dilated, fixed pupil. Which cause does this lecture pair with that finding?

C. Temporal lobe herniation — Unilateral dilated and fixed → temporal lobe herniation. The rest of the lecture's table: bilateral pinpoint → metabolic encephalopathy, pontine hemorrhage, drugs (morphine, heroin); bilateral dilated and fixed → post cardiac arrest, drugs (TCAs, atropine); bilateral dilated but reactive → drugs (cocaine, LSD, amphetamine).

Which pupillary defect accommodates but does not react, and what is the anatomical lesion?

B. Argyll Robertson pupil; bilateral damage to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain — Argyll Robertson pupil ("prostitute pupil"): pupils accommodate but do not react; bilateral damage to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain — neurosyphilis, diabetes mellitus. Marcus Gunn is decreased bilateral pupillary constriction from an afferent defect (CN II damage, retinal detachment); Adie's is a slow, sluggish reaction from postganglionic parasympathetic denervation; Horner is miosis, ptosis and anhidrosis from loss of sympathetic fibres (brainstem CVA, Pancoast tumor, syringomyelia).

On examining tone, the resistance you feel increases the faster you move the limb. Which lesion does this lecture attribute that to?

B. Corticospinal lesion — velocity-dependent spasticity — Assessing spasticity, e.g. velocity-dependent resistance — corticospinal lesion. The lecture separates this from identifying rigidity, e.g. "lead-pipe" resistance — Parkinson's disease and detecting hypotonia — cerebellar dysfunction. Tone is graded with the Modified Ashworth Scale (0 to 4).

A trauma patient has acute flaccid paralysis below T6. The bulbocavernosus reflex is ABSENT. What does this indicate?

B. Spinal shock — Bulbocavernosus reflex (S2–4): in a patient with acute paralysis from trauma — absent → spinal shock; present → spinal cord severance. The technique is to squeeze the glans penis or clitoris, or tug on an indwelling Foley catheter, with a normal response of contraction of the anal sphincter.

Which statement about Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs is correct according to the evidence cited in this lecture?

B. Both have 5% sensitivity and 100% specificity, so a negative sign adds no diagnostic value — Brudzinski's sign — sensitivity 5%, specificity 100%. Kernig's sign — sensitivity 5%, specificity 100%. The latter 2 add no diagnostic value to the diagnosis of meningitis if negative. Nuchal rigidity is sensitivity 30%, specificity 77%, and is frequently absent in a child under 2 years.

A patient stands steadily with eyes open but sways and nearly falls when the eyes close. Which system has failed, and which condition fits?

C. Proprioception; vitamin B12 deficiency or tabes dorsalis — Romberg's test requires 2 out of 3: proprioception, vision, and normal cerebellar and vestibular function. Closing the eyes removes vision; a fall then means proprioception has failed. Positive Romberg's test in conditions causing sensory ataxia, e.g. B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis), sensory peripheral neuropathies (DM), Ménière's disease. A cerebellar patient is unsteady with the eyes open.

Which reflex is the only one in which the examiner's own thumb is struck, and what is its root level?

B. Biceps, C5–6 — Biceps C5,6: provide support for the patient's forearm, place your thumb on the biceps tendon, and strike your thumb with the reflex hammer — the only reflex where the examiner's thumb is struck. Normal response is flexion of the elbow and contraction of biceps.

Which modality pair is carried by the dorsal columns as this lecture assigns them?

B. Vibration and proprioception — The lecture labels light touch (crude and fine), vibration and proprioception as dorsal column, and pin prick (pain) as spinothalamic tract. It also separates the testing strategy: pain, temperature and light touch: assess dermatomes; vibration and proprioception: assess fingers and toes, starting distal and moving proximally.

A child of 18 months has an extensor plantar response with fanning of the toes. How should this be interpreted?

B. Normal — present in babies up to 2 years of age — Present in babies up to 2 years of age — normal. Beyond that it is a sign of a UMN lesion (corticospinal tract), and the lecture lists amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig disease), brain tumor or injury, meningitis, multiple sclerosis, spinal injury/defect/tumor, and stroke.

Bottom Line
The lecture's own mnemonic
  • TCAs → Tachycardia · Cardiotoxicity · Anticholinergic effects · sexual dysfunction. The cardiotoxicity is the one that kills: fast sodium channel blockade → conduction block and arrhythmia → sodium bicarbonate, exactly as in the antiarrhythmic lectures' class I toxicity.
Bottom Line
The lecture's two mnemonics for this class
  • SSRIs — the 4 S's: Stomach upset · Sexual dysfunction · Serotonin syndrome · Size increase (weight gain). And for indications: SSRIs are Effective For Sadness, Panic, Compulsions — Escitalopram, Fluoxetine, Fluvoxamine, Sertraline, Paroxetine, Citalopram.
Bottom Line
This table makes the whole class predictable
  • Once you know a drug's receptor profile you can generate its side effects without memorising them separately: mirtazapine is a heavy H1 antagonist → sedation and weight gain; amitriptyline blocks α1, muscarinic and H1 → the full TCA burden; SSRIs touch none of them → only the serotonergic effects remain.
Exam Lock
The strength and the weakness are the same experiment
  • Reserpine depletes monoamines and causes depression; MAOIs preserve them and relieve it. That is the case for the hypothesis. But the transporter block happens in hours while the mood change takes weeks — so monoamine levels cannot be the whole story, which is why the lecture moves to downstream signal transduction. Expect to be asked for this discrepancy by name.
Exam Lock
Two syndromes, two antidotes
  • Serotonin syndrome → cyproheptadine (a serotonin antagonist) plus benzodiazepines. Cheese reaction → phentolamine or prazosin (α-blockade). Both start with stopping the offending agent, and the distinguishing features are hyperthermia + myoclonus + rigidity (serotonin) versus occipital headache + stiff neck after a meal (tyramine).
Exam Lock
Half-life explains both the discontinuation syndrome and the washout period (PHAR.00012)
  • The same property runs in both directions. A short half-life (paroxetine, venlafaxine) means abrupt withdrawal produces symptoms. A long half-life (fluoxetine) protects against withdrawal but demands a long washout before starting a MAOI — otherwise the two overlap and you get serotonin syndrome, the reason the washout exists at all.
Trap
Screen for bipolar disorder before you prescribe (PHAR.00016)
  • A major depressive episode may be the initial presentation of bipolar disorder, and treating such an episode with an antidepressant alone may precipitate mania. Before starting an antidepressant, patients with depressive symptoms should be screened for evidence of bipolar disorder.
Trap
The management of lithium-induced DI is deliberately counter-intuitive
  • Amiloride — a potassium-sparing diuretic from the diuretics lecture — is used because it blocks ENaC, the very channel through which lithium enters the principal cell. And thiazides, which normally *raise* lithium levels by reducing its clearance, are a second-line treatment for the polyuria. Both facts are examinable precisely because they look wrong.

Major depression = only depression. Bipolar depression = depression + mania.

The two MAOI emergencies — serotonin syndrome and the cheese reaction

Serotonin syndromeCheese reaction (tyramine-induced hypertension)
TriggerCombination of a MAOI with a serotonergic agent. An irreversible MAOI with a serotonergic agent is the most toxic combination. Any drug or combination that increases serotonin can cause it.Tyramine is contained in certain foods — aged cheeses and meats, chicken liver, soy products, pickled or smoked fish such as anchovies or herring, and red wines — and is normally inactivated by MAO in the gut. Patients on a MAOI cannot degrade dietary tyramine.
MechanismOverstimulation of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2 receptors.Tyramine causes the release of large amounts of stored catecholamines from nerve terminals.
PresentationHyperthermia, hypertension, muscle rigidity and myoclonus — "Hot (hyperthermia), Hyper(tension), and Hyperactive (myoclonus, hyperreflexia)". Life-threatening.Occipital headache, stiff neck, tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmias, seizures, and possibly stroke.
ManagementDiscontinuation of all serotonergic agents · supportive care · sedation with benzodiazepines · administration of the serotonin antagonist cyproheptadine.Phentolamine or prazosin are helpful in the management of tyramine-induced hypertension. The lecture's mnemonic: STOP (MAOI), DROP (BP), BLOCK (NE effects). Sympathomimetic drugs may also cause significant hypertension, so OTC cold preparations containing pseudoephedrine and phenylpropanolamine are contraindicated. The selegiline transdermal patch is better tolerated and safer — unlikely to cause tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis.

Choosing an antidepressant, and the clinical indications

StepChoice
1st lineSSRI or SNRI. Fluoxetine would be a reasonable first choice for adults or children not taking other drugs that may interact with it; citalopram or sertraline for adults taking other drugs that could interact with fluoxetine.
2nd lineIf no response after 4–8 weeks of an SSRI → switch to another SSRI or an SNRI, or add a drug from a different class (e.g. SSRI + bupropion).
AdjunctiveIf monotherapy is inadequate, add a second-generation antipsychotic: quetiapine, aripiprazole, olanzapine — the three approved for adjunctive treatment of major depressive disorder.
Other classesSARI (trazodone) — alternative if anxiety is not prominent; TCAs and MAOIs for moderate to severe disease.
