Rapid recall — stems and answers

Two days after a patient on phenelzine is started on sertraline for inadequate response, she develops fever 40 °C, hypertension, muscle rigidity and myoclonus. Which receptors are overstimulated, and what specific antidote does this lecture name?

B. 5-HT1A and 5-HT2 receptors; cyproheptadine — Serotonin syndrome — the combination of a MAOI with a serotonergic agent; an irreversible MAOI with a serotonergic agent is the most toxic combination. It is the result of overstimulation of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2 receptors, presenting with hyperthermia, hypertension, muscle rigidity and myoclonus — "Hot, Hyper(tensive) and Hyperactive". Management: discontinuation of all serotonergic agents, supportive care, sedation with benzodiazepines, and administration of the serotonin antagonist cyproheptadine.

A patient on tranylcypromine eats aged cheese and develops severe occipital headache, stiff neck and BP 220/130. What is the mechanism, and which agents manage it?

B. Tyramine cannot be degraded, releasing large amounts of stored catecholamines; phentolamine or prazosin — The cheese reaction. Tyramine is normally inactivated by MAO in the gut; patients on a MAO inhibitor are unable to degrade dietary tyramine, and tyramine causes the release of large amounts of stored catecholamines from nerve terminals, resulting in occipital headache, stiff neck, tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmias, seizures and possibly stroke. Phentolamine or prazosin are helpful in the management of tyramine-induced hypertension — STOP, DROP, BLOCK. The selegiline transdermal patch is unlikely to cause a tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis.

A 24-year-old takes a large amount of amitriptyline. ECG shows a widened QRS and ventricular arrhythmia. Which receptor/channel action explains this, and what is the treatment?

C. Cardiac fast sodium channel blockade; sodium bicarbonate — TCAs block α-adrenergic, muscarinic, histamine receptors and cardiac fast sodium channels; blockade of cardiac fast sodium channels → arrhythmias. TCAs have a narrow therapeutic index — five- to six-fold the maximal daily dose of imipramine can be lethal — and overdose can induce lethal arrhythmias. Sodium bicarbonate is useful in reversing conduction block.

A patient stable on nortriptyline is started on an SSRI and develops severe anticholinergic toxicity. Which SSRIs are most likely responsible, and by which enzyme?

B. Fluoxetine or paroxetine; CYP2D6 — Fluoxetine and paroxetine are potent inhibitors of CYP2D6 and therefore have a high potential for drug interactions. CYP2D6 is responsible for the elimination of TCAs, neuroleptic drugs, and some antiarrhythmic and β-blockers. Fluvoxamine inhibits CYP1A2, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4. Citalopram, escitalopram and sertraline are low interaction risk. Note also that 7% of the Caucasian population has a CYP2D6 polymorphism associated with slow TCA metabolism.

Which antidepressant is preferred for a depressed smoker who is distressed by sexual dysfunction on his current drug — and what is its principal overdose risk?

B. Bupropion; seizures — Bupropion inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine uptake and increases their release, assists in decreasing craving and attenuating withdrawal symptoms for nicotine (as effective as nicotine patches), and is not associated with sexual dysfunction because it is not serotonergic. Its overdose is associated with seizures. It is used for depression if anxiety is not prominent and is less effective than other antidepressants for anxiety.

Which antidepressant is described as extremely sedating, is most commonly used as an unlabelled hypnotic, and can cause priapism?

B. Trazodone — Trazodone — a SARI: a weak but selective inhibitor of SERT whose primary metabolite is a potent 5-HT2 antagonist; it also blocks α1 and H1 receptors, is extremely sedating, and is an excellent hypnotic — its most common use in current practice is as an unlabeled hypnotic, with the rare but troublesome adverse effect of priapism. Nefazodone is the SARI associated with hepatotoxicity and CYP3A4 inhibition.

Why do the immediate pharmacological actions of TCAs and MAOIs count as a WEAKNESS of the monoamine hypothesis?

B. Because the biochemical effect is immediate while the clinical effect takes weeks — Weaknesses of the monoamine hypothesis: the pharmacological actions of both tricyclic and MAO inhibitor classes of antidepressants are immediate; the clinical effects take weeks; discrepancy. This is why the lecture proposes that depression may be linked to a deficiency in signal transduction. The supporting evidence remains reserpine precipitating depression while depleting dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine, and iproniazid/isoniazid lifting depression while inhibiting MAO.

A patient on long-term lithium develops polyuria and polydipsia. Water deprivation fails to raise urine osmolality, and desmopressin does not help. Which drug does this lecture recommend, and why?

B. Amiloride; it blocks ENaC in the collecting duct, preventing lithium from entering principal cells and helping restore aquaporin-2 expression — Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Lithium enters kidneys via Na/Li channels → increased sodium excretion, decreased kidney response to ADH/aldosterone; lithium blocks aquaporin function → polyuria and dehydration. Management: adjust lithium therapy or discontinue if possible; amiloride blocks ENaCs in the collecting duct → prevents lithium from entering principal cells, reducing further damage and helping restore aquaporin-2 expression; if amiloride is insufficient, thiazides or NSAIDs.

A patient stable on lithium is started on a new drug and becomes toxic. Which of these reduces lithium's renal clearance according to this lecture?

C. Thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors or ARBs — Renal clearance of lithium is reduced by thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors and ARBs — these cause retention of lithium and need dose adjustments. Lithium's window is narrow (effective at 0.5–1 mM, toxic above 1.5 mM), and serum lithium concentrations, thyroid function and renal function must be regularly monitored. Acute intoxication gives vomiting, profuse diarrhea and coarse tremor.

A 29-year-old presents with a first major depressive episode. Why does this lecture insist on screening before prescribing an SSRI?

B. A major depressive episode may be the initial presentation of bipolar disorder, and an antidepressant alone may precipitate mania — A major depressive episode may be the initial presentation of bipolar disorder. Treating such an episode with an antidepressant alone may precipitate mania in patients with bipolar disorder. Before starting an antidepressant, patients with depressive symptoms should be screened for evidence of bipolar disorder. For bipolar depression the approved combination is olanzapine with fluoxetine.

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Succinylcholine is normally short-acting *because* it is destroyed in the plasma
  • The drug is not inactivated at the synapse at all — succinylcholine is not metabolized effectively at the synapse, therefore the membrane remains depolarized and unresponsive to additional impulses, and a flaccid paralysis results. Its brevity depends entirely on plasma BChE, so a BChE defect converts a 5–10 minute drug into hours of paralysis.
Bottom Line
Warfarin is the lecture's example of "multiple genes: pharmacokinetics + pharmacodynamics"
  • CYP2C9 changes how much drug is there (kinetics); VKORC1 changes how much the target responds (dynamics). The same drug is the worked example for both halves of PHAR.0316 — which is why it earns the only FDA label change quoted in the DLA.
Exam Lock
The three-way split is the exam's organising principle
  • Every example in this DLA is filed under one of the three. NAT2, BChE, CYP2D6, CYP2C19 and TPMT are pharmacokinetic. VKORC1 is pharmacodynamic. Warfarin is both. G6PD and RYR1 are idiosyncratic — and the lecture notes that idiosyncratic drug reactions are not caused by differences in either drug metabolism or drug targets; they seem to result from interactions between the drug and a unique aspect of the physiology of the individual patient.
Exam Lock
Prodrug or active drug decides which way the phenotype hurts
  • Active drug inactivated by CYP2D6 (metoprolol): poor metabolizer → toxicity. Prodrug activated by CYP2D6 (codeine, tramadol, tamoxifen): poor metabolizer → no effect; ultrarapid metabolizer → overdose. One enzyme, opposite errors, decided entirely by which side of the arrow the active molecule sits on.
Trap
Malignant hyperthermia's inheritance is the opposite of most of this DLA
  • NAT2 slow acetylation and BChE deficiency are autosomal RECESSIVE. Malignant hyperthermia is autosomal DOMINANT, incidence 1:12,000 — so a single affected parent, or a family history of an anaesthetic death, is enough to change your anaesthetic plan.

Pattern tables

N-acetyltransferase 2 and butyrylcholinesterase

N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2)Butyrylcholinesterase (BChE)
EnzymeA genetically polymorphic phase II enzyme that catalyzes acetylation.Plasma pseudocholinesterase — hydrolyses succinylcholine.
GeneticsSlow acetylators are homozygous for an autosomal recessive allele with lower activity levels. The rate of isoniazid acetylation is inherited (bimodal distribution).Defects in the BCHE gene; transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. Because of the rarity of these variants, testing is not a routine clinical procedure.
ConsequenceSlow acetylators are prone to toxicity of drugs that are inactivated by acetylation.Decreased rate of metabolism of succinylcholine → prolonged paralysis. Normally the onset of blockade is within 1 minute and the duration only 5–10 minutes because of rapid hydrolysis by BChE.
ExamplesIsoniazid → neuropathy, hepatotoxicity and systemic lupus erythematosus. Hydralazine and procainamide → systemic lupus erythematosus. Sulfonamides → hypersensitivity reactions, hemolytic anemia and systemic lupus erythematosus.Succinylcholine, mivacurium.
Management / testDose adjustment and awareness of the drug-induced lupus risk.Treated with continued mechanical ventilation until muscle function returns to normal. Dibucaine number — the percent of pseudocholinesterase activity inhibited by dibucaine: wild-type homozygotes ≥ 75; heterozygotes 40–70; atypical homozygotes ≤ 20

CYP2D6 — four metabolizer phenotypes and their opposite consequences

PhenotypeGenotypeConsequence
Poor metabolizersHomozygous for recessive alleles coding for enzymes with low activityAdverse drug effect with standard doses of agents that are INACTIVATED by CYP2D6 — e.g. metoprolol. Codeine is relatively ineffective, because it requires metabolism by CYP2D6 to form the more potent opioid morphine.
Extensive metabolizersHeterozygous or homozygous for the "wild type" alleleNormal response.
Ultrarapid metabolizersMultiple copies of the CYP2D6 gene — some have up to 13 copies.May require very high doses of drugs metabolized by CYP2D6, but can OVERDOSE with codeine — suffering respiratory depression or even respiratory arrest in response to standard doses.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 27-year-old is given codeine after surgery and reports no analgesia whatsoever. Which phenotype explains this, and what would the same phenotype do to metoprolol?

B. Poor CYP2D6 metabolizer; codeine cannot be converted to morphine, while metoprolol would accumulate and cause an adverse effect — Codeine is relatively ineffective in poor metabolizers because it requires metabolism by CYP2D6 to form the more potent opioid morphine. And poor metabolizers for CYP2D6 can potentially experience an adverse drug effect when treated with standard doses of agents such as metoprolol that are inactivated by CYP2D6. The mirror-image danger is the ultrarapid metabolizer, who can overdose with codeine, suffering respiratory depression or even respiratory arrest in response to standard doses.

After a brief procedure, a patient remains paralysed for two hours following succinylcholine. What is the mechanism, what is the treatment, and what test identifies it?

B. Butyrylcholinesterase deficiency; continued mechanical ventilation until muscle function returns; the dibucaine number — Patients with genetic variations in butyrylcholinesterase have a decreased rate of metabolism of succinylcholine, resulting in prolonged paralysis, treated with continued mechanical ventilation until muscle function returns to normal. The dibucaine number is the percent of pseudocholinesterase activity inhibited by dibucaine: wild-type homozygotes ≥ 75; heterozygotes 40–70; atypical homozygotes ≤ 20. Defects in the BCHE gene are transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait.

A patient started on azathioprine develops profound pancytopenia. Which enzyme is deficient, how common is the homozygous state, and what dose adjustment does the lecture give?

B. TPMT; approximately 1 in 300; about one-tenth of the standard dose — TPMT catalyzes the S-methylation of the anticancer thiopurines 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine; methylation inactivates them. Thiopurines have a narrow therapeutic window and some patients suffer life-threatening myelosuppression. Approximately 1/300 individuals are homozygous for a polymorphism that leads to low TPMT activity; homozygotes are at increased risk for myelosuppression at standard doses and have to be treated with approximately 1/10 of the standard dose.

A patient of West African descent is given primaquine and develops acute haemolysis with Heinz bodies on the film. Which step in the mechanism is impaired first?

B. Formation of NADPH, which is essential for maintaining the reduced glutathione pool — Diminished G6PD activity impairs the ability of the cell to form NADPH that is essential for the maintenance of the reduced glutathione pool → decreased detoxification of free radicals and peroxides → oxidation of sulfhydryl groups in proteins including haemoglobin → denatured proteins forming insoluble masses (Heinz bodies) → rigid, nondeformable cells removed by splenic and hepatic macrophages. The trigger drugs are sulfonamides, antimalarials (e.g. primaquine and chloroquine), and chloramphenicol, and the A− allele is present in 10–20% of Africans, thought to provide protection against malaria.

Which combination correctly matches the two genes that alter warfarin response to their type of variation?

B. CYP2C9 pharmacokinetic (metabolism of the more potent S-isomer); VKORC1 pharmacodynamic (the drug target) — Warfarin is a racemic mixture; S-warfarin is 3–5 times more potent than R-warfarin, and metabolism of the S isomer is mainly via CYP2C9 — a pharmacokinetic variation — while VKORC1 polymorphisms affect warfarin dose requirement, which may vary two-fold — a pharmacodynamic variation in the target. The FDA revised the warfarin label on August 16, 2007 to state that lower initial doses should be considered for patients with genetic variations in CYP2C9 and VKORC1.

Which statement about malignant hyperthermia matches this DLA?

B. Autosomal dominant, incidence about 1:12,000, triggered by volatile inhalation anaesthetics and succinylcholine, most reliably diagnosed by the in vitro caffeine-halothane contracture test — A potentially fatal genetic disorder of skeletal muscle triggered in susceptible individuals by volatile inhalation anesthetics (e.g. halothane) and depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxants such as succinylcholine. Transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait with a reported incidence of about 1:12,000; one of the main causes of death due to anesthesia. The syndrome is tachycardia and hypertension, severe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, hyperkalemia, and acidosis, caused by a defect in RYR1, and the most reliable test is the in vitro caffeine-halothane muscle contracture test.

A patient on hydralazine and procainamide develops a positive ANA with arthralgias and a malar rash. Which polymorphism increases this risk?

B. Slow acetylation via NAT2 — Slow acetylators are homozygous for an autosomal recessive allele of N-acetyltransferase 2 with lower activity levels, and are prone to toxicity of drugs that are inactivated by acetylation. The lecture's examples: isoniazid may cause neuropathy, hepatotoxicity and systemic lupus erythematosus; hydralazine and procainamide may cause systemic lupus erythematosus; sulfonamides may cause hypersensitivity reactions, hemolytic anemia and systemic lupus erythematosus.

DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss

DLA · Department of Clinical Skills · source pp. 2016–2027

Bottom line

Bottom Line
The over-the-counter sleeping aid is the point of the case
  • Every dementia history in this DLA ends with a medication review, and the list is specific: narcotics, benzodiazepines, tranquilizers, and anticholinergic medications such as antihistamines. A patient with cognitive decline on nightly diphenhydramine has a potentially reversible contributor sitting in the bathroom cabinet.

Exam locks

Exam Lock
"Acute on chronic" is the phrase the case turns on
  • A worsening over days to weeks on a baseline of gradual decline over months to years is highly suggestive of delirium in the setting of decreased cognitive reserve from dementia. That is not one diagnosis but two, and both need naming — the acute precipitant *and* the underlying substrate.

Memory loss — the major causes

TypeDefinition (verbatim)
MCIDepending on the definition used, between 5% and 16% per year will progress to dementia.
Alzheimer's diseaseDementia has an insidious onset and progresses steadily in the absence of focal neurologic signs or other identifiable causes. Autopsy reveals characteristic cortical degeneration with amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.
Vascular dementiaDementia is temporally related to a stroke or due to chronic cerebral ischemia. Classically, dementia progresses in a stepwise manner, but it may be steadily progressive. It may be difficult to distinguish from Alzheimer's disease. In the early stages, subcortical signs (e.g. depression, subtle gait disturbances) and language difficulties often outweigh memory impairment, in contrast to early Alzheimer's disease, in which memory loss typically predominates.
Mixed dementiaThe coexistence of Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

An 82-year-old with a two-year history of gradual forgetfulness becomes acutely confused over four days after several falls, with new headaches and urinary incontinence and no fever. What is the leading diagnosis, and what is the term for this pattern?

B. Subdural hematoma from trauma; "acute on chronic" — Most probable diagnosis: subdural hematoma from trauma. The history of trauma in an elderly patient leading to confusion over days to weeks suggests a subdural hematoma... The "acute on chronic" nature of a worsening over days to weeks on a baseline of a gradual decline over months to years is highly suggestive of delirium in the setting of a decreased cognitive reserve from dementia. There is no history of fever, so meningitis is less likely; seizures cause fluctuating symptoms and are of more rapid onset.

A patient becomes confused over a period of seconds. Which three diagnoses does the time-course table put at the top?

B. Seizure, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage — The lecture's table: sudden (over seconds) → seizure, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage; over minutes to hours → drug-induced, hypoxia, hypoglycemia; over hours to days → infection, renal failure, hepatic failure; gradual progression over months → dementia. The three factors that drive the whole approach are temporal course, presence of focal neurologic symptoms, and age of the patient.

Which feature best distinguishes early vascular dementia from early Alzheimer's disease in this DLA?

B. In early vascular dementia, subcortical signs such as depression and subtle gait disturbances and language difficulties often outweigh memory impairment, whereas memory loss predominates in early Alzheimer's disease — Vascular dementia is temporally related to a stroke or due to chronic cerebral ischemia; classically it progresses in a stepwise manner, but it may be steadily progressive. It may be difficult to distinguish from Alzheimer's disease. In the early stages, subcortical signs (e.g. depression, subtle gait disturbances) and language difficulties often outweigh memory impairment, in contrast to early Alzheimer's disease, in which memory loss typically predominates. Mixed dementia is the coexistence of both.

A patient has parkinsonian stiffness and shuffling gait that began three years ago, with memory problems starting this year. Which diagnosis does the DLA's question point to?

C. Parkinson's disease with dementia — The framing question is "Which came first, memory problems or stiffness and a shuffling gait?" — if memory problems came first, think about Lewy body dementia or vascular dementia; if memory problems began more than a year after parkinsonian symptoms, consider Parkinson's disease with dementia. Here the motor features preceded the cognitive ones by years.

Which screening statement matches this DLA?

B. In the absence of a memory complaint, screen approximately every 3 years from age 75 to 81 and then every other year; the MMSE is the most widely used instrument but does not cover executive function and is insensitive to very early impairment — In the absence of a complaint of memory loss, it is reasonable to screen patients for cognitive impairment approximately every 3 years from age 75 to 81, and then every other year thereafter. The most widely used screening instrument is the Folstein Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). However, the MMSE does not cover executive function (reasoning, judgment, organization, and planning) and is insensitive to very early impairment. Note the trap in option 4: well-preserved social skills may conceal deficits, which is a reason to screen, not to skip it.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
The single line that separates cerebellar from sensory ataxia
  • Eyes open makes no difference in cerebellar ataxia; eyes open rescues sensory ataxia. That is the whole of Romberg, and it is why the workbook holds the eyes closed for a full 30–60 seconds rather than a moment.
Trap
The 512 Hz fork is not the 128 Hz fork
  • Weber and Rinne use a 512 Hz fork (hearing); vibration sense in the sensory exam uses a 128 Hz fork (dorsal columns). Two forks, two purposes, and the frequencies are examinable.

Bottom line

Bottom Line
Where the answers live in this deck
  • Everything in Case 1 is in PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation: the ternary-complex figure (UFH vs LMWH), the monitoring table (aPTT vs PT/INR vs nothing), the HIT type II cycle with its management line, the DTI table (argatroban, bivalirudin, monitored by aPTT), and the management of DVT and PE table with its ≥ 5 days and INR therapeutic on 2 consecutive days bridging rule. Warfarin dose variability is in the Pharmacogenetics DLA — CYP2C9 and VKORC1.
Bottom Line
Where the answers live
  • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis and its protein C/S mechanism, plus the treatment (stop warfarin, vitamin K if needed, give UFH or LMWH), are on the warfarin adverse-effects slide of the coagulation lecture. The thrombolysis question is answered by the indications table: alteplase is indicated for acute massive pulmonary embolism, not for routine VTE. The PE presentation itself — pleuritic chest pain, tachypnoea, loud P2, hypoxia with hypocapnia — is in the CLSK dyspnoea material.
Bottom Line
Where the answers live
  • Case 3 → the coagulation lecture's Appendix 1: management of myocardial infarction (aspirin, oxygen, nitroglycerin, morphine; PCI with aspirin + ADP blocker ± GP IIb/IIIa and UFH or bivalirudin; fibrinolytics only for STEMI) and Appendix 2 for secondary prevention, plus L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease and Antianginal Drugs. Case 4 → the antianginal and antihypertensive lectures: the reason β-blockers alone are avoided in cocaine chest pain is unopposed α-mediated vasoconstriction, and labetalol has combined α and β blockade. Case 5 → Antiarrhythmic Drugs I & II for rate control (β-blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs, digoxin) and chemical cardioversion, and the coagulation lecture for anticoagulation in non-valvular AF.

PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs

PHAR · Dr Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology · source pp. 2057–2122

QuestionAnswer
What causes positive symptoms?Overactivity of the mesolimbic pathway — and D2 blockade there is the therapeutic action
What causes negative and cognitive symptoms?Hypoactivity of the mesocortical pathway — D2 blockade there may worsen them, which is why atypicals are more effective for negative symptoms
Where do EPRs come from?D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway → relative cholinergic excess → treat with antimuscarinics
Where does galactorrhoea come from?D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway → hyperprolactinaemia
Which agents give the most EPR?High-potency classicals: haloperidol and fluphenazine (++++). Least: clozapine and quetiapine (0/+)
Which give the most sedation and hypotension?Low-potency classicals (chlorpromazine, thioridazine) and clozapine — H1 and α1 blockade
The four EPRs and their treatmentsParkinsonism → benztropine / trihexyphenidyl / diphenhydramine / amantadine (never levodopa) · dystonia → the same anticholinergics · akathisia → clonazepam or propranolol · tardive dyskinesia → stop the drug, stop anticholinergics, tetrabenazine or valbenazine (VMAT inhibitors), benzodiazepine, clozapine
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeRigidity, tremor, hyperthermia, altered mental status, autonomic instability, ↑ WBC and CK, myoglobinaemia → dantrolene or bromocriptine
Drug-specific toxicitiesClozapine → agranulocytosis 1–2% (mandatory counts) and seizures · chlorpromazine → seizures and corneal/lens deposits · thioridazine → QT prolongation with a black box and retinal deposits
Metabolic burdenClozapine and olanzapine highest (+++ weight, glucose, lipids); aripiprazole lowest; all atypicals carry a hyperglycaemia/diabetes warning
Class black boxElderly patients with dementia-related psychosis have an increased risk of death
ChoiceAtypicals preferred; aripiprazole most prescribed in the US; clozapine reserved for refractory disease; long-acting IM formulations last 2–4 weeks for non-adherence
PregnancyCategory C; only clozapine is category B

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
The antiemetic exception is a two-drug list
  • Nearly every neuroleptic is an antiemetic through D2 blockade at the chemoreceptor trigger zone — but aripiprazole (a partial agonist, so it does not fully block) and thioridazine are the exceptions. Prochlorperazine and droperidol are the agents actually used for nausea and vomiting.
Bottom Line
Three hyperthermic emergencies, three antidotes — keep them apart
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (D2 blockade): rigidity, hyperthermia, ↑ CK → dantrolene or bromocriptine. Serotonin syndrome (from the antidepressant lecture): hyperthermia with myoclonus and hyperreflexia → cyproheptadine. Malignant hyperthermia (from the pharmacogenetics DLA, RYR1): triggered by volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine → dantrolene. Only dantrolene appears twice.
Exam Lock
Clozapine is the drug of last resort and of two exceptions
  • It is reserved for refractory patients because of agranulocytosis in 1–2% with mandatory blood counts, and it carries the highest metabolic burden and one of the two highest seizure risks. Yet it is also the agent recommended for patients with tardive dyskinesia who require antipsychotics and the only category B drug in pregnancy. Learn it as the exception, not the rule.
Trap
Anticholinergics treat three of the four — and worsen the fourth
  • Parkinsonism and dystonia respond to benztropine, trihexyphenidyl or diphenhydramine. Akathisia takes clonazepam or propranolol. But in tardive dyskinesia you must eliminate all drugs with central anticholinergic action — the opposite instruction. And levodopa is never used for drug-induced parkinsonism, because you would be feeding the psychosis.
Trap
The black box that applies to the whole class
  • Antipsychotics carry a Black Box Warning indicating that elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death. That is separate from thioridazine's own black box for QT prolongation — two different warnings, and both are examinable.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 24-year-old on haloperidol develops a sustained involuntary contraction of the neck muscles 36 hours after starting treatment. Which pathway is responsible, and what is the treatment?

B. Nigrostriatal; benztropine, trihexyphenidyl or diphenhydramine — Acute dystonia, an extrapyramidal reaction. The nigrostriatal pathway projects from the substantia nigra to the basal ganglia and is part of the extrapyramidal nervous system; blockade of D2 receptors in this system may lead to disorders of movement. Since dopaminergic neurons inhibit and cholinergic neurons excite the striatal output, D2 blockade creates a relative cholinergic excess, so dystonia can be controlled with benztropine, trihexyphenidyl, or diphenhydramine. Levodopa should never be used in these patients. Haloperidol is a high-potency agent (EPR risk ++++).

A patient on long-term antipsychotic therapy develops lateral jaw movements and fly-catching motions of the tongue. Which management step does this lecture specify that is the OPPOSITE of the treatment for acute EPRs?

B. Eliminate all drugs with central anticholinergic action — Tardive dyskinesia — a late-occurring syndrome of abnormal choreoathetoid movements; the most important adverse effect of antipsychotic drugs; disfiguring and potentially irreversible; probably due to long-term dopamine receptor blockade causing dopamine receptors to up-regulate. Management: discontinue the antipsychotic or reduce the dose; eliminate all drugs with central anticholinergic action; the VMAT inhibitors tetrabenazine or valbenazine; a benzodiazepine may help; clozapine is recommended for patients who require antipsychotics.

A patient started on an antipsychotic three days ago has a temperature of 40 °C, lead-pipe rigidity, fluctuating blood pressure, WBC 18,000 and CK 9,000. Which two agents does this lecture name as helpful?

B. Dantrolene or bromocriptine — Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — a rare and life-threatening disorder with rigidity, tremor, hyperthermia, altered mental status, autonomic instability, elevated WBC, elevated CK, and myoglobinemia with potential nephrotoxicity. Dantrolene or bromocriptine may be helpful. Contrast serotonin syndrome (myoclonus and hyperreflexia → cyproheptadine) and malignant hyperthermia (RYR1, anaesthetic-triggered → dantrolene).

Which antipsychotic requires mandatory regular blood counts, and why is it nonetheless recommended in a particular circumstance?

B. Clozapine; agranulocytosis in 1–2%, yet recommended for patients with tardive dyskinesia who require antipsychotics — Clozapine causes agranulocytosis in 1–2% of patients; regular blood cell counts are mandatory, and it is reserved for refractory patients. Yet it is also recommended for patients with tardive dyskinesia who require antipsychotics, is among the agents least likely to induce EPR (0/+), and is the only antipsychotic in pregnancy category B. Its costs are the metabolic burden (+++ weight gain, glucose, dyslipidaemia) and seizure risk.

Which drug is associated with retinal deposits and a black box warning for QT prolongation and torsade de pointes?

B. Thioridazine — Thioridazine is associated with a significant risk of QT prolongation and lethal torsade de pointes; the FDA has issued a "black box" warning recommending its use be reserved for patients who have failed adequate courses of other antipsychotics, and thioridazine causes retinal deposits while chlorpromazine causes deposits in the anterior portions of the eye (cornea and lens).

A woman on risperidone develops amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Which pathway is blocked, and which class is less likely to do this?

B. Tuberoinfundibular; atypical antipsychotics — The tuberoinfundibular pathway projects from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary; dopamine released from these neurons inhibits prolactin secretion, so blockade of dopamine receptors increases prolactin levels and may cause galactorrhea. In women: amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome and infertility; in men: loss of libido, infertility and impotence. Atypical antipsychotics are less likely to produce prolactin elevations — although risperidone is a notable atypical that still does.

Which statement contrasting classical and atypical antipsychotics is correct?

B. Atypicals have dual antagonism at 5-HT2A and D2, produce less EPR and tardive dyskinesia, are less likely to cause hyperprolactinaemia, and are more effective for negative symptoms — Common properties of atypical antipsychotics: dual antagonism at 5-HT2A and D2 receptors; part of their action is due to 5-HT receptor blockade; less EPRs; less tardive dyskinesia; less likely to cause hyperprolactinemia; more effective at treating negative symptoms; effective in refractory populations. Option 3 inverts the mechanism: atypicals have higher affinities for other receptors than for the D2 receptor.

Which two agents does this lecture name as carrying the greatest risk of seizures?

B. Chlorpromazine and clozapine — Chlorpromazine and clozapine are the agents with the greatest risk of seizures — the lecture's mnemonic is "C is for C-Zures." Note that sedation is a separate axis: it is more likely with low-potency antipsychotics and with the atypical agents, and is due to blockade of central H1 receptors.

An 82-year-old nursing-home resident with Alzheimer's disease is agitated. What class-wide warning applies?

B. A Black Box Warning states that elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death — Antipsychotics carry a Black Box Warning indicating that elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death. Note that control of disturbed behavior in Alzheimer's disease is nonetheless listed among the psychiatric indications — the warning shapes the risk-benefit discussion rather than forbidding use outright.

Which antipsychotic is an inverse agonist at 5-HT2A receptors with no significant affinity for dopamine receptors, and what is its approved indication?

B. Pimavanserin; hallucinations and delusions associated with Parkinson's disease psychosis — Pimavanserin is an inverse agonist at the 5-HT2A receptors with no significant affinity for dopamine receptors, and is approved for treatment of hallucinations and delusions associated with Parkinson's disease psychosis — which is precisely why the absence of dopamine blockade matters. Aripiprazole is a partial agonist at D2 and 5-HT1A and an antagonist at 5-HT2A, and is the most prescribed antipsychotic in the US.

CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination

CLSK · Dr. Morona Sukhoo-Pertab, MBBS · Department of Clinical Skills · source pp. 2123–2166

ElementWhat to carry into the exam
Evaluation sequenceHistory and physical → rule out general medical condition → rule out substance abuse → rule out malingering and factitious disorder → diagnose primary mental disorder
Three information domainsObservation and interview of the patient · collateral information · information from others and the medical record
ScreeningCAGE: dependence 91% sens / 87.8% spec; abuse 87.5% / 80.9%; but only 53% sensitive for unhealthy use. AUDIT (WHO): 0–40, ≥ 8 positive (>90% sens, 80% spec), ≥ 20 suggests dependence. Well-Being Index < 13 → test further for depression.
Which MSE toolbCAM → delirium (sudden disturbance of attention and awareness); MMSE → cognitive impairment/dementia (gradual decline in cognitive domains); MSE → psychiatric presentation
Six MSE componentsAppearance and behavior · mood and affect · language and speech · thoughts and perception · insight and judgement · cognition and memory
Mood vs affectMood = subjective, asked, long-term. Affect = objective, observed, short-term. Mood incongruence is common in psychotic disorders.
Thought process spectrumLogical → circumstantial → tangential → loose association → flight of ideas
HallucinationsVisual (most common) → organic; auditory → schizophrenia; tactile → alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal; olfactory → temporal lobe epilepsy, tumour, migraine, Parkinson's
Suicide riskPlan + lethal means + poor support + poor judgement + no safety contract → hospitalize. Otherwise evaluate, treat the disorder and the underlying cause, and monitor continuously
Insight grades1 denial → 2 slight awareness with denial → 3 blames others → 4 intellectual insight → 5 true emotional insight
Cognitive localisationFrontal = executive (digit span, WORLD backwards, serial 7s, letter fluency) · temporal = memory · mesial temporal R>L = facial recognition · left hemisphere = language · occipital and biparietal = visuospatial (pentagon copy) · left parietal = arithmetic
OrientationLost first to time, then place, last person

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Attention vs memory is the delirium/dementia split
  • The two definitions in this table are the distinction the confusion DLA also draws: delirium is a sudden disturbance of attention and awareness; dementia is a gradual decline in cognitive domains. That is why bCAM tests attention and the MMSE tests cognition — and why the MMSE is insensitive to very early impairment and does not cover executive function.
Exam Lock
The primary psychiatric diagnosis is the last one you make, not the first
  • The lecture's own sequence puts medical illness, substances, and malingering/factitious disorder ahead of the psychiatric diagnosis. This is the same discipline as the confusion DLA, where an acute onset demands a rapid search for a reversible, life-threatening cause before dementia is invoked.
Exam Lock
The modality points at the cause
  • Auditory → schizophrenia. Visual → organic. Tactile → alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Olfactory → temporal lobe epilepsy, tumour, migraine, Parkinson's. A patient with visual hallucinations is more likely to have a medical problem than a primary psychotic one — which is exactly why the evaluation sequence rules out medical causes first.
Trap
CAGE and AUDIT do not screen for the same thing
  • CAGE is a dependence/abuse instrument — excellent for those (91% / 87.5% sensitive) and poor for unhealthy use at 53% sensitivity. AUDIT covers the broader unhealthy-use question at > 90% sensitivity, with ≥ 20 suggesting dependence. Choosing the wrong instrument is choosing to miss the patient.
Trap
Education confounds three of these tests
  • The lecture flags it twice: attention testing asks you to consider poor math/spelling skills before calling serial 7s abnormal, and information and vocabulary depends on educational background. The confusion DLA makes the same point from the other side — a sixth-grade education was offered there as the reason a patient "never was very good at math."

Screening instruments — with their actual test characteristics

InstrumentWhat it screensPerformance (verbatim)
CAGE questionnaireAlcoholBest sensitivity for alcohol dependence (91%; specificity 87.8%) and for alcohol abuse (87.5%, specificity 80.9%). It is NOT a good screening tool for assessing unhealthy alcohol use (53% sensitive).
AUDITAlcohol — developed by the WHO to assess alcohol consumption, drinking behaviors, and alcohol-related problemsScore ranges 0 to 40. A score of 8 or greater is generally considered a positive test for unhealthy alcohol use, with greater than 90% sensitivity and 80% specificity. A score of 20 or greater suggests the presence of alcohol dependence.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A patient's family reports heavy drinking. You want to screen for unhealthy alcohol use, not dependence. Which instrument does this lecture support, and why not the other?

B. AUDIT, because CAGE is only 53% sensitive for unhealthy alcohol use while AUDIT is over 90% sensitive at a cut-off of 8 — The CAGE questionnaire presented the best sensitivity for alcohol dependence (91%; specificity 87.8%) and for alcohol abuse (87.5%, specificity 80.9%). It is NOT a good screening tool for assessing unhealthy alcohol use (53% sensitive). With a score that can range from 0 to 40, a score of 8 or greater on the AUDIT is generally considered a positive test for unhealthy alcohol use, with greater than 90 percent sensitivity and 80 percent specificity; a score of 20 or greater suggests the presence of alcohol dependence.

A 58-year-old with alcohol use disorder, admitted 48 hours ago, reports insects crawling on his skin. Which hallucination modality is this, and what does this lecture associate it with?

C. Tactile; alcohol withdrawal or benzodiazepine withdrawal — Tactile hallucinations are most common with alcohol withdrawal or benzodiazepine withdrawal. The rest of the list: visual (most common) occur most often in organic conditions such as Charles Bonnet syndrome, migraines, Lewy body dementia and metabolic encephalopathy; auditory are often seen in schizophrenia; olfactory (phantosmia) may occur in schizophrenia and mood disorder — consider temporal lobe epilepsy, chronic migraine headaches, brain tumor and Parkinson's disease.

A patient says "I know I have bipolar disorder and that my spending sprees come from the illness, but when I feel that way I still spend." Which grade of insight is this?

D. Grade 4 — intellectual insight without applying the knowledge to future experiences — Grade 4 — intellectual insight: admission of illness and recognition that symptoms or failures in social adjustment are due to irrational feelings or disturbances, without applying that knowledge to future experiences. Grade 5 is true emotional insight: emotional awareness of the motives and feelings within and of the underlying meaning of symptoms — the point at which the knowledge actually changes behaviour.

Which statement about mood and affect matches this lecture?

B. Affect is observed from facial expression and reflects short-term feeling; mood is inquired from the patient and reflects a longer-lasting inner state — Affect: observe the patient's facial expression (objective); the patient's feeling/emotion typically in response to an external event or a thought; reflects short-term feeling triggered by a specific event. Mood: inquire from the patient (subjective); refers to an inner state that persists for some time; reflects long-term feeling. Affect descriptors are range, intensity (blunted, flat, normal), congruence and appropriateness, and mood incongruence is common in psychotic disorders.

Which tool does this lecture pair with a sudden disturbance in attention and awareness?

B. Brief Confusion Assessment Method (bCAM) — Brief Confusion Assessment Method (bCAM) — indication: delirium — a sudden disturbance in attention (i.e. reduced ability to direct, focus, sustain, and shift attention) and awareness (reduced orientation to the environment). The MMSE is indicated for cognitive impairment (dementia): gradual decline from a previous level of performance in one or more cognitive domains, and the MSE for a psychiatric presentation.

In which order is orientation typically lost, according to this lecture?

C. Time, then place, then person — Progression of loss: 1st — time; 2nd — place; last — person. Orientation testing should not be superficial: person — do not limit to the patient's name only; place — patient's residence, name of current location, city, state; time — time of day, day of the week, month, season, date, year.

Serial 7s and WORLD-backwards primarily probe which lobe and function, per the lecture's localisation table?

B. Frontal lobe; executive function — The table gives frontal lobe → executive function → digit span, WORLD backwards, serial 7s, verbal (letter) fluency. Others: temporal lobe → memory (orientation, immediate and delayed recall); mesial temporal lobe (R > L) → facial recognition; left hemisphere → language; occipital and biparietal → visuospatial (pentagon copy); left parietal → arithmetic. Note that serial 7s appears twice — as attention and as arithmetic.

PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs

PHAR · Dr Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology · source pp. 2167–2234

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
"LOT" — the three benzodiazepines that skip phase I
  • Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam are conjugated directly, so they are the ones whose handling does not depend on CYP3A4 or on hepatic phase I capacity. That is why the lecture names lorazepam or oxazepam for patients with advanced liver disease in the drug-withdrawal indication.
Exam Lock
The time-course contrast is objective PHAR.00038 in one line
  • Benzodiazepines give rapid relief of acute anxiety symptoms; antidepressants take 4–6 weeks for the antianxiety response. That is exactly why the two are combined at the start and the benzodiazepine is then tapered — the fast drug covers the gap until the safe drug works.
Trap
Flumazenil is not a routine antidote
  • Its 1-hour half-life means a patient can re-sedate after it wears off, and it can precipitate withdrawal or unmask seizures in exactly the patients most likely to have overdosed. Note also that it reverses Z-drugs as well — they share the benzodiazepine site.

Pattern tables

Benzodiazepines — therapeutic uses and adverse effects

IndicationDetail (verbatim)
Anxiety disorders1. Rapid relief of acute anxiety symptoms. 2. Adjuncts to antidepressants. 3. Recommended only for short-term use. Alprazolam is effective for short- and long-term treatment of panic disorder but may cause withdrawal reactions.
Muscular disordersDiazepam is useful in the treatment of skeletal muscle spasms such as occur in muscle strain, and in treating spasticity from degenerative disorders like multiple sclerosis and cerebral palsy.
SeizuresClonazepam — used for some types of epileptic seizures. Lorazepam, midazolam and diazepam — used in status epilepticus.
Drug withdrawalUsed for management of ethanol withdrawal. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide are commonly used; lorazepam or oxazepam are used in patients with advanced liver disease.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

Which single difference in channel kinetics underlies the fact that barbiturates can cause fatal respiratory depression while benzodiazepines usually cannot?

B. Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of channel opening and require GABA; barbiturates increase the duration and at high doses open the channel directly, without GABA — Benzodiazepine-induced enhancement takes the form of an increase in FREQUENCY of channel opening events; in contrast to benzodiazepines, barbiturates increase the DURATION of the GABA-gated chloride channel openings, and at high concentrations barbiturates also directly activate chloride channels, independent of the presence of GABA. Because the benzodiazepine effect requires GABA, there is a ceiling: benzodiazepines do not produce significant respiratory depression, coma, or death unless combined with alcohol or other depressants.

A patient with alcoholic cirrhosis needs a benzodiazepine for ethanol withdrawal. Which agents does this lecture specify, and why?

B. Lorazepam or oxazepam, because they are conjugated directly and are not metabolized by the P450 system — Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide are commonly used for ethanol withdrawal, but lorazepam or oxazepam are used in patients with advanced liver disease — because oxazepam, lorazepam and temazepam are conjugated directly and are not metabolized by the P450 system. Contrast flurazepam, which is oxidized by liver enzymes to active metabolites with half-lives ranging from 30 to 100 hours.

Which anxiolytic has no hypnotic, anticonvulsant or muscle-relaxant effect, no dependence, no interaction with alcohol, and takes 2–3 weeks to work?

B. Buspirone — Buspirone — a partial agonist at 5-HT1A receptors; slow onset of 2–3 weeks (similar to antidepressants); no hypnotic, anticonvulsant, or muscle relaxant effects; less psychomotor impairment than benzodiazepines; no interaction with alcohol or benzodiazepines; no rebound anxiety or withdrawal on discontinuation; no dependence. It is a second-line agent in generalized anxiety disorder due to variable efficacy. Mnemonic: *"BUS rides SLOW, but safe."*

A patient who takes clonazepam for seizures presents obtunded after a mixed overdose. Why is flumazenil hazardous here?

B. It may cause seizures if a benzodiazepine is being used to control seizures, and may precipitate withdrawal in physiologically dependent patients — Flumazenil may precipitate withdrawal in physiologically dependent patients and may cause seizures if a benzodiazepine is used to control seizures. It also has a rapid onset and short duration — half-life about 1 hour due to rapid hepatic clearance — so frequent administration may be necessary to maintain reversal of long-acting benzodiazepines. It is the only benzodiazepine receptor antagonist available for clinical use, and it blocks the effects of benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.

Which hypnotic is contraindicated in narcolepsy, and what is its mechanism?

B. Suvorexant; dual orexin OX1 and OX2 receptor antagonism — Orexin A and B are neuropeptides that promote wakefulness through activation of the OX1 and OX2 receptors. Suvorexant and lemborexant are dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORA)... Contraindicated in narcolepsy. Their adverse effects are daytime somnolence and worsening of depression/suicidal ideation. Blocking the wake-promoting system in a patient who already cannot stay awake is the reason for the contraindication.

Which drug in this lecture is used for performance anxiety, and which for PTSD nightmares?

A. Propranolol for performance anxiety; prazosin for PTSD nightmares — Propranolol and other β-adrenergic receptor antagonists can reduce the autonomic symptoms associated with specific situational phobias; propranolol is widely used to control performance anxiety (stage fright). Prazosin crosses the blood-brain barrier and antagonizes central α1 receptors, blocking stress responses; through this mechanism prazosin can improve sleep and reduce nightmares associated with PTSD.

Which statement about the Z-drugs is correct?

B. They act only on the BZ1 subtype, are approved only as hypnotics, are antagonised by flumazenil, and have minimal muscle-relaxing and anticonvulsant effects — Z-drugs are positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptors; act only on the BZ1 subtype of benzodiazepine receptors; only approved as hypnotics; antagonized by flumazenil; minimal muscle relaxing and anticonvulsant effects; little or no tolerance; low incidence of adverse effects; have largely replaced benzodiazepines in the treatment of insomnia. Zaleplon has the shortest half-life (1 h, ultrashort duration); eszopiclone the longest (6 h).

Which benzodiazepine grouping matches the lecture's duration table?

B. Chlordiazepoxide, clonazepam, diazepam and flurazepam long-acting (1–3 days); alprazolam, lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam intermediate (10–20 h); midazolam and triazolam short-acting (3–8 h) — The lecture's table gives exactly that grouping, with half-lives of 1–3 days · 10–20 hours · 3–8 hours. It also notes the sleep-disorder favourites: intermediate-acting temazepam and short-acting triazolam, and that the onset of action of benzodiazepines is 30 to 60 minutes.

Why have antidepressants replaced benzodiazepines as first-line therapy for chronic anxiety, and how is the transition managed?

B. Antidepressants have a tolerable adverse-effect profile without dependence; a benzodiazepine may be combined during the first weeks and then tapered after 4–6 weeks — Antidepressants are considered first-line agents in the management of chronic anxiety. They have replaced benzodiazepines as the drugs of choice for chronic anxiety due to a tolerable adverse effect profile. The antianxiety response may take 4–6 weeks. They may be used alone or in combination with a benzodiazepine during the first weeks of treatment; after 4–6 weeks the benzodiazepine can be tapered. Benzodiazepines remain excellent for rapid relief of acute anxiety symptoms but are recommended only for short-term use.

A patient on long-term phenobarbital has subtherapeutic levels of warfarin and an oral contraceptive failure. Which barbiturate property explains both?

B. Induction of hepatic P-450 microsomal enzymes — Enzyme induction: barbiturates induce P-450 microsomal enzymes in the liver. This is one of the explicit contrasts with benzodiazepines, which have no enzyme induction, and it is the same mechanism that put barbiturates on the warfarin-inducer list in the coagulation lecture (with carbamazepine, phenytoin and rifampin).

NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus

PATH · Dr. Adesola Adeleye · Department of Pathology · source pp. 2235–2267

EntityEtiopathogenesisClinical / morphology
Vasogenic edemaDisruption of the blood-brain barrier — meningitis, encephalitis, trauma, metastasis; extracellular fluid, worsened by the paucity of lymphaticsHeadache, nausea and vomiting, altered mental status, seizures, deficits; flattened gyri; complications herniation, stroke, permanent injury
Cytotoxic edemaNeuronal, glial or endothelial cell membrane injury — hypoxia / ischemia, metabolic damage; intracellular fluidAs above
Non-communicating hydrocephalusObstruction of flow within the ventricles — aqueductal stricture, 4th ventricular tumourOnly the affected portion of the ventricle enlarges
Communicating hydrocephalusPoor absorption by arachnoid villi — post-meningitic scarring, SAH, leptomeningeal carcinomatosis; or excess production (choroid plexus papilloma)Entire ventricular system enlarged
Ex vacuoLoss of brain volume — infarction or neurodegenerationSecondary increase in CSF volume; not a pressure problem
Normal pressure hydrocephalusIdiopathic; a communicating type. Transient high CSF pressure enlarges the ventricles and distorts the corona radiata; enlargement then normalises pressureNormal opening pressure with enlarged ventricles; gait disturbance, dementia, urinary incontinence
Pseudotumor cerebriUnknown; overweight women of childbearing age; normal neuroimagingPositional headache, CN VI diplopia, vomiting, papilloedema → vision loss. Treat with lumbar punctures, acetazolamide, shunt
Subfalcine herniationCingulate gyrus under the falxCompresses the anterior cerebral artery → lower-limb motor and sensory deficits
Transtentorial (uncal)Uncus against the free tentorial marginIpsilateral blown pupil + contralateral hemiparesis; Kernohan phenomenon reverses both; Duret haemorrhages in the pons
Tonsillar herniationTonsils through the foramen magnumBrainstem compression → respiratory and cardiac arrest → death
ConcussionDysregulation of the reticular activating system; no permanent injuryTransient LOC, headache, amnesia; normal imaging; repetitive injury → chronic traumatic encephalopathy
ContusionBruising of the brain surface against the skull; coup and contrecoupOedema, depressions, haemorrhage; old lesions are depressed and yellow-brown
Diffuse axonal injuryShearing of axons because grey and white matter accelerate differentlyAxonal swelling and focal haemorrhages; ~50% of post-traumatic coma; no lucid interval
Epidural haematomaSkull fracture at the pterion → middle meningeal arteryLucid interval then deterioration over hours; lens-shaped, does not cross sutures
Subdural haematomaBridging veins; brain atrophy in the elderly, thin-walled veins in infantsAcute or delayed over days to weeks after trivial trauma; crescent-shaped, crosses sutures

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Ex vacuo is not really hydrocephalus
  • The ventricles are big because the brain has shrunk, not because CSF is under pressure — hence "ex vacuo", filling a vacuum. Contrast NPH, where the ventricles are enlarged with a normal opening pressure but the triad of gait disturbance, dementia and urinary incontinence is real and treatable.
Exam Lock
Three compartments, three diseases, one lecture
  • Brain → tumour and oedema. Blood → the four haemorrhages. Water → hydrocephalus. Every entity in this lecture is one compartment expanding inside a rigid box, and every complication is the box's answer: equilibration, then herniation, then failure of perfusion.
Exam Lock
Why Kernohan's notch is called a false localising sign
  • In ordinary uncal herniation the signs are ipsilateral pupil, contralateral hemiparesis. When the brainstem is pushed far enough across, the opposite cerebral peduncle is crushed against the tentorium, so the hemiparesis becomes ipsilateral to the mass and the pupil contralateral — pointing the examiner to the wrong side. Recognising it is the point of the slide.
Exam Lock
Artery, fracture, lucid interval, lens — or vein, atrophy, slow, crescent
  • The two haemorrhages differ on every line, and each line predicts the next. Arterial pressure explains the hours-long deterioration after a lucid interval; tight dural attachment at the sutures explains the lens shape. Venous, low-pressure bleeding in an atrophic brain explains days-to-weeks and the crescent that crosses sutures.
Trap
Diplopia here is a false localising sign
  • The CN VI palsy in raised ICP does not localise the lesion — the abducens nerve has the longest intracranial course and is compressed by pressure alone. Combine that with papilloedema and positional headache in an overweight woman of childbearing age, and a normal scan, and the diagnosis is made by exclusion.

Aggravating factorPaucity of lymphatics greatly impairs the resorption of excess extracellular fluid—

Interferes with or blocks normal CSF circulation from ventricles to subarachnoid space.Poor absorption of CSF by arachnoid villi — post-meningitic scarring, subarachnoid haemorrhage, leptomeningeal carcinomatosis. TraumaTrauma
Bleeding between dura mater and inner table of skullBleeding between dura mater and arachnoid mater
Associated with skull fracture (involving the pterion)Brain atrophy and mild trauma
