Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 19-year-old is struck on the side of the head, briefly loses consciousness, wakes and talks normally, then deteriorates over three hours. CT shows a lens-shaped hyperdensity that does not cross the suture. Which vessel and which fracture?

B. Middle meningeal artery; fracture involving the pterion — Epidural haemorrhage. Etiology: skull fracture involving the pterion. Pathogenesis: laceration of the middle meningeal artery → acute arterial blood accumulation in the potential space between dura and skull. Does not cross the sutural margin → lens-shaped appearance on imaging. Clinical: initial loss of consciousness followed by a so-called "lucid interval" with recovery of consciousness → continued bleeding and expansion of hematoma → deterioration over a period of hours.

An 84-year-old on no anticoagulant becomes progressively confused over three weeks after a minor fall. CT shows a crescentic collection crossing the coronal suture. What is the mechanism and the risk factor?

B. Rupture of bridging veins between arachnoid and dura; brain atrophy stretching the veins and allowing extra movement — Subdural haemorrhage — due to rupture of veins bridging arachnoid and dura → slower (venous) blood accumulation between dura and arachnoid membranes. Risk factor: in the elderly due to brain atrophy — bridging veins get stretched out and the brain has additional space to move; in infants bridging veins are thin-walled and easily ruptured. Can cross sutural margins and has a crescent-shaped lesion on brain imaging. Presentation may be acute (within hours) or delayed (days to weeks), especially in the elderly after trivial head injury.

A patient with a large right temporal mass has a dilated right pupil and left hemiparesis, then over the next hour develops a dilated LEFT pupil and RIGHT hemiparesis. What has happened?

C. Kernohan phenomenon — the contralateral cerebral peduncle and CN III are compressed against the tentorium — Kernohan phenomenon: further displacement of the uncus → contralateral blown pupil, contralateral impaired extraocular movements and ipsilateral hemiparesis. This is due to compression of the contralateral cerebral peduncle against the tentorium and compression of the contralateral cranial nerve III. The initial picture — ipsilateral blown pupil and contralateral hemiparesis — is ordinary uncal herniation. Duret haemorrhages are linear flame-shaped haemorrhages from stretching of the median and paramedian pontine arteries.

A 74-year-old has a magnetic gait, cognitive decline and urinary incontinence. Ventricles are enlarged and the LP opening pressure is normal. Which type of hydrocephalus is this?

C. Normal pressure hydrocephalus — a type of communicating hydrocephalus — Normal pressure: normal opening pressure on lumbar puncture. Hydrocephalus: pathologically enlarged ventricular size. Idiopathic; type of communicating hydrocephalus. Theory: transient high CSF pressure leading to ventricular enlargement → distorts fibers of corona radiata; ventricular enlargement normalizes pressure. Clinical features: 1. gait disturbances, 2. dementia, 3. urinary incontinence. Ex vacuo would be loss of brain volume with a secondary increase in CSF volume, not a treatable triad.

Which mechanism produces cytotoxic rather than vasogenic cerebral oedema?

B. Neuronal, glial or endothelial cell membrane injury from generalised hypoxia or ischaemia — Vasogenic edema: disruption of the blood-brain barrier; fluid from the vascular component into the extracellular space — meningitis, encephalitis, trauma and metastasis. Cytotoxic edema: neuronal, glial or endothelial cell membrane injury; increase in intracellular fluid — in generalized hypoxia/ischemia insult, metabolic damage, anything that injures the cells. The paucity of lymphatics greatly impairs the resorption of excess extracellular fluid, which is why the brain tolerates oedema poorly.

A 28-year-old woman with obesity has months of positional headache, transient visual obscurations, horizontal diplopia and papilloedema. MRI is normal. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

B. Pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension); lumbar punctures, acetazolamide, shunt — Pseudotumor cerebri: pseudo- false, tumor- mass, cerebri- brain → not due to a tumor. Epidemiology: overweight women of childbearing age. No obvious cause on neuroimaging: no masses, no bleeding, no hydrocephalus/increased ventricular size, no vasogenic or cytotoxic edema. Clinical features: increased intracranial pressure characterised by headache (positional), diplopia (CN-6 palsy), vomiting, and papilledema potentially leading to vision loss. Treatment: lumbar punctures, acetazolamide, shunt.

Which injury is seen in about half of patients comatose after trauma, has NO lucid interval, and arises from differential acceleration of grey and white matter?

C. Diffuse axonal injury — Diffuse axonal injuries: damage to the deep white matter regions. With trauma, denser gray matter doesn't accelerate/move as fast as white matter → shearing of axons away from the cell body as they are stretched beyond the elastic point → alterations in axoplasmic flow. Pathological findings: axonal swelling and focal hemorrhagic lesions. Seen in around 50% of patients in coma after trauma, even without contusions. No lucid interval seen. The lucid interval belongs to the epidural haematoma.

Which herniation compresses the anterior cerebral artery, and what deficit follows?

C. Subfalcine; motor and sensory deficits in the lower extremity and lower trunk — Subfalcine herniation: unilateral or asymmetrical expansion of a cerebral hemisphere displaces the cingulate gyrus under the falx cerebri → compresses the anterior cerebral artery → infarcts in the area supplied by the artery → motor and sensory deficits in the lower extremity and lower trunk. The ACA supplies the medial motor and sensory cortex — the leg area of the homunculus, which is why the deficit is in the lower limb.

PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease

PHAR · Dr Malcolm Antoine Jr · PCM500 Pharmacology · source pp. 2268–2361

Choice of treatment (PHAR.00058) — verbatim

DrugMechanismSignature point
LevodopaPrecursor that crosses the BBB on the L-system carrier and is decarboxylated to dopamine centrallyMost effective; 1–3% reaches the brain alone; response declines in years 3–5; wearing-off and on-off; does not stop progression
CarbidopaPeripheral dopa decarboxylase inhibitor that does not cross the BBBRaises brain delivery to 10% and cuts the levodopa requirement by 75%; removes the peripheral nausea, arrhythmia and hypotension
BromocriptineErgot D2 agonistNow rarely used; ergots cause fibrosis, digital vasospasm, erythromelalgia
Pramipexole, ropiniroleNon-ergot dopamine agonistsInitial therapy in younger patients; less dyskinesia than levodopa but less effective; uncontrollable somnolence and impulse control disorders
RotigotineNon-ergot agonistTransdermal, once daily
ApomorphineNon-ergot agonistSC or SL rescue for "off" episodes; highly emetogenic — pretreat with trimethobenzamide; 5-HT3 antagonists contraindicated
Selegiline, rasagilineIrreversible MAO-B inhibitionAdjunct to levodopa; selegiline → amphetamine metabolites → insomnia; 14-day rule with serotonergic drugs
EntacaponePeripheral COMT inhibitionPreferred COMT inhibitor; available with levodopa/carbidopa
TolcaponeCentral and peripheral COMT inhibitionFulminating hepatic necrosis — signed consent and LFTs every 2 weeks
Amantadine↑ dopamine release, ↓ reuptake, NMDA antagonismModest effect; decreases levodopa-induced dyskinesia; livedo reticularis
Benztropine, trihexyphenidylAntimuscarinicTremor and rigidity, not bradykinesia; avoid in glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, pyloric stenosis

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Why a COMT inhibitor only makes sense alongside carbidopa
  • Blocking dopa decarboxylase peripherally shunts levodopa down the COMT pathway, raising 3-O-methyldopa, which then competes with levodopa for the same L-system carrier at the gut and the blood-brain barrier. The COMT inhibitor closes that escape route. Two enzymes, one substrate, and the second block is needed because of the first.
Exam Lock
The same nigrostriatal circuit, read in two directions
  • In the antipsychotics lecture, D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway caused drug-induced parkinsonism treated with antimuscarinics. Here the same circuit fails from the other end — loss of dopaminergic neurons — and the treatment is the same two options: give dopamine back or block the acetylcholine.
Trap
PHAR.00056 in one line
  • Dopamine does not cross the blood-brain barrier — that is the whole answer to "why not just give dopamine?" Its immediate precursor levodopa does cross, using the facilitative L-transport system for neutral amino acids, and is then converted to dopamine in the brain.
Trap
Levodopa and antipsychotics cancel each other in both directions
  • Antipsychotics block D2 and cause parkinsonism — so they should not be used in parkinsonian patients. Levodopa raises dopamine and can precipitate psychosis — so it should not be given to psychotic patients. That is why the antipsychotics lecture insists levodopa should never be used for drug-induced parkinsonism, and why pimavanserin (no dopamine affinity) exists for Parkinson's disease psychosis.

Pattern tables

Inhibitors of dopamine metabolism, amantadine and antimuscarinics

Class / drugMechanismKey points
MAO-B inhibitors — selegiline, rasagilineSelegiline selectively and irreversibly inhibits MAO-B (which selectively metabolizes dopamine), retarding the breakdown of dopamine in the brain. Rasagiline is a second irreversible MAO-B inhibitor approved for PD.Enhances the effect of levodopa and allows the levodopa dose to be reduced; mainly used as an adjunct to levodopa. Selegiline is metabolized to methamphetamine and amphetamine — may cause insomnia if taken late in the day. Interactions: use of other MAO inhibitors, SNRIs, SSRIs, TCAs, St John's wort, methadone, tramadol or meperidine within 14 days could result in hypertensive crisis and/or serotonin syndrome and is contraindicated; methylphenidate, amphetamines or sympathomimetic amines can cause severe hypertension.
COMT inhibitors — tolcapone, entacaponeInhibition of dopa decarboxylase (by carbidopa) causes compensatory activation of the COMT pathway → increased plasma 3-O-methyldopa, which competes with levodopa for the active carrier that transports levodopa across the intestinal mucosa and the blood-brain barrier. Inhibiting COMT reverses this.Effects: decreased metabolism of levodopa · decreased plasma levels of 3-O-methyldopa · increased uptake of levodopa · higher dopamine levels in the brain. Fulminating hepatic necrosis is associated with tolcapone: its use in the US requires signed patient consent plus monitoring of liver function tests every 2 weeks. No such toxicity has been reported for entacapone, which is therefore preferred and is available in fixed-dose combinations with levodopa/carbidopa.
AmantadineAntiviral drug with antiparkinsonian actions. Its mode of action in PD is unclear; it may increase dopamine release and inhibit dopamine reuptake, and it is an antagonist of the NMDA receptor — suggesting an antidyskinetic effect.The effects of amantadine in PD are modest. Adverse effects: restlessness, agitation, confusion, hallucinations; at high doses acute toxic psychosis; peripheral edema (responds to diuretics); headache, heart failure, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, urinary retention, GI disturbances. Livedo reticularis sometimes occurs and usually clears within a month of withdrawing the drug. Caution with a history of seizures or heart failure.
Antimuscarinics — benztropine, trihexyphenidylAntagonists of acetylcholine — the other half of the treatment strategy.Adjuvant therapy. May improve tremor and rigidity; little effect on bradykinesia. Can produce mood changes, xerostomia, pupillary dilation, confusion, hallucinations and urinary retention. Cannot be used in patients with glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy or pyloric stenosis.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

Why is levodopa given rather than dopamine, and what does adding carbidopa achieve numerically?

B. Dopamine does not cross the blood-brain barrier while levodopa is carried across on the L-system; carbidopa raises brain delivery from 1–3% to about 10% and cuts the daily levodopa requirement by 75% — Dopamine does not cross the blood-brain barrier, but its immediate precursor levodopa is transported into the CNS and is converted to dopamine in the brain... Levodopa is transported into the brain by the facilitative L-transport system for neutral amino acids. Carbidopa is a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor that does not cross the blood-brain barrier... Concomitant administration of carbidopa may reduce the daily requirements of levodopa by 75%. The lecture's figures: levodopa alone 1–3% to brain; with carbidopa 10%.

A patient on levodopa/carbidopa has good mornings but predictable loss of benefit before each next dose. What is this called, and how does it differ from the on-off phenomenon?

B. Wearing-off reaction — fluctuations RELATED to the timing of levodopa intake; the on-off phenomenon is UNRELATED to dose timing and its mechanism is unknown — Wearing-off reactions: fluctuations related to the timing of levodopa intake. The on-off phenomenon: fluctuations in response unrelated to the timing of doses; the exact mechanism is unknown. For patients with severe off-periods who are unresponsive to other measures, apomorphine may provide benefit. The underlying reason both develop is that with time the number of neurons falls and there are fewer cells capable of taking up levodopa and converting it to dopamine.

Which COMT inhibitor requires signed patient consent and liver function tests every two weeks, and why?

B. Tolcapone; fulminating hepatic necrosis — Fulminating hepatic necrosis is associated with the use of tolcapone. Accordingly, its use in the US requires signed patient consent plus monitoring of liver function tests every 2 weeks. No such toxicity has been reported for entacapone, which is therefore preferred and is available as fixed-dose combinations with levodopa/carbidopa.

A patient on pramipexole develops new compulsive gambling and episodes of falling asleep at the wheel. Which two adverse effects are these, and what does the lecture say to do about the second?

B. Impulse control disorders and uncontrollable somnolence; the somnolence requires discontinuation of the medication — Confusion, hallucinations, delusions. Compulsive behaviors, defined as impulse control disorders (ICDs). And: Pramipexole, ropinirole and rotigotine: uncontrollable somnolence. This requires discontinuation of the medication. Note the class contrast — ergot agonists instead cause pulmonary infiltrates, pleural and retroperitoneal fibrosis, erythromelalgia and painless digital vasospasm.

Which statement about dopamine agonists versus levodopa matches the lecture?

B. Dopamine agonists are less effective than levodopa for motor symptoms but less likely to cause motor fluctuations or dyskinesia, and are favoured as initial therapy in younger patients — Dopamine agonists are less effective than levodopa in treating the motor symptoms of PD. They are less likely to cause motor fluctuations or dyskinesia. Many experts favor dopamine agonists as initial therapy in younger patients with PD, and levodopa as initial therapy in older patients who may be more vulnerable to the adverse cognitive effects of the dopamine agonists. And crucially: dopamine agonists do not require enzymatic conversion for activity; therefore they do not depend on the functional capacities of the nigrostriatal neurons.

A patient with PD on selegiline is prescribed tramadol for back pain. What is the risk, and what interval does the lecture specify?

B. Hypertensive crisis and/or serotonin syndrome; use within 14 days of an MAO-B inhibitor is contraindicated — Use of other MAO inhibitors, SNRIs, SSRIs, TCAs, St. John's wort, methadone, tramadol, or meperidine within 14 days of an MAO-B inhibitor could result in hypertensive crisis and/or serotonin syndrome and is contraindicated. Concomitant use of methylphenidate, amphetamines, or sympathomimetic amines such as pseudoephedrine with an MAO-B inhibitor can also result in severe hypertension. Selegiline's own metabolism to methamphetamine and amphetamine also explains insomnia if taken late in the day.

Which drug is an antiviral with an NMDA-antagonist action, decreases levodopa-induced dyskinesia, and can cause a reversible mottled rash?

B. Amantadine — Amantadine — an antiviral drug with antiparkinsonian actions; its mode of action in PD is unclear; it may increase dopamine release and inhibit dopamine reuptake, and it is an antagonist of the NMDA receptor, suggesting an antidyskinetic effect. Livedo reticularis sometimes occurs in patients taking amantadine and usually clears within a month of withdrawing the drug. It can be used as monotherapy in early PD and as an adjunct in later stages, and can decrease levodopa-induced dyskinesia.

Which supplement reduces levodopa's effectiveness, and by what mechanism?

B. Vitamin B6; it is a cofactor for dopa decarboxylase and increases peripheral metabolism of levodopa — Vitamin B6 is a cofactor for L-Dopa decarboxylase. Vitamin B6 increases peripheral metabolism of levodopa and decreases its effectiveness. Note the related pharmacokinetic point: certain amino acids can compete with the drug for absorption from the gut and for transport from the blood to the brain, and food delays the appearance of levodopa in the plasma.

Approximately what proportion of substantia nigra neurons are lost by the time symptoms first appear, and how much at autopsy?

B. At least 70% at onset; often 95% at autopsy — The extent of loss of dopaminergic neurons is profound. At least 70% of the neurons are destroyed at the time symptoms first appear. Often, 95% of the neurons are missing at autopsy. This is why treatment is symptomatic — relief provided by levodopa is only symptomatic and lasts only while the drug is present in the body, and levodopa does not stop progression of PD.

Which antiparkinsonian drug improves tremor and rigidity but has little effect on bradykinesia, and in whom is it contraindicated?

B. Benztropine; patients with glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy or pyloric stenosis — Benztropine and trihexyphenidyl are adjuvant therapy; they may improve tremor and rigidity with little effect on bradykinesia; can produce mood changes, xerostomia, pupillary dilation, confusion, hallucinations, and urinary retention; and cannot be used in patients with glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy or pyloric stenosis. They are the antagonists of acetylcholine arm of the treatment strategy — restoring the dopamine/ACh balance from the other side.

NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases

PATH · Dr. Adesola Adeleye · Department of Pathology · source pp. 2362–2387

EntityCause / mechanismKey features
Global ischemia / hypoxiaSevere systemic hypotension (MI, shock) or ↓ O₂ carrying capacity (CO poisoning); outcome set by severity and durationNeurons > glia; hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells most vulnerable; more severe impairment than focal ischemia
Watershed infarctBorder zones at the most distal reaches of arterial supply, after hypotensive episodes, classically after resuscitation from cardiac arrestGreatest risk: ACA–MCA border zone; also internal border zone (superficial vs deep MCA) and MCA–PCA
Embolic infarctMore common than thrombotic; cardiac mural thrombus or carotid atheromatous plaque; AF, myocardial dysfunctionFocal deficit in a named arterial territory
Thrombotic infarctThrombus on an atherosclerotic plaqueAnterograde extension; may fragment and embolize
Paradoxical embolusVenous embolus crossing a right-to-left shunt — PFO, ASD, VSDSystemic ischemia including stroke
Lacunar infarctHypertensive lipohyalinosis of penetrating (lenticulostriate) arteries obstructing the lumenDeep, small; the other outcome of lipohyalinosis is the Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm
Hypertensive intraparenchymal haemorrhageRupture of small penetrating vessels / Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms, commonly lenticulostriateBasal ganglia (most common), thalamus, pons, cerebellum; fatal if large or intraventricular
Cerebral amyloid angiopathySubintimal and medial amyloid in larger non-penetrating cortical vesselsSuperficial / lobar haemorrhage in contrast to the deep hypertensive bleed
Arteriovenous malformationTangled arteries and veins with no interposing capillaries; most common vascular malformation; M:F 2:1; age 10–30Seizure, intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage; high-output cardiac failure in newborns
Subarachnoid haemorrhageRupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm; 90% anterior circulation, at branch points of the circle of Willis; ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos; hypertension, smoking, ageThunderclap headache, rapid loss of consciousness, meningismus; CT blood in basal cisterns; LP with RBCs or xanthochromia; complications rebleed, vasospasm (nimodipine), communicating hydrocephalus

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Selective vulnerability explains the clinical picture after cardiac arrest
  • Neurons die before glia, and among neurons the hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells go first — which is why survivors of arrest show memory impairment and ataxia. Add the ACA–MCA watershed and you also get the classic "man-in-a-barrel" proximal arm weakness.
Exam Lock
The imaging line is the reason for the CT-first algorithm
  • A CT in the first hours is often normal in ischaemic stroke but shows haemorrhage immediately. That is precisely why the emergency CT is done — not to see the infarct, but to exclude the bleed before thrombolysis. It joins the 3–4.5-hour alteplase window from the coagulation lecture.
Exam Lock
Lipohyalinosis has two endings, and the lecture tests both
  • The same hypertensive small-vessel change either blocks the lumen → lacunar infarct or weakens the wall → Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm → hypertensive haemorrhage. Both happen in the lenticulostriate arteries, which is why the basal ganglia are the commonest site for each.
Exam Lock
Three complications, three time frames
  • Rebleed — immediately. Vasospasm — the early period after the haemorrhage (and nimodipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker from the antihypertensives lecture, prevents it). Communicating hydrocephalus — late, from meningeal fibrosis blocking the arachnoid granulations.
Trap
Lobar vs deep is the single most useful location rule
  • Hypertensive bleeds are DEEP — basal ganglia (commonest), thalamus, pons, cerebellum, from small penetrating vessels. Amyloid angiopathy bleeds are LOBAR/superficial — from larger non-penetrating cortical vessels. An elderly normotensive patient with a recurrent lobar haemorrhage is amyloid angiopathy until proven otherwise.

Pattern tables

Introduction — ischemic vs haemorrhagic stroke

Ischemic strokeHemorrhagic stroke
CauseEmbolic >> thrombotic; global hypoxia/ischemia (rare)Vascular rupture — can be intraparenchymal or subarachnoid
ImagingDiffusion-weighted MRI shows the lesion within 30 minutes of onset; CT shows the lesion within 6 to 24 hours.Both CT and MRI can identify the lesion immediately after onset.

Types of ischemic stroke — four mechanisms

MechanismDetail (verbatim)
Embolic infarctionsMore common than thrombotic. Source of emboli: cardiac mural thrombus or carotid atheromatous plaque. Predisposing factors: atherosclerotic plaque, atrial fibrillation, myocardial dysfunction.
Thrombotic occlusionUsually a thrombus superimposed on atherosclerotic plaques. Can have anterograde extension. Can fragment and embolize.
Paradoxical emboliWhen a venous embolus crosses over to the arterial side due to the presence of a right-to-left shunt (patent foramen ovale, atrial or ventricular septal defect) and can lead to ischemia on the systemic side, including stroke.
Lacunar infarctsOcclusion of penetrating arteries (commonly lenticulostriate), mostly due to hypertension causing lipohyalinosis of these arteries. Lipohyalinosis can obstruct the vessel lumen → lacunar infarct, or weaken the vessel wall → Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm.

Intracranial haemorrhage — the classification

Intraparenchymal haemorrhageSubarachnoid haemorrhage
Hypertensive: primary intraparenchymal hemorrhage · rupture of Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm · slit hemorrhageThe most important cause is non-traumatic rupture of a berry aneurysm.
Non-hypertensive: cerebral amyloid angiopathy · vascular malformation · coagulopathy · tumor hemorrhage · hemorrhagic conversion of ischemic stroke—

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 58-year-old hypertensive collapses with a dense left hemiplegia; CT shows a haemorrhage centred on the right putamen extending into the ventricle. Which vessels and which lesion?

B. Lenticulostriate arteries; Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms arising from lipohyalinosis — Hypertensive primary intraparenchymal haemorrhage — due to rupture of small intraparenchymal vessels which branch off major cerebral vessels; like Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms and lacunar infarcts, they commonly involve the lenticulostriate arteries, with typical locations: basal ganglia (most common), thalamus, pons and cerebellum, and it can be fatal if large or if it extends into the ventricular system. Lipohyalinosis weakens the wall → Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm.

An 81-year-old normotensive woman has her second lobar haemorrhage in two years. What is the mechanism, and why is the location different from a hypertensive bleed?

B. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy — amyloid deposits subintimally and in the media of larger non-penetrating cortical vessels, so the bleed is superficial/lobar, unlike the deep hypertensive bleed from small penetrating vessels — Amyloid angiopathy: the hemorrhage affects larger non-penetrating vessels supplying the cortex and is therefore typically superficial/lobar in location, unlike small penetrating vessels affected by hypertension which are typically subcortical/deep. Amyloid deposits inside the vessel wall (subintimal and medial deposition) which weakens the vessel and increases the risk of rupture and hemorrhage.

A 44-year-old collapses with the "worst headache of my life" and neck stiffness. CT is equivocal; LP shows xanthochromia. Which complication is prevented by nimodipine, and when does it occur?

B. Vasospasm, in the early period after the haemorrhage — Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm. The complications: rebleed — common and higher risk of mortality; vasospasm — in the early period after the hemorrhage (nimodipine helps prevent vasospasm); hydrocephalus — due to healing and meningeal fibrosis obstructing CSF absorption by arachnoid granulations. Xanthochromia is yellowish CSF due to release of bilirubin after RBC lysis.

Which associations does this lecture give for saccular (berry) aneurysms?

B. ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (congenital, younger age), plus hypertension, smoking and advanced age (acquired degeneration) — Saccular aneurysms are associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and other congenital diseases which can affect connective tissue of blood vessels — these occur at a younger age. Saccular aneurysms are also associated with acquired risk factors which cause degenerative changes of blood vessels, e.g. hypertension, smoking and advanced age. 90% are in the anterior circulation, at branch points of the circle of Willis. Note the ADPKD link back to the renal-vascular lecture's berry aneurysm extrarenal manifestation.

A patient resuscitated after prolonged cardiac arrest has bilateral proximal arm weakness and profound short-term memory loss. Which two vulnerabilities explain this?

B. Watershed infarction at the ACA–MCA border zone, and selective vulnerability of hippocampal pyramidal cells — Border zone infarcts occur in the regions that lie at the most distal reaches of the arterial blood supply. GREATEST RISK: border zone between the anterior and the middle cerebral artery distributions. Usually seen after hypotensive episodes; most commonly seen in patients resuscitated after cardiac arrest. And in global ischemia, the cell type matters: neurons >> glial cells, especially pyramidal cells of the hippocampus and cerebellar Purkinje cells.

Forty-eight hours after an ischaemic stroke, what will the histology show?

B. Tissue necrosis with an early influx of neutrophils, followed a few days later by macrophages — The lecture's timeline: up to 24 hours ("acute") — cytoplasmic eosinophilia, nuclear pyknosis and karyorrhexis → red neurons; 24 hours to 2 weeks ("subacute") — tissue necrosis causing early influx of neutrophils followed a few days later by influx of macrophages, later vascular proliferation and reactive gliosis; after 2 weeks ("repair") — removal of necrotic tissue and gliosis, leaving behind a glial scar and cystic space. Grossly at this point the brain is pale, soft and swollen.

A 26-year-old man presents with a seizure; imaging shows a tangle of vessels with no intervening capillary bed. Which lesion is this, and what is its presentation in a newborn?

B. Arteriovenous malformation; high-output congestive heart failure from arteriovenous shunting — Arteriovenous malformations: most commonly a tangled network of arteries and veins with no interposing capillaries. The most common vascular malformation; affects males twice more than females (2:1 M:F); age 10 to 30 years. Manifest with seizure, intracerebral hemorrhage or even a subarachnoid hemorrhage. In newborns: high output congestive heart failure because of blood shunting from arteries to veins.

Which imaging statement matches this lecture's comparison of ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke?

B. Diffusion-weighted MRI shows an ischaemic lesion within 30 minutes; CT shows it within 6 to 24 hours; both CT and MRI identify haemorrhage immediately — Ischemic stroke: diffusion-weighted MRI shows the lesion within 30 mins of onset; CT shows the lesion within 6 to 24 hours. Hemorrhagic stroke: both CT and MRI can identify the lesion immediately after onset. Note also that "stroke" is the clinical designation applied when symptoms last more than 24 hours.

Also flagged in this lecture

Exam Lock
Two EEG numbers and one negative
  • 3 Hz spike-and-wave = typical absence; 1.5–2.5 Hz diffuse spike-wave = atypical absence. And the single most useful bedside discriminator is no postictal confusion in typical absence — a child who stares, blinks and then carries straight on mid-sentence.
Exam Lock
Five minutes defines two different things
  • A febrile seizure needs treatment if it lasts > 5 minutes, and status epilepticus is defined as a single seizure lasting more than 5 minutes. The same number, and the same first drug class — a benzodiazepine — in both.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 7-year-old has 20 daily episodes of staring with eye fluttering, each under 10 seconds, with no postictal confusion. EEG shows 3-Hz spike-and-wave. Which drugs are first line, and by what mechanism?

B. Ethosuximide and valproate; inhibition of the T-type Ca²⁺ current that governs thalamic oscillatory activity — Typical absence seizures — brief loss of consciousness, abrupt staring, rapid eye blinking, usually < 10 seconds, no postictal confusion, 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharge, onset 3–5 years, often resolving by puberty. Absence seizures involve oscillatory neuronal activity between thalamus and cortex; the T-type Ca²⁺ current governs oscillatory responses in thalamic neurons; ethosuximide and valproate inhibit this current and are effective in absence seizures. Valproate is preferred if tonic-clonic seizures are also present.

A young woman with generalized epilepsy plans pregnancy. Which drug carries the highest malformation risk, and what two supplements does the lecture recommend?

B. Valproate; prophylactic folic acid for neural tube defects, and vitamin K for the mother in the final month and for the newborn — Valproate causes a significantly higher rate of fetal malformations compared to other antiepileptic drugs — and it is listed as teratogenic: avoid in females of childbearing age. Prophylactic folic acid decreases incidence of neural tube defects. Newborn hemorrhagic disease: enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs may increase degradation of vitamin K in the fetus... Vitamin K supplementation is recommended for the mother in the final month of pregnancy and for the newborn.

A patient started on lamotrigine two weeks ago develops a spreading rash with mucosal involvement. What is the correct action, and which other drugs share this black box?

B. Discontinue at the first sign of rash; lamotrigine and carbamazepine carry black box warnings for SJS/TEN, and phenytoin is also high risk — Antiepileptic drugs are associated with an increased risk for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN). Lamotrigine and carbamazepine have black box warnings regarding SJS/TEN reactions. They should be discontinued at the first sign of rash. High risk: phenytoin, lamotrigine, carbamazepine. The lecture also notes that lamotrigine's risk is high if titrated too quickly.

A seizure has continued for 8 minutes in the emergency department. Which is the correct first-phase therapy, and what follows if it fails?

B. IM midazolam or IV lorazepam or IV diazepam; then IV fosphenytoin, valproic acid or levetiracetam — Status epilepticus is a single seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between seizures. Phase 1 (5–20 minutes of activity): IM midazolam OR IV lorazepam OR IV diazepam. Phase 2 (20–40 minutes): IV fosphenytoin OR IV valproic acid OR IV levetiracetam; second-line, less preferred, IV phenobarbital. Phase 3: repeat second therapy / refractory management.

Which antiepileptic requires regular eye examinations, and why?

B. Vigabatrin; permanent visual field defects — Vigabatrin: permanent visual field defects (requires regular eye checks). Vigabatrin's mechanism is inhibition of GABA degradation — it inhibits GABA aminotransferase. Note the contrast with diplopia, which is a common, reversible dose-related effect of phenytoin, carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine.

Which antiepileptic INHIBITS cytochrome P450 — including its own metabolism — while the others listed induce it?

D. Valproate — Carbamazepine, phenobarbital and phenytoin induce cytochrome P450; oxcarbazepine is a weak P450 inducer. Valproate is a CYP450 inhibitor: hepatotoxicity; inhibits cytochrome P450; inhibits metabolism of several drugs; inhibits its own metabolism. This is the same inducer list that appeared in the coagulation lecture as drugs that stimulate warfarin metabolism and reduce anticoagulation.

A patient on phenytoin has a small dose increase and becomes ataxic with diplopia and levels far above expectation. Which pharmacokinetic property explains this?

B. Zero-order (saturation) kinetics — Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics of elimination (tricky to dose) — once the enzyme is saturated, a small dose increment produces a disproportionate rise in level, hence diplopia and ataxia. Its other signature effects are gingival hyperplasia, coarsening of facial features in children, hirsutism, and rash / Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Which drug pairing of mechanism is correct as this lecture classifies them?

B. Tiagabine inhibits GABA reuptake; vigabatrin inhibits GABA aminotransferase — Inhibition of the reuptake of GABA: tiagabine. Inhibition of degradation of GABA: vigabatrin inhibits GABA aminotransferase. And on the glutamate side: gabapentin and pregabalin decrease glutamate release by blocking presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; levetiracetam binds to synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A). Ethosuximide is a T-type Ca²⁺ blocker; phenytoin is a Na⁺ channel blocker.

Which non-pharmacological therapy involves stimulating the LEFT vagus nerve, and by how much does it reduce partial seizures?

B. Vagus nerve stimulation; by about one-third — Intermittent electrical stimulation of the left vagus nerve with an implanted pacemaker-like device reduces the number of partial seizures by 1/3. The patient can activate the device when they sense a seizure is imminent. Vagus nerve stimulation is used as an adjunct to anticonvulsant therapy. The other options in the lecture are surgery (resection or disconnection), deep brain stimulation, and the ketogenic diet (4:1 fat to protein and carbohydrate).

Which antiepileptic is listed as a first-line option for essential tremor?

C. Primidone — Primidone — essential tremor (first-line option); propranolol is also first line. The rest of the "other uses" table: carbamazepine — neuropathic pain and bipolar disorder; gabapentin — neuropathic pain and restless legs syndrome; lamotrigine — bipolar disorder; pregabalin — neuropathic pain; topiramate — migraine prophylaxis; valproate — bipolar disorder and migraine prophylaxis. Recall too that primidone is metabolized to phenobarbital, and its adverse effects mirror it.

NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases

PATH · Dr. Adesola Adeleye · Department of Pathology · source pp. 2447–2477

DiseaseAge / geneticsProtein and hallmarkClinicalMorphology
Alzheimer diseaseMost common cause of dementia in older adults; 5–10% familial early onset — APP (chr 21, Down), presenilin 1 (chr 14), presenilin 2 (chr 1); 90–95% sporadic late onset — ApoE ε4 on chr 19; homozygotes 95% risk by 85Aβ extracellular plaques + intracellular tau neurofibrillary tanglesEarly memory impairment, altered mood and behaviour, later aphasia and disorientation; motor and sensory systems usually intact; death from intercurrent pneumoniaFrontal, temporal and parietal atrophy; narrow gyri, wide sulci; ex vacuo ventriculomegaly; neuronal loss and gliosis
Frontotemporal lobar degenerationYounger age than ADFTLD-tau (Pick bodies) or FTLD-TDP-43Behaviour or language first; memory laterLobar frontal and temporal atrophy with knifelike gyri
Parkinson diseaseMostly sporadic; small percentage with α-synuclein gene mutationsα-Synuclein → Lewy bodies (cytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions)Asymmetric pill-rolling tremor, bradykinesia with shuffling gait, cogwheel rigidity; dementia < 1 year from motor onset = Lewy body dementia; > 1 year = dementia secondary to PDPallor and atrophy of the substantia nigra; loss of pigmented neurons with gliosis
Huntington diseaseAutosomal dominant; CAG repeat on chromosome 4 — 6–35 normal, ≥ 36 disease; longer repeat = earlier onset; expansion in spermatogenesis → paternal anticipationHuntingtin — ubiquitinated intranuclear inclusionsChorea, athetosis, forgetfulness to dementia, impulse control loss, aggression and increased suicide risk; death after an average course of 15 yearsSmall brain; marked caudate (± putamen) atrophy with dilated lateral and third ventricles; severe striatal neuronal loss with gliosis

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
The one-year rule ties three lectures together
  • The confusion DLA asked *"which came first, memory problems or stiffness and a shuffling gait?"*; this lecture gives the answer in numbers — dementia within 1 year of motor onset = Lewy body dementia; more than 1 year apart = dementia secondary to Parkinson disease. And the antipsychotics lecture supplies the drug for the hallucinations: pimavanserin.
Exam Lock
Three genes for the 5%, one allele for the 95%
  • Early-onset familial AD: APP (chr 21) · presenilin 1 (chr 14) · presenilin 2 (chr 1) — all of which increase Aβ production, and the presenilins are γ-secretase. Late-onset sporadic AD: ApoE ε4 on chr 19, with 95% risk by age 85 in ε4 homozygotes. The Down syndrome link is APP gene dosage on chromosome 21.
Exam Lock
The name is the pathology
  • "A-myo-trophic" = the lower motor neuron loss (muscle atrophy, fasciculations). "Lateral sclerosis" = the upper motor neuron loss (degeneration of the corticospinal tract in the lateral cord → spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski). And the four things that are spared — intellect, sensation, sphincters and eye movements — are what distinguish it from everything else in this lecture.
Trap
Two features separate FTLD from Alzheimer at the bedside
  • Younger age of onset and behaviour or language first, memory later — the exact reverse of Alzheimer disease, where early memory impairment dominates and behaviour follows. Note also the protein crossover: tau gene mutations increase the risk of FTLD, not of AD.

Pattern tables

Alzheimer disease — genetics and morphology

5–10%: INHERITED, EARLY ONSET90–95%: SPORADIC, LATE ONSET
Associated with gene mutations or chromosomal alterations that increase production of Aβ peptideApoE genotype on chromosome 19: three different allelic forms (ε2, ε3, ε4)
Amyloid precursor protein on chromosome 21 — Down syndromeIf homozygous for ε4: the risk of Alzheimer is much greater — a 95% chance by age 85
Presenilin 1 and 2 gene mutations on chromosomes 14 and 1, which code for the γ-secretase enzyme—

Rapid recall — stems and answers

Which combination of gene, chromosome and mechanism belongs to early-onset familial Alzheimer disease?

B. Presenilin 1 on chromosome 14, coding for γ-secretase, increasing Aβ production — 5–10% inherited, early onset: associated with gene mutations or chromosomal alterations that increase production of Aβ peptide — amyloid precursor protein on chromosome 21 (Down syndrome), and presenilin 1 and 2 gene mutations on chromosomes 14 and 1 which code for the γ-secretase enzyme. ApoE ε4 on chromosome 19 belongs to the 90–95% sporadic, late-onset group, where ε4 homozygotes have a 95% chance by age 85.

Which secretase combination generates the amyloidogenic product, and which is non-amyloidogenic?

B. β-secretase + γ-secretase gives the Aβ peptide (amyloidogenic); α-secretase + γ-secretase gives a non-amyloidogenic product — APP is broken down into different fragments by a group of secretases — β, α, γ. 1. α-secretase + γ-secretase = soluble fragment + non-amyloidogenic breakdown product. 2. β-secretase + γ-secretase = soluble fragment + Aβ peptide (amyloidogenic breakdown product). The Aβ monomer then forms oligomers → aggregates and fibrils → neuronal damage and extracellular plaques, and the oligomers activate kinases that hyperphosphorylate tau.

A 58-year-old develops disinhibition, socially inappropriate behaviour and progressive word-finding difficulty; memory is relatively preserved. Imaging shows knife-edge frontal and temporal atrophy. What is the diagnosis, and which two proteins define its subtypes?

B. Frontotemporal lobar degeneration; tau (Pick bodies) or TDP-43 — Frontotemporal lobar degeneration: disorders preferentially affecting the frontal and/or temporal lobes; tends to present at younger ages (differentiate from Alzheimer disease); progressive behavioral changes or language problems depending on the lobe affected primarily → memory disturbances occur later (differentiate from Alzheimer disease). FTLD-tau: accumulation of tau neurofibrillary tangles; one subtype is Pick disease, where Pick bodies are seen intracellularly. FTLD-TDP-43: intracellular accumulation of TDP-43, a DNA/RNA binding protein. Grossly: lobar atrophy with knifelike thinning of the gyri.

A man develops visual hallucinations and fluctuating cognition eight months after the onset of a resting tremor. What does the lecture call this, and what is the histological hallmark?

B. Lewy body dementia; Lewy bodies — cytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions of α-synuclein — When dementia arises within 1 year of motor symptoms it is Lewy body dementia; if more than 1 year apart it is called dementia secondary to Parkinson disease. The hallmark: "Lewy bodies" are found in the remaining neurons of the substantia nigra — single or multiple, cytoplasmic, eosinophilic inclusions; on ultrastructure, filaments composed of α-synuclein. Grossly there is pallor and atrophy of the substantia nigra.

A 38-year-old with chorea has a father who developed the same illness at 52. Which genetic principle explains the earlier onset, and what is the threshold repeat number?

B. Repeat expansion occurs during spermatogenesis, so paternal transmission is associated with earlier onset; 36 or more CAG repeats on chromosome 4 — CAG repeats on chromosome 4: 6–35 repeats is normal; 36 or more repeats causes Huntington disease. There is an inverse relationship between repeat number and age of onset (longer repeats = earlier onset). Repeat expansions occur during spermatogenesis → paternal transmission is associated with earlier onset in the next generation. The pathologic hallmark is intranuclear inclusions containing ubiquitinated huntingtin, and the gross picture is marked caudate atrophy with dilated lateral and third ventricles.

A 55-year-old has asymmetric hand weakness, tongue fasciculations, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response. Sensation, cognition and eye movements are normal. What is spared, and what is the prognosis?

B. Intellect, sensation, sphincter control and eye movements are spared; life expectancy 2–5 years after onset — Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Intellect, sensation, sphincter control and eye movements are spared. Manifests in the fifth decade or later; life expectancy 2–5 years after onset; males > females; most cases sporadic, ~10% familial with autosomal dominant inheritance. The mixed picture is diagnostic: loss of upper motor neurons → paresis, spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign and degeneration of the lateral corticospinal tract; loss of lower motor neurons → muscle atrophy, weakness and fasciculations.

Which pairing of disease and basal ganglia consequence is correct?

B. Parkinson's — decreased intentional movement from death of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra; Huntington's — increased unintentional movement from death of striatal cholinergic interneurons and GABAergic neurons — Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease both affect neurons in the basal ganglia — Parkinson's disease causes decreased intentional movement and Huntington's disease increased unintentional movement. Huntington disease: death of striatal cholinergic interneurons and death of striatal GABAergic neurons. Parkinson's disease: death of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. The lecture's mnemonic is CAG — Caudate loses Acetylcholine and GABA.

Which statement about neurofibrillary tangles is correct?

B. They develop intracellularly from hyperphosphorylated tau and persist extracellularly after neuronal death; tau gene mutations increase the risk of frontotemporal lobar degeneration — Neurofibrillary tangles: aggregation of tau (develop intracellularly) → persist extracellularly after neuronal death. Mutations in the tau protein gene increase risk for frontotemporal lobar degeneration. The mechanism: tau is a microtubule-associated protein present in axons; Aβ oligomers activate kinases → hyperphosphorylate tau → it loses its ability to bind microtubules → aggregates into tangles. Plaques, by contrast, are extracellular Aβ.

NicotineFull agonist at nicotinic receptors ON dopamine neurons — direct stimulationMild: irritability and sleeplessness — yet among the most addictive drugsNicotine replacement; bupropion (avoid if seizure risk); varenicline — partial agonist with greater affinity than nicotine
Opioidsμ agonism on the GABA interneuron → less GABA → disinhibited dopamineUnpleasant but not life-threatening: dysphoria, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, yawningMethadone or buprenorphine for agonist detoxification; naltrexone after detoxification in highly motivated patients
MarijuanaTHC at CB1 on GABAergic neurons → less GABA → more dopamine; CB1 brain, CB2 immune cells; both Gi-linkedTolerance and mild physical dependenceApproved cannabinoids: dronabinol and nabilone for chemotherapy-induced nausea; dronabinol for AIDS-related anorexia; CBD for Lennox-Gastaut, Dravet and tuberous sclerosis
LSD / mescaline / psilocybinAgonist at 5-HT2 receptorsNo addiction and no withdrawal syndromeBenzodiazepine for severe agitation on a "bad trip"
PCP (and ketamine)Non-competitive NMDA antagonism; also blocks NE and DA reuptake—No specific antidote; parenteral benzodiazepines for violence and for seizures
MDMAReverses transporters with preferential affinity for SERTDepressionWatch for hyperthermia with dehydration (may be fatal), serotonin syndrome and seizures
InhalantsN₂O — euphoria, analgesia, then loss of consciousness; solvents — exhilaration and light-headedness; nitrites — smooth muscle dilationNitrites are not addictiveSolvents implicated in cancer, cardiotoxicity, neuropathies and hepatotoxicity; 100% N₂O may cause asphyxia and death

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Naltrexone's mechanism drawn out
  • Ethanol evokes release of endorphins → activation of μ receptors inhibits the GABAergic interneuron → less GABA → the dopaminergic mesolimbic neuron is disinhibited → more dopamine. Naltrexone blocks the μ receptor → the interneuron is disinhibited → more GABA → less dopamine. That is route 1 of the addiction diagram, run forwards and then backwards.
Exam Lock
Dependence is not addiction
  • A patient on a β-blocker or a corticosteroid is physically dependent and will have a withdrawal syndrome if it is stopped abruptly — but has none of the four behaviours that define addiction. Getting this distinction right is the point of PHAR.00059, and it is the clinical reason opioid analgesia is not the same as opioid addiction.
Exam Lock
Nystagmus in both planes is the PCP giveaway
  • Both vertical AND horizontal nystagmus in an agitated, violent patient with hypertension, hyperthermia and rigidity is PCP, and the treatment is benzodiazepines for both the behaviour and the seizures — there is no specific antidote. Note the hyperthermia trio again: PCP, MDMA and serotonin syndrome all kill through temperature.
Trap
Cocaine blocks the transporter; amphetamine reverses it
  • Both raise synaptic dopamine, but by opposite manoeuvres. Cocaine sits on DAT and stops reuptake. Amphetamine is carried IN by DAT, empties the vesicles via VMAT, and then makes DAT run backwards. That is why amphetamine's effect survives vesicle depletion and cocaine's does not.

Pattern tables

The four terms — and why they are not synonyms

TermDefinition (verbatim)
AbuseThe excessive self-administration of any substance for nonmedical purposes.
AddictionBehaviors that include one or more of the following: impaired control over drug use · compulsive use · continued use despite harm · craving.
DependenceA state of adaptation manifested by the drug-class-specific withdrawal syndrome. The withdrawal syndrome can be produced by abrupt cessation, rapid dose reduction, or administration of an antagonist.
Withdrawal syndromePhysiological and behavioral changes directly related to sudden cessation or reduction in use of a drug to which the body has become adapted.
ToleranceA state of adaptation in which exposure to a drug induces changes that result in a diminution of one or more of the drug's effects over time. Tolerance may occur to both the desired and undesired effects of drugs, and may develop at different rates for different effects.

Cocaine and the amphetamines

CocaineAmphetamines
ScheduleSchedule II (DEA)Schedule II (DEA)
MechanismInhibits dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake. Prolongation of dopaminergic effects in the brain's limbic system produces the intense euphoria.Increase release of catecholamines; also weak inhibitors of MAO; possible direct catecholaminergic agonists. Taken up into neurons by biogenic amine transporters; once inside, they interfere with VMAT, depleting synaptic vesicles; cytoplasmic dopamine rises and is released into the synapse by reversal of the DAT.
CNS actionsStimulation of cortex and brainstem; increases mental awareness and produces a feeling of well-being and euphoria; paranoia may occur after repeated doses; at high doses tremors and convulsions, followed by respiratory and vasomotor depression.Behavioral effects similar to cocaine, due to release of dopamine; increased alertness, decreased fatigue, depressed appetite and insomnia; at high doses, psychosis and convulsions.
Sympathetic actionsPeripherally potentiates the action of norepinephrine → tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis and diaphoresisActivate receptors through norepinephrine release
PharmacokineticsAbuse liability and dependence are greatest with IV injection and freebase ("crack") smoking. Rapidly de-esterified and demethylated to benzoylecgonine, which is excreted in the urine — detection of this substance in the urine identifies a user.—
WithdrawalDysphoria, depression, sleepiness, fatigue, cocaine craving and bradycardia. Cocaine withdrawal is generally mild; treatment of withdrawal symptoms is usually not required.Tolerance can be marked. An abstinence syndrome can occur: increased appetite, sleepiness, exhaustion and mental depression. Antidepressants may be indicated.
Therapeutic usesMany agents, mainly antidepressants and dopamine agonists, have been tested as treatments for cocaine abuse. None have demonstrated clear efficacy.Attention deficit syndrome: amphetamine and methylphenidate. Narcolepsy: amphetamine and methylphenidate. Also appetite control.

Psychedelic agents

AgentMechanismPresentation and management
LSD (with mescaline and psilocybin)The hallucinogenic actions of LSD appear to be mediated by AGONIST effects at 5-HT2 receptors in the CNS.Patients present with a combination of somatic and psychomimetic symptoms. Somatic symptoms are due to sympathomimetic effects: mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, increased body temperature, flushing, sweating, tremors and piloerection. Users may require medical attention because of "bad trips"; severe agitation may require treatment with a benzodiazepine. LSD does not cause addiction and there is no withdrawal syndrome.
Phencyclidine (PCP)The dissociative properties of PCP are due to NON-COMPETITIVE ANTAGONISM at NMDA receptors. It also blocks reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, causes cholinergic and anticholinergic effects, and has actions at nicotinic and opioid receptors. *Originally used as an anesthetic; withdrawn in humans due to adverse effects; retained in veterinary practice.*Patients alternate from agitation to stupor. Paranoid behavior and extreme violence may occur unexpectedly. Both vertical and horizontal nystagmus is common. Pupils may be large or small. Hypertension, tachycardia and hyperthermia. Muscle rigidity, dystonias and seizures. Hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis resulting in myoglobinuria and renal failure. There is no specific antidote; violent psychotic behavior requires sedation with parenteral benzodiazepines, and seizures should be treated with benzodiazepines. Ketamine shares many structural, pharmacologic and clinical characteristics with PCP and is a popular drug of abuse.
MDMA ("ecstasy")A derivative of amphetamine. Like amphetamines, MDMA causes release of biogenic amines by reversing the action of their transporters; it has preferential affinity for SERT and therefore most strongly increases the concentration of serotonin in the synapse.Acute effects: enhanced sensory perception, increased extroversion, emotional warmth, empathy. Adverse effects: tachycardia, dry mouth, jaw clenching, muscle aches; at higher doses visual hallucinations, agitation, hyperthermia and panic attacks. Hyperthermia, along with dehydration, may be fatal. Other complications include serotonin syndrome and seizures. Withdrawal is characterized by depression.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A patient on long-term propranolol develops tachycardia and tremor when it is stopped abruptly. Which term does this lecture apply, and which does it NOT?

B. Physical dependence with a withdrawal syndrome; not addiction — Dependence: a state of adaptation manifested by the drug-class-specific withdrawal syndrome... Dependence and tolerance are normal responses that often occur with the persistent use of certain medications. Physical dependence may develop with chronic use of many classes of medications. These include β-blockers, α2-adrenergic agents, corticosteroids, antidepressants. Addiction requires the behaviours impaired control over drug use, compulsive use, continued use despite harm, craving, none of which are present here.

Sixty hours after his last drink, an alcohol-dependent man becomes disoriented with visual hallucinations, fever and autonomic instability. What is this, and which agents are preferred?

B. Delirium tremens; long half-life benzodiazepines — diazepam and chlordiazepoxide — The lecture's timeline: withdrawal begins with tremor, nausea and vomiting, sweating, agitation and anxiety, may be followed by hallucinations, generalized seizures may appear after 24–48 h, and after 48–72 h delirium tremens may appear. Management: long half-life benzodiazepines are the preferred agents — diazepam and chlordiazepoxide — because their long half-life makes withdrawal smoother and rebound symptoms less likely; lorazepam and oxazepam are intermediate-acting and may be preferable in the elderly and those with liver failure.

Which alcohol pharmacotherapy works by blocking μ opioid receptors, and how does that reduce dopamine release?

B. Naltrexone; ethanol-evoked endorphins normally inhibit the GABAergic interneuron, so blocking μ receptors restores GABA release and re-inhibits the mesolimbic dopamine neuron — Alcohol releases endogenous opioids, which activate μ receptors, resulting in dopamine release. Administration of the opioid antagonist naltrexone reduces craving for alcohol and decreases relapse to heavy drinking. The lecture animates it: ethanol → endorphins → μ activation inhibits the GABAergic interneuron → less GABA → dopaminergic mesolimbic neuron disinhibited → more dopamine. Naltrexone blocks μ → the interneuron is disinhibited → more GABA → less dopamine.

Which mechanism distinguishes amphetamine from cocaine?

B. Amphetamine is taken into the neuron, depletes vesicles via VMAT and reverses the DAT; cocaine blocks reuptake at DAT, NET and SERT — Cocaine inhibits dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake. Amphetamines are taken up into neurons by biogenic amine transporters; once in the neuron, amphetamines interfere with the VMAT, depleting synaptic vesicles; levels of dopamine in the cytoplasm increase and are released into the synapse by reversal of the DAT. Amphetamines are also weak inhibitors of MAO and possible direct catecholaminergic agonists.

A urine screen identifies benzoylecgonine. Which drug does this indicate, and which routes carry the greatest abuse liability?

B. Cocaine; IV injection and freebase ("crack") smoking — Cocaine is rapidly de-esterified and demethylated to benzoylecgonine, which is excreted in the urine; detection of this substance in the urine identifies a user. Abuse liability and dependence are greatest with IV injection and freebase ("crack") smoking. Withdrawal is dysphoria, depression, sleepiness, fatigue, craving and bradycardia — generally mild, and no agent has demonstrated clear efficacy for cocaine addiction.

A patient wants help stopping smoking but has a history of head injury with post-traumatic seizures. Which agent should be avoided, and which acts as a nicotinic partial agonist?

B. Avoid bupropion because of seizure risk; varenicline is the partial agonist that binds nicotinic receptors with greater affinity than nicotine — Bupropion is associated with seizures: patients with a history of seizure, stroke, brain tumor, brain surgery, or severe head injury should not take bupropion. Varenicline is a partial agonist at neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the CNS; it binds to the nicotinic receptor with greater affinity than nicotine, thus reducing the reward of smoking. The most common adverse effects are nausea.

Which cannabinoid receptor mediates the psychological effects of THC, and how does THC raise dopamine?

B. CB1 in the brain; THC binding to CB1 on GABAergic neurons decreases GABA release, disinhibiting dopaminergic neurons — Two cannabinoid receptor subtypes: CB1 and CB2; both are Gi protein-linked. CB1 receptors are found primarily in the brain and mediate the psychological effects of THC; CB2 receptors are present mainly on immune cells. CB1 receptors are present in GABAergic neurons; binding of THC to CB1 receptors decreases GABA release; decrease of GABA release disinhibits dopaminergic neurons, resulting in increased dopamine release.

An agitated, violent patient has both vertical and horizontal nystagmus, hypertension, hyperthermia and muscle rigidity, and later develops myoglobinuria. Which drug, and what is the treatment?

B. Phencyclidine; there is no specific antidote — parenteral benzodiazepines for the violent behaviour and for seizures — Phencyclidine: patients alternate from agitation to stupor; paranoid behavior and extreme violence may occur unexpectedly; both vertical and horizontal nystagmus is common; pupils may be large or small; hypertension, tachycardia and hyperthermia; muscle rigidity, dystonias and seizures; hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis resulting in myoglobinuria and renal failure. There is no specific antidote for PCP; extreme violent psychotic behavior requires sedation with parenteral benzodiazepines; seizures should be treated with benzodiazepines. Its dissociative properties are non-competitive antagonism at NMDA receptors.

Which statement about LSD is correct?

B. Its hallucinogenic actions are mediated by agonist effects at 5-HT2 receptors; it does not cause addiction and there is no withdrawal syndrome — The hallucinogenic actions of LSD appear to be mediated by agonist effects at 5-HT2 receptors in the CNS. LSD does not cause addiction. There is no withdrawal syndrome. The somatic symptoms are due to sympathomimetic effects: mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, increased body temperature, flushing, sweating, tremors and piloerection, and severe agitation may require treatment with a benzodiazepine.

Which inhalant is explicitly described as NOT addictive, and what was its original medical use?

C. Amyl nitrite; treatment of angina — Organic nitrites: amyl nitrite produces dilation of smooth muscle and has been used for treatment of angina. In recent years amyl nitrite and butyl nitrite have been used to enhance erection. They are not addictive. For contrast: nitrous oxide produces euphoria and analgesia and then loss of consciousness, usually taken as 35% N₂O mixed with O₂; administration of 100% N₂O may cause asphyxia and death, and volatile organic solvents are principally used by boys in early teen years from lower socioeconomic classes.

NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors

PATH · Dr. Adesola Adeleye · Department of Pathology · source pp. 2608–2643

EntityKey facts
Multiple sclerosisAutoimmune; activity separated in TIME, lesions separated in SPACE; young adults, F:M 2:1; risks smoking, low vitamin D, migration before puberty, HLA-DRB1 (each *1501 copy ≈ 3× risk), family history; Th1 → IFN-γ → macrophages; Th17 → IL-17 → neutrophils; plaques near ventricles, optic nerves, chiasm, brainstem, cerebellum, cord; CSF oligoclonal bands; periventricular plaques on MRI
ADEM / AHEMPost-infectious, monophasic; ADEM non-localizing over 1–2 weeks, rarely fatal; AHEM more devastating, children and young adults, rapid progression
Central pontine myelinolysisNon-immune oligodendrocyte damage after rapid correction of CHRONIC (> 2 days) hyponatraemia → quadriplegia, bulbar palsy, locked-in syndrome (only eye movement spared); extrapontine forms exist
Wernicke / KorsakoffThiamine (B1) deficiency; triad of confusion, ocular palsies and ataxia; ETKAC > 1.25; haemorrhage and necrosis of the MAMILLARY BODIES; thiamine reverses it, delay leaves Korsakoff — no new memories and confabulation
AlcoholPeripheral neuropathy, cerebellar degeneration (atrophic anterior vermis), withdrawal seizures, Wernicke-Korsakoff
Pilocytic astrocytomaGrade I; cerebellum; BRAF translocation; cystic with a mural nodule; ROSENTHAL FIBERS
IDH-mutant astrocytomaGrade II–III; hemispheres; IDH1/IDH2 driver, TP53 and ATRX; infiltrative with loss of the corticomedullary junction
GlioblastomaGrade IV; IDH wild-type; EGFR/PDGFR amplification, TP53, TERT promoter, CDKN2A deletion; "butterfly glioma" crossing the midline with haemorrhage and necrosis; microvascular proliferation and PSEUDOPALISADING NECROSIS
Oligodendroglioma4th–5th decade; frontal/temporal; seizures for years; 1p/19q codeletion and IDH mutation both good prognosis; "fried egg" cells and thin-walled capillaries; calcification
Ependymoma4th ventricle in the first 2 decades; spinal cord in adults (NF2); true rosettes and perivascular pseudorosettes
MedulloblastomaMost common CNS malignancy in children; cerebellum; Wnt-β-catenin and MYC; small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes; grade IV but very radiosensitive — 75% alive at 5 years
MeningiomaArachnoid meningothelial cells attached to dura; adults; whorls and psammoma bodies; chromosome 22q; multiple meningiomas + 8th nerve schwannoma = NF2
SchwannomaVestibular 8th nerve at the cerebellopontine angle; hearing loss and tinnitus; NF2, chromosome 22q; Antoni A and B with Verocay bodies
Metastases25–50% of intracranial tumours; lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, GIT; sharply demarcated masses at the grey–white junction; paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, limbic encephalitis, sensory neuropathy

Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
Rosettes are not one word
  • Homer Wright rosettes → medulloblastoma (cells around a fibrillary centre). True rosettes with a gland-like central lumen and perivascular pseudorosettes → ependymoma. "Fried egg" cells with perinuclear halos → oligodendroglioma. Three patterns, three tumours, and each is the fastest route to the answer on a histology stem.
Exam Lock
Time and space — then confirm with two tests
  • The definition itself is the diagnostic criterion: activity separated in time, lesions separated in space. The two confirmatory findings are oligoclonal bands in the CSF and periventricular white matter plaques on MRI.
Exam Lock
Wernicke is reversible; Korsakoff is what is left behind
  • Treatment with thiamine reverses the Wernicke triad. Delayed treatment leaves the irreversible memory disturbance of Korsakoff's syndrome — no new memories and confabulation. The lesion to name is haemorrhage and necrosis of the mamillary bodies.
Trap
The two-day rule is why acute hyponatraemia is safe to correct quickly
  • Osmotic demyelination needs a cell that has already exported its osmolytes — which takes about two days. That is the mechanistic reason the syndrome is a complication of chronic hyponatraemia only, and it is exactly the kind of "why" the exam builds a question around.
Trap
Chromosome 22q appears twice — and links them
  • Meningioma and schwannoma both map to chromosome 22q, and multiple meningiomas plus an eighth nerve schwannoma, or glial tumours, define neurofibromatosis type 2 — which also explains the adult spinal ependymoma association a slide earlier. One syndrome, three tumours.

Rapid recall — stems and answers

A 28-year-old woman has had optic neuritis, and two years later develops leg spasticity. MRI shows periventricular white matter plaques. Which CSF finding supports the diagnosis, and which T-cell subsets drive it?

B. Oligoclonal bands; Th1 releasing IFN-γ and Th17 releasing IL-17 — Multiple sclerosis — disease activity separated in time, producing white matter lesions separated in space. CSF analysis: elevated protein with increased immunoglobulin ("oligoclonal bands") and moderate pleocytosis; MRI shows white matter plaques, most commonly periventricular. Pathogenesis: Th1 and Th17 T cells react against myelin antigens; Th1 releases IFN-γ which attracts and activates macrophages, and Th17 releases IL-17 which attracts neutrophils → inflammation causing demyelination.

A patient's chronic hyponatraemia of 112 mmol/L is corrected to 132 over 8 hours. Two days later she develops quadriplegia and bulbar palsy with preserved eye movements. What is the mechanism, and why does chronicity matter?

B. Osmotic demyelination — oligodendrocytes have exported their osmolytes over ~2 days, so rapid correction drives fluid out, causing cell contraction and apoptosis — Central pontine myelinolysis: non-immune damage to oligodendrocytes of the pons typically after sudden correction of hyponatremia, that may result in a rapidly evolving quadriplegia and bulbar palsy → locked-in syndrome (only eye movement unaffected)... Only occurs in chronic hyponatremia (> 2 days) because osmolytes — potassium, chloride and organic osmolytes such as glucose and glutamine — are pushed out of the cell over a period of 2 days... When hyponatremia is corrected rapidly, there are no osmolytes within the cell to keep fluid from rapidly moving to the extracellular compartment → oligodendrocyte contraction and apoptosis.

A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder has confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Which structure shows haemorrhage and necrosis, and what happens if treatment is delayed?

B. Mamillary bodies; irreversible Korsakoff's syndrome with inability to form new memories and confabulation — Wernicke encephalopathy is characterized by the triad: encephalopathy presenting with confusion, ocular palsies, and ataxia... Pathological features include foci of hemorrhage and necrosis most commonly in the mamillary bodies... Treatment with thiamine reverses these deficits; delayed treatment leads to an irreversible memory disturbance called Korsakoff's syndrome — no new memories and confabulation. The laboratory marker is ETKAC > 1.25.

A 62-year-old has a rapidly enlarging hemispheric mass that crosses the corpus callosum with haemorrhage and necrosis. Histology shows microvascular proliferation and tumour nuclei arrayed around anucleate necrotic zones. Which tumour, grade and genetics?

B. Glioblastoma, IDH wild-type; grade IV; EGFR and PDGFR amplification, TP53 mutation, TERT promoter mutation, CDKN2A deletion — Glioblastoma, IDH wild-type — grade IV; cerebral hemispheres; EGFR and PDGFR gene amplification, TP53 mutation (resistant to apoptosis), telomerase mutation, biallelic deletion of CDKN2A, TERT promoter mutation; gross: infiltrating tumor with hemorrhage and necrosis crossing the midline ("butterfly glioma"); histology: microvascular proliferation with areas of "pseudo"-palisading necrosis.

A 7-year-old has a cerebellar cystic lesion with a mural nodule; histology shows bipolar cells with hair-like processes and brightly eosinophilic corkscrew inclusions. Which tumour and which genetic change?

B. Pilocytic astrocytoma; BRAF translocation — Pilocytic astrocytoma — grade I; cerebellum; BRAF translocations; gross: cystic lesion with a mural nodule; histology: bipolar cells with thin hair-like ("pilo") processes in a fibrillary meshwork with eosinophilic rod-like structures — ROSENTHAL FIBERS, seen at low magnification as a biphasic pattern with alternating loose and compact regions. It is one of the three commonest paediatric tumours, with medulloblastoma and ependymoma, all in the infratentorial posterior fossa.

Which histological feature belongs to ependymoma?

B. Perivascular pseudorosettes and true rosettes with a gland-like lumen — Ependymoma microscopy: regular cells with round-to-oval nuclei and abundant granular chromatin; variable fibrillary background; cells may form rosettes with long delicate processes extending into the lumen ("canals"); also seen are "pseudo"-rosettes which are perivascular, with tumor cells around vessels. Homer Wright rosettes → medulloblastoma; Rosenthal fibres → pilocytic astrocytoma; psammoma bodies → meningioma; Verocay bodies → schwannoma.

A 40-year-old has bilateral vestibular schwannomas and two meningiomas. Which chromosome and syndrome, and what other CNS tumour is associated?

B. Chromosome 22q; neurofibromatosis type 2; spinal ependymoma in adults — Meningioma: multiple meningiomas + 8th nerve schwannoma or glial tumors → neurofibromatosis type 2; genetics: chromosome 22q. Schwannoma: most commonly the vestibular portion of the eighth nerve at the cerebellopontine angle; associated with NF2; genetics: chromosome 22q. And adult ependymomas are mostly in the spinal cord, with an association with neurofibromatosis 2.

Which statement about metastatic brain tumours matches this lecture?

B. They account for 25–50% of intracranial tumours and form sharply demarcated masses at the grey-white matter junction; commonest primaries are lung, breast, melanoma, kidney and GIT — Most commonly metastatic carcinomas; account for 25% to 50% of intracranial tumors; most common primary sites: lung, breast, skin (melanoma), kidney and GIT; metastases form sharply demarcated masses (usually multiple but can be single) at the grey-white matter junction. Paraneoplastic syndromes can involve the central and peripheral nervous system; the common pattern is cerebellar degeneration (ataxia), limbic encephalitis (dementia) and sensory neuropathy.

Which finding carries a GOOD prognosis in oligodendroglioma?

B. Codeletion of 1p and 19q, and IDH1 or IDH2 mutation — Oligodendroglioma genetics: codeletion of 1p and 19q — good prognosis; IDH1 or IDH2 mutation — good prognosis. The tumour presents in the 4th–5th decade with several years of antecedent neurological symptoms, especially seizures, most often in the frontal and temporal lobes, and shows round nuclei with clear cytoplasm forming halos ("fried egg") and thin-walled capillaries with calcification on gross examination.
