Also flagged in this lecture

Bottom Line
The source deck spells the two mnemonics down the middle of the slide as letters: S-I-G E C-A-P-S on the depression side and D-I-G F-A-S-T on the manic side. Learn them as letters — the DSM counts symptoms, and you will be counting under time pressure.
    Bottom Line
    PDD trades severity for chronicity: fewer symptoms (2 beyond low mood), far longer clock (2 years). MDD trades the other way — more symptoms, only 2 weeks.
      Bottom Line
      Count discipline: GAD counts 3, panic counts 4. The two numbers are the single highest-yield fact on these two slides and they are trivially swappable under exam pressure.
        Exam Lock
        MDD must have
        • 5 symptoms from the depression list
        • and at least 1 is either ↓ mood / anhedonia
        • >2 weeks
        Exam Lock
        The cyclothymia clock
        • >2 years of oscillation, and
        • never symptom-free for more than 2 months — the gaps are what the criterion is measuring
        Exam Lock
        The only thing separating the two
        • Acute Stress disorder: >3 days but <1-month disturbance
        • Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: >1-month disturbance
        Trap
        Five symptoms is not enough on its own. A patient with insomnia, ↓ energy, ↓ concentration, guilt and weight loss for a month has five symptoms and no ↓ mood and no anhedonia — that is not MDD. One of the two gateway symptoms must be present.
          Trap
          Bipolar I does not require a depressive episode. One manic episode of >1 week is sufficient. Bipolar II is the mirror image: the depressive episode is mandatory and a full manic episode is disqualifying.
            Trap
            The two mood-plus-psychosis diagnoses are separated by when the psychosis happens. In schizoaffective disorder psychosis persists in the absence of the mood episode; if psychosis occurs only during mood episodes, it is a mood disorder with psychotic features.
              Trap
              Do not read schizoid or schizotypal as mild schizophrenia. Schizotypal has magical thinking with no hallucinations and no response to external stimuli — the absence of true psychosis is exactly what keeps it a personality disorder.

                Rapid recall — stems and answers

                A 34-year-old reports 3 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, 6 kg weight loss, early-morning waking, poor concentration and guilt. TSH is normal and she takes no substances. Which criterion set does she satisfy?

                B. Major depressive disorder — MDD must have 5 symptoms, at least 1 of which is either ↓ mood or anhedonia, for >2 weeks. She has six symptoms including both gateway symptoms, over three weeks. PDD would require ≥2 years; bipolar II requires hypomania AND MDD.

                A 41-year-old man has had persistently low mood for most of the day, more days than not, for the last 3 years, with low energy and poor concentration but no episode ever meeting full MDD criteria. Which is correct?

                B. Persistent depressive disorder — PDD: ↓ mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years, + 2 other symptoms. The diagnosis is defined by chronicity, not by severity — which is why students who count only symptoms miss it.

                A 22-year-old has an 8-day episode of elevated mood, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep and reckless spending. He has never had a depressive episode. Which diagnosis fits?

                C. Bipolar I disorder — Bipolar I must have ↑ mood and 3 other symptoms, >1 week. He has grandiosity, decreased need for sleep and painful-consequence activity over 8 days. A depressive episode is NOT required for bipolar I. Bipolar II would require hypomania AND MDD, and never a manic episode.

                A 29-year-old woman is referred for 'depression'. She has fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance and low mood for 4 months. Which step does the DLA place BEFORE assigning a psychiatric diagnosis?

                B. Assess for thyroid disease — Determine the extent to which a general medical illness may contribute to the signs and symptoms of a psychiatric disorder. The source slides print Thyroid disease? directly beneath the depression criteria. Weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation are the bodily signs that accompany the classic psychiatric presentation here.

                Which feature would EXCLUDE bipolar II disorder?

                C. A single manic episode lasting 9 days — Bipolar II must have hypomania AND MDD, and the patient must NEVER have had a manic episode. A 9-day manic episode is >1 week and reclassifies the patient as bipolar I.

                A 24-year-old has had auditory hallucinations, disorganized speech and avolition for 10 weeks. Urine drug screen is negative. Which diagnosis fits the duration?

                B. Schizophreniform disorder — Schizophreniform = >1 month but <6 months. Ten weeks is past the 1-month line and well short of 6 months. Brief psychotic episode is >1 day but <1 month; schizophrenia requires >6 months.

                A patient has had 2 years of delusions and negative symptoms. Manic episodes have occurred concurrently at times, but the delusions clearly persist during long periods when mood is normal. Which is correct?

                C. Schizoaffective disorder — Schizoaffective disorder: an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode concurrent with Criterion A of schizophrenia. The discriminator is that psychosis persists when the mood episode is absent — otherwise it would be a mood disorder with psychotic features.

                Which of the following is listed by the DSM as a NEGATIVE symptom in Criterion A?

                C. Diminished purposeful activities (avolition) — Criterion A lists delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized or abnormal motor behavior, and negative symptoms — diminished emotional expression and diminished purposeful activities (avolition). The other four options are all *positive* or motor features.

                A 38-year-old reports uncontrollable worry on most days for the past 9 months with restlessness, muscle tension and sleep disturbance. Which diagnosis fits?

                B. Generalized anxiety disorder — GAD: occurring most days and for at least 6 months, cannot control worry, 3 or more symptoms from restlessness, easily fatigued, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance. She has three. Panic disorder would need discrete unexpected attacks with 4 or more symptoms.

                Three weeks after surviving a motor-vehicle collision, a 27-year-old has flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance of driving and hypervigilance. Which diagnosis applies today?

                B. Acute stress disorder — Acute stress disorder = >3 days but <1-month disturbance; PTSD = >1-month disturbance. At three weeks the symptom set is identical to PTSD but the clock has not run out, so the diagnosis is acute stress disorder.

                A patient has no friends, avoids all social invitations, and states he simply prefers to be alone and is content that way. He is not distressed by the isolation. Which personality disorder fits?

                B. Schizoid — Schizoid: happy. Loners. Do not want any relationships. The absence of a wish for relationships is the discriminator. Avoidant patients are also loners but fear rejection and criticism — they want the relationships.

                A 45-year-old is rigid, perfectionistic and preoccupied with rules and order, but reports no intrusive thoughts and performs no rituals. Which is correct?

                B. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder — Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (Cluster C): rigid, perfectionist — no intrusive thoughts or forced compulsions. That parenthetical on the source slide is the whole discriminator against OCD, which requires true obsessions and compulsions.

                A 30-year-old has recurrent unexpected episodes of intense fear with palpitations, sweating, dyspnoea and a fear of dying, peaking within minutes, followed by 6 weeks of constant worry about the next episode and avoidance of the mall. What must be considered before the diagnosis is assigned?

                B. Whether a general medical condition explains the symptoms — The source slide prints General medical condition? under panic disorder — thyrotoxicosis, pheochromocytoma, arrhythmia and asthma all reproduce the attack. Her presentation otherwise satisfies ≥4 symptoms followed by 1 month of worry / maladaptive change.

                Which cluster and mnemonic pairing is correct?

                C. Cluster C — anxious or fearful — WORRIED — Cluster A — odd, eccentric; unable to develop meaningful relationships — WIRED. Cluster B — dramatic, emotional, or erratic — WACKY. Cluster C — anxious or fearful — WORRIED.

                NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)

                Source notes

                Source note
                The source deck carries this small group as image-only slides — a title, a slide number and a photomicrograph, with no written text. Reproduced here are the verbatim objectives and slide list, plus, for each numbered slide, the diagnostic criteria you are expected to state at the scope, drawn from the corresponding NCRS lectures already in this deck (Nephrotic Syndrome, Nephritic Syndrome, Tubulointerstitial Disease, Vascular Disease, UTI and Renal Tumors).

                  Also flagged in this lecture

                  Bottom Line
                  On any glomerular slide, work the same four questions in order: (1) is the glomerulus hypercellular or not? (2) is the GBM thickened? (3) are there crescents? (4) what does immunofluorescence show — linear, granular, or nothing? Those four answers separate every diagnosis in this session.
                    Bottom Line
                    Because the lesion is focal, an inadequate biopsy that samples only spared glomeruli reads as minimal change disease. The steroid-unresponsive "MCD" is FSGS until proven otherwise.
                      Bottom Line
                      Glomeruli are spared in acute pyelonephritis. If a slide shows heavy interstitial neutrophils *and* glomerular damage, reconsider — you are probably not looking at pyelonephritis.
                        Bottom Line
                        Renal cell carcinoma is the tumour that invades a vein. That single gross feature — a tumour thrombus climbing the renal vein into the IVC — separates it from almost everything else you will be shown.
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children
                          • Selective proteinuria (albumin)
                          • Dramatic response to corticosteroids
                          • Secondary associations: Hodgkin lymphoma, NSAIDs
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, and in African-American patients
                          • Non-selective proteinuria; poor steroid response; progresses to chronic kidney disease
                          • Secondary: HIV, heroin, sickle cell disease, obesity, reduced nephron mass
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Primary: autoantibody against phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) on podocytes — ~75%
                          • Secondary: hepatitis B, SLE, solid tumours (lung, colon), drugs (penicillamine, NSAIDs, captopril)
                          • Nephrotic syndrome in the adult; the most thrombogenic of the nephrotic lesions
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Child, 1–4 weeks after a group A streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection
                          • Nephritic syndrome: haematuria (cola-coloured urine), RBC casts, hypertension, periorbital oedema, mild proteinuria
                          • ↓ serum C3; ↑ ASO / anti-DNase B titres
                          • Excellent prognosis in children; ~95% recover
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Presents as a nephrotic–nephritic hybrid; slow progression to chronic renal failure
                          • Type I: immune-complex — hepatitis C (± cryoglobulins), hepatitis B, SLE, chronic infection
                          • Type II: C3 nephritic factor — an autoantibody stabilising C3 convertase → persistent complement activation and a persistently LOW C3
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Ascending infection — E. coli >> Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter
                          • Fever, costovertebral angle tenderness, pyuria and WBC casts — the cast is what locates the infection in the kidney rather than the bladder
                          • Predisposing: vesicoureteral reflux, obstruction, instrumentation, diabetes, pregnancy
                          • Complications: papillary necrosis, pyonephrosis, perinephric abscess
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Presents in the 4th–5th decade: flank pain, palpable kidneys, haematuria, hypertension
                          • Progresses to end-stage renal disease in ~50%
                          • Contrast autosomal recessive (ARPKD, PKHD1, chromosome 6) — presents in infancy, smooth-surfaced kidneys with radially arranged elongated cysts, with congenital hepatic fibrosis
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Genetics: clear cell — VHL gene on chromosome 3p (sporadic and von Hippel–Lindau); papillary — MET
                          • Risk factors: smoking (the strongest), obesity, hypertension, chronic dialysis with acquired cystic disease
                          • Classic triad — costovertebral pain, palpable mass, haematuria — present in only ~10%
                          • Paraneoplastic syndromes: EPO → polycythaemia; PTHrP → hypercalcaemia; renin → hypertension; ACTH → Cushing syndrome
                          • Metastasis is characteristically to lung and bone, often as the presenting event
                          Trap
                          A slide that looks normal on light microscopy is the answer, not a failed slide. If LM is normal and the child is nephrotic, you have already made the diagnosis — EM only confirms it.
                            Trap
                            Membranous (thick wall, no hypercellularity, subepithelial deposits) versus membranoproliferative (thick wall plus hypercellularity, tram-tracks, subendothelial deposits). The names are one syllable apart; the slides are not.
                              Trap
                              Crescents are a pattern, not a disease. Light microscopy tells you the kidney is failing fast; only immunofluorescence tells you which of the three mechanisms did it, and therefore whether the treatment is plasmapheresis, immunosuppression, or both.
                                Trap
                                Both slides are labelled "Slide 8" in the source deck. Read the titles: Benign Nephrosclerosis and Malignant Nephrosclerosis are separate images.

                                  Rapid recall — stems and answers

                                  A 5-year-old has periorbital oedema and 4+ proteinuria. The biopsy glomeruli are normal on light microscopy and immunofluorescence is negative. What will electron microscopy show?

                                  B. Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes — Minimal change disease: normal LM, negative IF, and diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on EM. It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and shows a dramatic response to corticosteroids.

                                  Which immunofluorescence finding is expected on Slide 3 (membranous glomerulopathy)?

                                  C. Granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall — Membranous glomerulopathy shows granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall, corresponding to subepithelial electron-dense deposits and the spikes-and-domes silver pattern. Linear IgG is anti-GBM disease; IgA in the mesangium is IgA nephropathy.

                                  A steroid-unresponsive adult nephrotic patient has a biopsy showing sclerosis of part of the tuft in 3 of 20 glomeruli. Which is the diagnosis, and what makes it easy to miss?

                                  B. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — a small biopsy may sample only spared glomeruli — FSGS is FOCAL (some glomeruli) and SEGMENTAL (part of the tuft), so an inadequate biopsy that samples only spared glomeruli reads as minimal change disease. FSGS is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and responds poorly to steroids.

                                  A 7-year-old develops cola-coloured urine and hypertension 2 weeks after a sore throat. Which set of findings is expected?

                                  B. Granular IgG and C3 with subepithelial humps and low C3 — Post-streptococcal GN: diffuse hypercellularity with neutrophils on LM, granular "starry-sky" IgG/C3 on IF, subepithelial humps on EM, and a LOW serum C3 with raised ASO / anti-DNase B. Prognosis in children is excellent.

                                  Slide 5 shows a hypercellular, lobular glomerulus with a double-contoured GBM on silver stain. IF shows C3 alone with no immunoglobulin. Which is correct?

                                  B. Dense deposit disease (MPGN type II), associated with C3 nephritic factor — C3 alone with no immunoglobulin is dense deposit disease (MPGN type II), driven by C3 nephritic factor — an autoantibody that stabilises C3 convertase, producing persistent complement consumption and a ribbon-like dense transformation of the lamina densa on EM. Type I shows granular C3 with IgG and subendothelial deposits.

                                  A 60-year-old with haemoptysis and rapidly rising creatinine has crescents in 70% of glomeruli and SMOOTH LINEAR IgG along the GBM. Which is the diagnosis?

                                  C. Goodpasture syndrome — Linear IgG along the GBM is type I (anti-GBM) RPGN — Goodpasture syndrome, antibodies against the α3 chain of type IV collagen shared by glomerular and alveolar basement membrane, hence lung + kidney. Wegener's / GPA and microscopic polyangiitis are pauci-immune (type III) with little or no staining.

                                  Slide 7 shows patchy interstitial neutrophils, intratubular neutrophil aggregates and normal glomeruli. Which urinary finding corresponds?

                                  C. WBC (leukocyte) casts — Acute pyelonephritis: patchy interstitial suppuration with intratubular neutrophil aggregates forming WBC casts, tubular necrosis, and characteristically spared glomeruli. The WBC cast is what localises the infection to the kidney rather than the bladder. RBC casts are nephritic; muddy-brown granular casts are acute tubular necrosis.

                                  A kidney has a 'flea-bitten' cortical surface, and arterioles show onion-skin thickening and fibrinoid necrosis. Which clinical picture accompanies it?

                                  B. Diastolic pressure >120 mmHg with papilloedema and acute renal failure — Malignant nephrosclerosis: flea-bitten kidney from petechial haemorrhages, hyperplastic "onion-skin" arteriolosclerosis and fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, occurring in malignant hypertension with diastolic pressure >120 mmHg — a medical emergency with papilloedema, encephalopathy and acute renal failure. Benign nephrosclerosis gives a finely granular grain-leather surface and hyaline arteriolosclerosis.

                                  A 45-year-old with bilateral flank masses and hypertension has a sudden severe headache. Which association explains this?

                                  C. Berry aneurysm rupture causing subarachnoid haemorrhage — ADPKD extrarenal associations: liver cysts (most common), berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse and colonic diverticula. A sudden severe headache in a patient with polycystic kidneys is berry aneurysm rupture → subarachnoid haemorrhage. The gene is PKD1 on chromosome 16 in ~85%.

                                  A smoker presents with polycythaemia and a golden-yellow upper-pole renal mass extending into the renal vein. Which gene is most likely involved?

                                  B. VHL on chromosome 3p — Clear cell renal cell carcinoma — the VHL gene on chromosome 3p, sporadic or as part of von Hippel–Lindau. Smoking is the strongest risk factor; the golden-yellow upper-pole mass with renal vein invasion is characteristic, and EPO production causes polycythaemia. MET drives the papillary type.

                                  Which single question, asked at the microscope, separates membranous glomerulopathy from membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis?

                                  B. Is there hypercellularity in addition to the thickened wall? — Both thicken the capillary wall. Membranous: thickened wall with NO hypercellularity, subepithelial deposits, spikes and domes. Membranoproliferative: thickened wall WITH hypercellularity, tram-track double contours, subendothelial (type I) deposits. That is the whole discriminator on light microscopy.

                                  NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness

                                  CLSK · Department of Clinical Skills · Dr. R. Hadmon, Dr. Miguel, Dr. Millette · source pp. 2685–2707

                                  Bottom line

                                  Bottom Line
                                  Heliotrope = violaceous periorbital rash. Gottron's papules = over the knuckles. Shawl sign = over the shoulders and upper back. All three plus proximal symmetric weakness = dermatomyositis, and dermatomyositis is a paraneoplastic flag in an adult — look for the malignancy.

                                    Exam locks

                                    Exam Lock
                                    Core difference
                                    • Compliance → passive obedience
                                    • Adherence → active participation

                                    Traps

                                    Trap
                                    Step 2 is the step students skip. Fatigue and true weakness are different conditions, but they can occur together or be confused. A patient who says "weak" and means "tired" will send you down the wrong VINDICATE branch for the whole encounter.
                                      Trap
                                      This is a counselling objective, not a treatment one. The examinable point is that three plausible-sounding preventive interventions are not blanket recommendations — and you must be able to say why to a patient who has read about them.

                                        Rapid recall — stems and answers

                                        A patient reports weakness that is worse at the end of the day and improves with rest, with ptosis and diplopia. Which localisation does this pattern indicate?

                                        C. Neuromuscular junction — Does your weakness get worse with exercise? → myasthenia gravis (and mitochondrial myopathies). Fatigability with ptosis and diplopia and no sensory loss localises to the neuromuscular junction. Weakness that gets better with exercise is Lambert-Eaton syndrome, classically with small-cell lung cancer.

                                        A 62-year-old has progressive weakness with visible muscle twitching, brisk reflexes and a Babinski sign, plus dysarthria and dysphagia — with entirely normal sensation. Which diagnosis best fits?

                                        B. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis — Fasciculations → ALS, and voice change / trouble swallowing → ALS. The combination of upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski) and lower motor neuron signs (atrophy, fasciculations) with NO sensory loss is the signature. Numbness and tingling with weakness would indicate neurologic disorders such as MS or stroke, not myopathies, and would argue against ALS.

                                        A patient has difficulty standing from a seated position and raising her arms above her head, with a violaceous periorbital rash and papules over the knuckles. What must be actively excluded?

                                        B. An underlying malignancy — Proximal weakness with heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules is dermatomyositis. The workbook lists rash or weight loss as pointing to vasculitis-associated mononeuritis, dermatomyositis, malignancy and hyperthyroidism — and adult dermatomyositis is a paraneoplastic presentation until proven otherwise.

                                        A 58-year-old asymptomatic man asks whether he should have a carotid ultrasound to prevent stroke. Which answer reflects the USPSTF position in Appendix D?

                                        B. Screening is recommended against in asymptomatic adults — The USPSTF recommends AGAINST screening for asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis. Narrowing causes only a small percentage of strokes; endarterectomy carries a 2–3% surgical risk of stroke or death, and no strong evidence shows screening reduces stroke risk overall. *Insufficient evidence* is the USPSTF's position on atrial fibrillation screening, a different question.

                                        Which statement correctly distinguishes adherence from compliance?

                                        B. Compliance means passive obedience; adherence means active participation — Compliance → passive obedience. Adherence → active participation. Compliance implies obedience to medical authority; adherence involves patient responsibility, engagement, and lifestyle change, with patients and providers working together in decision-making.

                                        NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness

                                        CLSK · Department of Clinical Skills · Dr. Miguel and Dr. Millette · source pp. 2708–2755

                                        StageWeakness (SG-11)Numbness (SG-12)
                                        First questionIs this TRUE weakness, or fatigue/asthenia?Where exactly, and how did it evolve? — localization + time course
                                        DistributionBoth sides → cord compression · one limb → nerve/root/MS/stroke · one side + face → stroke/TIA/hemiplegic migraine · proximal → myopathy · distal → neuropathyFace + body one side → brain or brainstem · face only → brainstem or cortex · arm + leg no face → cervical cord or medulla · bilateral → cord or neuropathy · stocking-glove → peripheral neuropathy
                                        Modality / modifierWorse with exercise → myasthenia · better with exercise → Lambert-Eaton · fasciculations → ALSPain and temperature → spinothalamic · vibration and proprioception → dorsal columns · light touch → less localizing
                                        Red flagCranial nerve signs → lesion above the foramen magnum; fever → abscess, venous sinus thrombosis, encephalitisUrinary retention / faecal incontinence → cauda equina syndrome; sensory level → cord
                                        Exam focusCN V, VII, IX/X, XII · full motor, reflexes, gait, sensation, coordinationLower-limb sensation (light touch, pain, vibration, proprioception) · lower-limb motor and reflexes · gait · heel-to-shin
                                        Then the sameProblem representation → illness script → ranked differential → investigations → closure → CIS feedback → SOAP note and critiqueIdentical structure; the roles rotate

                                        Also flagged in this lecture

                                        Bottom Line
                                        Metformin → B12 deficiency → dorsal column signs. A diabetic on metformin with impaired vibration and proprioception may have two neuropathies at once — the distal symmetric polyneuropathy of diabetes and a treatable B12 deficiency layered on top.
                                          Bottom Line
                                          The additional systems are not random. Conjunctival and mucosal inspection looks for pallor — and B12 or another nutritional deficiency is exactly the diagnosis that links anaemia to dorsal column numbness. Abdominal distention looks for urinary retention, which is the cauda equina flag.
                                            Exam Lock
                                            ADA-recommended foot exam
                                            • Temperature or pinprick sensation
                                            • Proprioception
                                            • Ankle reflexes
                                            • Vibration sense (128-Hz tuning fork)
                                            • Light touch sensation (10-g monofilament)
                                            • Inspection for skin breakdown, poor circulation, structural abnormalities
                                            Trap
                                            Urinary retention or faecal incontinence with lower-limb numbness is cauda equina syndrome — the one answer in this table that converts the encounter from a workup into an emergency.
                                              Trap
                                              Sensory ataxia versus cerebellar ataxia. Both give an unstable gait. Sensory ataxia is dorsal column loss and is worse with the eyes closed (Romberg positive); cerebellar ataxia is unchanged by vision and comes with dysmetria, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia.

                                                Rapid recall — stems and answers

                                                A patient has numbness of the LEFT side of the face and the RIGHT arm and leg, with diplopia. Where is the lesion?

                                                C. Brainstem — Brainstem lesions often produce CROSSED findings: ipsilateral face symptoms, contralateral body symptoms — plus cranial nerve deficits such as diplopia. A cortical lesion gives contralateral face + arm + leg together; a cervical cord lesion gives arm + leg without the face.

                                                A 45-year-old has bilateral stocking-distribution numbness and impaired vibration sense in both feet, developing over 2 years. He has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. Which additional cause must be considered?

                                                B. Vitamin B12 deficiency — Metformin is associated with B12 deficiency, and vitamin B12 and B6 neuropathy are listed under nutritional deficiencies. B12 deficiency causes dorsal column loss — sensory ataxia with impaired vibration and proprioception — which can layer on top of the distal symmetric polyneuropathy that accounts for ~75% of diabetic neuropathies.

                                                A patient with 3 days of ascending numbness in both legs now reports urinary retention. Which is the most urgent consideration?

                                                B. Cauda equina syndrome — Do you have urinary retention / fecal incontinence? → cauda equina syndrome. Bilateral lower-limb sensory symptoms with bowel/bladder dysfunction is the emergency pattern; CIDP and Charcot-Marie-Tooth are chronic, and the workbook places bowel/bladder dysfunction squarely under spinal cord lesions.

                                                On examination a patient cannot identify a coin placed in her hand with her eyes closed, and fails to perceive the left-sided touch when both hands are touched simultaneously. Where is the lesion?

                                                C. Right parietal cortex — Loss of stereognosis suggests cortical (parietal lobe) dysfunction; extinction — failure to perceive one of two simultaneous touches on symmetrical body areas — suggests a contralateral parietal lobe lesion. Left-sided extinction therefore localises to the right parietal cortex.

                                                A patient develops numbness over seconds that then remains constant. Which tempo category does this fit, and what is the leading cause?

                                                B. Hyperacute — stroke — Hyperacute (seconds to minutes): stroke · seizure · migraine · acute disc herniation · nerve infarct (vasculitis). The focused-question table also lists "did your numbness appear suddenly and remain constant?" → stroke, compressive neuropathy or radiculopathy. GBS is acute (hours to days); CIDP, tumour and B12 deficiency are subacute to chronic (weeks to years).

                                                NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood

                                                CLSK · Department of Clinical Skills · Dr. Michon Sukhoo-Pertab · source pp. 2756–2785

                                                StageWhat you must doThe instrument
                                                OpenBuild rapport before the sensitive topic; ask the two screening questions; use your own emotional response as a clue*"Over the past month, have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?"* / *"…little interest or pleasure in doing things?"*
                                                CountExplore the neurovegetative symptoms and confirm functional impairmentSIGECAPS (PHQ ≥10 = probable depressive disorder, but the PHQ is not used in this group)
                                                SeparateDistinguish depression from normal sadnessSWAG — Suicidality, Weight loss >5%, Anhedonia, Guilt
                                                RiskAsk directly about suicide; distinguish passive from active ideation; quantifySAD PERSONS — 0–2 home, 3–6 admit or discharge with follow-up, 7–10 admit
                                                ExcludeScreen the medical mimics and substance useMalignancy · hypothyroidism · autoimmune · CNS disease; single-item alcohol screen → CAGE / AUDIT-C / AUDIT → DSM-5 SUD criteria
                                                ExamineFull MSE plus two skills targeted at your leading differentialMSE six components; e.g. thyroid gland, pretibial myxedema, bradycardia, Woltman sign
                                                ReasonProcess list → problem representation → illness script → rank three differentials → investigations for eachVINDICATE, then narrow
                                                CloseInform, set short- and long-term goals, address somatic symptoms, check understanding"Small chunks" + pauses; "teach back" phrased as the clinician's responsibility

                                                Source notes

                                                Source note
                                                The mental status examination itself — its six components, the descriptors and the cognitive tests — is covered in the CLSK section *Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination* earlier in this deck. This section carries the workbook content that is unique to SG-13: the depressed-mood workup, suicide-risk assessment, alcohol screening, the abnormality tables the workbook adds to the MSE, and how to close the encounter with a depressed patient.

                                                  Also flagged in this lecture

                                                  Bottom Line
                                                  Use your own emotional response as data. That instruction is unusual in a physical examination workbook and it is deliberate — countertransference is an observation, not a distraction.
                                                    Bottom Line
                                                    This is why the SG-13 rubric asks for two additional examination skills. If your differential includes hypothyroidism, the workbook names them: inspect and palpate the thyroid gland · assess for pretibial myxedema · assess pulse for bradycardia · assess deep tendon reflexes in upper and lower extremities (Woltman sign).
                                                      Bottom Line
                                                      Some clinicians compare depression to other chronic illnesses with chemical deficiencies: *"Depression is a deficiency problem like diabetes. If your pancreas makes too little insulin, your sugar goes up. In depression certain parts of your brain make too little serotonin and the deficit seriously affects how you think and feel."*
                                                        Bottom Line
                                                        The definition of a delusion already carries the cultural safeguard in it: an abnormal belief "not shared by others from the same culture or cultural sub-group." That clause is the whole reason cultural competence sits inside the MSE and not beside it.
                                                          Exam Lock
                                                          If ONE of the following is documented, it is most likely that the patient is depressed
                                                          • S — Suicidality (serious thoughts or attempts at self-destruction)
                                                          • W — Weight loss (more than 5% of normal body weight without medical cause)
                                                          • A — Anhedonia (loss of pleasure or interest in usually pleasurable activities)
                                                          • G — Guilt (feelings of responsibility for negative life events when little or none exists)
                                                          Trap
                                                          Step 2 is the one that separates a symptom list from a diagnosis. Five symptoms without functional impairment is not clinical depression — and the workbook prints that requirement explicitly.
                                                            Trap
                                                            This is a counting convention, not a contradiction. The DSM says *five symptoms, at least one of which is depressed mood or anhedonia*. The workbook's phrasing — *4 of the symptoms plus depressed mood or anhedonia* — counts the gateway symptom separately and arrives at the same five. Know both forms so neither wording throws you.
                                                              Trap
                                                              Always screen for a past manic or hypomanic episode in a patient presenting with depression. Missing it and starting an antidepressant alone is the classic error — and it is why this question sits in the workbook's *associative symptoms* block rather than as an afterthought.
                                                                Trap
                                                                Hallucination = no stimulus. Illusion = a real stimulus, misread. That one line settles most exam items on this table.

                                                                  Pattern tables

                                                                  Focused questions — mapping answers onto diagnoses

                                                                  QuestionThink about
                                                                  How has your mood been lately? Have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless? How often? How long does it last?Depressed mood
                                                                  Have you lost interest in your usual activities? Do you get less pleasure from things you used to enjoy?Anhedonia
                                                                  How have you been sleeping? How does that compare to your normal sleep?Sleep disturbance
                                                                  Has there been any change in your appetite or weight?Appetite or weight change
                                                                  Have you noticed a decrease in your energy level?Decreased energy
                                                                  Have you been feeling fidgety or had problems sitting still? Have you felt slowed down, like you were moving in slow motion or stuck in mud?Increased or decreased psychomotor activity
                                                                  Have you been having trouble concentrating? Is it harder to make decisions than before?Decreased concentration
                                                                  Are you feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things? How would you describe yourself to someone who had never met you before?Guilt or feelings of worthlessness
                                                                  Have you felt that life is not worth living or that you would be better off dead?Suicidal ideation

                                                                  Focused questions — mapping answers onto diagnoses

                                                                  FindingDiagnosis
                                                                  At least 5 DSM symptoms including depressed mood or anhedoniaMajor depressive disorder
                                                                  Milder severity (<5 DSM symptoms) including depressed mood or anhedoniaDysthymic disorder · depressive disorder NOS · adjustment disorder
                                                                  Mild symptoms that do not impair functionTransient dysphoria

                                                                  Time course and associative symptoms

                                                                  QuestionThink about
                                                                  Did these symptoms begin after the death of a loved one?Bereavement
                                                                  Did these symptoms begin during a time of stress?Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
                                                                  Have you ever seen or experienced a traumatic event in which you or someone else's life was in danger? How about threat of serious injury?Posttraumatic stress disorder
                                                                  Have these symptoms been present on most days for at least 2 years?Dysthymic disorder or chronic major depressive disorder
                                                                  Do these episodes occur at a particular time of the year?Seasonal affective disorder
                                                                  Do your symptoms begin during the week prior to menses and remit within a few days of menses?Premenstrual dysphoric disorder
                                                                  Have you ever had periods where your mood was very good, or too good, for no reason — with racing thoughts, reduced need for sleep, or increased energy? Did it get you into trouble, for instance by spending too much money, impulsively traveling, or taking on too many projects?Bipolar disorder
                                                                  Have you ever had visions or seen things that other people could not see?Depressive disorder with psychotic features
                                                                  Have you heard things that other people could not hear, such as noises or the voices of people whispering or talking?Psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder
                                                                  Have you ever had a panic attack, where out of the blue you experienced intense anxiety, fear, or discomfort for no apparent reason?Panic disorder
                                                                  Have you felt nervous, anxious, or on edge on more than half the days in the last month?Generalized anxiety disorder

                                                                  Thought PROCESS abnormalities — the descriptor table

                                                                  TermDescriptionCharacteristic of
                                                                  CircumstantialNonlinear thought expressed as long-winded explanations and with multiple deviations from the central topic before a central idea is finally expressedSchizophrenia · bipolar disorder · epilepsy · intellectual disability · developmental delay
                                                                  Clang associationsThe use of words based on rhyme patterns rather than meaningSchizophrenia · manic states
                                                                  ConfabulationFabrication of facts or events in response to questions, to fill in the gaps from impaired memoryKorsakoff syndrome from alcoholism
                                                                  Flight of ideasThe quick succession of thoughts usually expressed as a continuous flow of rapid speech and abrupt changes in topicBipolar disorder (manic phase)
                                                                  Incoherence / Word saladSpeech that is incomprehensible and illogical, with lack of meaningful connections, abrupt changes in topic, or disordered grammar or word use. Flight of ideas, when severe, may produce incoherenceSevere psychotic disturbances (usually schizophrenia)
                                                                  Loose associations / derailmentsIncoherent thinking expressed as illogical, sudden, and frequent changes of topicSchizophrenia · other psychotic disorders
                                                                  PerseverationThe inappropriate repetition or persistence of behavior, speech, or soundsPsychoses · epilepsy · dementia · Parkinson disease · traumatic brain injury · stroke
                                                                  TangentialNonlinear thought expressed as a gradual deviation from a focused idea or question; multiple unnecessary details without actually answering the questionSchizophrenia · anxiety · delirium
                                                                  Thought blockingThe abrupt ending of a thought process expressed as a sudden stop in the middle of answering a questionSchizophrenia · other psychoses

                                                                  Circumstantial eventually arrives at the point; tangential never does. That is the single distinction most often tested from this table.

                                                                  Thought CONTENT — abnormal beliefs

                                                                  TermDefinition
                                                                  DelusionAn abnormal belief, held with total conviction, which is maintained in spite of proof or logical argument to the contrary and is not shared by others from the same culture or cultural sub-group. Types: persecutory · grandiose · jealous · erotomanic (the belief that another person is in love with the individual) · somatic (bodily functions or sensations) · unspecified, including delusions of reference — the belief that external events, objects, or people have a particular and unusual personal significance (e.g., commands from the radio or television)
                                                                  Magical thinkingAn irrational belief that certain actions and outcomes are linked, often culturally determined by folklore or custom, e.g. fingers crossed for good luck
                                                                  Overvalued ideasBeliefs that are held, valued, expressed and acted on, beyond the norm for the culture to which the person belongs
                                                                  Thought broadcastingThe belief that the patient's thoughts are heard by others
                                                                  Thought insertionThe belief that thoughts are being placed in the patient's head from outside
                                                                  Thought withdrawalThe belief that thoughts are being removed from the patient's head
                                                                  AnxietiesApprehensive anticipation of future danger or misfortune accompanied by feelings of worry, distress, and/or somatic symptoms of tension
                                                                  CompulsionsRepetitive behaviors that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession, aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or a dreaded event or situation; these behaviors are excessive and unrealistically connected to the provoking stimulus
                                                                  PhobiasPersistent irrational fears accompanied by a compelling desire to avoid the provoking stimulus

                                                                  Clinical correlate: compulsions, obsessions, phobias, and anxieties often occur in anxiety disorders. Delusions and feelings of unreality or depersonalization are often associated with psychotic disorders. Delusions may also occur in delirium, severe mood disorders, and dementia.

                                                                  Rapid recall — stems and answers

                                                                  A patient with low mood answers "yes" to having considered a specific method and says he thinks he might act on it in the near future. How does the workbook classify this?

                                                                  C. Very high risk for suicide — "There's a big difference between having a thought and acting on a thought. Do you think you might try to hurt yourself in the near future?" — a positive response puts the patient at VERY HIGH risk for suicide. A response of "not at all" to thoughts of self-harm is what puts a patient at low risk.

                                                                  Applying the SAD PERSONS scale, a patient scores 8. What does the scale suggest?

                                                                  C. Admit to hospital — 0–2 home with appropriate follow-up · 3–6 admit or discharge with appropriate follow-up · 7–10 admit to hospital. The workbook adds: this is a guide only and should not be used to replace clinical judgement.

                                                                  Which single screening question does the workbook name as the BEST INITIAL tool for unhealthy alcohol use?

                                                                  C. How many times in the past year have you had 5 (4 for women) or more drinks in a day? — Step 1 is the single-item screen — "How many times in the past year have you had 5 (4 for women) or more drinks in a day?", with ≥1 time being positive — described as the best initial screening tool. CAGE is best for identifying dependence and less sensitive for early/unhealthy use; AUDIT-C is more sensitive than CAGE for early detection.

                                                                  A patient asked about their medical history describes at length the hospitals they have stayed in, never mentioning their medical conditions. Which thought-process abnormality is this?

                                                                  B. Tangential — Tangential: nonlinear thought expressed as a gradual deviation from a focused idea or question — multiple unnecessary details WITHOUT actually answering the question. Circumstantial thought also wanders but a central idea is finally expressed.

                                                                  A patient mistakes rustling leaves for the sound of voices. What is this, and what is it NOT?

                                                                  B. An illusion — a misinterpretation of a real external stimulus — Illusions are misinterpretations of REAL external stimuli. Hallucinations are perception-like experiences that seem real but LACK actual external stimulation. Illusions occur in grief reactions, delirium, acute and posttraumatic stress disorders, and schizophrenia.

                                                                  A 68-year-old with alcohol use disorder cannot recall how he acquired a bruise and produces a detailed but fabricated story. Which term applies, and which syndrome is it characteristic of?

                                                                  B. Confabulation — Korsakoff syndrome from alcoholism — Confabulation: fabrication of facts or events in response to questions, to fill in the gaps from impaired memory — characteristic of Korsakoff syndrome from alcoholism. It is also the reason the workbook advises checking recent memory against answers you can verify from other sources.

                                                                  Which statement about the PHQ is correct per this workbook?

                                                                  B. It is a 9-item self-report tool; scores range 0–27 and ≥10 indicates a probable depressive disorder, but it is not used in this small group — The PHQ is a 9-item, self-report questionnaire assessing the 9 DSM signs and symptoms of major depressive disorder over the past 2 weeks; total scores range from 0 to 27; scores ≥10 indicate a probable depressive disorder. The PHQ questionnaire is not used in this small group — use SIGECAPS. The 30-point instrument with a <24 cut-off is the MMSE, a dementia screen.

                                                                  NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)

                                                                  PATH · Department of Pathology, SGU · Small Group 14 · source pp. 2786–2804

                                                                  SlideDiagnosisThe one finding that names it
                                                                  1Cerebral edemaFlattened gyri, narrowed sulci, compressed ventricles — vasogenic (extracellular) versus cytotoxic (intracellular)
                                                                  2HydrocephalusWide ventricles with NARROW sulci = true hydrocephalus; wide ventricles with WIDE sulci and normal pressure = ex vacuo
                                                                  3Epidural hematomaMiddle meningeal ARTERY; lens-shaped; does not cross sutures; lucid interval
                                                                  4Subdural hematomaBridging VEINS; crescent-shaped; crosses sutures; elderly/alcoholic, trivial trauma
                                                                  5Cerebral infarctionRed neurons → neutrophils → macrophages → gliotic cystic cavity
                                                                  6Intracerebral hemorrhageHypertensive rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms; basal ganglia / putamen
                                                                  7Berry aneurysm — subarachnoid hemorrhageSaccular aneurysm at a circle-of-Willis branch point; worst headache of life; vasospasm days 4–12
                                                                  8Alzheimer diseaseExtracellular Aβ neuritic plaques + intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles; cortical atrophy with ex vacuo ventricles
                                                                  9Multiple sclerosisPeriventricular plaques of differing age; demyelination with preserved axons; CSF oligoclonal bands
                                                                  10GlioblastomaPseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation; butterfly glioma
                                                                  11MeningiomaDural-based; whorls and psammoma bodies; NF2, chromosome 22
