                                                                  Source notes

                                                                  Source note
                                                                  The source deck carries this small group as image-only slides: a title, a slide number and a photograph. Reproduced here are the verbatim objectives and the twelve slide titles, plus, for each, the findings you are expected to name at the microscope or on the gross specimen, drawn from the NCRS neuropathology lectures already in this deck (Trauma and Hydrocephalus, Cerebrovascular Disease, Neurodegenerative Disease, Demyelinating Disease and CNS Tumors).

                                                                    Also flagged in this lecture

                                                                    Bottom Line
                                                                    Before the cranial sutures close, hydrocephalus enlarges the head. After they fuse, the same volume raises intracranial pressure instead — which is why the presentation is macrocephaly in the infant and headache, papilloedema and vomiting in the adult.
                                                                      Bottom Line
                                                                      Rosette discipline: Homer Wright (no lumen, fibrillary centre) — medulloblastoma and neuroblastoma. Perivascular pseudorosettes — ependymoma. Flexner-Wintersteiner (true lumen) — retinoblastoma. Psammoma bodies — meningioma (also papillary thyroid, serous ovarian, mesothelioma).
                                                                        Exam Lock
                                                                        Clinical consequence — herniation
                                                                        • Subfalcine (cingulate) — compresses the anterior cerebral artery
                                                                        • Transtentorial (uncal) — CN III palsy (blown pupil), posterior cerebral artery compression, Duret haemorrhages in the midbrain/pons
                                                                        • Tonsillar — cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum; brainstem compression and respiratory arrest
                                                                        Exam Lock
                                                                        The line that answers most questions
                                                                        • Artery, lens, does not cross sutures, lucid interval → EPIDURAL.
                                                                        • Vein, crescent, crosses sutures, elderly with trivial trauma → SUBDURAL.
                                                                        Exam Lock
                                                                        Genetics and clinical
                                                                        • Early-onset familial: APP (chr 21), presenilin-1 (chr 14), presenilin-2 (chr 1)
                                                                        • Risk allele: ApoE ε4 increases risk; ApoE ε2 is protective
                                                                        • Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) — virtually all develop Alzheimer pathology by age 40
                                                                        • Clinical: insidious memory loss progressing to global cognitive decline; the most common cause of dementia
                                                                        Exam Lock
                                                                        Compare — PATH.7032
                                                                        • MS — young adults, F:M 2:1, relapsing-remitting, HLA-DRB1*1501, periventricular white matter
                                                                        • ADEM / AHEM — post-infectious or post-vaccination, monophasic, children and young adults, PERIVENOUS demyelination; AHEM is the fulminant haemorrhagic form
                                                                        • Central pontine myelinolysis — too-rapid correction of hyponatraemia; symmetric loss of myelin in the BASIS PONTIS; locked-in syndrome; the >2-day rule protects against it
                                                                        Trap
                                                                        Big ventricles are not a diagnosis. Wide sulci with wide ventricles = ex vacuo (atrophy). Narrow sulci with wide ventricles = true hydrocephalus under pressure. That single comparison is what the slide is testing.
                                                                          Trap
                                                                          Berry aneurysms are NOT atherosclerotic aneurysms. They are congenital-ish defects in the media at arterial branch points, they lack an internal elastic lamina and media at the neck, and they rupture — they do not usually thrombose or dissect.
                                                                            Trap
                                                                            Tangle burden correlates with cognitive decline better than plaque burden. Plaques are extracellular and made of Aβ; tangles are intracellular and made of tau. Mixing up which is which is the most common error on this slide.

                                                                              Rapid recall — stems and answers

                                                                              A CT shows enlarged lateral ventricles AND widened cortical sulci in a 78-year-old with progressive memory loss. Measured CSF pressure is normal. Which is correct?

                                                                              C. Hydrocephalus ex vacuo from cerebral atrophy — Hydrocephalus ex vacuo is compensatory ventricular enlargement following loss of brain parenchyma — ventricles AND sulci enlarge, and CSF pressure is normal. A true hydrocephalus under pressure expands the ventricles while compressing the sulci. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus has normal measured pressure but the clinical triad of urinary incontinence, dementia and magnetic gait and does not widen the sulci.

                                                                              A 22-year-old is struck at the temple, briefly loses consciousness, converses normally for an hour, then deteriorates rapidly. The haematoma is lens-shaped and stops at the suture lines. Which vessel is torn?

                                                                              B. The middle meningeal artery — Epidural haematoma: middle meningeal ARTERY torn by a fracture at the pterion; lens-shaped (biconvex) because the dura is bound at the sutures so the collection does not cross them; the arterial pressure produces the classic lucid interval then rapid deterioration. A bridging vein tear gives a crescentic subdural that does cross sutures.

                                                                              A biopsy of a hemispheric mass in a 60-year-old shows serpentine necrosis with tumour cells aligned along its edge and florid endothelial proliferation. Which diagnosis?

                                                                              C. Glioblastoma — Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular (endothelial) proliferation define glioblastoma, WHO grade 4. Grossly it is variegated with haemorrhage and necrosis and may cross the corpus callosum as a butterfly glioma. Meningioma shows whorls and psammoma bodies; medulloblastoma shows Homer Wright rosettes in a child's cerebellum.

                                                                              Which pairing of inclusion and location is correct for Alzheimer disease?

                                                                              C. Neuritic plaques are extracellular Aβ; neurofibrillary tangles are intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau — Neuritic (senile) plaques are EXTRAcellular with an Aβ core derived from amyloid precursor protein (chromosome 21); neurofibrillary tangles are INTRAcellular, made of hyperphosphorylated TAU, and persist after neuronal death as ghost tangles. α-synuclein is Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.

                                                                              A 7-year-old has morning headaches, vomiting and truncal ataxia. Imaging shows a midline cerebellar mass; histology shows sheets of small round blue cells with rosettes lacking a central lumen. Which statement is correct?

                                                                              B. It is a WHO grade 4 tumour but is exquisitely radiosensitive and may seed the CSF — Medulloblastoma: children, cerebellar VERMIS, small round blue cells with HOMER WRIGHT rosettes, WHO grade 4 but exquisitely radiosensitive, and characteristically produces "drop metastases" seeding the CSF to the cauda equina. Arachnoid cap cells give meningioma; 1p/19q codeletion is oligodendroglioma.

                                                                              A hypertensive 65-year-old has a sudden dense hemiparesis. Autopsy shows haemorrhage centred on the putamen. Which lesion is responsible?

                                                                              B. Rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms — Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage arises from rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of the small penetrating arteries, on a background of hyaline arteriolosclerosis; the basal ganglia/putamen is the commonest site, then thalamus, pons and cerebellum. Berry aneurysm rupture produces subarachnoid haemorrhage; cerebral amyloid angiopathy produces lobar haemorrhages in the elderly.

                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics

                                                                              PHAR · Dr Mohit Kaur · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology · source pp. 2805–2894

                                                                              QuestionAnswer
                                                                              What is general anesthesia?Analgesia · amnesia · loss of consciousness · suppression of sensory and autonomic reflexes · skeletal muscle relaxation
                                                                              Why balanced anesthesia?No single drug achieves all the goals: inhaled agents are slow to induce and poor analgesics, paralysis needs a neuromuscular blocker, and combining drugs minimises the halogenated-hydrocarbon dose
                                                                              MechanismFacilitate GABA_A and glycine receptors; inhibit nicotinic receptors
                                                                              Potencyλ(oil:gas) ↑ → MAC ↓ (Meyer-Overton). 1/MAC = potency index. MAC = ED50 on a quantal curve; MAC values are additive
                                                                              Speedλ(blood:gas) ↓ → faster onset. High potency correlates with slow onset. ↑ inspired concentration and ↑ ventilation speed induction; ↑ cardiac output SLOWS it
                                                                              RecoveryRedistribution from the brain and exhalation. Low-solubility agents: recovery mirrors induction. High-solubility agents: recovery depends on duration, because fat is a reservoir
                                                                              Signature toxicitiesHalothane → hepatitis and catecholamine sensitisation. Methoxyflurane → fluoride nephrotoxicity. Sevoflurane → compound A. N₂O → closed-space expansion and megaloblastic anaemia. Enflurane → spike-and-wave at high dose
                                                                              Malignant hyperthermiaRYR1, autosomal dominant, ~1:12,000; triggered by halogenated agents ± succinylcholine; tachycardia, hypertension, rigidity, hyperthermia, hyperkalemia, acidosis; treat with DANTROLENE; diagnose with the caffeine-halothane contracture test
                                                                              IV agentsThiopental — redistribution, ↓ICP, no analgesia. Propofol — most popular, antiemetic, ↓ICP, hypotension via ↓PVR. Etomidate — for the hypotensive patient, adrenal suppression. Ketamine — NMDA blocker, dissociative, the only one with analgesia and CV stimulation, ↑ICP, emergence phenomena
                                                                              AdjuvantsBenzodiazepines (amnesia) · opioids (analgesia) · neuromuscular blockers (relaxation, competitive block reversed by neostigmine) · ondansetron (PONV) · antimuscarinics (amnesia, secretions, bradycardia)

                                                                              Also flagged in this lecture

                                                                              Bottom Line
                                                                              The rule generalises: any closed gas-filled space is a contraindication. If the question describes a cavity that cannot vent, nitrous oxide is the wrong answer.
                                                                                Bottom Line
                                                                                Methionine synthase is the B₁₂-dependent enzyme. N₂O irreversibly oxidises the cobalt in cobalamin — which is why the picture is a functional B₁₂ deficiency: megaloblastic anaemia, and with long exposure, subacute combined degeneration.
                                                                                  Bottom Line
                                                                                  Redistribution, not metabolism, ends the effect. That is why a single induction dose wears off in minutes but repeated dosing accumulates — the fat compartment fills, and then only hepatic clearance can remove the drug.
                                                                                    Exam Lock
                                                                                    The safety statement you should be able to quote
                                                                                    • General anesthetics are among the most dangerous drugs approved for general use, as their margin of safety is small.
                                                                                    • Therapeutic indices range from about 2–4 — the dose that produces circulatory failure may be only 2 to 4 times that which produces adequate anesthesia
                                                                                    Exam Lock
                                                                                    MAC values are ADDITIVE
                                                                                    • Nitrous oxide can be used as a "carrier" gas, decreasing the anesthetic requirement of other anesthetics.
                                                                                    • Example: 0.7 MAC of isoflurane + 0.3 MAC of nitrous oxide = 1 MAC.
                                                                                    Exam Lock
                                                                                    The two sentences to memorise
                                                                                    • There is an INVERSE relationship between blood solubility of an anesthetic and the rate of rise of its tension in arterial blood. A low blood:gas partition coefficient determines a FASTER onset of anesthesia.
                                                                                    • Anesthetics with larger λ(oil:gas) tend to have larger λ(blood:gas) — which means MORE POTENT INHALED ANESTHETICS TEND TO HAVE SLOWER ONSETS.
                                                                                    Exam Lock
                                                                                    Rank order of metabolism
                                                                                    • Methoxyflurane > halothane > enflurane > sevoflurane > isoflurane > desflurane > nitrous oxide
                                                                                    Exam Lock
                                                                                    N₂O should be avoided in the following clinical settings
                                                                                    • Pneumothorax
                                                                                    • Obstructed middle ear
                                                                                    • Air embolus
                                                                                    • Obstructed loop of bowel
                                                                                    • Intraocular air bubble
                                                                                    • Pulmonary bulla
                                                                                    • Intracranial air
                                                                                    Exam Lock
                                                                                    Establishing susceptibility
                                                                                    • The most reliable test is the in vitro CAFFEINE-HALOTHANE MUSCLE CONTRACTURE TEST — a small piece of muscle is obtained from the thigh under regional or general anesthesia, attached to a device measuring force of contraction, and exposed to halothane or caffeine
                                                                                    • A response to halothane, or a response to LOW concentrations of caffeine, is diagnostic for malignant hyperthermia-susceptible muscle
                                                                                    • Genetic testing can also be used
                                                                                    • During anesthesia, watch for TRISMUS from muscular contraction
                                                                                    Trap
                                                                                    Height and weight do not change MAC. It is an alveolar *concentration*, not a dose per kilogram — which is exactly why it is the standard of comparison.
                                                                                      Trap
                                                                                      Increased cardiac output slows inhalational induction. This is counter-intuitive and it is examined precisely because it is counter-intuitive — more blood flowing past the alveolus means more blood to saturate, so alveolar and arterial tension climb more slowly.
                                                                                        Trap
                                                                                        Muscular dystrophies are a separate trap. Patients with undiagnosed Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy receiving succinylcholine and halogenated anesthetics can develop life-threatening HYPERKALEMIA and RHABDOMYOLYSIS — due to upregulation of extra-junctional ACh receptors depolarizing the whole cell. This is not malignant hyperthermia, though it is triggered by the same two drug classes.
                                                                                          Trap
                                                                                          Ketamine is the exception on almost every axis. Every other IV agent reduces intracranial pressure and provides no analgesia; ketamine raises ICP and does provide analgesia. Learn it as the exception and the rest of the table stays simple.

                                                                                            Pattern tables

                                                                                            Organ effects of the inhaled anesthetics

                                                                                            SystemEffect
                                                                                            CardiovascularMost inhaled anesthetics depress normal cardiac contractility (dose-dependent) and decrease mean arterial pressure through vasodilation. Halothane and enflurane reduce arterial pressure mainly by MYOCARDIAL DEPRESSION (reduced cardiac output) with little effect on vascular resistance; isoflurane, desflurane and sevoflurane produce greater VASODILATION with minimal effect on cardiac output — so they may be better choices for patients with impaired myocardial function. Nitrous oxide is less likely to lower blood pressure than other inhaled anesthetics. Halothane SENSITIZES THE MYOCARDIUM TO CIRCULATING CATECHOLAMINES, which may lead to ventricular arrhythmias — less marked for isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane
                                                                                            RespiratoryAll volatile anesthetics have BRONCHODILATING properties and all are RESPIRATORY DEPRESSANTS. Isoflurane and enflurane are the most depressant; nitrous oxide is the least. Isoflurane and desflurane are PUNGENT, making them less suitable for induction in patients with bronchospasm; halothane, sevoflurane and nitrous oxide are NONPUNGENT.
                                                                                            CNSInhaled anesthetics increase cerebral blood flow because they reduce cerebral vascular resistance — this may increase intracranial pressure, clinically undesirable in patients with raised ICP from brain tumor or head injury. Nitrous oxide increases blood flow the least. At higher doses enflurane may produce a spike-and-wave pattern and mild generalized muscle twitching (tonic-clonic movements); this seizure-like activity does not have adverse clinical consequences. Nitrous oxide has low anesthetic potency but exerts marked ANALGESIC and AMNESIC actions.
                                                                                            KidneyAll inhaled anesthetics decrease glomerular filtration rate and renal blood flow.
                                                                                            LiverAll inhaled anesthetics decrease hepatic blood flow.
                                                                                            Uterine smooth muscleHalogenated hydrocarbon anesthetics are potent UTERINE RELAXANTS — usable when profound uterine relaxation is required for intrauterine fetal manipulation or manual extraction of a retained placenta. Nitrous oxide has little effect on uterine musculature.

                                                                                            IV anesthetics — one comparison table

                                                                                            ThiopentalPropofolEtomidateKetamine
                                                                                            MechanismGABA_AGABA_AGABA_ANMDA receptor blockade
                                                                                            AnalgesiaNone — may cause hyperalgesiaNoneNoneYES
                                                                                            Intracranial pressure↓↓↓↑

                                                                                            Rapid recall — stems and answers

                                                                                            Two agents have λ(oil:gas) values of 19 and 960 respectively. Which statement is correct?

                                                                                            B. The agent with λ(oil:gas) 960 is more potent and has slower onset — Meyer-Overton: potency increases as liposolubility increases — as λ(oil:gas) increases, MAC decreases. λ(oil:gas) 960 is methoxyflurane, MAC 0.16 — the most potent. And because anesthetics with large λ(oil:gas) tend to have large λ(blood:gas), high potency correlates with SLOW onset (methoxyflurane λ(blood:gas) = 12, very slow onset and recovery).

                                                                                            A patient in septic shock has a high cardiac output. What effect does this have on inhalational induction?

                                                                                            B. It slows induction because a larger volume of blood is exposed, increasing blood 'capacity' — An increase in pulmonary blood flow (increased cardiac output) SLOWS the rate of rise in arterial tension, because increased pulmonary blood flow exposes a larger volume of blood to the anesthetic; blood "capacity" increases and tension rises slowly. The effect is greatest for agents with moderate to high blood solubility.

                                                                                            Which combination yields exactly 1 MAC?

                                                                                            B. 0.7 MAC isoflurane plus 0.3 MAC nitrous oxide — MAC values are ADDITIVE. Nitrous oxide can be used as a "carrier" gas, decreasing the anesthetic requirement of other anesthetics: 0.7 MAC of isoflurane and 0.3 MAC of nitrous oxide yield 1 MAC.

                                                                                            Which of the following would DECREASE MAC?

                                                                                            C. Concurrent opioid analgesia — MAC is decreased by hypothermia, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, and adjuvant drugs such as opioid analgesics or sedative-hypnotics — so the inspired concentration should be decreased accordingly. MAC is increased by anxiety and thyrotoxicosis. Sex, height and weight do not significantly affect MAC.

                                                                                            A patient is being ventilated after a bowel obstruction. Which inhaled agent must be avoided, and why?

                                                                                            C. Nitrous oxide — it enters closed gas spaces faster than nitrogen escapes — N₂O exchanges with nitrogen in air-containing cavities; it enters the cavity faster than nitrogen escapes, increasing the volume and/or pressure of the cavity. Avoid in pneumothorax, obstructed middle ear, air embolus, obstructed loop of bowel, intraocular air bubble, pulmonary bulla and intracranial air.

                                                                                            A dental assistant working in a poorly ventilated suite develops megaloblastic anaemia. Which agent and mechanism?

                                                                                            C. Nitrous oxide — decreased methionine synthase activity — Prolonged exposure to nitrous oxide decreases METHIONINE SYNTHASE activity and causes megaloblastic anemia — a potential occupational hazard for staff working in poorly ventilated dental operating suites. Methionine synthase is the B₁₂-dependent enzyme, so the picture is a functional B₁₂ deficiency.

                                                                                            Thirty minutes into a sevoflurane and succinylcholine anaesthetic, a patient develops masseter spasm, generalised rigidity, tachycardia and a rising temperature. Which is the immediate pharmacological treatment and what is the underlying defect?

                                                                                            B. Dantrolene — a defect in the RYR1 ryanodine receptor gene — Malignant hyperthermia: an autosomal dominant defect in the ryanodine receptor gene RYR1, incidence ~1:12,000, triggered by halogenated inhalation anesthetics and succinylcholine. Abnormal RYR1 receptors release calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum without control → sustained contraction, heat, acidosis, hyperkalemia and rhabdomyolysis. Treat with DANTROLENE, which prevents Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, plus cooling and correction of electrolytes and acid-base balance. Trismus during anesthesia is the sign to watch for.

                                                                                            Which IV anesthetic would you choose to induce a hypotensive trauma patient with a normal ICP, and what is its characteristic long-term risk?

                                                                                            C. Etomidate — adrenocortical suppression through inhibition of 11-β-hydroxylase — Etomidate is primarily used for anesthetic induction of patients at risk for hypotension because it causes minimal cardiovascular and respiratory depression. It inhibits 11-beta hydroxylase, causing adrenocortical suppression via inhibitory effects on steroidogenesis with decreased plasma hydrocortisone — adrenal suppression with prolonged infusions.

                                                                                            A patient in septic shock needs induction. Which agent's cardiovascular profile makes it particularly useful, and what is the mechanism?

                                                                                            C. Ketamine — central sympathetic stimulation and inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake — Ketamine is the only IV anesthetic that possesses both analgesic properties and the ability to produce CV stimulation: heart rate, arterial pressure and cardiac output increase, due to stimulation of the central sympathetic nervous system and to inhibition of the reuptake of norepinephrine at sympathetic nerve terminals. Very useful for poor-risk geriatric patients and high-risk patients in cardiogenic or septic shock.

                                                                                            A head-injured patient with raised intracranial pressure requires induction. Which agent is specifically contraindicated by that concern?

                                                                                            D. Ketamine — Ketamine INCREASES intracranial pressure; in this regard it resembles inhaled anesthetics as a potentially dangerous drug when intracranial pressure is elevated. Thiopental, propofol and etomidate all REDUCE intracranial pressure — the lecture singles out thiopental as much more desirable than the inhaled anesthetics for patients with cerebral swelling.

                                                                                            A single induction dose of thiopental wears off in minutes. What terminates its effect, and what is required for elimination?

                                                                                            B. Redistribution from the brain terminates the effect; hepatic metabolism is required for elimination — The anesthetic effects of the ultra-short acting barbiturates are terminated by REDISTRIBUTION from the brain to other tissues, but HEPATIC METABOLISM is required for their elimination from the body. The redistribution sequence runs vessel-rich group (brain, liver, kidneys) → muscle group → fat group.

                                                                                            Which adjuvant reversal pairing is correct?

                                                                                            B. Competitive neuromuscular block is reversed by an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor such as neostigmine — The effects of the COMPETITIVE neuromuscular blockers (e.g. pancuronium) can be reversed by an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor such as neostigmine — the depolarizing blocker succinylcholine cannot be reversed that way. Opioids are reversed by an antagonist such as naltrexone.

                                                                                            Which statement about propofol is correct?

                                                                                            C. It has antiemetic actions and causes hypotension mainly through decreased peripheral vascular resistance — Propofol produces NO analgesia, REDUCES intracranial pressure, has ANTIEMETIC actions so postoperative vomiting is uncommon, is rapidly metabolized in the liver at a rate ten times FASTER than thiopental, and causes hypotension primarily through decreased peripheral vascular resistance.

                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics

                                                                                            PHAR · Dr Malcolm Antoine Jr · Department of Microbiology, Immunology & Pharmacology · source pp. 2895–2931

                                                                                            QuestionAnswer
                                                                                            MechanismBlock voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, binding near the INTRACELLULAR end. State-dependent: higher affinity for activated and inactivated channels, so the effect is greater in rapidly firing axons.
                                                                                            Which form does whatUncharged base crosses the membrane; the CATION binds the receptor. pK 8–9, so most is cation at pH 7.4. Low pH (infected tissue) → less uncharged drug → the block fails.
                                                                                            Potency and durationLiposolubility ↑ → potency ↑, duration ↑, and toxicity ↑
                                                                                            OnsetpKa closer to body pH → faster onset
                                                                                            Order of blockB (preganglionic autonomic) and C (pain) and A-δ (pain, temperature) first; A-α/β/γ (postural, touch, pressure, motor) last. Pain first, motor last.
                                                                                            Ester vs amideEsters — plasma/tissue esterases, short, PABA metabolite → allergy. Amides — hepatic CYP450, longer, allergy extremely rare, toxicity ↑ in liver disease. Amides have two "i"s.
                                                                                            Restricting the drug to its siteAdd a vasoconstrictor (epinephrine): ↓ systemic absorption, ↑ neuronal uptake, ↓ systemic toxicity. In spinal anesthesia epinephrine also acts on α₂-adrenoceptors to inhibit substance P release — hence clonidine and dexmedetomidine as adjuncts. Risks: delayed wound healing, tissue edema, necrosis. Cocaine vasoconstricts by itself.
                                                                                            Signature toxicitiesCNS: stimulation → convulsions → depression → respiratory failure; prophylax with a benzodiazepine. CV: bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic. Blood: prilocaine → o-toluidine → methemoglobinemia, treat with methylene blue. Allergy: esters, via PABA. Cocaine: vasoconstriction, hypertension, arrhythmias, nasal septal damage.
                                                                                            Drug interactionProcaine → PABA → antagonises sulfonamides (which compete with PABA for dihydropteroate synthetase).

                                                                                            Also flagged in this lecture

                                                                                            Bottom Line
                                                                                            A useful spelling trick: amide local anesthetics have two "i"s in the name — lidocaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine, ropivacaine. Esters have one: procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, cocaine.
                                                                                              Bottom Line
                                                                                              Use-dependence explains why a nerve that is actively transmitting pain is blocked more readily than one at rest — the drug needs the channel to open before it can reach its binding site.
                                                                                                Exam Lock
                                                                                                Use-dependence — state-dependent block
                                                                                                • The blockade of sodium channels by most local anesthetics is VOLTAGE- and TIME-DEPENDENT.
                                                                                                • Channels in the RESTED state, which predominate at more negative membrane potentials, have a LOWER affinity for local anesthetics than ACTIVATED (open) and INACTIVATED channels, which predominate at more positive membrane potentials.
                                                                                                • Thus the effect of a given drug concentration is more marked in RAPIDLY FIRING axons than in resting fibers.
                                                                                                Exam Lock
                                                                                                How a vasoconstrictor restricts the drug to its site (PHAR.00089)
                                                                                                • Preparations of local anesthetics often contain a vasoconstrictor, usually EPINEPHRINE.
                                                                                                • Vasoconstrictors reduce systemic absorption from the depot site by decreasing blood flow in these areas.
                                                                                                • As a consequence, neuronal uptake of the drug is ENHANCED due to the higher local drug concentration, and the SYSTEMIC TOXIC EFFECTS ARE REDUCED.
                                                                                                • Cocaine itself constricts blood vessels by potentiating the action of norepinephrine; therefore it prevents its own absorption.
                                                                                                Trap
                                                                                                The classic exam application: do not use epinephrine-containing solutions in end-artery territories — fingers, toes, nose, ears, penis — where vasoconstriction risks ischaemia and necrosis. That is exactly what the lecture's own vignette about the lacerated index finger is testing.

                                                                                                  Pattern tables

                                                                                                  Toxicity by system

                                                                                                  SystemToxic effects and management
                                                                                                  Central nervous systemFollowing absorption, local anesthetics may cause STIMULATION of the CNS, producing restlessness and tremor that may proceed to CLONIC CONVULSIONS. Central stimulation is followed by CNS DEPRESSION; death is usually caused by RESPIRATORY FAILURE. More serious toxic reactions are due to convulsions from excessive blood levels — prevented by administering the smallest dose required for adequate anesthesia. When large doses must be given, premedication with a BENZODIAZEPINE (e.g. diazepam) provides significant prophylaxis against seizures.
                                                                                                  Peripheral nervous systemWhen applied at excessively high concentrations, ALL local anesthetics can be toxic to nerve tissue. The mechanism of neurotoxicity is unknown, but it does NOT result from excessive sodium channel blockade.
                                                                                                  CardiovascularEffects result partly from direct actions on cardiac and smooth muscle membranes and partly from indirect effects on autonomic nerves. Local anesthetics block sodium channels and thus DEPRESS cardiac pacemaker activity, excitability and conduction; at very high concentrations they may also block Ca²⁺ channels. With the EXCEPTION OF COCAINE, they also depress the strength of cardiac contraction and cause arteriolar dilation, leading to HYPOTENSION. Cardiovascular collapse and death usually occur only after large doses, but may occasionally result from the small amounts used for infiltration anesthesia especially if BUPIVACAINE is the agent used — bupivacaine is more cardiotoxic than other local anesthetics.
                                                                                                  Cocaine — the exceptionBlockade of norepinephrine uptake results in VASOCONSTRICTION and HYPERTENSION. It may also precipitate cardiac arrhythmias. The vasoconstriction produced by cocaine can lead to ischemia and, in chronic abusers, to ulceration of the mucous membrane and even damage to the NASAL SEPTUM.
                                                                                                  BloodLarge doses of PRILOCAINE during regional anesthesia may lead to accumulation of the metabolite O-TOLUIDINE, an oxidizing agent capable of converting hemoglobin to METHEMOGLOBIN. Reducing agents such as METHYLENE BLUE may be given IV to convert methemoglobin back to hemoglobin.
                                                                                                  Allergic reactionsMore common with ESTER types, due to the PABA metabolite. Amides are not metabolized to PABA and allergic reactions to them are extremely rare.

                                                                                                  Rapid recall — stems and answers

                                                                                                  A 75-year-old man undergoes carpal tunnel release under local anaesthesia with bupivacaine. Which best explains the pharmacologic effect of this drug on the membrane of his neurons?

                                                                                                  C. Decreased permeability to Na⁺ — The primary mechanism of action of local anesthetics is blockade of VOLTAGE-GATED SODIUM CHANNELS — they bind receptors near the intracellular end of the channel and block it, decreasing Na⁺ permeability. Calcium channel block occurs only at very high concentrations and is not the primary effect. *(This is the lecture's own vignette.)*

                                                                                                  A 30-year-old construction worker needs a laceration of his right index finger sutured. Which agent is CONTRAINDICATED in the local anesthetic solution?

                                                                                                  A. Epinephrine — Vasoconstrictors such as epinephrine reduce systemic absorption by decreasing blood flow — but in an end-artery territory such as a digit that same vasoconstriction risks ischaemia and necrosis. The lecture explicitly lists delayed wound healing, tissue edema, or necrosis among the vasoconstrictor's adverse effects. *(This is the lecture's own vignette.)*

                                                                                                  A dentist reports that lidocaine fails to anaesthetise an abscessed tooth. What is the pharmacological explanation?

                                                                                                  B. The low extracellular pH of infected tissue shifts the drug to the ionized form, so little uncharged drug diffuses into the cell — The cationic form is the most active form at the receptor site, but the UNCHARGED form is required for penetration of biological membranes because the receptor is not accessible from the external side. Infected tissues have a LOW extracellular pH, so a very low fraction of nonionized local anesthetic is available for diffusion into the cell.

                                                                                                  A patient develops cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen after a large dose of a local anesthetic for regional block. Which drug and which treatment?

                                                                                                  C. Prilocaine — intravenous methylene blue — Large doses of PRILOCAINE during regional anesthesia may lead to accumulation of the metabolite O-TOLUIDINE, an oxidizing agent capable of converting hemoglobin to METHEMOGLOBIN. Reducing agents such as METHYLENE BLUE may be given IV to convert methemoglobin to hemoglobin.

                                                                                                  A patient has a documented allergy to procaine. Which statement guides your choice?

                                                                                                  C. Amide local anesthetics are not metabolized to PABA and allergic reactions to them are extremely rare — Ester-type local anesthetics are metabolized to p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) derivatives, and these metabolites are responsible for allergic reactions in a small percentage of the population. Amides are NOT metabolized to PABA, and allergic reactions to agents of the amide group are extremely rare. Procaine is an ester, so an amide such as lidocaine is the substitute.

                                                                                                  During an axillary block a patient reports circumoral tingling and tinnitus, then becomes restless with tremor. What is happening, and what would have reduced the risk?

                                                                                                  B. Early systemic local anesthetic toxicity; premedication with a benzodiazepine when large doses must be given — Following absorption, local anesthetics may cause CNS stimulation — restlessness and tremor that may proceed to clonic convulsions — followed by CNS depression, with death usually caused by respiratory failure. Serious reactions are prevented by administering the smallest dose required; when large doses must be given, premedication with a benzodiazepine such as diazepam provides significant prophylaxis against seizures. Paresthesias in the mouth and tongue and tinnitus are listed among the early toxic symptoms.

                                                                                                  Which local anesthetic raises blood pressure rather than lowering it, and why?

                                                                                                  B. Cocaine — blockade of norepinephrine uptake causing vasoconstriction — With the exception of COCAINE, local anesthetics depress the strength of cardiac contraction and cause arteriolar dilation leading to hypotension. Cocaine's blockade of norepinephrine uptake results in VASOCONSTRICTION and HYPERTENSION; it may also precipitate cardiac arrhythmias, and its vasoconstriction can cause ischemia and, in chronic abusers, ulceration of the mucous membrane and damage to the nasal septum.

                                                                                                  NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf Pain

                                                                                                  CLSK · Department of Clinical Skills · Dr. Gonzague, reviewed by Dr. Miguel · source pp. 2932–2943

                                                                                                  DiagnosisKey clinical featuresTypical clinical courseFirst investigation
                                                                                                  Deep venous thrombosisUnilateral calf swelling and tenderness, often subtle; calf >3 cm larger; pitting oedema; collateral superficial veins. Risk: immobility, surgery, trauma, pregnancy, malignancy, previous DVT, oral contraceptives, family historyMay progress; the danger is PULMONARY EMBOLISM, especially from proximal DVTWells score → D-dimer or compression ultrasound; anticoagulation
                                                                                                  CellulitisWarm, red, swollen, tender skin with fever; erysipelas is raised and sharply demarcatedAcute; spreads along skin and can seed lymphatics (red streaks, tender nodes = acute lymphangitis)Clinical diagnosis; antibiotics
                                                                                                  Superficial thrombophlebitisRedness, tenderness and a PALPABLE CORD along a superficial vein (often the saphenous); risk from immobility, venous stasis, IV linesAcute over days; usually benign but can extend to the deep systemUltrasound to exclude deep extension; walking and supportive care
                                                                                                  Ruptured (dissecting) Baker cystSwelling BEHIND THE KNEE preceding the calf pain; known osteoarthritis of the kneeSudden calf pain and swelling mimicking DVT once the cyst rupturesUltrasound — it is the test that separates it from DVT
                                                                                                  Chronic venous insufficiencyDiffuse aching legs, worse later in the day and with prolonged standing; oedema, BROWN pigmentation (haemosiderin), stasis dermatitis, possible ulcers (medial malleolus)Chronic and progressive; relieved by elevation and walkingVenous duplex to assess valve competence; compression therapy

                                                                                                  Also flagged in this lecture

                                                                                                  Bottom Line
                                                                                                  Bilateral calf pain with a blood pressure of 160/94 in a patient sent to an outpatient clinic is the vignette telling you the answer is vascular and the risk factor is hypertension. Read the vitals before you read the complaint.
                                                                                                    Bottom Line
                                                                                                    Buerger's test and calf measurement are the two that get skipped and are on the rubric. Buerger's test — elevate to 45° looking for pallor, then hang the leg down looking for reactive hyperaemia — is the bedside test for arterial insufficiency; the calf circumference difference feeds straight into the Wells score (>3 cm).
                                                                                                      Exam Lock
                                                                                                      The ankle-brachial index (ABI) — the main screening test
                                                                                                      • Abnormal: <0.90
                                                                                                      • Easy, reliable, done in the office
                                                                                                      • High specificity (99%) · lower sensitivity (15–20%)
                                                                                                      • USPSTF: does NOT recommend routine screening (insufficient evidence)
                                                                                                      • AHA: screening with ABI is REASONABLE in high-risk patients
                                                                                                      Trap
                                                                                                      Task 5 is unique to this simulation and is a gift. You are allowed back into the encounter to fill gaps before you reason and before you write. Plan to use it — decide during task 4 what you still need.
                                                                                                        Trap
                                                                                                        Cellulitis and DVT look the same from the doorway. Both give a red, warm, swollen calf. The history — fever and a portal of entry versus immobility, malignancy and previous DVT — is what separates them, and getting it wrong in either direction is dangerous.
                                                                                                          Trap
                                                                                                          High specificity, low sensitivity is exactly why the ABI is a good confirmatory test and a poor screening test — a normal ABI does not exclude PAD, which is also why the USPSTF stops short of recommending routine screening.

                                                                                                            Rapid recall — stems and answers

                                                                                                            A patient reports calf pain that comes on after walking exactly two blocks every time and stops after standing still for two minutes. Pedal pulses are weak and the skin is cool and hairless. Which is the diagnosis and the confirming test?

                                                                                                            B. Peripheral arterial disease; ankle-brachial index — Vascular (arterial) claudication: pain on walking, at a REPRODUCIBLE distance, relieved by standing still for 1–3 minutes, with cool hairless skin, weak pulses and pallor on elevation. The screening test is the ankle-brachial index — abnormal <0.90, specificity 99%, sensitivity 15–20%. Neurogenic claudication is relieved by sitting or leaning forward, with normal pulses.

                                                                                                            A 62-year-old has leg pain relieved by leaning forward on a shopping trolley and worsened by standing upright. Pedal pulses are normal. Which diagnosis?

                                                                                                            B. Lumbar spinal stenosis — "Is the pain relieved by leaning forward and aggravated by bending backwards?" → spinal stenosis. Flexion opens the canal; extension narrows it. Normal pulses argue against an arterial cause, and the workbook also links thigh, buttock or hip pain to lumbar spinal stenosis.

                                                                                                            A 35-year-old heavy smoker has ischaemic ulceration of two toes with claudication of the feet and Raynaud phenomenon. What is the diagnosis and the single most important intervention?

                                                                                                            B. Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease); smoking cessation — Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease): inflammatory occlusion of small and medium vessels in SMOKERS, affecting the digits and toes, aggravated by exercise and smoking, relieved by rest and SMOKING CESSATION, with ischaemic ulcers and gangrene that may involve multiple limbs. The workbook lists Raynaud's phenomenon in Buerger's disease among the associated features and names smoking as the major risk factor.

                                                                                                            A patient with known knee osteoarthritis reports a swelling behind the knee for weeks, then sudden calf pain and swelling. Which diagnosis must be considered alongside DVT?

                                                                                                            B. Ruptured Baker cyst — "Did you have swelling behind your knee prior to the calf pain? Do you have osteoarthritis of the knee?" → dissecting Baker cyst. It mimics DVT exactly once it ruptures, which is why ultrasound is the discriminating investigation.

                                                                                                            Using the workbook's Wells questions, which item SUBTRACTS points?

                                                                                                            C. Is another diagnosis more likely? — "Is another diagnosis more likely?" scores –2 points. Every other listed item — paralysis, bedridden >3 days or major surgery within 4 weeks, local tenderness, cancer, entire leg swollen, calf swelling >3 cm, pitting oedema, previous DVT and collateral superficial veins — scores +1.

                                                                                                            A patient with an aching, swollen leg that is worse at the end of the day has brown pigmentation over the medial ankle and relief with elevation. Which diagnosis?

                                                                                                            B. Chronic venous insufficiency — Chronic venous insufficiency: venous valve failure causing chronic congestion — diffuse aching legs, worse later in the day, aggravated by prolonged standing, relieved by ELEVATION and WALKING, with edema, brown pigmentation and possible ulcers. Arterial disease is the opposite: elevation aggravates it and dangling relieves it.

                                                                                                            Which statement about the ankle-brachial index reflects the guideline positions in Appendix C?

                                                                                                            B. The USPSTF does not recommend routine screening, while the AHA considers ABI screening reasonable in high-risk patients — USPSTF: does NOT recommend routine screening (insufficient evidence). AHA: screening with ABI is reasonable in high-risk patients. Abnormal is <0.90, with HIGH SPECIFICITY (99%) but LOWER SENSITIVITY (15–20%). Most of the 236 million people with PAD worldwide do not have classic claudication.
