                                                                                                            Cardiovascular — every lock on one sheet

                                                                                                            73 locks across the block

                                                                                                            LectureLockWhat it says
                                                                                                            L01 · ArteriosclerosisWhy this revision slide is not optionalEvery entity in this lecture is defined by which layer it damages: atheroma = intima; Mönckeberg = media; fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia = intima; hyaline and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis = small vessel wall.
                                                                                                            L01 · ArteriosclerosisWhy this revision slide is not optionalRobbins Basic Pathology, 11th Ed. Chapter 8, p.275 — regional specialisations of the vasculature.
                                                                                                            L01 · ArteriosclerosisMemory line for the orderA-C-P-I-C — the vessels get smaller and more proximal-to-distal as you go down the list; the abdominal aorta below the renals is the single most involved segment, which is why AAA is infrarenal.
                                                                                                            CLSK · Peripheral Vascular SystemThe mnemonic the slide ends onPulseless · Pallor · Paresthesia · Pain · Paralysis — the arterial-occlusion Ps. Add Poikilothermia (cold) and you have the classic six.
                                                                                                            CLSK · Peripheral Vascular SystemArterial vs neurogenic claudicationArterial claudication is reproducible at a fixed walking distance, relieved by standing still, with absent pulses. Neurogenic (spinal stenosis) claudication is relieved by flexion — leaning on a shopping trolley, cycling — and the pulses are normal.
                                                                                                            DLA · Clinical approach to leg swellingMap every differential back to one of the fiveCHF → hydrostatic · nephrotic and cirrhosis → oncotic · cellulitis → permeability · filariasis and post-radiotherapy → lymphatic obstruction · NSAIDs and CCBs → Na⁺ and water retention.
                                                                                                            DLA · Clinical approach to palpitationsThe one-line rule the session is built to teachSyncope in association with palpitations should prompt a work-up for serious arrhythmia — and the diagnosis of an anxiety disorder does not preclude the diagnosis of an arrhythmia.
                                                                                                            L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & DissectionThe single sentence that separates the twoIn malignant hypertension, the vascular damage is acute. In benign hypertension, vascular damage is chronic. Everything else — the morphology, the organ damage, the urgency of treatment — follows from that one word.
                                                                                                            L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & DissectionThe morphology term to attachCystic medial degeneration — marked elastin fragmentation with areas devoid of elastin that resemble cystic spaces, against the regular layered pattern of elastic tissue in normal media.
                                                                                                            L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular System3 / 2 / ≤1The count is the whole classification: 3 features = typical, 2 = atypical, 1 or 0 = non-cardiac. Learn the three features as a set — quality, provocation, relief.
                                                                                                            L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular SystemNever forget the four “killer” causes of chest painMyocardial infarction or ischemia · Pulmonary embolism · Aortic dissection · Pneumothorax. Alongside them, always ask: is the patient stable or unstable, what are the characteristics of the pain, and what are the risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease?
                                                                                                            L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular SystemPlatypnea is the one people missOrthopnea and PND both point at heart failure. Platypnea is the reverse — worse sitting up, better lying down — and it points at an atrial myxoma or hepatopulmonary syndrome.
                                                                                                            L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular SystemTiming S1 at the bedsidePalpate the carotid artery while auscultating. S1 occurs with the pulse; S2 does not.
                                                                                                            L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular SystemThe two that move the other wayHCM and MVP are the exceptions: less filling makes them louder, more filling makes them softer. Everything else follows preload.
                                                                                                            L05 · VasculitidesThe clinical decision this lecture is really aboutPathogenesis is either immune-mediated or direct infection, and it is very important to differentiate between them: immunosuppressives are used for immune-mediated conditions and will be counterproductive in an infectious pathology.
                                                                                                            L05 · VasculitidesGiant cell vs Takayasu — the only reliable separatorThe histology is essentially the same. Age is the discriminator: > 50 = giant cell; < 50 = Takayasu. Territory helps — temporal/ophthalmic vs aortic arch and great vessels.
                                                                                                            L05 · VasculitidesThree questions separate all threeUpper airway involved? → Wegener's. Asthma and eosinophilia? → Churg-Strauss. Neither, plus no granuloma, all lesions the same age? → microscopic polyangiitis.
                                                                                                            L05 · Vasculitides“All lesions the same age” is the MPA lockPAN shows different stages of activity at the same time; MPA shows lesions all of the same age. That single phrase is how a histology stem separates them.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)Calcium is the whole loop-vs-thiazide questionLoops lose calcium (they abolish the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ reabsorption) → used in hypercalcemia. Thiazides keep calcium → used in hypercalciuria / recurrent stones. Loops Lose calcium; Thiazides Take it back.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)Loop-specific extras the reading addsLoops abolish the lumen-positive potential from K⁺ recycling → ↑ Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ excretion; loop diuretics should be avoided in postmenopausal osteopenic women because increased Ca²⁺ excretion may have deleterious effects on bone metabolism. Loops also induce COX-2 expression — the prostaglandins mediate part of the diuretic/natriuretic action, which is why NSAIDs blunt them.
                                                                                                            L07 · Heart FailureTwo numbers that decide autopsy questionsA left ventricle over 1.5 cm is hypertrophied. A heart over ~360 g (male) is enlarged. And because valves are avascular and nourished by diffusion, they heal by scarring, not regeneration — which is why rheumatic valve disease is progressive.
                                                                                                            L07 · Heart FailureTwo named appearancesHeart failure cells = hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the lung, from left failure. Nutmeg liver = chronic passive congestion with hemorrhagic centrilobular necrosis, from right failure. If a stem gives you one, it is telling you which side failed.
                                                                                                            L07 · Heart FailureThe definition of acute coronary syndrome used in this moduleThe term acute coronary syndrome is applied to any of the three catastrophic manifestations of IHD: unstable angina, MI, and sudden cardiac death.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)Special considerations with black patients (current guidelines, verbatim)Hypertension occurs at a younger age and is often more severe; black patients are particularly vulnerable to strokes and hypertensive kidney disease — 3–5 times as likely to have renal complications and end-stage kidney disease. They usually respond well to calcium channel blockers and diuretics but have smaller blood pressure reductions with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and β-blockers. Appropriate combination therapies provide powerful responses that are similar in black or white patients.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)Two safety linesHigh doses of short-acting dihydropyridines can increase the risk of MI (excessive vasodilation and reflex cardiac stimulation) — sustained-release preparations are preferred.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)Two safety linesNon-dihydropyridines (verapamil & diltiazem) are relatively contraindicated in patients taking β-blockers, or with 2nd or 3rd degree AV block, or severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Patients with bradycardia, conduction defects or heart failure should not be given CCBs, especially verapamil and diltiazem.
                                                                                                            L09 · Ischemic Heart DiseaseThe one that breaks the patternPrinzmetal angina gives ST elevation with normal troponin and normal arteries. Every other combination of those three findings points somewhere else — ST elevation *with* raised troponin is an infarct; no ST elevation with raised troponin is NSTEMI.
                                                                                                            L09 · Ischemic Heart DiseaseThe two-minute / twenty-minute ruleContractility stops at < 2 minutes — that is why a wall-motion abnormality appears on echocardiography long before any necrosis. Irreversible injury begins at 20–40 minutes — that is the window reperfusion is racing.
                                                                                                            L09 · Ischemic Heart DiseaseContraction band necrosis has three homesReperfused infarct · catecholamine excess (cocaine, pheochromocytoma) · around the edge of any infarct. All three are the same mechanism — calcium flooding a myocyte with no ATP.
                                                                                                            L09 · Ischemic Heart DiseaseWhy CK-MB still mattersTroponin stays up for 7–10 days, so it cannot tell you whether a patient who reinfarcts on day 4 has a *new* event. CK-MB clears by 72 hours, so a second rise is a second infarct.
                                                                                                            L09 · Ischemic Heart DiseaseThe single most examinable relationship in this lecturePeak macrophage activity (days 3–7) = maximum softening = maximum rupture risk. The heart is weakest exactly when the patient feels best, which is why day-4 sudden deterioration after an uncomplicated MI is rupture until proven otherwise.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)Why both preserve renal blood flowCentral sympatholysis lowers pressure without constricting the renal vasculature. That is why these two survive in patients where renal perfusion matters — and why methyldopa remains the classic choice in pregnancy, where uteroplacental flow must be preserved.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)Objective PHAR.0245 — why nitrate + sildenafil is dangerousBoth act on the same pathway: nitrates donate NO which raises cGMP, and sildenafil blocks the PDE5 that degrades cGMP. Together they cause runaway cGMP accumulation → profound, refractory hypotension — potentially fatal. This same pairing reappears in the Antianginal Drugs lecture.
                                                                                                            L11 · Valvular Heart DiseaseThe asymmetry to rememberStenosis is always the leaflet, and always chronic. Regurgitation can be leaflet or apparatus, and can be acute — which is why a ruptured chord or papillary muscle presents as sudden flash pulmonary oedema, while stenosis never does.
                                                                                                            L11 · Valvular Heart DiseaseThree sterile-vegetation tellsCancer + bland thrombus + no inflammation = NBTE. SLE + vegetations on *both* surfaces = Libman-Sacks. Previous rheumatic fever + tiny warty nodules on the line of closure = RHD.
                                                                                                            L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1Why NBTE is step 2 of infective endocarditisThe sterile platelet–fibrin thrombus of NBTE is the scaffold that circulating bacteria adhere to. That is why the pathology and microbiology lectures describe the same lesion from two directions, and why any condition producing endothelial injury is a risk factor.
                                                                                                            L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1The time-based rule for prosthetic valvesEarly PVE (< 1 year, usually < 2 months) = skin flora introduced at surgery → coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus. Late PVE (> 1 year) behaves like native-valve disease — the organism comes from the community, not the theatre.
                                                                                                            L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial DiseaseThe four infiltratesLymphocytes → viral. Neutrophils + lymphocytes + plasma cells → fungal. Eosinophils → hypersensitivity (methyldopa, sulfonamides). Giant cells → giant cell myocarditis. The cell in the infiltrate *is* the answer.
                                                                                                            L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial DiseaseBeck's triad is in the slide, unnamedFaint distant heart sounds + distended neck veins + declining cardiac output (hypotension) is Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade. The lecture lists all three and adds shock as the endpoint.
                                                                                                            L14 · Cardiovascular Infections 2Two tests separate all fourCatalase splits staph from strep/enterococcus. Then coagulase splits S. aureus from S. epidermidis, and MSA/haemolysis splits S. sanguinis (alpha, no growth on MSA) from E. faecalis (gamma, yellow on MSA).
                                                                                                            L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac NeoplasmsWhy prostaglandins are the whole storyMade in the placenta, destroyed in the lungs. Cut the placenta and inflate the lungs and PG levels collapse — the duct closes. That is why PGE₁ keeps a duct open (transposition, preductal coarctation) and indomethacin closes it (isolated PDA).
                                                                                                            L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac NeoplasmsTwo counting mnemonics from the lectureAcyanotic = the three D's (ASD, VSD, PDA). Cyanotic = the T's — and the number of letters counts the anatomy: 1 vessel (truncus), 2 switched (transposition), 3 (tricuspid atresia), 4 (tetralogy), 5 (total anomalous pulmonary venous connection).
                                                                                                            L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac NeoplasmsPosition-dependent syncope is the myxoma questionA left atrial mass that obstructs the mitral orifice only in certain positions produces syncope on standing or bending, a crescendo mid-diastolic murmur (from the palpitations DLA), and constitutional symptoms from IL-6. It is the one cardiac tumour with a classic bedside story.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)Why the mortality drugs are all anti-compensatoryChronic activation of the SNS and RAAS is associated with cardiac tissue remodeling, which prompts additional neurohumoral activation — a vicious cycle. Every drug that prolongs survival (ARNI/ACEI/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) blocks a compensation. Every drug that only relieves symptoms (diuretics, digoxin) treats the consequence.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)Objective PHAR.0253 in one lineChronic HF = block the compensations (ARNI, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) and relieve congestion (loop diuretic). Acute decompensated HF = relieve congestion first (IV loop diuretic), then support the pump short-term (milrinone, dobutamine) — never long-term, because PDE inhibitors increase mortality.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs IUse / state-dependence — one idea that explains the whole classDrugs bind more rapidly to open or inactivated Na⁺ channels, so they have a greater effect in tissues that are more frequently depolarizing. Cells discharging at abnormally high frequency are preferentially blocked — which is why an antiarrhythmic can suppress a tachycardia while barely touching normal myocardium, and why toxicity appears in hypoxia and acidosis, when normal cells behave abnormally.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs IIWhy lidocaine works only where the tissue is sickClass IB drugs are less prominent blockers of Na⁺ channels at rest but effectively block channels in depolarized tissue. In ischaemic tissue, cells are partly depolarized because they lack sufficient ATP to run the sodium pump, so their Na⁺ channels spend more time inactivated — and IB drugs have the greatest affinity for the inactivated state. That is the whole reason lidocaine is a post-MI drug.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antianginal DrugsObjectives PHAR.0275, 0278 and 0279 on one slideWhy nitrate + β-blocker (or CCB) is better than either alone: nitrates ↓ preload but cause reflex tachycardia and increased contractility; β-blockers and rate-limiting CCBs ↓ heart rate and contractility but increase end-diastolic volume. Together, each cancels the other's compensatory penalty.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antianginal DrugsObjectives PHAR.0275, 0278 and 0279 on one slideWhy nitrate + sildenafil is dangerous: sildenafil inhibits PDE5, the enzyme that breaks down cGMP; nitrates raise cGMP. Combined, cGMP accumulates unopposed → profound hypotension.
                                                                                                            DLA · Cardiac Arrhythmias 1 & 2Above vs below the bundle of HisMobitz I is above the His bundle — the node is fatiguing, so the PR stretches before it fails, and the block is usually benign and vagally responsive. Mobitz II is below it — an all-or-nothing infranodal failure that progresses to complete block, which is why it needs a pacemaker.
                                                                                                            SG03 · SG04 · SG06 — Cardiovascular simulations & SOAPDeep inspiration is the fastest discriminator at the bedsidePain that worsens on deep inspiration is pleuritic — PE, pneumothorax, pericarditis, pleuritis, musculoskeletal. Pain unaffected by breathing or position but reproduced by exertion is ischaemic. Pain relieved by sitting forward is pericarditis.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of CoagulationVitamin K sits on both sides of the balanceVitamin K is required for factors II, VII, IX and X *and* for the anticoagulant proteins C and S (PHAR.0281). A drug that blocks vitamin K therefore lowers procoagulants and anticoagulants — and the anticoagulants fall first.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of CoagulationThe anuclear-platelet argument is the whole answerAny question asking *why aspirin's antiplatelet effect outlasts its plasma half-life*, or *why 5–7 days must elapse before surgery*, is answered by the same sentence: irreversible COX acetylation in a cell that cannot make new protein, so the effect lasts the platelet's 10-day lifetime and recovers only as new platelets are produced.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation15% and "no effect"Two numbers carry this objective: only 15% of absorbed clopidogrel is activated, and polymorphisms have no effect on prasugrel. If a stem gives you a poor metabolizer on a PPI with recurrent stent thrombosis, the answer is to switch agent — prasugrel or ticagrelor — not to raise the clopidogrel dose.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of CoagulationThe two-line versionaPTT → intrinsic + common → UFH and parenteral DTIs. PT/INR → extrinsic + common → warfarin. Everything modern (LMWH, fondaparinux, DOACs) is predictable and unmonitored; that predictability *is* the selling point.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of CoagulationManagement of HIT (PHAR.0290) — verbatimPatients are treated by discontinuance of heparin and administration of a direct thrombin or factor X inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin, dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban) or fondaparinux.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of CoagulationThe bridging rule, verbatimFor treatment of acute venous thromboembolism, heparin, LMWH, or fondaparinux is usually continued for at least 5 days after warfarin therapy is begun, and until the INR is in the therapeutic range on 2 consecutive days. This overlap allows for adequate depletion of the vitamin-K-dependent coagulation factors.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of CoagulationSkin necrosis is a protein C/S problem, not a bleeding problemThe paradox resolves once you remember PHAR.0281: proteins C and S are vitamin-K-dependent anticoagulants with short half-lives, so warfarin creates a transient hypercoagulable window before the procoagulant factors fall. That is why the treatment includes heparin, not more warfarin.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of CoagulationThe four antidotes, in one blockProtamine sulfate → heparin (partial for LMWH, inactive against fondaparinux). Vitamin K → warfarin (fresh frozen plasma if immediate). Idarucizumab → dabigatran (antibody Fab fragment). Andexanet alfa → apixaban / rivaroxaban (decoy modified factor Xa).
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation3 – 4.5 hoursThis is the single most examinable number in the lecture. Alteplase is the only agent listed for acute ischemic stroke, and the window is 3–4.5 hours from onset with a measurable neurologic deficit. Reteplase and tenecteplase are STEMI only.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of CoagulationLong term vs short term is the whole pointDAPT after a noncardioembolic stroke/TIA is a short-term strategy only; extending it long term trades ischemic benefit for hemorrhage. Note also the word noncardioembolic — a cardioembolic stroke (e.g. AF) is an anticoagulation problem, not an antiplatelet one.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic DrugsThe one number from this sectionThe relationship between LDL and CHD risk is log-linear: for every 30 mg/dL reduction in LDL, the relative risk for CHD is reduced by about 30%. This is the quantitative justification for treating to a target rather than to a threshold.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic DrugsThe two statin sentences most likely to be testedHigh-dose statin immediately after ACS regardless of lipid levels — the benefit is not a lipid-number benefit. And homozygous FH benefits much less — no functional LDL receptor means the drug's final common pathway is missing, which is precisely why PCSK9 inhibitors appear in the FH row of the treatment table.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic DrugsNiacin's profile in one lineFlush (aspirin-preventable, prostaglandin-mediated) · hyperglycemia · hyperuricemia/gout · hepatotoxicity. A diabetic with gout is the patient in whom niacin is hardest to justify — especially since adding niacin to a statin has not been shown to reduce ASCVD risk.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic DrugsIf a question pairs a fibrate with a statin, the answer hinges on which fibrateBoth drugs independently cause myositis; the danger is pharmacokinetic and belongs to gemfibrozil alone — two mechanisms (blocked hepatic uptake and competition for glucuronosyl transferases), both raising statin levels. Fenofibrate does not do this. Add renal insufficiency to the stem and the risk rises further.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic DrugsWhy PCSK9 inhibitors and statins add upStatins upregulate LDL receptors, and PCSK9 inhibitors increase LDL receptors on the membrane of the hepatocyte — PCSK9 inhibitors are complementary to statins. Two different points in the receptor's life cycle: synthesis versus recycling.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic DrugsThree superlatives run this tableBiggest LDL drop → PCSK9 monoclonals (60–70%). Biggest HDL rise → niacin (20–35%). Biggest TG drop → fibrates (30–60%). And two classes move something the wrong way: fibrates can raise LDL, resins raise TG.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic DrugsThe pregnancy answer is a resinStatins are category X. The only category B drug in the lecture is colesevelam, and the resins are separately named drugs of choice for pregnant women and for children. That is two independent statements pointing at the same answer.
                                                                                                            NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf PainThe ankle-brachial index (ABI) — the main screening testAbnormal: <0.90
                                                                                                            NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf PainThe ankle-brachial index (ABI) — the main screening testEasy, reliable, done in the office
                                                                                                            NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf PainThe ankle-brachial index (ABI) — the main screening testHigh specificity (99%) · lower sensitivity (15–20%)
                                                                                                            NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf PainThe ankle-brachial index (ABI) — the main screening testUSPSTF: does NOT recommend routine screening (insufficient evidence)
                                                                                                            NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf PainThe ankle-brachial index (ABI) — the main screening testAHA: screening with ABI is REASONABLE in high-risk patients

                                                                                                            Renal — every lock on one sheet

                                                                                                            20 locks across the block

                                                                                                            LectureLockWhat it says
                                                                                                            L17 · Introduction to Renal PathologyThe compartment triad is the diagnostic algorithmGlomerulus → immune. Tubule/interstitium → toxic, ischaemic, infectious. Vessels → local or systemic vascular disease. Every lecture that follows sits in exactly one of these three rows, and the urinalysis tells you which.
                                                                                                            L17 · Introduction to Renal PathologyDeposit location is the single most efficient fact in the renal blockSubepithelial humps → post-strep. Regular subepithelial → membranous. Subendothelial → lupus and MPGN. Mesangial → IgA. Learn these four before any of the individual diseases and half of the nephritic lecture becomes recall.
                                                                                                            L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic SyndromesTwo barriers, two failuresThe filtration barrier is both a size barrier (slit diaphragm) and a charge barrier (anionic GBM). Albumin is anionic, so charge loss alone lets albumin through — which is why minimal change disease produces massive selective proteinuria with a normal light microscope. Structural collapse (FSGS, membranous) adds size failure, and the proteinuria becomes non-selective.
                                                                                                            L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic SyndromesPATH.6007 in one sentenceThe thrombotic risk in nephrotic syndrome is two-hit: antithrombotic factors are lost in the urine through the damaged glomerulus, and the liver's compensatory protein synthesis increases pro-thrombotic factors. Renal vein thrombosis is the named complication — and it is listed again under membranous nephropathy.
                                                                                                            L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic SyndromesPLA2R + membrane attack complexMembranous is an in situ immune-complex disease: the antibody meets its antigen (PLA2R) *on the podocyte itself*, which is why the deposits are subepithelial. The injury is done by C5–C9, not by neutrophils — which is why the light microscope shows thickening without hypercellularity and the urine is nephrotic rather than nephritic.
                                                                                                            L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic SyndromesThe three negatives are the diagnosisNo LM finding · no IF pattern · no deposits on EM. All that is left is foot-process effacement. Add no hypertension, preserved renal function, selective proteinuria and >90% steroid response and MCD becomes the most "negative" disease in the lecture — which is exactly how it is recognised.
                                                                                                            L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic SyndromesThree columns, four diseases, one exam questionThe stem gives you one of the three columns and asks for the disease, or gives the disease and asks for a column. Spike and dome + granular IgG/C3 + subepithelial deposits → membranous. Nothing + nothing + effacement → minimal change. Segmental sclerosis + (IgM/C3 sometimes) + diffuse effacement → FSGS. Nodules + no pattern + earliest GBM thickening → diabetic.
                                                                                                            L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic SyndromesNormal complement with mesangial IgA is the giveawayThe lecture states plainly that IgA nephropathy's pathogenesis involves activation of the alternative complement pathway, yet C3/C4 are normal — production is keeping up with consumption. If a stem gives you gross hematuria after a sore throat with normal complement, the answer is IgA nephropathy; low complement moves it to PSGN.
                                                                                                            L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic SyndromesThree eponymous appearances, one diseaseLumpy-bumpy and starry sky are the immunofluorescence; humps are the electron microscopy. All three belong to post-streptococcal GN. Compare with membranous nephropathy, whose subepithelial deposits give spike and dome on silver stain light microscopy — the same anatomical compartment, different stain, different disease.
                                                                                                            L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic SyndromesC3NeF is the mechanism you must be able to stateAn autoantibody that stabilises an enzyme rather than blocking it: it protects the alternative-pathway C3 convertase from inactivation, so C3 is consumed continuously. Serum C3 falls with normal C1 and C4 — the signature of pure alternative-pathway consumption — and Factor B and properdin fall with it. Recurrence after transplant in 90% follows from the fact that the antibody, not the kidney, is the disease.
                                                                                                            L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic SyndromesLinear · granular · nothingThree immunofluorescence patterns map one-to-one onto the three mechanisms. Linear = an antibody bound continuously along the GBM (anti-GBM). Granular = discrete immune complexes. Pauci-immune = no antibody in the tissue at all, because the antibody (ANCA) is acting on neutrophils, not on the GBM. Any RPGN question resolves to this row.
                                                                                                            L23 · Tubular and Interstitial DiseasesWhat makes this lecture different from the last twoGlomerular disease announces itself in the glomerular urine — protein and red cell casts. Tubulointerstitial disease announces itself as failure of tubular jobs: concentrating urine (polyuria, nocturia), reabsorbing salt (salt wasting), and excreting acid (metabolic acidosis). Learn the three failures and most of the clinical pictures follow.
                                                                                                            L23 · Tubular and Interstitial DiseasesThe potassium flipsMaintenance → HYPERkalemia (you cannot excrete it). Recovery → HYPOkalemia (you are losing it in a 3 L/day diuresis through tubules that still cannot reabsorb). Same patient, opposite emergency, a week apart — and this is exactly how it is asked.
                                                                                                            L23 · Tubular and Interstitial DiseasesFever + rash + eosinophilia + sterile pyuria ≈ 15 days after a new drugThat tetrad is the entire diagnosis, and sterile pyuria is the finding that separates it from pyelonephritis — white cells in the urine with no growth on culture. Treatment is withdrawal of the drug; steroids help recovery.
                                                                                                            L23 · Tubular and Interstitial DiseasesPapillary necrosis — the four-cause mnemonic the lecture hands youDiabetes · Sickle cell disease · Chronic obstruction · Analgesic excess. The presentation is fever plus renal colic, because the sloughed papilla behaves like a stone.
                                                                                                            L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous DisordersHyaline vs hyperplastic — the one-word answerBenign → hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Malignant → hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ("onion-skin") plus fibrinoid necrosis of the afferent arteriole. The mechanistic reason is in the diagrams: benign disease reduces pressure transmission downstream, while malignant hypertension causes breakthrough transmission of high pressure that injures the endothelium directly.
                                                                                                            L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous DisordersThe two kidneys look different — and that is the diagnosisThe stenotic kidney is protected from the systemic pressure and becomes atrophic and ischemic; the contralateral kidney takes the full pressure and develops hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Asymmetric kidneys in a hypertensive patient with a bruit is the classic picture.
                                                                                                            L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis"Uncomplicated" is a definition, not an impressionIt means a healthy, pre-menopausal, non-pregnant woman with no risk factors and no treatment failure. Everything else — men, pregnancy, catheters, stones, diabetes, structural abnormality, recurrence — is complicated, and that word changes the diagnostic pathway (urine culture required) and the complication list.
                                                                                                            L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and PyelonephritisWhy a negative nitrite does not exclude a UTIThe nitrite test detects the conversion of nitrates to nitrites by bacterial nitrate reductase — an enzyme E. coli, Klebsiella and Proteus have but S. saprophyticus does not (nitrite test negative). A young sexually active woman with dysuria and a negative nitrite is the classic S. saprophyticus stem.
                                                                                                            L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and PyelonephritisP fimbriae are named after the disease they causeType 1 fimbriae bind the bladder urothelium — and are the target of Tamm-Horsfall protein. P fimbriae — pyelonephritis-associated pili (PAP) are what let UPEC ascend and colonise the kidney. Same organism, different adhesin, different level of the tract.

                                                                                                            Nervous system — every lock on one sheet

                                                                                                            86 locks across the block

                                                                                                            LectureLockWhat it says
                                                                                                            CLSK · Nervous System I — History and Cranial NervesLocalise before you nameThe lecture's own four-step map puts "where" between the findings and the diagnosis. In neurology the level of the lesion — cortex, brainstem, cord, root, nerve, junction, muscle — is usually a stronger discriminator than the symptom itself, which is why the examination is organised by system rather than by complaint.
                                                                                                            CLSK · Nervous System I — History and Cranial NervesOne pupil beats four in an emergencyBilateral pinpoint → opioids or pons. Bilateral dilated + fixed → post-arrest or anticholinergic. Bilateral dilated + reactive → sympathomimetic. Unilateral dilated and fixed → temporal lobe (uncal) herniation — the only one in the table that is a surgical emergency of mass effect, and it links straight to the herniation figure in the pathology lectures.
                                                                                                            CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, GaitThe Babinski sign, and when it is normalPresent in babies up to 2 years of age — normal. After that it is a sign of a UMN lesion (corticospinal tract): the lecture lists amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig disease), brain tumor or injury, meningitis, multiple sclerosis, spinal injury / defect / tumor, and stroke.
                                                                                                            CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, GaitWhy the numbers matter clinicallyBrudzinski's and Kernig's signs add no diagnostic value to the diagnosis of meningitis if negative — at 5% sensitivity they miss 19 of 20 cases. They are 100% specific, so a *positive* sign is close to diagnostic. This is the cleanest example in the module of the rule that a specific test rules in (SpPin) and a sensitive test rules out (SnNout).
                                                                                                            PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant DrugsThe strength and the weakness are the same experimentReserpine depletes monoamines and causes depression; MAOIs preserve them and relieve it. That is the case for the hypothesis. But the transporter block happens in hours while the mood change takes weeks — so monoamine levels cannot be the whole story, which is why the lecture moves to downstream signal transduction. Expect to be asked for this discrepancy by name.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant DrugsTwo syndromes, two antidotesSerotonin syndrome → cyproheptadine (a serotonin antagonist) plus benzodiazepines. Cheese reaction → phentolamine or prazosin (α-blockade). Both start with stopping the offending agent, and the distinguishing features are hyperthermia + myoclonus + rigidity (serotonin) versus occipital headache + stiff neck after a meal (tyramine).
                                                                                                            PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant DrugsHalf-life explains both the discontinuation syndrome and the washout period (PHAR.00012)The same property runs in both directions. A short half-life (paroxetine, venlafaxine) means abrupt withdrawal produces symptoms. A long half-life (fluoxetine) protects against withdrawal but demands a long washout before starting a MAOI — otherwise the two overlap and you get serotonin syndrome, the reason the washout exists at all.
                                                                                                            PHAR · DLA · PharmacogeneticsThe three-way split is the exam's organising principleEvery example in this DLA is filed under one of the three. NAT2, BChE, CYP2D6, CYP2C19 and TPMT are pharmacokinetic. VKORC1 is pharmacodynamic. Warfarin is both. G6PD and RYR1 are idiosyncratic — and the lecture notes that idiosyncratic drug reactions are not caused by differences in either drug metabolism or drug targets; they seem to result from interactions between the drug and a unique aspect of the physiology of the individual patient.
                                                                                                            PHAR · DLA · PharmacogeneticsProdrug or active drug decides which way the phenotype hurtsActive drug inactivated by CYP2D6 (metoprolol): poor metabolizer → toxicity. Prodrug activated by CYP2D6 (codeine, tramadol, tamoxifen): poor metabolizer → no effect; ultrarapid metabolizer → overdose. One enzyme, opposite errors, decided entirely by which side of the arrow the active molecule sits on.
                                                                                                            DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss"Acute on chronic" is the phrase the case turns onA worsening over days to weeks on a baseline of gradual decline over months to years is highly suggestive of delirium in the setting of decreased cognitive reserve from dementia. That is not one diagnosis but two, and both need naming — the acute precipitant *and* the underlying substrate.
                                                                                                            SG08 · Nervous System Skills Examination (Student Workbook)The single line that separates cerebellar from sensory ataxiaEyes open makes no difference in cerebellar ataxia; eyes open rescues sensory ataxia. That is the whole of Romberg, and it is why the workbook holds the eyes closed for a full 30–60 seconds rather than a moment.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antipsychotic DrugsClozapine is the drug of last resort and of two exceptionsIt is reserved for refractory patients because of agranulocytosis in 1–2% with mandatory blood counts, and it carries the highest metabolic burden and one of the two highest seizure risks. Yet it is also the agent recommended for patients with tardive dyskinesia who require antipsychotics and the only category B drug in pregnancy. Learn it as the exception, not the rule.
                                                                                                            CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status ExaminationThe primary psychiatric diagnosis is the last one you make, not the firstThe lecture's own sequence puts medical illness, substances, and malingering/factitious disorder ahead of the psychiatric diagnosis. This is the same discipline as the confusion DLA, where an acute onset demands a rapid search for a reversible, life-threatening cause before dementia is invoked.
                                                                                                            CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status ExaminationThe modality points at the causeAuditory → schizophrenia. Visual → organic. Tactile → alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Olfactory → temporal lobe epilepsy, tumour, migraine, Parkinson's. A patient with visual hallucinations is more likely to have a medical problem than a primary psychotic one — which is exactly why the evaluation sequence rules out medical causes first.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic DrugsThe time-course contrast is objective PHAR.00038 in one lineBenzodiazepines give rapid relief of acute anxiety symptoms; antidepressants take 4–6 weeks for the antianxiety response. That is exactly why the two are combined at the start and the benzodiazepine is then tapered — the fast drug covers the gap until the safe drug works.
                                                                                                            NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and HydrocephalusThree compartments, three diseases, one lectureBrain → tumour and oedema. Blood → the four haemorrhages. Water → hydrocephalus. Every entity in this lecture is one compartment expanding inside a rigid box, and every complication is the box's answer: equilibration, then herniation, then failure of perfusion.
                                                                                                            NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and HydrocephalusWhy Kernohan's notch is called a false localising signIn ordinary uncal herniation the signs are ipsilateral pupil, contralateral hemiparesis. When the brainstem is pushed far enough across, the opposite cerebral peduncle is crushed against the tentorium, so the hemiparesis becomes ipsilateral to the mass and the pupil contralateral — pointing the examiner to the wrong side. Recognising it is the point of the slide.
                                                                                                            NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and HydrocephalusArtery, fracture, lucid interval, lens — or vein, atrophy, slow, crescentThe two haemorrhages differ on every line, and each line predicts the next. Arterial pressure explains the hours-long deterioration after a lucid interval; tight dural attachment at the sutures explains the lens shape. Venous, low-pressure bleeding in an atrophic brain explains days-to-weeks and the crescent that crosses sutures.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson DiseaseThe same nigrostriatal circuit, read in two directionsIn the antipsychotics lecture, D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway caused drug-induced parkinsonism treated with antimuscarinics. Here the same circuit fails from the other end — loss of dopaminergic neurons — and the treatment is the same two options: give dopamine back or block the acetylcholine.
                                                                                                            NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular DiseasesThe imaging line is the reason for the CT-first algorithmA CT in the first hours is often normal in ischaemic stroke but shows haemorrhage immediately. That is precisely why the emergency CT is done — not to see the infarct, but to exclude the bleed before thrombolysis. It joins the 3–4.5-hour alteplase window from the coagulation lecture.
                                                                                                            NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular DiseasesLipohyalinosis has two endings, and the lecture tests bothThe same hypertensive small-vessel change either blocks the lumen → lacunar infarct or weakens the wall → Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm → hypertensive haemorrhage. Both happen in the lenticulostriate arteries, which is why the basal ganglia are the commonest site for each.
                                                                                                            NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular DiseasesThree complications, three time framesRebleed — immediately. Vasospasm — the early period after the haemorrhage (and nimodipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker from the antihypertensives lecture, prevents it). Communicating hydrocephalus — late, from meningeal fibrosis blocking the arachnoid granulations.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antiepileptic DrugsTwo EEG numbers and one negative3 Hz spike-and-wave = typical absence; 1.5–2.5 Hz diffuse spike-wave = atypical absence. And the single most useful bedside discriminator is no postictal confusion in typical absence — a child who stares, blinks and then carries straight on mid-sentence.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Antiepileptic DrugsFive minutes defines two different thingsA febrile seizure needs treatment if it lasts > 5 minutes, and status epilepticus is defined as a single seizure lasting more than 5 minutes. The same number, and the same first drug class — a benzodiazepine — in both.
                                                                                                            NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative DiseasesThree genes for the 5%, one allele for the 95%Early-onset familial AD: APP (chr 21) · presenilin 1 (chr 14) · presenilin 2 (chr 1) — all of which increase Aβ production, and the presenilins are γ-secretase. Late-onset sporadic AD: ApoE ε4 on chr 19, with 95% risk by age 85 in ε4 homozygotes. The Down syndrome link is APP gene dosage on chromosome 21.
                                                                                                            NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative DiseasesThe name is the pathology"A-myo-trophic" = the lower motor neuron loss (muscle atrophy, fasciculations). "Lateral sclerosis" = the upper motor neuron loss (degeneration of the corticospinal tract in the lateral cord → spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski). And the four things that are spared — intellect, sensation, sphincters and eye movements — are what distinguish it from everything else in this lecture.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs of AbuseDependence is not addictionA patient on a β-blocker or a corticosteroid is physically dependent and will have a withdrawal syndrome if it is stopped abruptly — but has none of the four behaviours that define addiction. Getting this distinction right is the point of PHAR.00059, and it is the clinical reason opioid analgesia is not the same as opioid addiction.
                                                                                                            PHAR · Drugs of AbuseNystagmus in both planes is the PCP giveawayBoth vertical AND horizontal nystagmus in an agitated, violent patient with hypertension, hyperthermia and rigidity is PCP, and the treatment is benzodiazepines for both the behaviour and the seizures — there is no specific antidote. Note the hyperthermia trio again: PCP, MDMA and serotonin syndrome all kill through temperature.
                                                                                                            NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS TumorsTime and space — then confirm with two testsThe definition itself is the diagnostic criterion: activity separated in time, lesions separated in space. The two confirmatory findings are oligoclonal bands in the CSF and periventricular white matter plaques on MRI.
                                                                                                            NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS TumorsWernicke is reversible; Korsakoff is what is left behindTreatment with thiamine reverses the Wernicke triad. Delayed treatment leaves the irreversible memory disturbance of Korsakoff's syndrome — no new memories and confabulation. The lesion to name is haemorrhage and necrosis of the mamillary bodies.

                                                                                                            NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low MoodIf ONE of the following is documented, it is most likely that the patient is depressedW — Weight loss (more than 5% of normal body weight without medical cause)

                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Clinical consequence — herniationSubfalcine (cingulate) — compresses the anterior cerebral artery
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Clinical consequence — herniationTranstentorial (uncal) — CN III palsy (blown pupil), posterior cerebral artery compression, Duret haemorrhages in the midbrain/pons
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Clinical consequence — herniationTonsillar — cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum; brainstem compression and respiratory arrest
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)The line that answers most questionsArtery, lens, does not cross sutures, lucid interval → EPIDURAL.
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)The line that answers most questionsVein, crescent, crosses sutures, elderly with trivial trauma → SUBDURAL.
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Genetics and clinicalEarly-onset familial: APP (chr 21), presenilin-1 (chr 14), presenilin-2 (chr 1)
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Genetics and clinicalRisk allele: ApoE ε4 increases risk; ApoE ε2 is protective
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Genetics and clinicalTrisomy 21 (Down syndrome) — virtually all develop Alzheimer pathology by age 40
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Genetics and clinicalClinical: insidious memory loss progressing to global cognitive decline; the most common cause of dementia
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Compare — PATH.7032MS — young adults, F:M 2:1, relapsing-remitting, HLA-DRB1*1501, periventricular white matter
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Compare — PATH.7032ADEM / AHEM — post-infectious or post-vaccination, monophasic, children and young adults, PERIVENOUS demyelination; AHEM is the fulminant haemorrhagic form
                                                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)Compare — PATH.7032Central pontine myelinolysis — too-rapid correction of hyponatraemia; symmetric loss of myelin in the BASIS PONTIS; locked-in syndrome; the >2-day rule protects against it
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsThe safety statement you should be able to quoteGeneral anesthetics are among the most dangerous drugs approved for general use, as their margin of safety is small.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsThe safety statement you should be able to quoteTherapeutic indices range from about 2–4 — the dose that produces circulatory failure may be only 2 to 4 times that which produces adequate anesthesia
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsMAC values are ADDITIVENitrous oxide can be used as a "carrier" gas, decreasing the anesthetic requirement of other anesthetics.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsMAC values are ADDITIVEExample: 0.7 MAC of isoflurane + 0.3 MAC of nitrous oxide = 1 MAC.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsThe two sentences to memoriseThere is an INVERSE relationship between blood solubility of an anesthetic and the rate of rise of its tension in arterial blood. A low blood:gas partition coefficient determines a FASTER onset of anesthesia.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsThe two sentences to memoriseAnesthetics with larger λ(oil:gas) tend to have larger λ(blood:gas) — which means MORE POTENT INHALED ANESTHETICS TEND TO HAVE SLOWER ONSETS.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsRank order of metabolismMethoxyflurane > halothane > enflurane > sevoflurane > isoflurane > desflurane > nitrous oxide

                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsEstablishing susceptibilityThe most reliable test is the in vitro CAFFEINE-HALOTHANE MUSCLE CONTRACTURE TEST — a small piece of muscle is obtained from the thigh under regional or general anesthesia, attached to a device measuring force of contraction, and exposed to halothane or caffeine
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsEstablishing susceptibilityA response to halothane, or a response to LOW concentrations of caffeine, is diagnostic for malignant hyperthermia-susceptible muscle
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsEstablishing susceptibilityGenetic testing can also be used
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General AnestheticsEstablishing susceptibilityDuring anesthesia, watch for TRISMUS from muscular contraction
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · Local AnestheticsUse-dependence — state-dependent blockThe blockade of sodium channels by most local anesthetics is VOLTAGE- and TIME-DEPENDENT.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · Local AnestheticsUse-dependence — state-dependent blockChannels in the RESTED state, which predominate at more negative membrane potentials, have a LOWER affinity for local anesthetics than ACTIVATED (open) and INACTIVATED channels, which predominate at more positive membrane potentials.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · Local AnestheticsUse-dependence — state-dependent blockThus the effect of a given drug concentration is more marked in RAPIDLY FIRING axons than in resting fibers.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · Local AnestheticsHow a vasoconstrictor restricts the drug to its site (PHAR.00089)Preparations of local anesthetics often contain a vasoconstrictor, usually EPINEPHRINE.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · Local AnestheticsHow a vasoconstrictor restricts the drug to its site (PHAR.00089)Vasoconstrictors reduce systemic absorption from the depot site by decreasing blood flow in these areas.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · Local AnestheticsHow a vasoconstrictor restricts the drug to its site (PHAR.00089)As a consequence, neuronal uptake of the drug is ENHANCED due to the higher local drug concentration, and the SYSTEMIC TOXIC EFFECTS ARE REDUCED.
                                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · Local AnestheticsHow a vasoconstrictor restricts the drug to its site (PHAR.00089)Cocaine itself constricts blood vessels by potentiating the action of norepinephrine; therefore it prevents its own absorption.
